AI.tldr: AniGS enables scene-level animation of large, cluttered 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions by learning a time-conditioned deformation field and using a diffusion-based video refinement pipeline to introduce ambient motion (e.g., vegetation) while preserving static structures.
AI.motivation: Static reconstructions lack ambient motion, limiting immersion; existing object-centric animation methods do not scale to large, navigable scenes with clutter.
AI.method: Represent scene with canonical 3DGS; model motion with a time-conditioned deformation field; animate via a pretrained video diffusion model; iterative dataset-model updates with render-and-refine to expand viewpoint coverage; video-to-video refinement to constrain motion to targeted regions.
AI.result: Characterized on five real-world, large-scale outdoor scenes; AniGS yields natural ambient dynamics and high-quality novel-view videos, improving immersion in reconstructed environments.
AI.conclusion: AniGS extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to whole-scene animation, delivering scalable, controllable ambient motion for large scenes while preserving rigid structures; relies on diffusion-based generation and iterative refinement to maintain quality and region-specific motion.

title: Phionyx: A Deterministic AI Runtime Architecture with Structured State Management and Pre-Response Governance
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Reference implementation, reproducibility pack, and evaluation artifacts available via GitHub (https://github.com/halvrenofviryel/phionyx-research) and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20027534)
summary: We present Phionyx, a deterministic AI runtime architecture derived from the broader Echoism interaction framework that introduces a governance-first approach to AI engineering: treating large language model (LLM) outputs as noisy sensor measurements rather than direct decisions. Unlike probabilistic agents, Phionyx enforces deterministic state evolution via a structured state vector governed by deterministic state-evolution equations, enabling reproducible behavior in applications requiring auditability and governance. The architecture integrates three layers: (1) a deterministic evaluation kernel processing noisy sensor measurements through a canonical 46-block pipeline, (2) a unified safety layer providing pre-response control and architectural privacy enforcement, and (3) a semantic time-based memory system implementing impact-weighted cache eviction. Experimental validation on single-instance deployments demonstrates approximately 31% reduction in computational overhead vs. post-hoc filtering (at 30% unsafe input ratio, simulated cost model) and up to 24% improvement in high-value data retention vs. LRU (72% vs. FIFO, same cache capacity, benchmark-verified), deterministic execution verified across 100 repeated runs with zero variance in control signals (hash-verified), and zero unplanned restarts in single-instance deployment testing (see Appendix C for methodology and scope). This paper presents the architecture, its analytic structure, and scoped experimental evidence; generalization to distributed or multi-tenant deployments remains future work.

AI.tldr: Deterministic, governance-first AI runtime (Phionyx) with a 46-block evaluation pipeline, safety layer, and time-based memory; single-instance experiments show reduced overhead and improved data retention, with future work on distributed/multi-tenant deployments.
AI.motivation: Address auditability, reproducibility, and governance in AI systems by replacing probabilistic agents with deterministic state evolution and a governance-centric architecture.
AI.method: Three-layer architecture: (1) deterministic evaluation kernel processing noisy LLM outputs via a canonical 46-block pipeline; (2) unified safety layer for pre-response control and architectural privacy; (3) semantic, time-based memory with impact-weighted cache eviction. Experimental evaluation on single-instance deployments using a simulated cost model and benchmarked memory policies, focusing on reproducibility (100 runs with zero variance) and reliability (no restarts).
AI.result: Reported outcomes include ~31% reduction in computational overhead vs post-hoc filtering at a 30% unsafe input ratio; up to ~24% improvement in high-value data retention versus LRU under equal cache capacity (with a noted 72% vs FIFO figure in benchmarks); deterministic execution validated across 100 runs with zero variance; zero unplanned restarts in single-instance deployment.
AI.conclusion: The paper articulates the architecture, analytic framework, and scoped experimental evidence for Phionyx, while acknowledging that generalization to distributed or multi-tenant deployments remains for future work.

title: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap under Real-Time Constraints in Autonomous Racing
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE 104th Vehicular Technology Conference (VTC2026-Fall). 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Autonomous racing exposes the sim-to-real gap under extreme operating conditions characterized by high speed, tight stability margins, and stringent real-time constraints. Although simulation is indispensable for development, controllers that perform well in simulation often degrade abruptly on physical platforms due to interacting effects of dynamics mismatch, estimation delay, and execution-layer latency. This paper frames sim-to-real transfer in autonomous racing as a full-stack, real-time systems problem. We introduce a structured three-layer perspective (Physical/Cyber/Execution) to analyze how mismatches propagate and amplify through closed-loop feedback. We present diagnostic metrics beyond nominal lap time, including performance flip, stability-oriented measures, sensitivity to delay and noise, and latency distribution characterization. Mitigation strategies are synthesized from a deployment-oriented viewpoint, emphasizing execution-aware and delay-aware design. Finally, we outline benchmarking guidelines that enable reproducible and fair sim-to-real evaluation under compute and timing constraints. The resulting framework clarifies cross-layer failure mechanisms and provides practical design principles for deployable autonomous racing systems operating near dynamic limits.

AI.tldr: Introduces a full-stack three-layer framework (Physical/Cyber/Execution) to analyze and close the sim-to-real gap in autonomous racing, with new diagnostic metrics, deployment-aware mitigation strategies, and benchmarking guidelines.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing exposes severe sim-to-real transfer challenges under extreme operating conditions (high speed, tight margins, real-time constraints). Dynamics mismatch, estimation delays, and execution latency cause abrupt performance degradation; a cross-layer, deployment-oriented analysis is needed.
AI.method: Proposes a three-layer Physical/Cyber/Execution model to trace how mismatches propagate through closed-loop control; defines diagnostic metrics beyond lap-time (e.g., performance flip, stability metrics, delay/noise sensitivity, latency distributions); synthesizes mitigation strategies emphasizing execution-aware and delay-aware design; outlines benchmarking guidelines for reproducible, fair sim-to-real evaluation under compute/time constraints.
AI.result: The framework clarifies cross-layer failure mechanisms and provides practical design principles for deployable autonomous racing systems operating near dynamic limits.
AI.conclusion: A structured framework to diagnose, prevent, and benchmark sim-to-real transfer in high-speed autonomous racing, enabling deployable systems that approach dynamic limits.

title: Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Runtime-Tunable Transit Signal Priority
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the 29th IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026). Code: https://github.com/urbanAIthi/morl-tsp
summary: Transit signal priority (TSP) requires balancing competing objectives: reducing bus delay while limiting adverse impacts on non-bus traffic and avoiding extreme waits for a subset of vehicles. Existing reinforcement-learning (RL) approaches to TSP typically encode transit-aware features (e.g., occupancy and schedule deviation) but optimize a fixed reward or fixed scalarization, which limits operational flexibility when agency priorities change across time-of-day or disruption conditions. We present a preference-conditioned TSP controller, $π(a \mid s,w)$, that selects the next signal phase under minimum/maximum green and transition-feasibility constraints and can be tuned at runtime via a preference parameter $w$ to trade off bus-priority emphasis against overall traffic delay without retraining. We implement this on top of IntersectionZoo by introducing a constrained signal-control/TSP wrapper, and we extend scenario generation with bus-prevalence augmentation and timetable-based bus insertion to address sparse transit-priority events during training. Experiments against fixed-time control, a rule-based TSP overlay, and fixed-weight PPO specialists show that a single learned conditioned policy spans a smooth empirical trade-off frontier across runtime preferences, outperforms fixed-time and rule-based baselines, and maintains constraint feasibility, while tail-delay diagnostics reveal that non-bus externalities remain limited for moderate preference settings but can increase substantially under high bus-priority weights. The source code of this work is available at https://github.com/urbanAIthi/morl-tsp.

AI.tldr: A single, preference-conditioned RL controller for transit signal priority (TSP) enables runtime trade-offs between bus priority and overall traffic delay, achieving better performance than baselines while maintaining feasibility; high bus-priority weights can increase non-bus delays.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-TSP approaches use fixed rewards or weightings, limiting adaptability when priorities change across times of day or disruptions. A tunable, at-runtime preference captures operator flexibility without retraining.
AI.method: Introduce a preference-conditioned policy π(a|s,w) that selects signal phases under green/transition constraints. Integrate a constrained signal-control/TSP wrapper on IntersectionZoo, augment training with bus prevalence and timetable-based bus insertion. Compare against fixed-time control, a rule-based TSP overlay, and fixed-weight PPO specialists across a range of w to map an empirical trade-off frontier.
AI.result: A single conditioned policy spans a smooth trade-off frontier across runtime preferences, outperforming fixed-time and rule-based baselines while maintaining feasibility. Tail-delay analysis shows non-bus externalities are limited for moderate w but can rise under high bus-priority weights.
AI.conclusion: Preference-conditioned TSP control is viable and flexible, enabling runtime prioritization adjustments without retraining and with acceptable feasibility. The approach balances bus service performance with general traffic impacts and provides a scalable path for operator-driven TSP under varying conditions.

title: Recti-Q: Feature-Space Rectification for Out-of-Distribution-Robust Quantized Perception in Edge Robotics
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Robotic perception pipelines increasingly rely on large vision backbones deployed on SWaP-constrained edge platforms, making post-training quantization (PTQ) attractive for real-time inference. However, while PTQ often preserves clean in-distribution accuracy, we show that it can substantially degrade reliability under deployment-relevant distribution shifts (e.g., sensor noise, severe weather, and novel operating environments), creating a Quantization-Induced Robustness Gap. Across foundational vision benchmarks (ImageNet-C and PACS), 4-bit PTQ models exhibit pronounced robustness degradation despite negligible ID accuracy loss. To address this, we propose Recti-Q, a lightweight feature-space rectification framework that freezes the quantized backbone and trains a small classifier-head LoRA adapter using only source data. Recti-Q is architecture-agnostic across CNNs and Transformers, supports efficient teacher-free training, and recovers a significant portion of the lost robustness, in some cases matching or exceeding FP32 performance. At less than 1% parameter overhead (as small as 6 KB), Recti-Q preserves over 99% of PTQ memory savings, adds negligible compute, and enables low-bandwidth Over-The-Air (OTA) resilience patching for deployed robotic fleets operating in unpredictable physical environments.

AI.tldr: 4-bit post-training quantization degrades robustness under distribution shifts; Recti-Q introduces a lightweight, source-data LoRA adapter on top of a frozen quantized backbone to recover robustness with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization (PTQ) preserves in-distribution accuracy but can substantially reduce robustness to deployment-relevant distribution shifts, creating a Quantization-Induced Robustness Gap on edge vision models.
AI.method: Recti-Q freezes the quantized backbone, trains a small classifier-head LoRA adapter using only source data, architecture-agnostic across CNNs and Transformers, with teacher-free training and low parameter overhead (~<1%), enabling OTA patching.
AI.result: Recti-Q recovers a substantial portion of the robustness loss caused by 4-bit PTQ, in some cases matching or surpassing FP32; preserves over 99% of PTQ memory savings, adds negligible compute, and requires as little as 6 KB extra parameters.
AI.conclusion: Recti-Q provides a practical, low-overhead remedy for the robustness degradation introduced by PTQ in edge vision systems, compatible with OTA updates for deployed robotic fleets.

title: Integro-differential equations in angular stabilization of drone motion by distributed feedback control
summary: In this paper, we propose angular stabilization of drone motion using distributed feedback control in the form of an integral operator. It should be stressed that the memory of this integral operator could be unbounded. It is intuitively clear that large length of the observation time open new possibilities to construct better control based on previous states of the control object. Unbounded memory in control requires the creation of a certain approach different from standard ones to the study of integro-differential equations. One of the goals of this article is to propose a certain universal approach that allows us to study the stability of integro-differential equations in the case of unbounded memory in the integral operator specifying the feedback control in stabilization. The approach we propose allows us to reduce the study of integro-differential equations to the analysis of systems of ordinary differential equations. In general, such systems can consist of an infinite number of equations. In relation to the so-called linear approximation in the problem of angle stabilization manages to limit itself to relatively simple exponential kernels in the integral control and arrive at a system with a finite number of equations. The examples explain that more complex kernels, for example, linear combinations of the exponential kernels, can enhance the stabilization capabilities. We obtain new unexpectable results on the exponential stability of integro-differential equations. Then we apply them to stabilization of drone flight.

AI.tldr: Proposes angular stabilization of drone motion via distributed integral feedback with potentially unbounded memory, and introduces a universal approach to analyze stability of integro-differential equations with unbounded memory by reducing them to (possibly infinite) ODE systems; using exponential kernels yields finite-dimensional approximations, and combining kernels can enhance stabilization; reports new exponential-stability results and applies them to drone stabilization.
AI.motivation: Stabilize drone angular dynamics using integral feedback while addressing the analytical challenge of unbounded memory in the controller; to provide a universal framework to analyze the stability of integro-differential equations arising from such control schemes.
AI.method: Develop a universal approach that reduces integro-differential stability problems to the analysis of ordinary differential equation systems. For linear approximation, use exponential kernels in the integral control to obtain a finite set of equations; explore more complex kernels (e.g., sums of exponentials) to potentially improve stabilization.
AI.result: New exponential-stability results for integro-differential equations with unbounded memory; demonstration that exponential kernels and their combinations can enhance stabilization; application of the theoretical results to drone angular stabilization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed universal framework provides a viable method to study stability under unbounded-memory integral feedback and can yield improved stabilization via kernel design; the approach is applicable to drone stabilization and potentially other systems governed by integro-differential dynamics.

title: Intelligent Multi-UAV Navigation in ITNTNs: A Hierarchical LLM Approach
comment: This paper has been accepted by IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
summary: The deployment of high-speed Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in 3D aerial highways necessitates robust coordination of physical flight kinematics and multi-tier network handovers. While Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers rapid tactical control, it lacks the zero-shot strategic reasoning required to quickly adapt to dynamic Integrated Terrestrial and Non-Terrestrial Networks (ITNTNs). Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at semantic reasoning but suffer from high inference latency, rendering them unsuitable for real-time aerodynamic control. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel Hierarchical LLM-driven control framework. A massive cloud-based LLM deployed on a High-Altitude Platform Station (HAPS) manages slow-timescale global load balancing, while lightweight edge-LLMs on individual UAVs translate local observations into tactical sub-goals. These sub-goals guide a fast-timescale physical DRL controller to execute collision-free, handover-aware trajectories. Simulation results demonstrate that our agentic architecture significantly reduces collision rates and improves aggregate system throughput compared to existing baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hierarchical LLM-driven control framework for high-speed UAVs on 3D aerial highways that fuses cloud-based semantic reasoning with edge-driven tactical sub-goals to guide fast DRL flight control, improving safety and throughput in simulations.
AI.motivation: DRL enables rapid tactical control but lacks zero-shot strategic reasoning; LLMs provide semantic reasoning but have high latency for real-time control; need an integrated approach for dynamic ITNTN environments.
AI.method: A two-tier system: a massive cloud-based LLM on a High-Altitude Platform Station (HAPS) handles slow-timescale global load balancing and network management; lightweight edge LLMs on each UAV generate tactical sub-goals from local observations; a fast-timescale DRL controller executes collision-free, handover-aware trajectories based on these sub-goals.
AI.result: Simulation results show the agentic architecture significantly reduces collision rates and increases aggregate system throughput compared with existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical LLM-driven control can combine global strategic reasoning with local tactical execution to enhance safety and performance in ITNTN-integrated UAV networks, validating the framework and motivating further real-world evaluations.

title: BearingNAS: Obtaining In-Sensor Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems for Bearings Using a Laptop
comment: Accepted to IEEE COINS 2026 in Special Session 7: Edge AI technologies
summary: This paper introduces BearingNAS, a Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search (HW-NAS) framework designed to shift the intelligence directly onto the sensor die via in-sensor processing. BearingNAS frames the search as a constrained optimization problem targeting extreme micro-budgets (4 to 8 kiB of RAM and 16 to 32 kiB of Flash). To eliminate the reliance on expensive discrete GPUs, we propose a lightweight, derivative-free search strategy paired with a single data-flow search space that leverages a decaying kernel growth formulation to prevent parameter explosion. We evaluate our framework on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing benchmark, optimizing architectures for three STMicroelectronics targets: two commodity microcontrollers and the LSM6DSO16IS Intelligent Sensor Processing Unit (ISPU). Running entirely on a laptop CPU, the search converges in less than an hour. The resulting best in-sensor architecture achieves a highly competitive diagnostic accuracy of 99.50\% on the ISPU. These results demonstrate the viability of shifting the machine learning workload inside the sensor package, enabling low-cost, production-scale bearing fault diagnosis.

AI.tldr: BearingNAS is a hardware-aware NAS that optimizes ultra-small in-sensor neural architectures within tight micro-budgets (4–8 kiB RAM, 16–32 kiB Flash) for bearing fault diagnosis, using a derivative-free, single data-flow search with decaying kernel growth; it converges on CPU in under an hour and achieves 99.50% accuracy on ISPU for CWRU bearing data.
AI.motivation: Enable intelligent processing directly on sensor hardware to minimize data movement, power, and cost. Address the challenge of deploying NAS within extreme RAM/Flash constraints on commodity MCUs and ISPU platforms, enabling scalable, production-grade bearing fault diagnosis.
AI.method: Formulate HW-NAS as a constrained optimization problem with ultra-tight memory budgets. Employ a lightweight, derivative-free search strategy over a single data-flow search space. Use a decaying kernel growth formulation to mitigate parameter explosion. Validate on the CWRU bearing benchmark across three STMicroelectronics targets (two commodity MCUs and ISPU LSM6DSO16IS). Runs entirely on a laptop CPU; converges in under one hour.
AI.result: The best in-sensor architecture achieves 99.50% diagnostic accuracy on the ISPU, demonstrating competitive performance and viability of embedding ML workloads inside sensor packages for bearing fault diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: BearingNAS demonstrates the practicality of in-sensor ML under severe hardware constraints, enabling low-cost, production-scale bearing fault diagnosis by shifting computation from cloud/GPU to the sensor die.

title: Physics Closure Matters for Machine Olfaction: A Maxwell--Stefan Graph Solver for Identifiable Dynamic Gas Unmixing
summary: Machine olfaction for gas unmixing is an underconstrained inverse problem in which gas compositions must be inferred from low-dimensional, delayed, and entangled sensor responses produced by interacting chemical transport, surface adsorption, and sensor transduction. One of the key obstacles is physics closure misspecification, where a neural network is designed to fit sensor traces rather than infer a physically closed olfactory process. In this work, we formulate gas unmixing as a multi-physics-constrained inverse problem governed by Maxwell--Stefan multicomponent transport PDEs, competitive adsorption ODEs, and nonlinear sensor transduction ODEs. Directly solving such a high-dimensional coupled system is computationally expensive and often numerically unstable. To this end, we propose UnMixNet, a physics-closed graph neural solver that embeds this multi-physics forward process into end-to-end gas unmixing. UnMixNet discretizes Maxwell--Stefan cross-diffusion on spatial graphs and formulates the multicomponent flux on each edge. This design enables local, differentiable, and flux-conservative inference for multicomponent cross-diffusion. Evaluations on SmellNet show improved single-odor recognition, seen-mixture unmixing, and unseen-mixture generalization. In addition, an external validation on UCI Dynamic Gas Mixtures shows that the inferred concentration process agrees with ground truth concentration set points under dynamic transitions. Process-consistency diagnostics further show that the proposed model learns transferable dynamic physical fingerprints that better satisfies transport, conservation, adsorption, and readout closure.

AI.tldr: UnMixNet is a physics-closed graph neural network for gas unmixing, embedding Maxwell–Stefan multicomponent transport, adsorption, and sensor dynamics into a differentiable, flux-conservative forward model; it improves odor recognition, mixture unmixing, and generalization, with external validation against ground-truth concentration setpoints.
AI.motivation: Gas olfaction via chemical sensors yields entangled, delayed responses that are underconstrained and prone to physics-closure misspecification. A physically closed, end-to-end model is needed to infer true gas compositions while respecting transport, adsorption, and transduction dynamics.
AI.method: Formulate a multi-physics inverse problem incorporating Maxwell–Stefan cross-diffusion on spatial graphs, competitive adsorption ODEs, and nonlinear sensor transduction ODEs. Introduce UnMixNet, a physics-closed graph neural solver that discretizes the forward transport on edges, enabling local, differentiable, flux-conservative inference for multicomponent diffusion and the associated adsorptive and sensor dynamics.
AI.result: On SmellNet, the approach yields improved single-odor recognition, seen-mixture unmixing, and unseen-mixture generalization. External validation on UCI Dynamic Gas Mixtures shows inferred concentrations align with ground-truth set points during dynamic transitions. Diagnostics indicate the model learns transferable dynamic physical fingerprints that satisfy transport, conservation, adsorption, and readout closure.
AI.conclusion: A physics-closed, graph-based solver can effectively couple transport, adsorption, and sensor models for gas unmixing, delivering better physical fidelity and generalization than opaque neural surrogates.

title: MILP-Evo: Closed-Loop Fully Automatic Design of MILP Solvers
summary: Machine learning methods have shown that data-driven policies can accelerate mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers, but many such approaches remain difficult to inspect, adapt, and deploy because the learned policy is represented as an external predictor or other opaque model. By contrast, explicit solver logic is easier to understand and integrate, but is usually hand-designed rather than learned from solver feedback. We study whether the automatic design of MILP solver logic can instead be cast as LLM-guided closed-loop search over executable white-box components evaluated directly by end-to-end solver behavior. To this end, we propose a closed-loop program evolution framework for MILP solver auto-design, implemented through PySCIPOpt, and instantiate it on the joint design of a cut selector and a branching rule. Candidate programs are iteratively generated, loaded into SCIP, and evaluated by direct execution on MILP instances, with the resulting feedback guiding performance-based selection, targeted repair, diagnostic reflection, and diversity-aware population maintenance. The method outputs explicit solver components that can be inspected, modified, and deployed within standard solver workflows. Across four benchmark families, we find that LLM-guided program evolution can discover competitive domain-specialized policies in several settings.

AI.tldr: LLM-guided closed-loop search over executable MILP solver components to automatically design domain-specific, interpretable solver logic, yielding competitive policies and deployable components.
AI.motivation: Address the opacity and limited adaptability of learned MILP policies and the rigidity of hand-designed solver logic by enabling automatic design of solver components that are transparent and directly optimized by end-to-end solver performance.
AI.method: A closed-loop program evolution framework (via PySCIPOpt) jointly designs a cut selector and a branching rule. Candidate programs are iteratively generated, loaded into SCIP, and evaluated on MILP instances. Feedback drives performance-based selection, targeted repair, diagnostic reflection, and diversity-aware population maintenance, producing explicit, inspectable solver components.
AI.result: Across four benchmark families, the approach discovers competitive domain-specialized policies. The output components are explicit, inspectable, and deployable within standard solver workflows.
AI.conclusion: LLM-guided program evolution can automate the design of interpretable MILP solver logic, achieving competitive performance and enabling deployment of transparent, end-to-end-validated solver components.

title: On the Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry, Dynamics, and Sample Complexity
summary: Reachability analysis is central to safety-critical control, robotics, and neural network verification, but classical computational methods, such as Hamilton--Jacobi reachability and set propagation, scale poorly with state dimension. Sampling-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative, often providing finite-sample guarantees that bound the probability-mass left uncovered. However, an explicit account of how the geometry of the initial set, the dynamics, and the sampling law affect the accuracy of the estimator is not fully available in the literature. We study this by casting sampling-based reachable-set recovery as geometric support estimation over a family of problems specified by an initial set, its dynamics, and a sampling law. First, we identify two regularity properties, positive reach of the initial set's complement and Lipschitz continuity of the dynamics, that together make recovery well-posed: a probability-mass coverage guarantee can be upgraded to accuracy $r$ in Hausdorff distance. Second, we bound the resulting sample complexity: recovery is achievable with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big((e^{3LT}/r)^n\big)$ samples, exponential in both the state dimension and the time horizon. Third, we show that neither can be removed: an minimax lower bound of $Ω\big((e^{LT}/r)^n\big)$ holds for every estimator, so the exponential dependence on dimension and the degradation over the horizon are both intrinsic, not artifacts of a particular method. Experiments on nonlinear systems confirm that adversarial sampling improves constants but not the scaling.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes sampling-based reachability as geometric support estimation, showing that initial-set geometry and dynamics regularity yield Hausdorff accuracy guarantees, with intrinsic exponential sample complexity in state dimension and horizon; minimax lower bounds confirm this scaling is unavoidable, and adversarial sampling improves constants but not the rate.
AI.motivation: To provide explicit, finite-sample guarantees for sampling-based reachable-set recovery by linking accuracy to geometric and dynamical regularity, and to quantify the fundamental sample-complexity limits.
AI.method: Cast reachability as geometric support estimation over problem family defined by initial set, dynamics, and sampling law. Identify two regularity properties (positive reach of the initial set’s complement and Lipschitz dynamics) that ensure well-posed recovery. Derive a probabilistic coverage bound that translates to Hausdorff-distance accuracy r. Establish upper bound on sample complexity ~ O((e^{3LT}/r)^n). Prove a minimax lower bound Ω((e^{LT}/r)^n) for any estimator. Validate with nonlinear-system experiments comparing adversarial vs i.i.d. sampling.
AI.result: Recovery is achievable with roughly (e^{3LT}/r)^n samples; a universal lower bound requires at least (e^{LT}/r)^n samples. Adversarial sampling improves constants but not the scaling law; experiments on nonlinear systems corroborate the theory.
AI.conclusion: Exponential dependence on dimension and horizon is intrinsic to this problem under the stated regularity; geometry and sampling strategy jointly determine accuracy. While sampling-based methods enable finite-sample guarantees, achieving tight scaling remains computationally hard, with practical gains arising from smarter sampling rather than breaking the exponential rate.

title: Multi-Timescale Latent-Action DRL for Joint Optimization in Edge-Cloud Networks
summary: Load imbalance across edge and cloud layers degrades latency performance in hierarchical edge-cloud computing (HECC) systems under dynamic task arrivals and heterogeneous resources, leading to severe queuing delays and inefficient resource utilization. To address this challenge, we study a joint service placement, computational delegation, and power control (JSCP) problem to minimize the average end-to-end (e2e) latency. The resulting JSCP problem is a mixed-integer nonconvex and NP-hard optimization problem due to the strong coupling between discrete and continuous variables. To enable tractable optimization and stable system adaptation, we exploit the inherent difference in decision dynamics and decompose the problem into long-term system configuration and short-term resource allocation subproblems. Based on this formulation, we propose a two-timescale multi-layer deep reinforcement learning framework with a latent action space (2T-MDRL-LA) to jointly optimize service placement, user association, computational delegation, task offloading, and user transmit power. A latent action representation based on a variational autoencoder is introduced to efficiently compress the high-dimensional combinatorial action space. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively adapts to dynamic network conditions and achieves near-optimal performance compared to branch-and-bound solutions. It achieves up to a 20.8% reduction in average e2e latency and a 13% improvement in resource utilization over the scheme without the computational delegation, while converging approximately 50% faster than conventional proximal policy optimization.

AI.tldr: A two-timescale deep reinforcement learning framework with latent actions optimizes joint service placement, delegation, offloading, and power in hierarchical edge-cloud computing to reduce end-to-end latency and improve resource utilization, achieving near-optimal performance with faster convergence than PPO and faster than baseline without delegation.
AI.motivation: HECC systems suffer from load imbalance, dynamic task arrivals, and heterogeneous resources causing high latency due to queuing and suboptimal resource use. The JSCP problem is mixed-integer nonconvex and NP-hard, requiring tractable, adaptive optimization.
AI.method: Decompose JSCP into long-term system configuration and short-term resource allocation subproblems. Propose a two-timescale multi-layer deep reinforcement learning framework with a latent action space (2T-MDRL-LA). Use a variational autoencoder to compress high-dimensional combinatorial actions into a latent representation. Jointly optimize service placement, user association, computational delegation, task offloading, and user transmit power through learning.
AI.result: Simulation results show the framework adapts to dynamic network conditions and achieves up to 20.8% reduction in average end-to-end latency and 13% improvement in resource utilization versus a scheme without computational delegation, while converging about 50% faster than conventional proximal policy optimization (PPO). Near-optimal performance compared to branch-and-bound baselines.
AI.conclusion: A latent-action, two-timescale DRL framework can effectively solve the JSCP in HECC, offering substantial latency reductions and resource efficiency with faster convergence, demonstrating strong adaptability to dynamic conditions.

title: Text-conditioned Segmentation for Tomato Phenotyping via Procedural Synthetic Data
summary: Vision-based automation is an excellent candidate for reducing manual labor in greenhouse crop production and phenotyping. However, progress is constrained by the lack of annotated training data. Recent advances in vision-based foundational models have shown promising results in zero-shot generalization to novel domains, but their performance drops in complex agricultural environments. In this work, we present a sim-to-real framework for tomato plant segmentation that combines synthetic data generation with fine-tuning of a foundation model. We model a commercial cherry tomato greenhouse and use it to generate a large-scale synthetic dataset under diverse viewpoints, lighting conditions, and plant morphology. Subsequently, we fine-tune the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) on the synthetic dataset, specializing its text-conditioned segmentation behavior for greenhouse crop organs while retaining the general visual prior that makes zero-shot transfer possible. By evaluating our framework on multiple real-world greenhouse datasets, we demonstrate that combining synthetic data with SAM 3 fine-tuning significantly improves segmentation performance and model confidence. To support community benchmarking, we publicly release the procedural model, the generated synthetic dataset, and our fine-tuned SAM 3 weights.

AI.tldr: Sim-to-real framework for tomato plant segmentation: build a synthetic greenhouse dataset and fine-tune SAM 3 on it, yielding improved segmentation and confidence on real data; public release of dataset, model, and weights.
AI.motivation: Address the data scarcity problem in greenhouse vision by combining synthetic data with a foundation model to enable better segmentation of tomato plant organs while preserving zero-shot capabilities.
AI.method: Construct a realistic, commercial cherry tomato greenhouse model to generate a large-scale synthetic dataset across diverse viewpoints, lighting, and plant morphology. Fine-tune Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) on this synthetic data to specialize its text-conditioned segmentation for greenhouse organs while preserving its general visual priors.
AI.result: On multiple real greenhouse datasets, the synthetic-data–driven fine-tuning of SAM 3 significantly improves segmentation performance and model confidence compared to baselines relying on either synthetic data alone or zero-shot SAM 3. The approach also demonstrates good transferability across real-world conditions.
AI.conclusion: Combining synthetic data with fine-tuning of a foundation model is effective for targeted plant segmentation in greenhouse environments, and public release of the procedural model, synthetic dataset, and fine-tuned weights will support community benchmarking.

title: Beyond Accuracy and Cost: Latency-Aware LLM Query Routing for Dynamic Workloads
summary: Modern language query routers improve inference efficiency by assigning each query to a model that balances response quality and monetary cost. However, current query routers are largely latency-agnostic and do not consider the generation latency experienced by queries at model instances. In practice, latency is often controlled by load-balancing policies such as round-robin or join-the-shortest-queue, which do not account for model accuracy or inference cost. Incorporating query latency into routing is challenging as it depends not only on the query's prompt length, but also on the current prefill and decode workload at the model instance and the scheduling and batching policy of the serving framework. We design a lightweight latency estimator that simulates autoregressive token batch processing in the serving framework and estimates the time-to-first-token (TTFT) of queries. We incorporate this latency estimator into a latency-aware router that jointly optimizes latency, accuracy, and cost when assigning queries to model instances. Our experimental results indicate that this joint optimization yields up to 40% improvement in accuracy--cost utility while maintaining the same latencies as standard load-balancing approaches.

AI.tldr: Latency-aware routing for LLM inference: estimates time-to-first-token (TTFT) with a lightweight simulator and jointly optimizes latency, accuracy, and cost, achieving up to 40% better latency-utility at the same latency as baseline routers.
AI.motivation: Current language-model query routers are largely latency-agnostic and ignore generation latency, which depends on prompt length, model workload, and serving-framework scheduling/batching. Incorporating latency estimates into routing promises improved efficiency (accuracy vs. cost) without increasing latency.
AI.method: Develop a lightweight latency estimator that simulates autoregressive token batch processing in the serving framework to estimate TTFT. Integrate this estimator into a latency-aware router that jointly optimizes latency, accuracy, and cost when assigning queries to model instances, considering prompt length, prefill/decode workload, and batching policies.
AI.result: Experimental results show the joint optimization yields up to 40% improvement in accuracy–cost utility while maintaining the same latency as standard load-balancing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Latency-aware routing guided by a TTFT estimator can substantially improve the accuracy-cost efficiency of multi-model inference systems without increasing latency, highlighting the importance of accounting for generation latency in routing decisions.

title: End-to-end Conditional Diffusion for Realistic and Controllable Visual Traffic Scenario Generation
summary: Generating closed-loop traffic scenarios that are both realistic and controllable is crucial for evaluating autonomous driving systems, especially under rare safety-critical interactions. Existing learning-based methods often struggle to balance controllability and realism, offering either limited fine-grained control over traffic behavior or controllable scenarios at the expense of behavioral plausibility. This paper presents E2E-CDiff, an end-to-end conditional diffusion framework for controllable and realistic scenario generation. Conditioned on front-view visual observations, E2E-CDiff jointly denoises future motion states and executable low-level controls for route-interacting background vehicles. This unified state-action generation mitigates the planning-control mismatch in conventional two-stage trajectory-then-controller pipelines. Differentiable guidance further regulates speed, enforces drivable-area compliance, and supports collision-avoidance or collision-seeking behaviors, enabling both naturalistic and safety-critical scenario generation. Experiments on Bench2Drive show that E2E-CDiff achieves a favorable controllability-realism trade-off compared with representative reinforcement- and imitation-learning baselines, while its collision-guided variant induces challenging interactions across multiple autonomous driving systems. E2E-CDiff also performs competitively as a learning-based ego planner, demonstrating the generality of end-to-end state-action diffusion.

AI.tldr: End-to-end conditional diffusion for controllable, realistic traffic scenario generation using front-view observations; jointly predicts future motion and low-level controls; differentiable guidance for speed, drivable-area compliance, and collision behavior; shows favorable controllability-realism trade-off and competitive ego-planning ability.
AI.motivation: Need for realistic yet controllable synthetic traffic scenarios to test autonomous systems, addressing planning-control mismatch and limited realism in two-stage pipelines.
AI.method: Propose E2E-CDiff: an end-to-end conditional diffusion model conditioned on front-view visuals; jointly denoises future motion states and executable low-level controls for background vehicles; includes differentiable guidance for speed, drivable-area compliance, and collision-avoidance or -seeking; evaluation on Bench2Drive; includes collision-guided variant.
AI.result: Demonstrates favorable trade-off between controllability and realism vs RL/IL baselines; collision-guided variant yields challenging interactions across autonomous systems; competitive ego planner performance suggests generality of end-to-end state-action diffusion.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end state-action diffusion with differentiable guidance provides a unified and versatile framework for generating realistic, controllable traffic scenarios and potentially robust ego planning performance.

title: Towards Principled Continual Anomaly Detection: A Systematic Framework and Benchmark Scenarios
summary: Continual anomaly detection (CAD) studies how models can adapt to evolving data distributions while retaining performance on previously observed regimes. CAD benchmarks, however, depend critically on how tasks are defined, filtered, ordered, and validated. In tabular domains, task boundaries are rarely given, and arbitrary splits can create unlearnable, redundant, or overly transferable tasks that obscure genuine continual-learning behavior. To this end, we introduce a systematic framework for reproducible benchmark scenario design from existing tabular anomaly-detection datasets. The framework discovers candidate tasks, filters unsuitable tasks, and derives principled orderings that expose diverse dynamics. The framework allows us to deliver five benchmark-ready scenarios from three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets, yielding both single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings.

AI.tldr: A framework to design reproducible CAD benchmarks for tabular anomaly detection, producing five benchmark-ready scenarios from three cybersecurity datasets, with candidate-task discovery, filtering, and principled task ordering, enabling single- and multi-dataset CAD evaluations.
AI.motivation: In tabular CAD, arbitrary task splits undermine comparability and mask genuine continual-learning behavior; a principled, reproducible scheme is needed to define tasks, orderings, and validations.
AI.method: Develop a systematic framework that (1) discovers candidate tasks within existing tabular anomaly-detection datasets, (2) filters out unsuitable tasks, and (3) derives principled task orderings to reveal diverse dynamics; applies framework to three large-scale cybersecurity datasets to produce five benchmark-ready CAD scenarios, available in both single-dataset and multi-dataset settings.
AI.result: Five benchmark-ready CAD scenarios derived from three datasets; supports both single-dataset and multi-dataset continual anomaly detection evaluations; enhances reproducibility and exposure to diverse dynamics in tabular cybersecurity anomaly data.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables reproducible, analyzable CAD benchmarking for tabular data, clarifies task definitions and evaluation dynamics, and demonstrates practical applicability in cybersecurity contexts; potential to standardize comparisons across continual learning approaches.

title: Attention Without Grounding: Causal Evaluation of Visual Explanations in Medical VLMs
summary: Attention and saliency heatmaps are widely used to explain medical Vision-Language Model (VLM) outputs on chest X-rays, yet whether they truly highlight the image evidence driving predictions has not been causally tested. We audit faithfulness via overlap with radiologist bounding boxes on PadChest (n=637), attribution mass within radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and 16x16 patch-occlusion maps that record which regions, when hidden, change the answer. We study three MedGemma-4B variants, cross-family probes on LLaVA-RAD and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and the specialist CheXagent-2-3b, with two CXR-trained classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50) as positive controls. A heatmap is faithful only if the model uses the image and attention concentrates on regions whose occlusion alters the prediction. No evaluated VLM meets both criteria. MedGemma and Qwen3-VL use the image, but attention anti-correlates with patch-occlusion importance (rho < 0 with 95% bootstrap CIs below zero). LLaVA-RAD's attention correlates positively, but the model is almost text-only (99.1% text-only agreement, near-zero causal mass), so correlation ties two near-zero signals. Attention also misses annotated anatomy: overlap with true regions never beats shifted or random controls, and no method places more than 22% of its mass inside radiologist masks. The two CXR classifiers pass all metrics, indicating the failure is specific to VLM heatmaps, not the evaluation. These heatmaps are visually reassuring but not faithful; clinical explanations require controlled localization metrics and causal perturbation, not visual inspection alone.

AI.tldr: Across multiple medical VLMs and datasets, attention/heatmaps fail faithfulness tests: they do not overlap meaningfully with radiologist regions nor show causal sensitivity to occlusion; two dedicated CXR classifiers pass, indicating the issue is specific to VLM heatmaps.
AI.motivation: To causally test whether visual explanations (attention/heatmaps) from medical Vision-Language Models truly reflect image evidence driving predictions, rather than being visually reassuring artefacts.
AI.method: Evaluate faithfulness via (1) overlap with radiologist bounding boxes on PadChest (n=637), (2) attribution mass within radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and (3) 16x16 patch-occlusion maps to identify regions whose occlusion alters predictions. Analyze three MedGemma-4B variants, cross-family probes LLaVA-RAD and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, specialist CheXagent-2-3b, and two CXR-trained classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50) as positives.
AI.result: No VLM heatmap satisfies both criteria for faithfulness: (a) attention either anti-correlates with occlusion-based importance (MedGemma, Qwen3-VL) or, for LLaVA-RAD, shows positive correlation but is largely text-driven (99.1% text-only agreement, near-zero causal mass). (b) Overlaps with true radiologist regions do not outperform shifted/random controls, and no method concentrates more than 22% of its mass inside radiologist masks. The two CXR classifiers pass all metrics, indicating the limitation is specific to VLM heatmaps rather than evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Visual heatmaps from medical VLMs are not faithful explanations of image evidence. Reliable clinical explanations require controlled localization metrics and causal perturbation analyses rather than visual inspection alone.

title: Cross-Dialect Generalization Without Retraining: Benchmarks and Evaluation of Schema-Derived Constrained Decoding for MLIR
comment: 27 pages (9 main + bibliography + appendix), 9 figures, 9 tables. Code, benchmarks, and reproducibility Docker image at https://github.com/plawanrath/slm-to-mlir-constrained-emitter
summary: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) underlies modern ML compiler infrastructure (TensorFlow, JAX/StableHLO, PyTorch Inductor, IREE), yet appears only in trace amounts in code-LM pretraining corpora. MLIR is also extensible by design: new dialects ship per application domain, so a fine-tuned model per dialect does not scale. We ask whether inference-time priors derived mechanically from each dialect's Operation Definition Specification (ODS) can substitute for gradient-based adaptation. First, we release four natural-language-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects - MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, and StableHLO-Held-Out-200 - totaling 410 in-scope NL-to-MLIR pairs, plus a 25-program out-of-grammar stress set and a hand-authored n=30 functional reference set, shipped under Apache-2.0 with Gebru datasheets and Croissant 1.0 metadata. Second, we build a three-layer schema-derived constraint stack: a CFG over op signatures(C1), type-domain splits from an ODS-extracted type lattice (C2), and an SSA-scope validator driving five-retry rejection sampling (C3). Porting from arith+func+memref+linalg to StableHLO required no new constraint-layer code. On dialects whose verifier semantics are dominated by structural constraints, schema-derived priors let SmolLM2-1.7B match or exceed 15B-34B code LMs at 8-25x the per-generation speed: on linalg, SmolLM2 reaches 80.0% verify-valid (three-seed mean, n=125), beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping CIs. On arith+func and on the templated parametric StableHLO-Held-Out-200, where verifier semantics turn on attribute values rather than structure, the same baselines match or beat the SLM; we scope these as non-win cells. We release benchmarks, decoder, all per-prompt generations, and a reproducibility Docker image.

AI.tldr: Inference-time priors derived from MLIR dialect ODS can rival or exceed gradient-based adaptation for structurally constrained dialects, demonstrated on NL-to-MLIR benchmarks with a three-layer constraint stack; SmolLM2 shows substantial speedups and competitive verify rates on linalg, with broader benchmark release.
AI.motivation: MLIR has many dialects; data scarcity in pretraining means fine-tuning per dialect is not scalable. Mechanically derived priors from operation definitions could provide scalable, cross-dialect guidance at inference time.
AI.method: Introduce four NL-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects (MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, StableHLO-Held-Out-200) totaling 410 NL-to-MLIR pairs, plus an out-of-grammar stress set and a functional reference set. Develop a three-layer constraint stack: (C1) CFG over op signatures, (C2) SSA-type-lattice from ODS types, (C3) SSA-scope validator with five-retry rejection sampling. Porting from arith+func+memref+linalg to StableHLO required no new constraint-layer code. Evaluate SmolLM2-1.7B against larger code LMs on verify-valid rate; release benchmarks, decoder, all per-prompt generations, and reproducibility Docker image.
AI.result: In structurally-constrained dialects, schema-derived priors enable SmolLM2-1.7B to match or exceed 15B-34B code LMs at 8-25x per-generation speed. On linalg, SmolLM2 reaches 80.0% verify-valid (three-seed mean, n=125), beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping CIs. On arith+func and templated StableHLO-Held-Out-200 (where verifier semantics rely on attribute values), the same baselines match or beat the SLM, categorized as non-win cells. Benchmarks, decoder, per-prompt generations, and a reproducibility Docker image released.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time, schema-derived priors from dialect ODS can substitute for gradient-based adaptation in dialects where verification is dominated by structural constraints, enabling faster, competitive NL-to-MLIR generation. Results are dialect-dependent; structural constraints yield gains, while attribute-driven cases see no clear wins. Comprehensive benchmarks and reproducibility artifacts are released.

title: Fabric Pneumatic Artificial Muscles Based on the Drawstring Principle
summary: Pneumatic artificial muscles have wide applications in robotics and industrial fields. Conventional pneumatic artificial muscles generate extra radial deformation during axial contraction, which severely wastes available working space. Inspired by the widely adopted drawstring principle in textile products, this paper proposes a novel drawstring fabric pneumatic artificial muscle (DPAM). Unlike traditional counterparts, the proposed DPAM produces no extra radial deformation during contraction, greatly improving structural compactness. The DPAM exhibits outstanding mechanical performance: a load capacity over 800 times its self-weight, a maximum contraction ratio of 44%, and a power density up to 4.98 kW/kg, alongside excellent scalability. Two representative application scenarios, bionic robots and industrial production lines, are demonstrated to validate its practicability. The DPAM can be easily expanded within a two-dimensional plane, as verified by the fabricated DPAM matrix. This work not only presents a high-performance novel pneumatic artificial muscle but also inspires researchers to draw design inspiration from conventional textile structures to address existing challenges in soft robotics.

AI.tldr: A drawstring fabric pneumatic artificial muscle (DPAM) eliminates unwanted radial expansion during axial contraction, yielding a compact, high-performance actuator with strong scalability.
AI.motivation: Conventional pneumatic artificial muscles have poor workspace efficiency due to extraneous radial deformation; adopting a textile drawstring concept aims to enhance axial actuation and packaging density.
AI.method: Introduce a DPAM that uses drawstring-inspired fabric mechanisms to constrain radial expansion, preventing extra radial deformation during contraction; demonstrate 2D expandability via a DPAM matrix and validate in bionic robots and industrial lines.
AI.result: DPAM achieves >800x its self-weight in load capacity, contraction up to 44%, and power density up to 4.98 kW/kg, with good scalability and demonstrated practicality in multiple applications.
AI.conclusion: The DPAM delivers a high-performance, compact pneumatic actuator and illustrates the value of integrating conventional textile design principles into soft robotics, opening pathways for scalable, plane-expandable actuator arrays.

title: SechKAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hyperbolic Secant Functions
summary: In recent years, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have attracted increasing attention due to their effectiveness in machine learning and scientific computing tasks, offering a new paradigm for neural network design. In this paper, we present SechKAN, a KAN architecture based on hyperbolic secant (sech) functions. The hyperbolic secant basis is used for its smooth bell-shaped form, localized responses, and stable gradients. We employ 1D linear transformations to reduce the number of parameters, allowing SechKAN to remain comparable to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in model size. Experimental results indicate the effectiveness of SechKAN in function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification tasks on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. SechKAN achieves superior performance compared to MLPs and other KAN variants while maintaining a similar number of parameters. However, its running time, while better than that of other KAN variants, is slightly longer than that of MLPs.

AI.tldr: SechKAN is a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network variant using hyperbolic-secant basis with 1D linear transforms, achieving competitive performance with a parameter count similar to MLPs across function fitting, PDEs, and image classification, though with slightly longer runtime than MLPs.
AI.motivation: Investigate a new KAN-based architecture employing smooth, localized sech basis to improve learning stability and performance while keeping parameter efficiency comparable to MLPs.
AI.method: Introduce SechKAN, a KAN architecture based on hyperbolic secant activations. Use 1D linear transformations to reduce parameters. Evaluate on function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, comparing against MLPs and other KAN variants.
AI.result: SechKAN achieves superior performance relative to MLPs and other KAN variants while maintaining a similar parameter count. Running time is better than other KAN variants but slightly longer than MLPs.
AI.conclusion: SechKAN demonstrates that a sech-based KAN can deliver strong accuracy across diverse tasks with parameter efficiency, though runtimes may lag behind plain MLPs; the architecture provides a viable alternative within the KAN family and motivates further optimization of computational efficiency.

title: Norm or Direction? Decoding Vision Mambas for High-Resolution Vision
summary: Vision Mamba models replace quadratic self-attention with linear complexity selective state space models (SSMs), emerging as efficient visual backbones. However, MambaOut demonstrates that a Gated CNN block can match or exceed VMamba on image classification, questioning the necessity of SSMs for vision. This raises a fundamental question: do VMamba and MambaOut encode visual information differently at the representation level? To investigate, we apply cross model centered kernel alignment (CKA) analysis and find that VMamba's final stage blocks form representations distinctly different from both MambaOut and its own preceding blocks. We therefore focus on the final block features, decomposing each spatial token into magnitude and direction. MambaOut concentrates class-discriminative information in high-norm foreground tokens that align with Grad-CAM attribution. VMamba, by contrast, produces high-norm tokens predominantly in background regions, misaligned with Grad-CAM, yet preserves discriminative signals primarily in token directions. These observations reveal that the two models rely on different encoding strategies. We connect this difference to high-resolution classification and semantic segmentation. VMamba distributes logit support broadly across object regions, whereas MambaOut relies on sparse dominant tokens, a strategy that becomes less stable as token counts grow. Under full fine-tuning for segmentation, VMamba consistently outperforms MambaOut. These results suggest that VMamba's advantage in dense prediction stems not merely from the SSM mechanism or sequence length, but from how semantic evidence is organized across token magnitude, direction. Ultimately, we conclude that token magnitude and directional structure serve as critical axes for improving visual backbones, particularly under dense supervision.

AI.tldr: VMamba and MambaOut encode visual information differently; VMamba uses broad high-level semantic token directions and broadly distributed logit support favorable for dense prediction, while MambaOut relies on sparse high-norm tokens aligned with Grad-CAM; cross-model CKA reveals distinct representations, especially in the final block; for segmentation, VMamba outperforms MambaOut; token magnitude and direction are key axes for backbone design.
AI.motivation: To determine whether VMamba and MambaOut encode visual information differently and how this affects dense prediction tasks; to connect representation geometry to semantic segmentation and high-resolution classification.
AI.method: Use cross-model centered kernel alignment (CKA) to compare representations; decompose final block token representations into magnitude and direction; analyze token-level distribution relative to Grad-CAM; evaluate on high-resolution classification and semantic segmentation with full fine-tuning; assess stability with increasing token counts.
AI.result: CKA shows VMamba final-block representations are distinct from MambaOut and from its own preceding blocks; MambaOut concentrates class-discriminative information in high-norm tokens aligned with Grad-CAM; VMamba produces high-norm tokens in background yet preserves discriminative signals primarily in token directions; VMamba distributes logit support broadly across object regions, whereas MambaOut relies on sparse dominant tokens whose stability declines as token counts grow; under full segmentation fine-tuning, VMamba consistently outperforms MambaOut.
AI.conclusion: Token magnitude and directional structure are critical axes for visual backbone improvement; VMamba’s advantage in dense prediction stems from how semantic evidence is organized across token magnitude and direction, not solely the SSM mechanism or sequence length.

title: Semantic Cooperative Games for Contribution Attribution in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Contribution attribution has become a central problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems, where final outputs are produced through multiple agents, message exchanges, and ordered workflow dependencies. Existing attribution methods often rely on counterfactual valuation, such as removing agents or comparing score changes across altered agent subsets. In language-mediated workflows, these methods require repeated model calls, introduce high variance, and do not explicitly capture the intermediate semantic states through which agents produce, preserve, and transform task-relevant information. We propose Semantic Cooperative Games (SCG), a framework that represents a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph and induces an agent-level semantic value function on this structure. We define the Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) to allocate contribution over semantic support logic, and introduce SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that constructs the semantic hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets. We prove that SSV reduces to the classical Shapley value under standard set-based, fully observable, and no-order-dependence conditions. On a medical benchmark satisfying these conditions, SLIC reduces computation cost by 93.3% while remaining highly consistent with a Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and exposes cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge. Overall, SLIC provides a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: SCG with Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) and SLIC enables fast, interpretable attribution in LLM-based multi-agent workflows by constructing a semantic generation hypergraph and avoiding reruns of agent subsets; it reduces computation and aligns with Shapley under standard conditions while exposing cases where semantic contribution diverges from failure impact.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods rely on counterfactuals, require repeated model calls, exhibit high variance, and miss intermediate semantic states. There is a need for a fast, counterfactual-free, and semantically aware attribution framework for language-mediated multi-agent workflows.
AI.method: Represent a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph, define an agent-level semantic value function, and introduce Semantic Shapley Value (SSV). Propose SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that constructs the hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets.
AI.result: SSV reduces to the classical Shapley value under standard set-based, fully observable, and no-order-dependence conditions. In a medical benchmark with these conditions, SLIC cuts computation cost by 93.3% and stays highly consistent with Monte Carlo Shapley. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and reveals cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge.
AI.conclusion: SLIC offers a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: MVP-Tac: A Miniaturized Dual-Modal Vision and Photoelastic Tactile Sensor for Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. To appear in IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: Robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RMIS) offers major benefits over open and conventional laparoscopic procedures, yet it still lacks tactile feedback for palpation while operating under strict requirements to preserve reliable vision for navigation and safety. In practice, visual feedback is indispensable, and tactile solutions that cannot coexist with vision are difficult to translate into RMIS tools. To address both needs, we introduce MVP-Tac, a compact, vision-based tactile sensor that provides co-located vision and tactile sensing. MVP-Tac uses reflective photoelastic imaging: a thin photoelastic elastomer produces stress-dependent interferograms under contact that are captured by an embedded camera through a miniaturized reflective polariscope. A semi-transparent membrane and controllable illumination enable switching between visual mode and tactile mode, enabling tactile perception without sacrificing vision. We validate MVP-Tac through force calibration in the 0 to 2 N range and demonstrate its potential for tumor palpation via video-based hardness classification on tissue phantoms, achieving 97% accuracy for exposed-tumor classification and 92% accuracy for subdermal-tumor classification. Finally, we conduct a simulated colonoscopy to validate both visual and tactile modalities in a constrained lumen, including vision-guided 3D photomapping of the luminal wall and in situ hardness classification of localized nodules. Overall, MVP-Tac provides a practical path toward restoring clinically useful palpation in RMIS while maintaining essential visual feedback. The design, fabrication, and firmware of MVP-Tac are open-sourced at https://mvp-tac.github.io/

AI.tldr: A compact, vision-enabled tactile sensor (MVP-Tac) enables co-located vision and tactile sensing for RMIS; validated via force calibration, tissue phantom palpation, and simulated colonoscopy; open-source hardware and firmware.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of tactile feedback in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RMIS) that can coexist with essential visual navigation; enable palpation without compromising vision.
AI.method: Develop MVP-Tac: a thin photoelastic elastomer that shows stress-dependent interferograms under contact; embedded camera through a miniaturized reflective polariscope captures the tactile signal; a semi-transparent membrane and controllable illumination switch between visual and tactile modes; validation includes force calibration in 0–2 N range, video-based hardness classification on tissue phantoms (97% exposed-tumor, 92% subdermal-tumor), and a simulated colonoscopy with vision-guided 3D luminal photomapping and in situ nodular hardness classification; open-source design, fabrication, and firmware.
AI.result: Demonstrated accurate tactile sensing integrated with real-time vision; high tumor-hardness classification accuracy; successful 3D mapping and tactile classification in constrained luminal environments; sensor design supports practical RMIS palpation with preserved visualization.
AI.conclusion: MVP-Tac offers a viable path to restore clinically useful palpation in RMIS while maintaining vision; its compact, co-located sensing approach and open-source availability facilitate adoption and further development.

title: Dual-domain fused LSTM modeling for efficient time-dependent reliability analysis
summary: Time-dependent reliability analysis is crucial for ensuring the long-term safety and performance of engineering systems under uncertainties. However, traditional surrogate model methods often struggle to incorporate time-independent random variables and capture their complex interactions with time-dependent stochastic processes. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a dual-domain fused long short-term memory (DDF-LSTM) model for efficient and accurate time-dependent reliability analysis. A novel network architecture is developed to jointly process information from both time-dependent and time-independent domains. Specifically, the time-independent variables are embedded into the initial hidden states, and a fully connected layer is introduced to map both LSTM outputs and time-independent variables into the final output space. Furthermore, an improved loss function is designed to emphasize the model's sensitivity to minimum responses, thereby improving the precision of failure probability estimation. The proposed method effectively captures the dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and the temporal behavior of limit state functions. Once trained, the DDF-LSTM model enables efficient Monte Carlo simulation to estimate time-dependent failure probabilities with minimal computational cost. Four case studies validate the proposed method's enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: A dual-domain fused LSTM (DDF-LSTM) for time-dependent reliability analysis that jointly handles time-dependent and time-independent variables, embedding time-independent inputs in initial hidden states and using a final FC layer; improved loss biased towards minimum responses; validated on four case studies; achieves efficient MC-based reliability estimation.
AI.motivation: Time-independent random variables are difficult to integrate with time-dependent stochastic processes in reliability analysis using standard surrogates, hindering accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce DDF-LSTM architecture that processes both domains; embed time-independent variables in initial hidden state; FC layer maps combined LSTM outputs and time-independent variables to output; a loss function emphasizing sensitivity to minimum responses; use with Monte Carlo simulation.
AI.result: Method improves computational efficiency and predictive accuracy; captures dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and temporal limit-state behavior; validated by four case studies.
AI.conclusion: DDF-LSTM provides a robust, efficient framework for time-dependent reliability analysis with time-independent variables, enabling accurate Monte Carlo based reliability estimation across complex stochastic dynamics.

title: Seeing Before Generating: Object Perception Enhances Single-View 3D Reconstruction
summary: The relationship between object perception and reconstruction is well established in human vision, yet remains underexplored in computer vision. In this paper, we demonstrate that learnt object perception can significantly enhance 3D reconstruction. Focusing on the challenging task of single-view 3D object reconstruction, we propose a method that leverages perceptual signals extracted from pretrained perception models capturing semantic and geometric information to drive the reconstruction of an object from its single image. Our approach is model-agnostic and can be integrated into various reconstruction methods in a plug-and-play manner. Experiments with two state-of-the-art single-view 3D reconstruction pipelines in a benchmark dataset show consistent and substantial improvements achieved by our method, validating the effectiveness of incorporating perception into generation. We provide in-depth analysis of various aspects of our method and its application. Our project page is at https://ynhuhuynh.github.io/perception-3d/.

AI.tldr: Leverages perceptual signals from pretrained models to boost single-view 3D object reconstruction; plug-and-play, model-agnostic enhancement that improves two state-of-the-art pipelines on a benchmark.
AI.motivation: Explore the link between object perception and reconstruction in computer vision and leverage semantic/geometric cues from pretrained perception models to enhance 3D reconstructions from a single image.
AI.method: Extract perceptual signals (semantic and geometric information) from pretrained perception models and incorporate them into existing single-view 3D reconstruction pipelines in a plug-and-play, model-agnostic manner.
AI.result: Demonstrates consistent, substantial improvements over two state-of-the-art single-view 3D reconstruction pipelines on a benchmark dataset; provides in-depth analysis and validation of perception-guided generation.
AI.conclusion: Integrating perceptual signals into reconstruction is effective and flexible, enabling improved performance across approaches; a project page is provided for further details.

title: PEARL: Solver-in-the-Loop Interactive Optimization Modeling from Natural Language
summary: Optimization modeling is the process of translating real-world decision problems, often described in natural language, into formal mathematical formulations and executable solver code. While recent advances in large language models have shown promise in automating this process, most existing approaches remain one-shot: a model produces a formulation once, without executing it, conditioning on solver feedback, or iteratively revising errors. This stands in sharp contrast to real-world optimization modeling, which is inherently interactive and proceeds through repeated solve-debug-revise cycles. We introduce PEARL, a system for interactive optimization modeling that uses Python execution and mathematical programming solvers inside this loop. Rather than relying on a fixed repair workflow, PEARL learns when to test partial models, how to revise from solver diagnostics, and when to stop. It operates in a multi-turn tool-integrated setting where intermediate execution results, feasibility signals, and solution checks are used to improve both formulations and solver code before finalization. Across diverse optimization benchmarks, PEARL substantially improves verified solve rates over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines; notably, our PEARL-Qwen3-\textbf{4B} model outperforms the much larger DeepSeek-V3.2-\textbf{685B} in both macro- and micro-averaged accuracy on optimization modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: PEARL enables interactive optimization modeling by integrating Python execution and solver feedback into a multi-turn loop; a small 4B-parameter model (PEARL-Qwen3-4B) matches or beats a 685B model on optimization tasks by learning when to test, revise, and stop.
AI.motivation: One-shot LLM approaches for optimization modeling fail to emulate the iterative debugging cycles used in practice; there is a need to exploit solver diagnostics and intermediate results to improve formulations.
AI.method: A multi-turn system PEARL that uses Python execution and solvers within the loop; learns decision policy for testing partial models, revising from diagnostics, and stopping; operates with intermediate results, feasibility signals, solution checks to refine formulations and solver code before finalization; evaluated across diverse optimization benchmarks.
AI.result: Significant improvements in verified solve rates over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines; PEARL-Qwen3-4B outperforms the 685B DeepSeek-V3.2 in macro- and micro-averaged accuracy on optimization modeling tasks.
AI.conclusion: Interactive, tool-augmented optimization modeling with solver feedback is effective; smaller, well-integrated models can surpass larger baselines and generalize across benchmarks, reducing reliance on end-state single-shot formulations.

title: How defensive driving enhances driving safety: A driving simulator study on drivers' defensive driving behaviors
summary: Defensive driving is widely recognized as an advanced driving skill. However, whether and how defensive driving affects driving safety remains insufficiently investigated. This study examines the behavioral characteristics of defensive driving, its impact on driving safety, and the underlying mechanisms. First, defensive driving is defined regarding operational timing and application scenario. Then, 82 participants are recruited for driving simulator experiments, with their behavioral and eye movement data being collected. Following the experiments, participants are categorized into groups based on the frequency of defensive driving behaviors exhibited. Finally, both inter-group and inter trial comparisons are performed on the experimental data.
