Experimental results demonstrate that in the inter-group comparison, the high defensive driving capability group exhibits higher acceleration and deceleration magnitudes, lower average speeds, and larger average absolute yaw angles compared to the low capability group, alongside shorter fixation durations and reduced fixation frequencies. Moreover, we observe that these participants tend to initiate defensive or evasive actions earlier, resulting in lower scenario risk. Regarding the inter-trial comparison, we observe similar trends exclusively in the low capability group, whereas most metrics show no significant differences between Trial 1 and Trial 2 in the high capability group. These results reveal that drivers possessing defensive driving capabilities tend to execute more intense driving maneuvers and identify risks and take action earlier, thereby enhancing driving safety. Findings support the promotion of defensive driving and provide a basis for relevant training programs. Meanwhile, they offer insights for the training of autonomous driving algorithms with defensive driving capabilities.

AI.tldr: High defensive driving capability correlates with safer driving in a simulator: more intensive maneuvers, earlier risk detection, and reduced risk, supporting defensive driving training and autonomous-driving design.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap in understanding how defensive driving affects safety and the mechanisms by which it operates.
AI.method: 82 participants in a driving-simulator study; behavioral and eye-movement data collected; defensive-driving frequency used to group participants into high vs. low capability; inter-group and inter-trial comparisons.
AI.result: High capability drivers exhibit larger acceleration/deceleration magnitudes, lower average speeds, larger absolute yaw angles, shorter fixation durations, and fewer fixations; they initiate defensive/evasive actions earlier, leading to lower scenario risk. In inter-trial comparisons, similar trends appear mainly in the low-capability group; high-capability group shows few significant trial differences.
AI.conclusion: Defensive driving capabilities enhance safety by enabling earlier risk identification and more decisive actions; supports training programs and has implications for incorporating defensive-driving behavior into autonomous driving algorithms.

title: Reliability Scales Inversely: Bigger Models Compound Mistakes Faster via a Hidden Auto-Regressive Risk Regime
summary: As language models scale, answers start truer but degrade faster: scaling buys capability but erodes reliability. The knowledge-gap account - more data, retrieval, or scale - misses an auto-regressive risk residual that scale sharpens: the model commits to a low-probability token, conditions on it as established, and snowballs. We track this through per-position disagreement $δ= \log p_M - \log p_O$ against a stronger same-family oracle, whose second moment splits exactly into bias$^2$ $\mathrm{KL}(p_M \,\|\, p_O)^2$ and risk $\mathrm{Var}[δ]$. We present four findings: (i) under scaling, the knowledge gap falls $\approx$$6\times$ while knowledge degradation grows $11$-$39\times$; (ii) at a fabrication, felt uncertainty $H(p_M)$ relaxes quickly while oracle-referenced risk persists up to $17\times$ longer, leaving a confident-but-precarious risk regime that bridges consecutive fabrications ($+69\%$ at $14$B); (iii) this regime is causal - an on-policy, fixed-$\mathrm{KL}$ variance contraction cuts web-verified hallucination by $35$-$74\%$ across three model families; and, (iv) it structurally evades self-monitoring, with $p_M$-only detectors (e.g. semantic entropy) firing $\approx$$30\%$ less ($p<10^{-16}$) on the risky branch holding nearly $4\times$ more fabrications. Bigger models snowball mistakes faster, through a failure mode that is dominant, self-perpetuating, causal and invisible to the model itself.

AI.tldr: Scaling improves capability but introduces a persistent auto-regressive risk residual that reduces reliability faster than knowledge-gap improvements; the paper formalizes this via per-position disagreement against a stronger oracle and decomposes its variance into bias and risk, yielding four major findings about scaling, fabrication regimes, causality, and self-monitoring evasion.
AI.motivation: To understand why larger language models become more capable yet less reliable, by isolating a risk residual that is not captured by traditional knowledge-gap metrics and quantifying it with a per-token disagreement framework.
AI.method: Define δ = log p_M - log p_O against a stronger same-family oracle p_O. Analyze the second moment of δ, which splits into bias^2 = KL(p_M || p_O)^2 and risk Var[δ]. Empirically evaluate across model families, focusing on scaling effects, fabrications, on-policy KL-constrained variance contraction, and detectors that rely on p_M only.
AI.result: Four findings: (i) under scaling, knowledge gap falls ~6x while knowledge degradation grows 11–39x; (ii) at fabrications, felt uncertainty H(p_M) relaxes quickly, while oracle-referenced risk persists ~17x longer, yielding a confident-but-precarious risk regime bridging fabrications (+69% at 14B); (iii) this regime is causal—on-policy, fixed-KL variance contraction reduces web-verified hallucination by 35–74% across three model families; (iv) self-monitoring is evaded: p_M-only detectors (e.g., semantic entropy) fire ~30% less (p<1e-16) on the risky branch, which contains nearly 4x more fabrications. Conclude: bigger models snowball mistakes via a dominant, self-perpetuating, and model-invisible failure mode.
AI.conclusion: Scaling yields a paradox: larger models acquire capability but accumulate a distinct auto-regressive risk that grows with regime complexity and remains poorly tracked by self-monitoring or standard knowledge-gap metrics. Effective mitigation requires targeting this risk via on-policy variance control and reference-based detectors, as the risk is causal and structurally embedded in the autoregressive process.

title: Deep Learning Estimation of Sex, Age, Height, and Weight from CT-derived Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs
summary: Purpose: To develop and validate a deep learning ensemble for estimating adult sex, age, height, and weight from coronal digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) generated from diagnostic CT. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 128,621 CT examinations from 80,004 adults at nine institutions in Japan. Three multitask models-ConvNeXt-Base, ViT-Base/16, and MaxViT-Base-were fine-tuned using coronal DRRs and combined by weighted averaging. Data were split by institution into training (114,147 examinations; seven institutions), tuning (4,305; one institution), and test (10,169; one institution) sets; generalizability was assessed on two non-Japanese datasets. Accuracy and mean absolute error (MAE) were used to evaluate sex classification and age, height, and weight regression, respectively. Body surface area (BSA)-corrected heart and liver volume trends were compared using true versus estimated height and weight. Results: In the test set (median age, 69.9 years; 4,899 of 10,169 [48.2%] male), overall sex-classification accuracy was 0.997 (95% CI, 0.996-0.998), and MAEs were 3.57 years (3.51-3.63), 2.59 cm (2.54-2.64), and 3.40 kg (3.34-3.47) for age, height, and weight, respectively. In examinations covering the chest through pelvis, accuracy was 1.000, and MAEs were 3.15 years, 2.28 cm, and 3.18 kg, respectively. BSA calculated from estimated values reproduced age-related heart and liver volume trends obtained using true values. On non-Japanese datasets, height error increased but was reduced by continued fine-tuning. Conclusion: The ensemble estimated adult sex, age, height, and weight from CT-derived DRRs, with generally lower errors in examinations with broader anatomical coverage.

AI.tldr: Deep learning ensemble estimates adult sex, age, height, and weight from coronal DRRs derived from diagnostic CT; achieves high accuracy and low MAE, with strong performance across a broad anatomical range and partial generalization to non-Japanese data after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Provide noninvasive, rapid anthropometric and demographic estimation from CT-derived radiographs to improve imaging workflows, dosimetry, and risk stratification without additional scanning.
AI.method: Retrospective multicenter study (128,621 CT exams from 80,004 adults, 9 Japanese institutions). Three multitask models (ConvNeXt-Base, ViT-Base/16, MaxViT-Base-w) fine-tuned on coronal DRRs and ensembling by weighted averaging. Data split by institution into training (n=114,147), tuning (n=4,305), and test (n=10,169). Generalizability assessed on two non-Japanese datasets.
AI.result: Sex classification accuracy: ~0.997 overall; MAE for age 3.57 years, height 2.59 cm, weight 3.40 kg. In chest-to-pelvis subset: accuracy 1.000; MAEs 3.15 years, 2.28 cm, 3.18 kg. BSA-corrected heart/liver volume trends matched true values. Height errors on non-Japanese data increased but improved with continued fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: A robust ensemble can estimate sex, age, height, and weight from CT-derived DRRs with low errors, particularly for broader anatomical coverage, with reasonable cross-population generalization after domain-adaptive fine-tuning.

title: S2T-RLHF: Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Stable Preference-Based RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with preference-based reward models often exhibits unstable training dynamics. A key contributing factor is that standard RLHF relies on a single sequence-level scalar reward, which is propagated to token-level policy updates and leaves credit assignment within a response inherently ambiguous. Recent work has attempted to address this issue by refining rewards into denser token-level supervision, often relying on the implicit assumption that finer-grained credit assignment improves optimization. We argue that this assumption is incomplete: when preference signals are noisy and only defined at the response level, overly fine-grained reward refinement can amplify reward uncertainty and destabilize learning. To address this problem, we propose a granularity-aware principle for hierarchical credit assignment, emphasizing stability-oriented reward design rather than maximal allocation precision. Under this principle, sentences serve as a natural intermediate granularity, balancing semantic coherence with robustness to token-level noise. Guided by this view, we introduce S2T-RLHF. This sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework first allocates sequence-level preference rewards across sentences and then applies bounded token-level refinement within each sentence, without reward-model retraining or token-level supervision. Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings show that S2T-RLHF improves training stability and robustness while maintaining competitive preference alignment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a granularity-aware, sentence-to-token reward framework (S2T-RLHF) for RLHF that stabilizes training by distributing sequence-level preferences across sentences and bounded token-level refinement, improving stability without retraining reward models or full token-level supervision.
AI.motivation: Single sequence-level rewards in RLHF propagate to tokens, making credit assignment unstable; finer token-level refinement can amplify reward uncertainty when signals are noisy. A stability-first design with natural intermediate granularity is needed.
AI.method: Introduce a granularity-aware hierarchical credit assignment principle. Use sentences as the intermediate granularity to distribute sequence-level preferences across sentences, then apply bounded token-level refinement within each sentence. Do not retrain the reward model or require token-level supervision. Implemented as S2T-RLHF (sentence-to-token reward decomposition).
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings show improved training stability and robustness with competitive alignment to human preferences.
AI.conclusion: A granularity-aware, sentence-to-token reward decomposition provides stability benefits in RLHF without sacrificing alignment, offering a practical approach to robust preference-based learning.

title: RoboInter1.5: A Holistic Intermediate Representation Suite for Embodied World Modeling and Robotic Manipulation
comment: 28 pages. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2602.09973
summary: Existing robot datasets remain expensive to curate, embodiment-specific, and insufficiently annotated with the fine-grained structure required for generalizable reasoning, execution, or long-horizon environment dynamics simulation. Building on our prior work, RoboInter1.0, we present RoboInter1.5, an extended and holistic suite of intermediate representations for both robotic manipulation and embodied world modeling. RoboInter1.5 provides a unified resource of data, benchmarks, and models centered on dense manipulation-oriented intermediate representations. Specifically, RoboInter-Data contains over 230k manipulation episodes across 571 scenes with dense per-frame annotations covering more than ten types of intermediate representations, including subtasks, primitive skills, object and gripper grounding, segmentation, affordance, grasp poses, contact points, motion traces, etc. Built upon these annotations, RoboInter-VQA introduces spatial and temporal embodied VQA tasks to benchmark and improve the intermediate-representation reasoning capabilities of our RoboInter-VLM. RoboInter-VLA further studies how such representations benefit action execution through implicit, explicit, and modular plan-then-execute paradigms. To better model the physical world, we further introduce RoboInter-World, which leverages intermediate representations as structured conditioning signals for controllable prediction of future world states. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RoboInter1.5 provides a unified spatiotemporal scaffolding for intermediate representations. Rather than treating intermediate representations merely as interpretable signals, RoboInter1.5 conceptualizes them as a bidirectional interface that both regularizes low-level action spaces and constrains the latent rollouts of open-world physical simulators.

AI.tldr: RoboInter1.5 extends RoboInter1.0 with a dense, multi-representation dataset and associated tasks to unify manipulation and world modeling through bidirectional intermediate representations that regularize actions and constrain world-models.
AI.motivation: Current robot datasets are costly, embodiment-specific, and lack fine-grained, generalizable intermediate representations necessary for generalizable reasoning, execution, and long-horizon environment dynamics simulation.
AI.method: Introduce RoboInter-Data with 230k manipulation episodes over 571 scenes and 10+ per-frame representations; develop RoboInter-VQA for spatiotemporal embodied reasoning; study RoboInter-VLA for plan-then-execute action execution; add RoboInter-World for controllable future-state prediction using these representations; evaluate as a unified spatiotemporal scaffold.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show RoboInter1.5 provides a unified framework of dense, manipulation-oriented representations that improve reasoning, planning, and predictive modeling; representations serve as a bidirectional interface that regularizes low-level actions and constrains latent world-rollouts.
AI.conclusion: RoboInter1.5 offers a holistic, bidirectional intermediate-representation framework that enhances data efficiency, generalization, and long-horizon robotic reasoning by unifying data, benchmarks, and models across manipulation and embodied world modeling.

title: One Student, Many Teachers: Multi-Task On-Policy Distillation via Soft-Prompt Privileged Context
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) teaches large language models new skills through a teacher that shares the student's backbone and supervises its own rollouts. Existing teachers either inject privileged context at the input -- inducing post-hoc rationalization -- or fine-tune weights, accumulating drift and forgetting across tasks. We propose \method, whose teacher differs from the student only by a learnable soft prompt: trained on $(x, y_\text{gold})$ pairs with the backbone frozen, the prompt yields a task-specific teacher that preserves the student's exact representational geometry. \method\ extends naturally to multi-task settings by routing each example in a merged corpus to its corresponding soft-prompt teacher, allowing a single student to absorb knowledge from $K$ teachers in parallel; at inference, all prompts are discarded. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Phi-4-mini-instruct across four tasks (Science, Tool Use, Biology, Math), the single-task variant (OPD with a PT teacher) matches or exceeds full fine-tuning while training orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and the multi-task variant achieves the best overall average ($56.2$ on Qwen3-1.7B-Base) while preserving general-capability benchmarks -- in contrast to sequential SFT, which degrades both.

AI.tldr: OPSD uses a learnable soft-prompt teacher with a frozen backbone to distill knowledge, enabling a single-task or multi-task student to absorb from multiple teachers with minimal parameter updates; outperforms or matches full fine-tuning and preserves general benchmarks, while avoiding drift seen in weight-tuning.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of existing teacher paradigms that inject privileged context (risking post-hoc rationalization) or fine-tune weights (causing drift/forgetting across tasks). Propose a backboned student guided by a soft-prompt teacher that preserves representational geometry and scales to multi-task settings.
AI.method: Train a soft prompt to create a task-specific teacher while keeping the backbone fixed; for multi-task, route each example to its corresponding soft-prompt teacher and sum or combine supervision; at inference, discard all prompts. This yields OPS D (on-policy self-distillation) with PT teacher variant in a single-task setting and a multi-task variant that handles K teachers.
AI.result: In experiments on Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Phi-4-mini-instruct across four tasks, the single-task OPS D with a PT (prompt-tuned) teacher matches or exceeds full fine-tuning with far fewer trainable parameters; the multi-task variant achieves the best average performance (56.2 on Qwen3-1.7B-Base) while preserving general benchmarks, unlike sequential SFT which degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: Soft-prompt-based on-policy self-distillation provides an efficient, scalable alternative to weight-tuning for single- and multi-task learning, maintaining representation geometry and achieving competitive or superior performance with substantial parameter efficiency.

title: Fluid-SDF: Ultra-Lightweight and Editable Implicit Shape Representation via Differentiable Primitives
summary: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have become the standard for continuous 2D shape modeling, but they suffer from black-box uneditability, vulnerability to noise, and high parameter counts that severely hinder deployment on edge devices. We introduce Fluid-SDF, a highly compressed, differentiable Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) framework that models shapes using explicit geometric primitives blended via a smooth minimum function. By replacing traditional multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with a parameterized primitive engine, Fluid-SDF reconstructs complex, non-convex topologies using strictly under 100 parameters, achieving comparable or superior intersection-over-union (mIoU) to standard neural baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Fluid-SDF acts as a powerful geometric prior, inherently resisting high-frequency dataset noise where capacity-matched neural networks catastrophically overfit. Finally, unlike standard INRs, Fluid-SDF's explicit parameter space allows for direct, zero-shot user editing of local and global shape features without retraining. By bypassing expensive on-device gradient updates entirely, Fluid-SDF is uniquely suited for mobile AI, augmented reality, and resource-constrained embedded environments

AI.tldr: Fluid-SDF is a compact, differentiable, explicit-geometry framework that uses a parameterized primitive engine with smooth minimum blending to model shapes in under 100 parameters, achieving competitive mIoU with enhanced noise robustness and enabling zero-shot editing for edge-device deployment.
AI.motivation: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) offer continuous 2D shape modeling but suffer from black-box uneditability, vulnerability to noise, and large parameter counts, hindering on-device deployment and user editing; a compact, editable alternative is desirable.
AI.method: Replace MLP-based representations with a parameterized primitive engine that blends explicit geometric primitives via a smooth minimum function to form Fluid-SDF; achieve highly compact models (under 100 parameters) capable of representing non-convex topologies; maintain differentiability for training and editing.
AI.result: Achieves comparable or superior mIoU to neural baselines with far fewer parameters; acts as a strong geometric prior resistant to high-frequency noise; enables zero-shot editing of local and global shape features without retraining; eliminates on-device gradient updates, facilitating deployment on mobile/AR/embedded devices.
AI.conclusion: Fluid-SDF demonstrates that a compact, explicit-geometry representation with differentiable blending can match or outperform neural-ID-based approaches while providing editability and robustness, making it well-suited for resource-constrained settings.

title: Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering for Trustworthy LLM Inference
summary: Steering vectors (SVs), an inference-time intervention technique for large language models (LLMs), guide the generation process by adding a concept-specific direction vector to intermediate activations during inference. However, existing SV methods frequently yield representation-incoherent behaviors that undermine interpretability and fine-grained control, largely because prior work has focused on binary positive-negative steering evaluation while employing discrete clustering metrics that fail to capture the continuous spectrum of semantic alignment. In this work, we present the Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS) framework for LLM inference. PCS preserves original task competence while providing controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias through concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration.

AI.tldr: PCS introduces Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering for LLMs, a framework that uses concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration to provide continuous, safety-oriented semantic bias while preserving task performance, addressing representation incoherence and coarse binary steering in prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing steering-vector methods for LLMs suffer from representation-incoherent behaviors and rely on binary positive/negative steering with discrete clustering metrics, failing to capture the continuous spectrum of semantic alignment and compromising interpretability and fine-grained control.
AI.method: Propose PCS framework with concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration to inject semantically meaningful, continuous bias into intermediate activations during inference, preserving task competence while enabling controllable safety-oriented bias.
AI.result: Claims to maintain original task competence while providing controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias through probabilistic steering; suggests improved interpretability and finer-grained control over semantic alignment compared to prior binary SV approaches.
AI.conclusion: PCS provides a principled approach to steer LLMs along a continuum of concepts with probabilistic strength control, enabling safer and more interpretable manipulation of model outputs without sacrificing performance.

title: Confidence-Gated Vision-Only Heading Alignment for UAV-UGV Cooperative Systems
summary: Vision-based heading prediction is useful for UAV--UGV cooperation, but accurate prediction alone does not guarantee that every predicted heading should be issued directly as a control command. This paper investigates the decision problem of when and how a fixed vision-based heading predictor should be trusted for command issuance. A lightweight confidence-gated framework is proposed in which execution decisions are made using two interpretable reliability proxies derived from the perception stream: bounding-box area as a visibility-related proxy and short-window variation in predicted heading as a stability-related proxy. During low-confidence intervals, the framework compares the baseline freeze-HOLD policy with a bounded-blend fallback that updates the issued command conservatively. The method is evaluated on a real UAV--UGV dataset under clean and perturbed conditions. The results show that confidence gating creates a clear trade-off among execution rate, executed-frame accuracy, issued-command accuracy, and smoothness. The results further show that sparse execution can cause severe stale-command error under the baseline freeze-HOLD policy, whereas the bounded-blend fallback substantially improves command-level behavior under the same gate decisions. These findings highlight that reliable perception-driven autonomy depends not only on prediction accuracy, but also on decision-aware command issuance during low-confidence

AI.tldr: Confidence-gated heading prediction improves decision-making for command issuance in UAV-UGV coordination by using visibility and stability proxies; the bounded-blend fallback mitigates stale commands compared to a baseline freeze-HOLD policy.
AI.motivation: To ensure safe and reliable autonomous control when perception is uncertain; prediction accuracy alone is insufficient; need decision-aware execution policies.
AI.method: Lightweight framework using two interpretable proxies: bounding-box area as visibility proxy; short-window heading variation as stability proxy; gate decisions; evaluate baseline freeze-HOLD versus bounded-blend fallback under clean and perturbed conditions on real UAV-UGV data.
AI.result: Confidence gating yields trade-offs among execution rate, executed-frame accuracy, issued-command accuracy, and smoothness; bounded-blend reduces stale-command risk and improves command-level behavior under gating; baseline suffers from stale commands with sparse execution.
AI.conclusion: Reliability requires both perception accuracy and decision-aware command issuance during low-confidence; the proposed gating approach enhances autonomous robustness in perception-driven control.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for AI-Driven Crash Simulation Surrogates: A Comparative Study of Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensemble on Open-Source Bumper Beam Benchmark
summary: Machine learning surrogate models are increasingly being explored in engineering product development to augment simulation-driven design, offering near-instantaneous predictions that complement computationally expensive high-fidelity analyses. However, a critical gap limits their adoption in safety-critical workflows: a point prediction without an accompanying uncertainty estimate cannot tell an engineer when the model should not be trusted. This work presents a systematic, head-to-head comparison of two widely used uncertainty quantification approaches -- Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles -- applied to an open-source surrogate pipeline built on NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. A key contribution is the use of concrete dropout, a built-in PhysicsNeMo capability that eliminates the dropout rate as a manual hyperparameter by learning it end-to-end during training, directly addressing the most common criticism of Monte Carlo Dropout-based uncertainty quantification. Automotive crash simulation is used as the application domain, with a steel bumper beam impact problem serving as the benchmark. Both methods are evaluated on identical held-out simulations and compared on point accuracy, uncertainty band calibration, and computational cost. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration that challenges the common assumption that deep ensembles are the default gold standard for surrogate uncertainty quantification. The findings demonstrate that well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates are achievable within a fully open-source engineering workflow at a fraction of the computational cost of ensemble approaches.

AI.tldr: Comparative study of Monte Carlo Dropout (with concrete dropout) vs Deep Ensembles for uncertainty quantification in an open-source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo surrogate; highlights a calibration–accuracy trade-off and demonstrates calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification for ML surrogates in safety-critical engineering workflows is essential; current methods (MC Dropout, deep ensembles) have limitations in calibration, cost, and hyperparameter tuning.
AI.method: Head-to-head benchmark on automotive crash simulation (steel bumper beam impact) using an open-source PhysicsNeMo-based surrogate. Identical held-out simulations are used to compare point accuracy, calibration of uncertainty intervals, and computational cost. Concrete dropout is employed to learn dropout rates end-to-end, removing a common hyperparameter.
AI.result: There is a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration; deep ensembles do not consistently dominate MC-based methods. Well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates are achievable within an open-source workflow at substantially lower computational cost than ensembles.
AI.conclusion: Hyperparameter-free, calibrated UQ is feasible in open-source engineering pipelines and can outperform or match ensembles in calibration while reducing cost, challenging the default preference for deep ensembles as the gold standard in surrogate uncertainty quantification.

title: DeforM: Reasoning-Guided Physics-Aware Video Generation via Spatial-Temporal Masking
summary: Video generation models achieve high visual quality but often struggle to generate physics-aware videos. Unlike rigid-body motion, which can be described by explicit trajectories or formulas, complex deformation dynamics remain challenging to synthesize. We observe that a lack of physical reasoning for localizing dynamic areas allows irrelevant regions to dilute the model's attention, leading to generation failure. In this paper, we propose DeforM, a reasoning-guided image-to-video generation framework that directs the model's focus toward physics-critical regions. To reason about and localize these critical regions, we introduce a VLM-guided physical reasoning module, DeforM-Reason, to identify target objects and generate spatial-temporal masks. For physical guidance, we develop two alternative strategies: DeforM-Free for training-free mechanism analysis and DeforM-Injection as a powerful training-based generator. Experimental results demonstrate that DeforM improves the realism of generated deformation scenarios, outperforming baseline models in both visual quality and physical consistency.

AI.tldr: DeforM uses a VLM-guided reasoning module to locate physics-critical regions and produce spatial-temporal masks, guiding image-to-video generation. It offers two modes: DeforM-Free (training-free analysis) and DeforM-Injection (training-based generator), achieving improved realism and physical consistency over baselines.
AI.motivation: Current video generation often lacks physics-aware localization of dynamic regions; without physics reasoning, attention is diluted in irrelevant areas, leading to deformation failures.
AI.method: Introduce DeforM-Reason, a VLM-guided physical reasoning module that identifies target objects and generates spatial-temporal masks highlighting physics-critical regions. Two strategies: DeforM-Free for training-free analysis and DeforM-Injection as a training-based generator that injects these masks into the generation process to steer deformation dynamics.
AI.result: Experimental results show improved realism in deformation scenarios and superior visual quality and physical consistency compared to baseline models.
AI.conclusion: DeforM provides a flexible, reasoning-guided framework for physics-aware video generation, with training-free and training-based options, enhancing the synthesis of deformation dynamics.

title: FindStatBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Combinatorial Code Synthesis
summary: We introduce FindStatBench, an execution benchmark for evaluating large language models on combinatorial code synthesis. Built from FindStat, it contains 2,329 tasks across 24 collections and 5.52M hidden instances, covering statistic synthesis, which maps objects to integers, and map synthesis, which maps objects to objects. Each task gives a mathematical description and at most five public input-output examples; a model must emit one Python solve function with no retrieval, tool use, execution feedback, voting, or reranking. Submissions are scored by exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects. We evaluate eleven systems: four closed-source production models and seven open-weight models served through one inference provider. FindStatBench reveals three main patterns. First, the strongest open- and closed-source systems converge within 1 pp instance accuracy, and both an oracle over all systems and five-way sampling from one mid-tier model yield only limited task-accuracy gains. Second, examples can hurt: several classical bijections are solved perfectly with zero examples but fail under five-example prompts. Third, some failures reflect output-budget mechanics, as reasoning can exhaust the visible response before code is emitted. Overall, statistic synthesis is much easier than map synthesis, some collections remain near-zero, long prompts cause a sharp accuracy cliff, and exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.

AI.tldr: FindStatBench is a large benchmark for evaluating LLMs on combinatorial code synthesis, with 2,329 tasks across 24 collections and 5.52M hidden instances, requiring a single Python solve() function and exact sandboxed execution. It uncovers three patterns: strong convergence between top open- and closed-source models, examples can hurt performance, and output-budget mechanics limit reasoning-driven code emission; statistic synthesis is easier than map synthesis, while exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.
AI.motivation: Assess and diagnose LLM capabilities in mathematical code generation for combinatorial tasks, without tool use or external retrieval, and reveal systematic failure modes in reasoning and symbolic rule induction.
AI.method: Construct FindStatBench from FindStat, comprising 2,329 tasks across 24 collections with up to 5 public I/O examples and 5.52M hidden instances. Each task yields a mathematical description and requires one Python solve() function. Submissions are judged by exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects. No retrieval, tool use, execution feedback, voting, or reranking is allowed. Eleven systems are evaluated (four closed-source, seven open-weight) via a single inference provider.
AI.result: Three main patterns emerge: (1) strongest open- and closed-source systems converge within about 1 percentage point of instance accuracy; an oracle over all systems or five-way sampling from a mid-tier model yields only limited gains. (2) Examples can hurt: many classical bijections are solvable with zero examples but fail with five examples. (3) Output-budget mechanics cause failures: reasoning may exhaust the visible response before code is emitted. Additionally, statistic synthesis is substantially easier than map synthesis; some collections remain near-zero; long prompts correlate with sharp accuracy drops; exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.
AI.conclusion: FindStatBench exposes clear limits in LLMs' ability to perform combinatorial code synthesis, particularly for map synthesis, highlights the impact of prompt length and output budgets, and underscores the brittleness of symbolic rule induction, suggesting careful prompt and evaluation design for future work.

title: Correct-by-Construction Behavior Tree Synthesis from Signal Temporal Logic Specifications with Application to Robotic Missions
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Behavior Trees (BTs) are widely adopted for complex task execution in robotics, providing modular, reactive control but lacking formal guarantees. However, existing correct-by-construction synthesis from Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) cannot express quantitative timing constraints. This letter synthesizes correct-by-construction BTs from Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. The workspace is modeled as a timed transition system and abstracted into a zone graph, and an augmented state space tracking both logical progress and timing constraints is introduced. A hierarchical fixed-point algorithm computes winning sets for an STL fragment encompassing safety, reachability, response, recurrence, and persistence, yielding BT subtrees with a runtime constraint function. Correctness guarantees are proven and complexity bounds are derived. Simulations demonstrate specification satisfaction with strictly positive robustness, and a physical quadrotor experiment with six STL specifications validates practical deployability.

AI.tldr: Extends correct-by-construction BT synthesis to timed specifications by synthesizing BTs from STL using a zone-graph abstraction and a hierarchical fixed-point computation to generate subtrees with timing constraints; validated by simulations and a quadrotor experiment.
AI.motivation: BTs provide modular, reactive control but lack formal guarantees for timing; STL offers quantitative timing constraints, enabling formally guaranteed timed task execution in robotics.
AI.method: Model workspace as a timed transition system, abstract to a zone graph, and augment state space with both logical progress and timing constraints. Use a hierarchical fixed-point algorithm to compute winning sets for an STL fragment (safety, reachability, response, recurrence, persistence) and extract BT subtrees with a runtime constraint function. Prove correctness and derive complexity bounds.
AI.result: Formal correctness guarantees with positive robustness; complexity bounds established. Simulations show specification satisfaction with strictly positive robustness, and a six-specification quadrotor experiment validates practical deployability.
AI.conclusion: STL-based correct-by-construction BT synthesis is feasible and useful for providing formal timed task guarantees in robotics, with demonstrated theory and practical validation; future work could expand STL coverage, scalability, and online applicability.

title: On the Limits of Support-Preserving Alignment and Bounded Filtering
summary: We study whether alignment schemes that reshape a base model's output distribution, combined with bounded safety filters, can drive the probability of harmful behavior to zero in modern large language models. Recent research suggests that harmful behaviors can persist under preference-based alignment and that external filtering can be computationally hard in the worst case, but it remains unclear whether practical alignment pipelines that largely preserve internal representations can eliminate harmful behavior entirely rather than merely suppressing its most visible forms. We formalize this setting using support-preserving alignment operators together with bounded filtering algorithms under black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access, and analyze their ability to approximate an ideal eliminator that removes all harmful mass. Building on this framework, we provide computational and information-theoretic arguments indicating that, under these constraints, bounded filtering may fail to eliminate all harmful outputs supported by the base model's distribution. To evaluate these limits empirically, we analyze a range of state-of-the-art open-weight and hosted LLMs accessed via OpenRouter under bounded black-box, white-box, and statistical-query filters on adversarial prompts drawn from curated cybersecurity scenarios and PKU-SafeRLHF. Across models, filter classes, and query budgets, the estimated harmful-output rate decreases with additional filtering compute but consistently plateaus above zero, suggesting a persistent empirical harm floor.

AI.tldr: Under practical constraints of support-preserving alignment and bounded safety filters, a theoretical and empirical harm floor persists: complete elimination of harmful outputs is unlikely, as filtering cannot remove all harm mass.
AI.motivation: Assess whether practical alignment pipelines that largely preserve internal representations can entirely suppress harmful behavior, or whether an irreducible harm floor exists.
AI.method: Formalize alignment as support-preserving operators with bounded filters under black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access; provide computational and information-theoretic arguments; empirically evaluate open-weight and hosted LLMs via OpenRouter on adversarial cybersecurity prompts and PKU-SafeRLHF across various filters and budgets.
AI.result: Theory suggests bounded filtering may fail to eliminate all harmful outputs; empirically, harmful-output rates decrease with more filtering compute but plateau above zero across models, filters, and budgets.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating all harmful mass with the proposed bounded-filter approach is unlikely; persistent empirical harm requires alternative or more robust alignment strategies.

title: MissingBench-Verified: Probing Vision-Language Models' Inability to Detect Missing Object Parts
comment: Submitted to the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Explainable Computer Vision (eXCV). 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are well known for hallucinating non-existent objects in images. Objects with missing parts present a unique challenge for VLMs, stemming from both real-world knowledge bias and the scarcity of such images in training data. We present MissingBench-Verified, a benchmark designed to evaluate a specific and practically relevant scenario: when vision-language models fail to recognize that an essential component of an object has been removed. Across ten leading models, we observe consistent and significant failure rates that persist even when external tool evidence explicitly contradicts the model's visual perception. We further ask whether granting models access to image processing tools (e.g., cropping, contrast adjustment) enables autonomous inspection to resolve these failures. We find that existing mitigation strategies, including tool-assisted verification, autonomous visual reasoning, longer reasoning durations, and fine-tuning on an easier dataset, provide negligible improvement, indicating that this failure mode cannot be addressed through current prompting or post-hoc correction techniques. Our findings highlight a fundamental limitation of current VLM for inspection and monitoring tasks and underscore the need for architectural or training-level interventions that enable models to override internal expectations when confronted with contradictory evidence.

AI.tldr: VLMs fail to detect missing essential object components; across ten models, failures persist even when external evidence contradicts perception; standard mitigation (tool use, longer reasoning, fine-tuning) yields little improvement; calls for architectural/training-level fixes.
AI.motivation: Evaluate a practically relevant yet under-studied failure: when removing a key part alters object identity, can VLMs recognize the change and override prior knowledge?
AI.method: Introduce MissingBench-Verified benchmark; evaluate ten leading VLMs on cases where an object's essential component is removed; test remediation strategies including tool-assisted verification, autonomous visual reasoning, longer reasoning, and fine-tuning on easier data.
AI.result: Observed consistent and significant failure rates across models; external evidence does not reconcile model outputs; mitigation strategies provide negligible gains.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs have a fundamental limitation for inspection/monitoring tasks; prompting and post-hoc corrections are insufficient; solutions require architectural or training-level interventions to override internal expectations when confronted with contradictory evidence.

title: When JSON Is Not Enough: Semantic Reliability of Schema-Constrained LLM Ordering Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used as transaction compilers: a user states an intent in natural language, and the model emits a structured object that an API can execute. JSON Schema and provider-level structured-output modes are useful because they remove a large class of parse failures, but they do not by themselves decide whether the object is a safe, faithful transaction. We introduce OrderBench, a deterministic benchmark for restaurant ordering agents that separates syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, exact item semantics, constraint preservation, and unsafe acceptances. Across 2,400 Nebius Token Factory calls to four open models in prompt-only and JSON-schema modes, we find that schema-valid output can still have large semantic error rates. In the strongest model, both modes achieve 100% schema validity, yet semantic success remains near 80%; in weaker models, schema-valid unsafe acceptances occur in double digits. The result is a concrete engineering warning: structured output is a necessary interface layer, not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution.

AI.tldr: Structured-output interfaces (JSON Schema) reduce parsing failures but do not ensure safe, faithful transactions in LLM-driven order systems; OrderBench shows semantic errors persist even with schema validity.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether schema-validated, structured outputs suffice for safe, faithful transactions in LLM-based agents; isolate syntactic, semantic, and safety errors.
AI.method: Benchmark using OrderBench with 2,400 calls across four open models, comparing prompt-only vs. JSON-schema modes, and evaluating syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, item semantics, constraint preservation, and unsafe acceptances.
AI.result: Schema-valid outputs can still be semantically incorrect. In the strongest model, both modes reach 100% schema validity but ~80% semantic success; weaker models show schema-valid unsafe acceptances in double digits.
AI.conclusion: Structured output is necessary but not sufficient; domain verification and fail-closed execution are essential to ensure safe, faithful transactions.

title: Motion Primitive Discovery in a Humanoid Robot via Self-Organising Maps for Phase Recognition
summary: Understanding the computational basis of action recognition is a central challenge in social cognition as well as in human-robot interaction. Inspired by the Mirror Neuron System (MNS), we propose a two-level architecture for motor primitive discovery and online phase recognition applied to the NICO humanoid robot. At the first level, two Self-Organising Maps (SOMs) learn topographic representations of arm kinematics (A-SOM) and hand kinematics (H-SOM) from simulated trials covering seven motor actions. The maps are trained on non-redundant features identified through hierarchical correlation analysis of motion trajectories. The results show that the two SOMs encode complementary aspects of motor behaviour. At the second level, an Echo State Network (ESN) evaluates whether temporal trajectories of SOM activations, represented by consecutive best-matching units, are sufficient for online recognition of the currently executed movement phase. The results show that SOM-based trajectories preserve the dominant phase-discriminative structure of the movement, while contextual information provides only a secondary refinement. Our contribution is the integration of established SOM and ESN methods within an MNS-inspired architecture for motor primitive representation and online phase recognition. The results are compatible with the computational hypothesis that self-organised motor representations, when temporally integrated, can support accurate online recognition of ongoing movement phases.

AI.tldr: Two-level, MNS-inspired architecture using self-organising maps to learn arm and hand kinematics (A-SOM and H-SOM) from simulated trials, followed by an Echo State Network to recognize online movement phases from trajectories of best-matching units. The SOMs capture complementary motor representations, and temporal integration via ESN supports online phase recognition with context providing only minor refinement.
AI.motivation: Address the computational basis of action recognition in social cognition and human-robot interaction by emulating mirror-neuron system concepts to discover motor primitives and enable online phase recognition.
AI.method: Train two SOMs (A-SOM for arm, H-SOM for hand) on non-redundant features selected through hierarchical correlation analysis of motion trajectories. Then feed the sequence of active BMUs into an Echo State Network to decide online movement phase. Evaluate whether SOM trajectories preserve phase-discriminative structure and whether contextual information improves recognition.
AI.result: SOMs encode complementary aspects of motor behavior. SOM-based trajectories retain the dominant phase-discriminative structure; contextual information provides only secondary refinement. The ESN can perform online recognition based on SOM activation trajectories, supporting the hypothesis that temporally integrated self-organised motor representations enable online recognition of ongoing actions.
AI.conclusion: Integrates SOM and ESN within an MNS-inspired framework to represent motor primitives and enable online phase recognition; supports the computational hypothesis that temporally integrated self-organised motor representations underpin accurate online action recognition.

title: A Better Start for Language Models: Domain-Conditional Position Offsets
summary: Autoregressive language models are least accurate at the beginning of a sequence, where little context forces reliance on a generic pretraining prior. We show that this cold-start penalty is domain dependent and reduce it with a domain-conditional position offset: a single learned vector added to the embedding activation at the first sequence positions while all model weights remain frozen. The offset trains in minutes on roughly one hundred documents, switches between domains without added sequence state, and has no measurable latency overhead. Across eight Mamba, GPT-NeoX, and Llama models spanning 410M to 8B parameters, it reduces held-out in-domain perplexity by up to 27%; the effect persists at 70B, and one position captures most of the benefit. A matched, converged direct logit-bias correction reaches at most only 7.9% and leaves later-token loss unchanged, showing that the offset propagates through model state rather than merely recalibrating the output prior. A tuned LoRA reaches lower perplexity but uses two to three orders of magnitude more parameters and an active low-rank weight path, while soft prompts add sequence positions. With wrong-domain controls, offsets improve retrieval reranking and domain classification when decisions depend on early in-domain tokens, For the few-shot reasoning whose signal occurs later, the results maintains unchanged. Position-aware prefill application also help generation tasks, whereas naive application at every cached decoding step causes repetition. The offset is therefore not the strongest adapter, but a lightweight, hot switchable tool for short in-domain scoring and calibration.

AI.tldr: A single domain-conditional position offset vector added to the first token embeddings significantly mitigates the cold-start penalty in autoregressive LMs across multiple model families, with minimal changes to latency and no weight updates.
AI.motivation: To address the domain-dependent cold-start penalty in autoregressive language models, enabling faster, parameter-efficient domain adaptation without retraining the full model.
AI.method: Introduce a learned vector added to embeddings at initial sequence positions, with all model weights frozen; train quickly on ~100 documents; evaluate across 8 models (410M–8B) and later up to 70B, comparing against logit-bias, LoRA, and soft prompts; test in-domain and cross-domain tasks including retrieval and classification; assess generation and few-shot reasoning.
AI.result: The offset reduces in-domain perplexity by up to 27% and remains effective at larger scales; most gains come from a single position; a direct logit-bias correction yields at most 7.9% improvement and affects only early tokens, implying state propagation; LoRA can achieve larger reductions but with higher parameter cost; soft prompts add sequence positions; wrong-domain application improves early-token tasks like retrieval/classification; naive per-step use can cause repetition; overall, the offset is a lightweight, hot-switchable adapter rather than a top-performing full adapter.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight domain-aware, position-specific offset is a practical tool for short in-domain scoring/calibration, offering quick adaptation with negligible latency and without updating model weights; not the strongest adapter but valuable for targeted early-token enhancements and domain-sensitive tasks.

title: Cross-Dataset Generalization in Breast MRI Tumor Classification via Class-Wise Dataset Mixing
summary: Breast MRI is highly sensitive for detecting breast tumors, but exams contain many slices and require substantial reading time. Deep learning models often perform well on internal splits but can fail across institutions because of domain shift and dataset-origin bias. We study this failure mode for binary breast MRI tumor classification. EfficientNet-B3 and WaveViT-Small are trained using Duke Breast Cancer MRI and fastMRI, and evaluated only on the independent multi-center MAMA-MIA cohort. In a deliberately confounded setup, where label is perfectly correlated with dataset origin, external accuracy is near chance (0.5048--0.5265), despite very high recall. We then construct a mixed training set in which each class contains samples from both Duke and fastMRI, while preserving patient-level splitting, augmentation, and leakage controls. On MAMA-MIA, dataset mixing improves accuracy/F1 to 0.8463/0.8625 for WaveViT-Small and 0.8884/0.8994 for EfficientNet-B3. These results show that controlling dataset-origin bias is important for reliable breast MRI classification.

AI.tldr: Dataset-origin bias can severely degrade external accuracy in binary breast MRI tumor classification; training with mixed data from multiple sources improves cross-site performance on an independent multi-center cohort.
AI.motivation: Evaluate how domain shift and dataset-origin bias affect generalization in breast MRI classification and demonstrate the need to control origin bias for reliable cross-institution results.
AI.method: Train EfficientNet-B3 and WaveViT-Small on Duke Breast Cancer MRI and fastMRI datasets; evaluate on the independent MAMA-MIA cohort. In a deliberately confounded setup where label correlates with dataset origin, external accuracy hovers near chance (0.50–0.53) despite high recall. Then construct a mixed training set with samples from both datasets for each class, maintaining patient-level splitting, augmentation, and leakage controls. Evaluate on MAMA-MIA.
AI.result: In the confounded setup, external accuracy is near chance (0.5048–0.5265) with very high recall. With dataset mixing in training, accuracy/F1 on MAMA-MIA improves to 0.8463/0.8625 for WaveViT-Small and 0.8884/0.8994 for EfficientNet-B3.
AI.conclusion: Dataset-origin bias is a key pitfall for cross-site breast MRI classification; deliberate mixing of data from multiple sources can mitigate this bias and yield strong external performance across institutions.

title: ProbSPARQL: Querying Knowledge Graphs with Multi-dimensional, Uncertain Numeric Data
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Preprint. Supplementary material and reproducibility artifacts are available online
summary: The SFB 1574 Circular Factory is building a shared knowledge graph infrastructure for integrating data about returned products. A central challenge is that circular-factory data include numeric measurements that (i) originate from sensors or are derived from sensor-based measurements, (ii) are frequently multi-dimensional, and (iii) are inherently uncertain, while downstream triage, validation, reliability-modeling, and reassembly-planning modules require queryable uncertainty representations. Current RDF and SPARQL technologies lack native support for harmonized querying and analysis of such uncertain numeric measurement data. To address this gap, we present ProbSPARQL, an upward-compatible SPARQL extension developed as an early-stage query-layer pilot for this infrastructure. ProbSPARQL models uncertain numeric values as random variables whose distributions are encoded by probabilistic RDF literal datatypes, and supports distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins. We implement ProbSPARQL on Apache Jena ARQ and expose it through a Fuseki-compatible execution layer. We assess real-data applicability using project-derived measurement fragments covering GMM-encoded uncertainty and histogram-based empirical roughness distributions, and evaluate scalability separately on controlled ontology-conformant benchmarks with up to 5,000 angle-grinder instances and 1.5M triples. The results show feasible in-engine execution, filter-pushdown speedups over application-layer post-processing, and latency-accuracy trade-offs among divergence-join decision strategies.

AI.tldr: ProbSPARQL extends SPARQL with probabilistic literals and distribution-aware constructs to query uncertain numeric measurements in RDF, enabling in-engine processing and showing speedups and trade-offs on real and synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Circular-factory data involve uncertain, multi-dimensional numeric measurements from sensors. RDF/SPARQL lacks native support for harmonized querying of uncertainty, hindering triage, validation, reliability modeling, and reassembly planning.
AI.method: Introduce ProbSPARQL as an upward-compatible SPARQL extension. Model uncertain numeric values as random variables encoded via probabilistic RDF literal datatypes. Provide distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins. Implement on Apache Jena ARQ with a Fuseki-compatible execution layer. Validate with real-data fragments (GMM-encoded uncertainty and histogram-based roughness), and scalability tests on benchmarks up to 5,000 instances and 1.5M triples.
AI.result: Demonstrates feasible in-engine execution and filter-pushdown speedups over application-layer post-processing. Shows latency-accuracy trade-offs for different divergence-join strategies. Real-data and synthetic benchmarks indicate practical applicability and scalable performance within the tested scope.
AI.conclusion: ProbSPARQL is a viable early-stage query-layer solution for harmonizing and querying uncertain numeric data in RDF graphs, bridging a gap in current RDF/SPARQL capabilities. It achieves in-engine processing and measurable performance benefits, while highlighting trade-offs and areas for future standardization and optimization.

title: Koopman DCM: Unstable Eigenfunctions as Data-driven Representations for Legged Balancing
summary: In legged locomotion, divergent components of motion (DCMs) have emerged as characteristic states for balance control. They isolate the unstable mode of the dynamics but, in existing formulations, apply only to reduced models such as the linear inverted pendulum. In this study, we show how DCMs can be more generally formulated as Koopman eigenfunctions. Whereas Koopman analysis typically targets eigenvalues near zero, which capture conserved or slowly varying quantities, our investigation leads us to deliberately search for unstable eigenpairs with large eigenvalues. The resulting Koopman DCMs are data-driven observables trained using only real-robot data. On a real biped, DCMs learned from one hour of robot data improve tracking of reference walking patterns. We further show how learned DCMs provide state-based viability constraints when combined with model predictive control.

AI.tldr: A Koopman-eigenfunction formulation of divergent components of motion (DCMs) for legged locomotion, including unstable eigenpairs, learned from real-robot data; improves walking tracking and yields state-based viability constraints for MPC.
AI.motivation: Generalize DCMs beyond reduced models (e.g., linear inverted pendulum) by using Koopman theory to capture unstable dynamics, learned directly from real-robot data to enhance balance control.
AI.method: Compute Koopman eigenfunctions corresponding to unstable, high-magnitude eigenvalues; train data-driven DCM observables from about one hour of real-biped data; integrate these observables as viability constraints within model predictive control (MPC).
AI.result: DCMs learned from ~1 hour of real-robot data improve tracking of reference walking patterns on a real biped; they provide state-based viability constraints when combined with MPC.
AI.conclusion: Koopman-based DCMs offer a general, data-driven framework for balance control in legged robots, extending beyond reduced models and enabling improved tracking and constraint-based control.

title: TD-DPO: Difference-Aware Preference Optimization for Mitigating Sycophancy in Clinical Autism Intervention Dialogue
summary: The sycophancy of large language models can increase the safety risk in intervention dialogue for autistic children. Supervised fine-tuning can somewhat reduce sycophancy, but relying solely on positive examples is often insufficient to identify and correct failure patterns. We observe that sycophancy behaviors can often be localized to a limited span within the model response. In this regime, sequence-level preference optimization can over-update preference-irrelevant tokens and degrade intervention ability. To address this, we propose the \textbf{M}inimal \textbf{E}dit \textbf{D}ata \textbf{A}ugmentation (MEDA) strategy to construct controlled, stable, minimal edit preference pairs and \textbf{T}oken-level \textbf{D}ifference \textbf{D}irect \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization (TD-DPO), which upweights difference tokens between chosen and rejected responses while downweighting shared tokens to suppress background drift. Extensive experiments across multiple backbones and evaluators show that TD-DPO achieves a better trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and intervention ability retention in our offline settings, highlighting its potential as a practical alignment approach for autism intervention.

AI.tldr: Proposes MEDA data augmentation and TD-DPO token-level preference optimization to reduce sycophancy in LLMs for autism intervention without eroding intervention ability; shows offline improvements across backbones and evaluators.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy in LLMs can pose safety risks in intervention dialogue for autistic children. Supervised fine-tuning insufficient; sycophancy often localized to small spans and sequence-level methods can over-update non-relevant tokens, degrading performance.
AI.method: MEDA constructs controlled, stable, minimal edit preference pairs; TD-DPO upweights tokens that differ between chosen and rejected responses and downweights shared tokens to suppress background drift. Evaluated offline across multiple backbones and evaluators.
AI.result: TD-DPO achieves a better balance between reducing sycophancy and retaining intervention ability in offline settings across diverse backbones and evaluators.
AI.conclusion: TD-DPO with MEDA provides a practical alignment approach for autism intervention, mitigating sycophancy while preserving intervention capability; potential applicability to other safety-critical alignment tasks.

title: Dual-Edged Homogeneous-Modality Similarity: Towards Visible-Infrared Modality-Incomplete Person Re-Identification with Modality Adaptive Matching
summary: Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification (VI-ReID) operates under a closed-world assumption, where queries and galleries are from heterogeneous modalities. However, in open-world scenarios, both sets are likely to contain homogeneous and heterogeneous modality images. A query may consist of visible-only, infrared-only, or mixed-modality images, while galleries present multi-modal images over long-term collection. Under these conditions, VI-ReID methods, built on a heterogeneous-modality retrieval paradigm, suffer from three trustworthiness challenges: matching conflicts due to high homogeneous-modality similarity, interference from modality uncertainty, and robustness degradation induced by unknown modality combinations. They fail to meet the requirements of trustworthy visual recognition in reliability, consistency, and dynamic adaptability. To address these challenges, we formalize the Visible-Infrared Modality-Incomplete Re-Identification (VIMI-ReID) task. We reorganize existing datasets to construct the SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI benchmarks. The unpredictable modality combinations and inherent similarity of homogeneous-modality samples in VIMI-ReID cause a significant performance drop in existing VI-ReID methods. We propose the Modality Adaptive Matching Transformer (MAMT). It employs a Divergence Transformer Module (DTM) and a Shared Transformer Module (STM) to extract modality-specific and modality-shared features, respectively. Guided by a divergence loss, the DTM enriches modality-specific features with modality-style information to enhance discriminability within the same modality. A Modality Adaptive Matching Module (MAM) dynamically fuses features according to the query-gallery modality relationship, enabling stable matching under arbitrary and uncertain modality conditions. Extensive experiments on the VIMI benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and adaptability of MAMT.

AI.tldr: Defines VIMI-ReID for open-world cross-modality person re-identification, introduces SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI benchmarks, and proposes Modality Adaptive Matching Transformer (MAMT) with Divergence Transformer Module (DTM) and Shared Transformer Module (STM) for robust, modality-aware matching under uncertain modality conditions.
AI.motivation: In open-world VI-ReID, queries and galleries can contain both homogeneous and heterogeneous modalities. Existing heterogeneous-modality retrieval methods suffer from high within-modality similarity, modality uncertainty, and unknown modality combinations, leading to unreliable, inconsistent, and non-adaptive recognition.
AI.method: Formalize the VIMI-ReID task; construct SYSU-VIMI and RegDB-VIMI benchmarks; propose MAMT consisting of a Divergence Transformer Module (DTM) to enrich modality-specific features with modality-style information guided by a divergence loss, and a Shared Transformer Module (STM) to extract modality-shared features. A Modality Adaptive Matching Module (MAM) dynamically fuses features based on the query-gallery modality relationship to enable stable matching across arbitrary modality conditions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the VIMI benchmarks demonstrate that MAMT achieves effective and adaptable matching under diverse modality conditions, improving robustness and reliability in open-world VI-ReID.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a new task and benchmarks for modality-incomplete VI-ReID and presents a flexible transformer-based framework (MAMT) that effectively handles modality diversity and uncertainty, advancing trustworthy visual recognition in open-world settings.

title: Position: AI/ML Deepfake Research is Misaligned with AI-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AIG-NCII)
comment: Position paper accepted to ICML 2026, Spotlight
summary: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is not adequately addressed in AI/ML literature regarding AI-generated media, commonly referred to as "deepfakes". While research on deepfakes currently focuses on its epistemic harms -- or harms relating to truth and authenticity -- this is misaligned with the dominant reality of generative AI abuse involving sexualized imagery. We conduct a landscape analysis of highly-cited works to demonstrate that technical interventions addressing deepfakes almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII, limiting the research ecosystem to authenticity detection tools. In this position paper, we argue that existing interventions address viewer-centric epistemic harms, such as fraud or scams, but ignore subject-centric dignity harms, such as AIG-NCII. We illustrate that knowing an image is synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may, in some cases, even exacerbate them. We conclude by offering recommendations to realign the field, including updating threat models to consider subject-centric harms and addressing AIG-NCII in AI safety research. Finally, we caution that researchers should only engage in this high-risk domain if they implement safety guardrails for both subjects and researchers and establish partnerships with domain experts in sexual violence prevention.

AI.tldr: AIG-NCII is under-addressed in AI/ML deepfake research, which focuses on authenticity detection and viewer-centric harms; this misalignment neglects subject-centric harms and safety, calling for updated threat models and safety guardrails with domain partnerships.
AI.motivation: Deepfake research prioritizes epistemic harms (truth/authenticity) but real-world abuse centers on sexualized, non-consensual imagery that harms subjects; current interventions fail to address subject dignity and safety.
AI.method: Landscape analysis of highly-cited deepfake works to identify focus areas and gaps; critical position paper advocating realignment of research priorities and inclusion of AIG-NCII in safety research.
AI.result: Findings show that technical interventions largely ignore AIG-NCII; notifying users that an image is synthetic does not mitigate victim harms and may worsen them; a need to expand threat models to include subject-centric harms and to integrate safety-focused governance.
AI.conclusion: Call for realignment of AI safety and research to cover subject-centric harms like AIG-NCII, update threat models, engage domain experts in prevention of sexual violence, and implement safety guardrails for researchers and subjects.

title: Beyond Transformers: Linear Attention Policy for Open-Vocabulary Object Goal Navigation
summary: Open-Vocabulary Object Goal Navigation (OVON) requires agents to operate under partial observability, making effective internal state updates critical for navigation performance. This update is implemented by the policy network, where recent approaches adopt Transformer-based backbones with self-attention over a context window to integrate temporal information. However, our controlled experiments show that performance does not scale with context length under Transformer-based policies, questioning the suitability of self-attention for state integration in navigation. To this end, we propose Linear Attention-based Navigation (LANav), which adopts linear attention (LA) as the policy backbone to maintain a structured state update rather than self-attention over the context window. Across multiple LA variants evaluated under identical settings, LANav consistently outperforms Transformer-based baselines. Performance improves as state update mechanisms become more structured and regulated, highlighting the importance of state update design. To improve state update effectiveness, we introduce Weighted State-Expansion Linear Attention (WSLA), which expands each attention head's state into multiple sub-states and uses learnable weighted readout to aggregate expanded sub-states. Equipped with WSLA, LANav achieves 36.4% average success rate (SR) on HM3D-OVON, outperforming Transformer-based counterparts by 6.3 percentage points in macro-averaged SR, while maintaining computational efficiency. Distance-stratified results show larger gains in long-distance episodes, while HSSD transfer and fine-tuning demonstrate robustness across scene distributions. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 further achieves an 82% success rate over 50 trials, supporting the practical feasibility and sim-to-real transfer of LANav.

AI.tldr: LANav with WSLA (linear attention-based policy) yields structured state updates for OVON, outperforming Transformer baselines and enabling real-world transfer.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary object-goal navigation under partial observability relies on effective temporal state integration. Self-attention over a context window may not scale for state updates, prompting exploration of structured, efficient alternatives.
AI.method: Introduce Linear Attention-based Navigation (LANav) as the policy backbone and Weighted State-Expansion Linear Attention (WSLA) to enrich and aggregate state sub-states. Evaluate multiple LA variants under identical settings and compare to Transformer baselines on HM3D-OVON; assess long-distance performance, HSSD transfer, fine-tuning, and sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go2.
AI.result: LANav outperforms Transformer-based baselines across variants. WSLA yields 36.4% averageSR on HM3D-OVON, a 6.3-point macro SR improvement. Gains are larger in long-distance episodes; robustness across scene distributions via HSSD transfer and fine-tuning. Real-world deployment on Unitree Go2 achieves 82% success over 50 trials, indicating practical feasibility and sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: State update design is crucial for OVON. Linear attention with structured state updates (via WSLA) provides effective navigation, achieving higher accuracy and real-world transfer while maintaining computational efficiency compared to self-attention-based transformers.

title: The Information Shadow: Measuring Structural Limits on What Language Models Can Learn
summary: Some limits on what language models know are not gaps in data coverage but structural properties of learning from text. We introduce the information shadow: the region of phenomena that a text-trained learner cannot acquire regardless of scale, comprising (I) structures language cannot express, (II) functions that are statistically non-identifiable from the training distribution, and (III) functions that are representable but unreachable by gradient-based training. We give each type a probe that is decisive because the premise of the shadow is, in that setting, provable. For Type I, Language Compression Residuals compare a text learner, which sees only a lossy text-like encoding of the signal, against a full-signal learner, which sees the underlying signal directly. The text learner sits at a computable expressibility ceiling while the full-signal learner pulls away by a gap that stays flat across 300x more data, so the deficit is a property of the channel, not of training. For Type II, the Counterfactual Distinction Test trains models on data exactly consistent with two incompatible rules. Across a provable string task and a language-like agreement task, behavior on counterfactuals is set by the model's inductive bias, while 5% disambiguating data steers the learned rule bidirectionally to either target (r = +/-1.0, p < 1e-10). For Type III, Basin Escape Mapping exhibits a function that is representable at 100% (by hand construction) yet reached 0% of the time by standard training and instantly from a nearby initialization, with width scaling providing no help (p = 1.6 x 10^-14). Each effect is isolated by a control that rules out a capacity or modality artifact. We release the probe suite and discuss implications for benchmark design, capability auditing, and shadow-aware uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Introduces the notion of the "information shadow": fundamental limits on what text-trained learners can acquire, due to three distinct types of unreachable phenomena. Proposes decisive probes for each type—Language Compression Residuals for expressibility limits, Counterfactual Distinction Test for identifiability limits, and Basin Escape Mapping for optimization/induction limits—and demonstrates results on provable string tasks and language-like tasks. The work culminates in releasing a probe suite with implications for benchmark design, capability auditing, and shadow-aware uncertainty.
AI.motivation: To understand why merely scaling data may not enable language models to learn certain phenomena; formalize the inherent limits of learning from text and provide provable probes to isolate the resulting "information shadows".
AI.method: Three probes targeting separate origins of the shadow: Type I Language Compression Residuals comparing a text-only learner to a full-signal learner to expose an expressibility ceiling; Type II Counterfactual Distinction Test training on data consistent with two incompatible rules and evaluating counterfactual behavior to reveal inductive bias with small disambiguating data; Type III Basin Escape Mapping showing a function that is constructible by hand but rarely reached by standard gradient-based training, unaffected by width scaling; experiments include provable string tasks and language-like agreement tasks with controls to rule out capacity/modality artifacts; release of a public probe suite.
AI.result: Identification of a multi-faceted information shadow, with Type I revealing a fixed expressibility gap due to the channel; Type II showing inductive-bias-governed counterfactual behavior, tunable with minimal disambiguating data; Type III demonstrating a representable function that standard training almost never reaches, with no help from seemingly broader architectures; all effects controlled to exclude trivial capacity artifacts; the authors release the probes for broader benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: The concept of the information shadow has practical implications for benchmark design, capability auditing, and uncertainty explanation in language models, advocating shadow-aware evaluation and tooling to distinguish data-coverage limits from fundamental learning constraints.

title: Attributes Should Come from Images, Not Class Names: Distribution-Conditioned Attribute Selection for Vision-Language Models
summary: A popular route to interpretable zero-shot classification asks a large language model (LLM) to describe each class name and prompts CLIP with the resulting descriptors. We show that these descriptors carry little visual evidence of their own: removing the class name from the prompt collapses ImageNet accuracy from 59.5% to 15.5%. The diagnosis is that the descriptors are conditioned on the label rather than on the images, so they describe the concept in general and mislead exactly when the data shifts; an LLM insists that strawberries are red, but every strawberry in ImageNet-Sketch is a colorless line drawing.
