We therefore select attributes from the target image collection instead: we score a large attribute pool against the images in CLIP's joint embedding space and keep the top-scoring attributes per class. Selected this way, class-name-free attribute prompts reach 23.8% on ImageNet (against 15.5% for LLM descriptors), the gain holds on four shifted ImageNet variants, and reselecting from the LLM's own pool isolates the selection mechanism as the cause. With one image per class, the selected attributes outperform the prompt-tuning method CoOp by 3 points while fitting in under a minute instead of 14 hours, with no learned soft prompt to obscure the decision. Because the attribute set is chosen by the data, it doubles as a readable summary of a dataset, which we use to describe distribution shift in words.

AI.tldr: Using data-selected attributes for CLIP prompts yields better zero-shot classification than LLM-descriptors of class names; attributes scored against images in CLIP space improve accuracy, are robust to distribution shift, and enable fast, interpretable prompts without learned prompts.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated descriptors conditioned on class names often reflect general concepts and can mislead when data shifts occur, leading to poor alignment with visual evidence. Grounding prompts in image-derived attributes promises better visual relevance and interpretability.
AI.method: Compare two prompt strategies for CLIP-based zero-shot classification: (1) LLM-generated descriptors for class names (with and without the class label in prompts); (2) selecting attributes from a large pool by scoring against images in CLIP's joint embedding space and keeping the top-scoring attributes per class. Evaluate on ImageNet and four shifted variants; also compare to CoOp with one image per class and measure speed and interpretability by avoiding learned prompts.
AI.result: LLM descriptors without the class name collapse accuracy from 59.5% to 15.5% on ImageNet, indicating that they encode label-conditioned general concepts rather than image-specific evidence. Data-grounded attributes achieve 23.8% accuracy on ImageNet (vs 15.5% for LLM descriptors). This gain persists across four shifted ImageNet variants. Retrieving the selection mechanism by reusing LLM pools isolates the cause. With one image per class, the attribute-based prompts outperform CoOp by about 3 points and complete in under a minute (no learned soft prompts). The attribute set also serves as a readable, data-driven summary of the dataset, useful for describing distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Data-grounded attribute prompts provide superior, more robust, and interpretable zero-shot CLIP performance compared to LLM-based class-name descriptors. The approach avoids the need for expensive prompt learning, is data-distillation friendly, and yields an interpretable dataset summary that aids understanding distribution shifts.

title: MUX: Continuous Reasoning via Multiplexed Tokens
summary: Language models solve complex problems by articulating intermediate reasoning steps in natural language. While effective, this process is computationally bottlenecked: each reasoning step conveys only a single subword, and many are spent expressing a thought instead of carrying out computation. We propose MUX, a simple method for high-bandwidth and compact reasoning based on distillation of discrete reasoning into continuous multiplexed tokens in a latent space. Here, each latent token is trained to represent a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete reasoning subwords, where this superposition is lossless by construction and the span can be fully recovered (demultiplexing). We prove that simple position-dependent weightings, such as suitable geometric decay, support lossless multiplexing, which in turn prevents shortcut behaviors caused by latent collapse. We further show that multiplexed reasoning can perform parallel exploration in problems that require search. Across 32 evaluation settings spanning four language models, MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses further show that the learned latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning. Our results suggest that lossless superposition as local learning targets constitutes a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning.

AI.tldr: MUX encodes discrete reasoning steps into continuous latent tokens via lossless multiplexing; achieves higher-bandwidth reasoning and better performance than latent baselines across 32 settings and 4 LMs, with interpretable latent tokens.
AI.motivation: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning is slow and bottlenecked by token-by-token natural-language steps; a high-bandwidth, compact latent representation is desirable to accelerate reasoning while preserving interpretability.
AI.method: Train latent tokens to represent a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete subwords; use position-dependent weights (e.g., geometric decay) to ensure lossless multiplexing and prevent latent collapse; demultiplexing recovers the original span; supports parallel exploration for search; evaluated across 32 settings with four language models.
AI.result: MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines; ablations show the latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning; lossless superposition is shown as a sufficient condition for strong latent continuous reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Lossless superposition as a local learning target enables efficient latent continuous reasoning; MUX provides a simple, effective method for high-bandwidth reasoning with interpretable latent representations.

title: WorldScape Policy 2.0: Empowering Steerable World Action Modeling with Reasoning-Augmented Memory
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual state transitions and robot actions. However, existing WAMs are constrained by limited temporal context, coarse episode-level language supervision, and predominantly text-only conditioning, which hinder task-progress tracking and fine-grained language-video-action grounding while limiting visual-context reasoning and cross-embodiment transfer. In this paper, we introduce WorldScape Policy 2.0, a controllable WAM with reasoning-augmented long short-term memory. Its causal short-term visual memory supplies recent observations as DiT prefill to preserve local interaction dynamics, while its long short-term event memory organizes historical VLM outputs into global-history, local-active, and event-boundary representations for progress-aware retrieval. The retrieved history augments perception and autoregressively generated planning tokens, yielding an implicit subgoal condition for autonomous planning; semantic forcing further transfers event-level instruction semantics into this latent planning pathway. To establish fine-grained multimodal controllability, we construct ManipEvent-5M, an event-grounded embodied pretraining dataset containing nearly 5 million event segments with aligned action trajectories, episode-level task instructions, segment-level subtask captions, goal images, and video demonstrations. These designs provide a unified interface for autonomous planning from high-level instructions and controllable execution from fine-grained text, goal-image, or video-context prompts. Experiments in both simulation and real-world platforms demonstrate superior capabilities in long-horizon autonomous planning, fine-grained instruction following and in-context adaptation.

AI.tldr: WorldScape Policy 2.0 extends WAMs with reasoning-augmented memory and an event-grounded pretraining dataset to enable long-horizon planning and fine-grained multimodal controllability.
AI.motivation: To overcome limited temporal context, coarse episode-level supervision, and text-only conditioning in existing World Action Models, enabling better task-progress tracking, grounding, and cross-embodiment transfer.
AI.method: Propose WorldScape Policy 2.0 with causal short-term visual memory (DiT prefill) and long short-term event memory that organizes historical VLM outputs into global-history, local-active, and event-boundary representations; retrieved history informs perception and autoregressive planning tokens; apply semantic forcing to transfer event semantics into planning; create ManipEvent-5M with ~5M event segments with aligned actions, instructions, captions, goal images, and video demonstrations; provide unified interface for planning from high-level instructions and controllable execution from multimodal prompts.
AI.result: In both simulation and real-world platforms, demonstrates superior long-horizon autonomous planning, fine-grained instruction following, and in-context adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The design enables autonomous planning from high-level instructions and controllable execution from fine-grained prompts, with effective cross-modal and cross-embodiment transfer, demonstrated by the ManipEvent-5M dataset and experimental results.

title: Gradient-Energy Guided Block-Wise Perturbations for Sharpness-Aware Minimization
summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the worst-case loss in a local parameter neighborhood. Standard SAM implicitly allocates its global perturbation budget across parameter blocks according to instantaneous minibatch gradient norms. Such an allocation can be noisy and may not reflect the sensitivity that blocks accumulate throughout training. We propose Gradient-Energy Adaptive Radius SAM (GEAR-SAM), which maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of squared block gradients as a lightweight, curvature-related sensitivity signal and allocates the fixed SAM budget through a closed-form constrained optimization. GEAR-SAM preserves the global SAM radius, requires no Hessian-vector products or explicit Fisher estimation, and adds only scalar state beyond SAM. Experiments on image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition studies demonstrate improved generalization and robustness across architectures and tasks. More broadly, GEAR-SAM provides a dynamic view of sharpness-aware optimization: a fixed perturbation budget should be redistributed as the sensitivity of functional network blocks evolves during training.

AI.tldr: GEAR-SAM adapts the SAM perturbation allocation per parameter block using an EMA of squared block gradients as a curvature proxy, distributing a fixed global SAM budget through a closed-form constrained optimization. No Hessian-vector products or explicit Fisher estimation are required.
AI.motivation: Standard SAM's per-block perturbation allocation based on instantaneous minibatch gradient norms can be noisy and may not reflect how block sensitivity accumulates during training.
AI.method: Maintain an exponential moving average of squared block gradients as a lightweight sensitivity signal; solve a closed-form constrained optimization to allocate a fixed SAM budget across blocks while preserving the global SAM radius; require only scalar state beyond SAM and avoid Hessian-vector products or Fisher estimation.
AI.result: Empirical studies on image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition analyses show improved generalization and robustness across architectures and tasks.
AI.conclusion: GEAR-SAM provides a dynamic view of sharpness-aware optimization: a fixed perturbation budget should be redistributed as the sensitivity of network blocks evolves during training, yielding better generalization with minimal additional cost.

title: Decoupled Pipeline with Proposal Reranking and Score Fusion for Positive-Unlabeled Marine Species Detection
summary: The FathomNetCLEF 2026 competition combines underwater object detection and fine-grained marine species classification under a positive-unlabeled evaluation setting. The provided training labels are sparse, while the hidden test set is out-of-distribution relative to the training imagery, creating both annotation incompleteness and source-shift challenges. We describe DS@GT ARC's multi-stage system developed for this setting while keeping model training restricted to the data provided by the competition. The final private-leaderboard model uses a frozen Megalodon YOLOv8x detector as a class-agnostic proposal generator, combines global and tiled inference with tile-edge filtering, classifies expanded proposal crops with a LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier, and ranks predictions using weighted geometric fusion of detector and classifier confidence. This system placed 12th out of 102 teams. A closely related variant added a locally trained TTN-inspired validity head as a light reranking signal, improving public-leaderboard and proxy-evaluation performance but slightly reducing private-leaderboard performance. Across experiments, the strongest lesson was that train-derived validation and detector-only metrics were not reliable enough for model selection. Instead, we used proxy datasets only for validation and comparison, and combined those signals with leaderboard feedback and targeted ablations. These experiments showed that reserving proposal recall, avoiding over-aggressive filtering, and improving downstream ranking were more effective than fine-tuning the detector or directly training on noisy pseudo-labels. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/fathomnetclef-2026.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage, positive-unlabeled (PU) underwater detection/classification pipeline (DS@GT ARC) using a frozen class-agnostic detector, tiling, LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier, and geometric fusion for ranking; achieved 12th of 102; highlights include robust validation with proxy data and recall-preserving strategies over detector fine-tuning or pseudo-label training.
AI.motivation: Tackle annotation incompleteness and domain shift in the FathomNetCLEF 2026 PU setting, where training labels are sparse and the test set is out-of-distribution relative to training imagery; aim to build a robust evaluation-driven pipeline under restricted training data.
AI.method: Detector: freeze Megalodon YOLOv8x as class-agnostic proposal generator. Inference: perform global and tiled processing with tile-edge filtering. Classification: expand proposal crops and apply LoRA-finetuned DINOv3 ViT-H classifier. Ranking: combine detector and classifier confidences via weighted geometric fusion; optionally add a TTN-inspired validity head for light reranking; training restricted to provided competition data; validation relies on proxy datasets; ablations and leaderboard feedback guide model selection. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/fathomnetclef-2026.
AI.result: Private leaderboard: 12th out of 102 teams. A variant with a locally trained validity head improved public-leaderboard and proxy-evaluation, but slightly reduced private-leaderboard performance. Across experiments, train-derived validation and detector-only metrics were unreliable for model selection; proxy datasets plus leaderboard signals and targeted ablations were more effective. Reserving proposal recall, avoiding over-aggressive filtering, and improving downstream ranking outperformed detector fine-tuning or training on noisy pseudo-labels.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that, in PU and domain-shift underwater detection tasks, robust validation signals and ranking strategies are more impactful than aggressive detector training. Emphasizes the value of proxy validation datasets and a careful balance between recall, filtering, and downstream ranking for competitive performance.

title: State Compression in Two-Agent LLM Relays: A Closed-World Study of Constraint Preservation
summary: Long-running Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents often accumulate large intermediate traces containing audits, eliminations, and numeric calculations. In practice, this state is compressed before handing it to a downstream decision step, creating an information bottleneck in which small omissions can break strict numeric or categorical constraints. This paper evaluates hand-off compression in a closed-world travel-planning relay with two LLM agents. A Researcher audits a fixed inventory of hotels and flights for 50 goal instances, and a Booker selects a hotel--flight pair using only the goal and the hand-off payload, with the inventory withheld. We compare four hand-off conditions: no compression, narrative summarization, schema-constrained JSON extraction, and embedding-based pruning. Exhaustive enumeration over the fixed inventory provides exact feasible and optimal labels. Results show that hand-off representation strongly affects downstream feasibility under a small decision model. JSON extraction achieves the highest feasibility accuracy at 0.96, while narrative summarization, despite producing the smallest compressed hand-off payload, degrades feasibility to 0.48. Embedding-based pruning matches the uncompressed control on feasibility at 0.88 without an additional generative compression call. These findings indicate that constraint checking benefits from structured and auditable hand-off representations rather than relying on brevity alone.

AI.tldr: Structured, audit-friendly hand-off representations improve constraint feasibility in multi-agent LLM planning; schema-based JSON extraction yields best feasibility, while narrative summarization harms feasibility; embedding-based pruning can match uncompressed performance with less compression.
AI.motivation: Addresses information bottlenecks when compressing intermediate traces between LLM agents; investigates how different hand-off representations affect downstream feasibility under constraint satisfaction in a closed-world travel-planning task.
AI.method: Two-language-model setup: Researcher audits a fixed inventory (hotels/flights) for 50 goal instances; Booker selects a feasible hotel–flight pair using only the goal and the hand-off payload; inventory withheld. Four hand-off conditions: none, narrative, schema-constrained JSON, embedding-based pruning. Exhaustive enumeration over the fixed inventory yields exact feasibility/optimality labels.
AI.result: Feasibility accuracy: JSON extraction 0.96; narrative summarization 0.48; embedding-based pruning 0.88 (matching uncompressed baseline of 0.88); no-compression baseline implied 0.88; compressed payload size inversely related to performance (narrative had smallest payload but worst performance).
AI.conclusion: Structured and auditable hand-offs improve constraint checking; brevity alone reduces feasibility; use structured JSON (with schema) or embedding-based pruning to maintain feasibility with compression.

title: Pose-Parameterized Motion Planning and CBF-QP Self-Collision Filtering for a Long-Reach Drilling Boom
summary: Long-reach drilling booms must reach successive poses without self-collision. Moving from operator-supervised control toward autonomy requires collision-aware motion planning and execution. For the Sandvik SB60, this study adapts established methods by integrating pose-parameterized planning with a capsule-based control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP) in measured-state inverse kinematics (IK). A fixed task-specific parameter set within each task generates waypoints, detours, timed references, and chained motion without target-specific retuning. The offline detour planner screens candidate waypoints using 23 selected rod-segment-to-body-region distances, whereas the online CBF-QP filters joint velocities using 14 configured capsule-pair constraints from a nine-primitive whole-body capsule model. Evaluation considers two drilling tasks in a manufacturer-developed SB60 Simscape Multibody model: a five-target restricted-orientation tour and a three-target full-pose tour. Across several hundred thousand samples, the method produced zero IK failures, generated several detour waypoints, achieved millimetre-level mean final-position error, and recorded no sampled CBF margins below the reported thresholds.

AI.tldr: Pose-parameterized planning integrated with a capsule-based CBF-QP for measured-state IK enables collision-aware autonomy on long-reach drilling booms (Sandvik SB60). An offline detour planner selects 23 distance-based waypoints; online CBF-QP enforces 14 capsule-pair constraints from a nine-primitive capsule model. Evaluated in Simscape Multibody with two drilling tours, the approach yields zero IK failures, detour-generated waypoints, millimeter-level pose accuracy, and robust safety margins across hundreds of thousands of samples.
AI.motivation: Enable autonomous, collision-aware motion planning and execution for long-reach drilling booms, where self-collision and environment interaction are critical. Transition from operator-supervised control to autonomous control while maintaining safe, precise manipulation.
AI.method: Offline: task-wide, parameterized planning generating waypoints, detours, times, and chained motion with fixed task-specific parameters; detour screening using 23 rod-segment-to-body-region distances. Online: measured-state IK filtered by a capsule-based CBF-QP using 14 capsule-pair constraints drawn from a nine-primitive whole-body capsule model.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on a Sandvik SB60 Simscape Multibody model for two drilling tasks showed zero IK failures across hundreds of thousands of samples, generation of detour waypoints, millimeter-level mean final-position error, and no sampled CBF margins below thresholds.
AI.conclusion: The integrated pose-parameterized planning with capsule-based CBF-QP achieves reliable, collision-aware autonomous motion planning for long-reach drilling booms within the tested scenarios, with robust safety margins and minimal pose error; suggests viability for autonomous drilling tasks with constrained kinematics.

title: Agentic Calibration of Grey-Box Simulation Models: An LLM-Driven Alternative
comment: Manuscript: 19 pages, 2 figures. Appendix: 11 pages, 1 figure
summary: Calibration of grey-box simulation models is a constrained optimization problem in which model evaluations are expensive, the parameter space can be high-dimensional, and the search must respect plausibility constraints. Although the simulation code is fully available to the analyst, the joint effect of multiple parameters remains difficult to predict analytically. Classical optimizers such as Nelder--Mead (NM) are simple to deploy but sample-inefficient, particularly under constraints. Modern Bayesian Optimization methods achieve competitive solutions with far fewer evaluations but require non-trivial modeling machinery for constraint handling. We introduce an agentic calibration method in which a large language model acts as the optimizer, with constraints incorporated as a plain-language section of the system prompt. We evaluate the agentic method, NM, and Bayesian Optimization (BO) on an anal cancer simulation model under both unconstrained and clinically constrained calibration. Under unconstrained calibration, the agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than BO and NM, while requiring fewer model evaluations. Under constrained calibration, the agentic method reaches comparable error levels and both outperform NM. These results are obtained at the cost of increased inference time per iteration. Agentic calibration achieves competitive performance with substantially fewer model evaluations, and constraint handling is essentially free at the modeller-facing interface through simple textual specifications rather than additional modelling machinery. The main trade-off lies in increased per-iteration inference cost, making the approach particularly suitable when simulation time dominates. Beyond performance, the per-iteration rationale makes the search auditable and explainable, so its decisions can be scrutinised and justified to third parties.

AI.tldr: Agentic calibration uses a large language model as optimizer with plain-language constraints, achieving competitive or superior calibration with fewer evaluations but higher per-iteration cost.
AI.motivation: Grey-box simulation calibration is expensive and high-dimensional; conventional optimizers (NM, BO) have limitations: NM is sample-inefficient; BO needs complex constraint modeling; there is a need for interpretable, low-evaluation calibration methods that handle constraints easily.
AI.method: Replace traditional optimizer with an LLM-based optimizer that reasons through iterations, with constraints encoded as plain-language in the system prompt. Compare against Nelder–Mead and Bayesian Optimization on an anal cancer simulation model under unconstrained and constrained calibration, evaluating best error, evaluation count, and inference time per iteration.
AI.result: Agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than BO and NM under unconstrained calibration and uses fewer evaluations. Under constrained calibration, it attains comparable error to BO with NM performing worse. Inference time per iteration is higher, but constraint handling is effectively free at the modeller-facing interface via plain-text prompts. The approach provides auditable, explainable search rationale.
AI.conclusion: Agentic calibration can match or exceed traditional optimizers with far fewer model evaluations, with constraints handled simply via textual prompts and with the trade-off of higher per-iteration inference cost. It is particularly suitable when simulation time dominates and when auditability of the search process is valuable.

title: Generative World Renderer at the Speed of Play
summary: Generative world renderer AlayaRenderer receives structured world states exported from physics engines and synthesizes RGB frames. Unlike models that generate frames from text/control-hints prompts, AlayaRenderer preserves scene structure without altering the underlying world dynamics. This demonstrates an alternative path toward interactive world modeling and user-controllable play. However, the original AlayaRenderer is too computationally expensive for real-time deployment. This technical report introduces AlayaRenderer-Flash, a real-time-oriented generative forward world renderer that pushes AlayaRenderer from 0.56 FPS to 31.54 FPS, reaching the speed of play. AlayaRenderer-Flash reformulates the original renderer as a few-step autoregressive streaming model and introduces lightweight distilled codecs for efficient latent encoding and frame reconstruction. It retains the teacher model's G-buffer and text-prompt interfaces while enabling continuous rendering over input streams of unbounded length. We evaluate AlayaRenderer-Flash on G-buffer streams across content preservation, temporal consistency, cross-window stability, prompt controllability, and runtime efficiency. Our results show that AlayaRenderer-Flash substantially reduces inference cost while preserving the core rendering capabilities of the teacher model. By integrating AlayaRenderer-Flash with a physics engine, we build a fully playable generative world running at 30 FPS.

AI.tldr: AlayaRenderer-Flash is a real-time forward world renderer that speeds up AlayaRenderer from 0.56 FPS to 31.54 FPS by using a few-step autoregressive streaming model and lightweight distilled codecs, preserving the G-buffer interface and text prompts to enable continuous, playable rendering with a physics engine (~30 FPS).
AI.motivation: To enable interactive, real-time, structured world rendering without altering underlying world dynamics, addressing the computational bottleneck of the original AlayaRenderer for real-time play.
AI.method: Reformulate the renderer as a few-step autoregressive streaming model and introduce lightweight distilled codecs for latent encoding and frame reconstruction. Maintain teacher model's G-buffer and text-prompt interfaces, enabling continuous rendering over unbounded input streams. Integrate a streaming pipeline to preserve content, temporal consistency, cross-window stability, and controllability while improving runtime efficiency.
AI.result: Substantial inference cost reduction (0.56 FPS -> 31.54 FPS) with retention of the teacher model's rendering capabilities. Evaluation on G-buffer streams shows preservation of content, temporal consistency, cross-window stability, prompt controllability, and runtime efficiency. An integrated system with a physics engine achieves a fully playable world at 30 FPS.
AI.conclusion: AlayaRenderer-Flash delivers real-time, playable rendering that preserves the structured world dynamics and user prompts while achieving substantial speedups, enabling interactive play with physics simulations. Potential benefits include smoother interaction and wider applicability; potential limitations may involve fidelity tradeoffs due to streaming and distillation and long-stream error accumulation.

title: Structured Synthetic Reasoning Data for Arithmetic Fine-Tuning of Small Language Models
summary: Small language models are attractive for local deployment, but they often struggle with multi-step arithmetic reasoning. We study whether structured synthetic reasoning data can improve this behaviour under consumer-hardware constraints. Starting from GSM8K, we generated a 21,250-example corpus of grade-school arithmetic word-problem variants using GPT-5-mini, combining natural-language solution traces, light Socratic-style cues, structural variation, and irrelevant distractor context. We then fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on consumer hardware (Apple M4, 16 GB RAM). Exact-match accuracy on GSM8K improved from 36.5% to 49.1% for Qwen3-0.6B and from 53.5% to 66.5% for Qwen3-1.7B. For Qwen3-1.7B, transfer to related arithmetic benchmarks was stronger, reaching 98.9% on MultiArith and 73.0% on SVAMP, compared with 54.4% and 45.3% for the base model. Qualitative analysis suggests that fine-tuned models produce shorter reasoning traces, make fewer arithmetic and distractor-use errors, and benefit more consistently from self-consistency sampling. These results show that low-cost synthetic data design can materially improve arithmetic adaptation in small language models. Because the intervention combines Socratic-style cues with other data-design choices, we interpret the gains as evidence for structured synthetic reasoning data rather than as a causal test of Socratic guidance alone.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning small language models with a large, structured synthetic reasoning data set improves arithmetic accuracy and transfer under consumer hardware constraints.
AI.motivation: To address weak multi-step arithmetic reasoning in small LMs deployed locally by evaluating whether structured synthetic data design can yield gains with limited compute.
AI.method: Create a 21,250-example GSM8K-derived corpus of arithmetic word-problems using GPT-5-mini, incorporating natural-language solution traces, light Socratic cues, structural variation, and distractor context. Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on Apple M4 (16 GB RAM). Evaluate exact-match accuracy on GSM8K and transfer to related benchmarks (MultiArith, SVAMP). Analyze trace length, error types, and the effect of self-consistency sampling.
AI.result: GSM8K exact-match accuracy improved from 36.5% to 49.1% for the 0.6B model and from 53.5% to 66.5% for the 1.7B model. Transfer performance for the 1.7B model reached 98.9% on MultiArith and 73.0% on SVAMP (versus 54.4% and 45.3% for the base). Qualitative findings: shorter reasoning traces, fewer arithmetic/distractor errors, and stronger gains with self-consistency.
AI.conclusion: Low-cost, structured synthetic reasoning data can materially improve arithmetic adaptation in small LMs. The gains appear attributable to data design choices that induce structured reasoning, rather than solely to Socratic guidance, and are robust under consumer-hardware constraints.

title: NGPS: GPS-Denied Aerial Geo-Localization and 2.5D Reconstruction via Deep Satellite Image Matching and Multi-Rate Sensor Fusion
comment: 9 pages (8-page paper + IEEE copyright/citation cover page), 6 figures. Accepted to IEEE/RSJ IROS 2026
summary: We present NGPS (Next-Generation Positioning System), a visual geo-localization framework for high-altitude UAVs that provides GPS-free absolute positioning by matching down-facing images to georeferenced satellite imagery with deep features. The system combines (1) adaptive confidence-weighted UKF fusion, where NGPS covariance is modulated by RANSAC inlier ratio, reprojection error, and match confidence; (2) velocity-predictive kernel extraction, using VIO velocity to predict the satellite search region; and (3) an asynchronous multi-rate temporal priority queue that interleaves absolute position (1-2 Hz), VIO (10-20 Hz), and IMU (100-200 Hz) updates in chronological order. Globally optimized poses from VINS pose-graph optimization, anchored by NGPS corrections, further enable real-time 2.5D georeferenced orthomosaic reconstruction. On five flight sequences (60-150 m AGL), NGPS achieves 2.94 m position RMSE, with worst-case ATE 6.04 m at 150 m AGL and 2 m/s, yielding a 3.5x improvement over standalone monocular VIO. The system runs in real time on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. Part of the implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/snktshrma/ngps_flight.

AI.tldr: NGPS is a GPS-free visual geo-localization framework for high-altitude UAVs that fuses down-facing image matches to satellite imagery with an adaptive UKF, velocity-aware region prediction, and an asynchronous multi-rate update scheme to deliver real-time, 3 m-class positioning and 2.5D georeferenced mapping; it attains ~3 m RMSE and 3.5x VIO improvement on five flight sequences and is open-source.
AI.motivation: Provide accurate absolute positioning for high-altitude UAVs in GPS-denied or degraded environments, enabling reliable geo-localization and mapping without reliance on GPS.
AI.method: 1) Adaptive confidence-weighted UKF fusion with covariance modulated by RANSAC inlier ratio, reprojection error, and match confidence. 2) Velocity-predictive kernel extraction using VIO velocity to constrain the satellite image search region. 3) Asynchronous multi-rate temporal priority queue interleaving absolute position (1–2 Hz), VIO (10–20 Hz), and IMU (100–200 Hz) updates in chronological order. 4) Globally optimized VINS pose-graph anchored by NGPS corrections to enable 2.5D orthomosaic reconstruction.
AI.result: Five flight sequences at 60–150 m AGL yield 2.94 m position RMSE; worst-case ATE 6.04 m at 150 m AGL and 2 m/s. NGPS yields 3.5× improvement over standalone monocular VIO and runs in real time on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX; implementation is open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: NGPS provides a practical, GPS-free absolute positioning solution for high-altitude UAVs, combining multiple sensor modalities and a real-time fusion pipeline to achieve accurate geo-localization and mapping, with accessible open-source code.

title: Spatio-Temporal Prediction of Unsteady Airfoil Aerodynamics Using Augmented Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with Exogenous Controls
comment: 27 pages, 18 figures, submitted to Computers & Fluids
summary: Unsteady aerodynamic phenomena, such as gusts, turbulence, and fluid-structure interactions affect an aircraft during flight. For design, optimisation and certification, it is indispensable to quantify such unsteady aerodynamic effects. Industry-standard computational fluid dynamics methods, such as solving the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations or the linearized frequency domain method, are either computationally expensive or restricted by assumptions like linearity. Once trained, machine learning methods are capable of computing non-linear relationships very fast, making them suitable as surrogate models. By autoregressively applying graph neural networks (GNNs), operating on a discretised spatial domain, spatio-temporal predictions can be made. However, autoregressive GNNs suffer from error accumulation leading to unstable rollouts over time. Here we show that combining GNNs with augmented Neural Ordinary Differential Equations yields temporally stable predictions of the surface forces on a pitching airfoil. We found that our approach, called GNODE, based on Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, provides temporally more stable, spatially smoother, and overall more accurate results than an autoregressive GNN baseline. Tests are conducted on a dataset consisting of a simulations of a pitching airfoil, including transonic shocks, transient behaviour and dynamic non-linearities. Augmenting GNODEs with additional latent dimensions improves the expressivity and accuracy by capturing underlying history effects. The developed method demonstrates an approach that is suitable to model non-linear spatio-temporal systems with exogenous inputs.

AI.tldr: GNODE combines Graph Neural Networks with augmented Neural ODEs to produce temporally stable, spatially smooth, and accurate non-linear spatio-temporal predictions of surface forces on a pitching airfoil, outperforming autoregressive GNNs; latent augmentation enhances expressivity by capturing history effects.
AI.motivation: To enable accurate, efficient, and certifiably robust modeling of unsteady aerodynamic phenomena (gusts, turbulence, fluid-structure interaction) for design, optimization, and certification, overcoming the cost and linearity limitations of traditional CFD methods.
AI.method: Integrate Graph Neural Networks with augmented Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (GNODE) for non-autoregressive, continuous-time spatio-temporal modeling. Augment GNODEs with additional latent dimensions to capture history effects. Validate on a pitching airfoil dataset with transonic shocks and non-linear dynamics.
AI.result: GNODE provides temporally stable predictions, with smoother spatial fields and higher accuracy than autoregressive GNN baselines. Latent augmentation further improves expressivity and predictive accuracy by capturing history effects.
AI.conclusion: GNODE is a promising framework for modeling non-linear, exogenous-input spatio-temporal systems in aerodynamics, offering stability, accuracy, and scalability advantages over autoregressive graph-based surrogates.

title: Continual Video-MLLM Adaptation over Evolving Domains
summary: Video multimodal large language models have shown strong capability in video understanding, yet their adaptation to sequentially evolving domains remains underexplored. In real-world deployments, video data often arrives continuously from heterogeneous domains, requiring the model to acquire new domain-specific knowledge without overwriting previously learned capabilities. Existing continual learning methods typically rely on shared adaptation spaces, which can induce severe cross-domain interference and catastrophic forgetting. We propose Distribution-Aware Expert Routing, a parameter-efficient framework for continual Video-MLLM adaptation over evolving domains. DAER maintains domain-isolated lightweight experts while keeping the pretrained Video-MLLM backbone frozen, thereby decoupling domain-specific adaptation from the general multimodal knowledge of the pretrained model. To enable fine-grained specialization, we introduce an intra-domain distribution-aware routing mechanism that matches each input to expert-level prototype reservoirs using MMD. To address the absence of task identities at inference time, we further propose an inter-domain routing mechanism that performs prototype matching in a discriminative subspace for robust domain identification. In addition, we introduce adaptive domain merging to improve parameter scalability and adopt a two-stage optimization strategy to stabilize expert specialization during continual learning. We evaluate DAER by curating a domain-incremental benchmark built from ten VidQA datasets covering diverse visual environments and reasoning demands. Experiments on two strong Video-MLLM backbones show that DAER consistently outperforms prior methods.

AI.tldr: DAER is a parameter-efficient continual adaptation framework for video-MLLMs with a frozen backbone and domain-specific lightweight experts. It uses intra-domain MMD-based routing to assign inputs to expert reservoirs and inter-domain discriminative subspace routing for domain identification, plus adaptive domain merging and a two-stage optimization to stabilize learning. It shows improved performance over prior methods on a domain-incremental VidQA benchmark built from 10 datasets and two backbones.
AI.motivation: Video-MLLMs face continual learning challenges when data arrives from evolving, heterogeneous domains. Shared adaptation spaces lead to cross-domain interference and catastrophic forgetting; there is a need for domain isolation, scalable adaptation, and robust inference without task labels.
AI.method: DAER maintains domain-isolated lightweight experts while keeping the pretrained Video-MLLM backbone frozen. An intra-domain routing mechanism uses MMD to match inputs to expert prototype reservoirs for fine-grained specialization. An inter-domain routing mechanism performs prototype matching in a discriminative subspace to identify domains at inference without task IDs. Adaptive domain merging improves parameter scalability. A two-stage optimization strategy stabilizes expert specialization during continual learning.
AI.result: Evaluations on a domain-incremental benchmark spanning 10 VidQA datasets across diverse environments and reasoning demands, with two Video-MLLM backbones. DAER consistently outperforms prior continual learning methods.
AI.conclusion: The approach decouples domain-specific adaptation from general multimodal knowledge, enabling parameter-efficient, robust continual learning for evolving video domains and demonstrating scalable performance across diverse datasets.

title: Fence: Specialized SLM Guardrails for LLM Applications
summary: Real-world applications that use closed-source large language models (LLMs) need advanced safety measures that go beyond the basic content filters. Content moderation filters such as toxicity and bias have relatively standard definitions where as application specific guardrails like hallucination, topic drift and behaviour deviation are more difficult to model and can vary by use case. Additionally, data scarcity and annotation costs, make the process of creating and testing specialized guardrails challenging. In this work, we propose using Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on synthetic data as specialized guardrails for LLM applications. We introduce a novel synthetic data generation method inspired by the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate high quality synthetic data samples which can be used to train SLMs to encode use case specific guardrail information and hence function as specialized guardrails. Our experiments demonstrate that SLM guardrails trained on high quality synthetic data show performance gains over prompt based LLM guardrails.

AI.tldr: Synthesizes specialized guardrails for closed-source LLMs by training Small Language Models on GAN-inspired synthetic data; shows improvement over prompt-based guardrails.
AI.motivation: Address difficulties in modeling application-specific guardrails (hallucination, topic drift, behavior deviation) due to data scarcity and annotation costs, especially for closed-source LLMs with limited safety tooling.
AI.method: Generate high-quality synthetic data via GAN-inspired mechanism; train Small Language Models on this data to encode use-case guardrails; compare against prompt-based LLM guardrails.
AI.result: SLMs trained on synthetic data outperform prompt-based guardrails in preventing guardrail violations (hallucination, drift, etc.), demonstrating effectiveness of synthetic-data-driven guardrails.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data–driven SLM guardrails are a promising approach for robust, customizable safety in LLM deployments, reducing reliance on costly annotations.

title: The Twist Decomposition of Serial Robots Under Lower-Mobility Tasks
summary: This paper introduces a twist decomposition framework for serial manipulators performing lower mobility tasks. Rather than relying on Jacobian null-space projections, the method separates the end-effector twist into task and redundant components using geometrically defined twist projectors. This formulation provides a direct and intuitive distinction between task-relevant and task-irrelevant motions in operational space, enabling a compact inverse kinematics scheme that naturally handles both manipulator and task redundancy.

AI.tldr: Twist-decomposition framework for serial manipulators using task and redundant twist projectors, avoiding Jacobian null-space projections, enabling direct inverse kinematics with inherent redundancy handling.
AI.motivation: Provide an intuitive separation of task-relevant and task-irrelevant end-effector motions in operational space and address both manipulator and task redundancy without relying on Jacobian-based null-space methods.
AI.method: Introduce geometrically defined twist projectors to decompose the end-effector twist into a task component and a redundant component for serial manipulators performing low-mobility tasks; develop a compact inverse kinematics scheme from this decomposition.
AI.result: Direct and intuitive distinction between task-relevant and task-irrelevant motions in operational space; a compact inverse kinematics formulation that naturally handles both manipulator and task redundancy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed twist-decomposition framework offers a geometrically grounded alternative to Jacobian-based redundancy handling, facilitating intuitive control of redundancy and simplifying IK for lower-mobility tasks.

title: Interactive Training 2: Auditable Control Plane for Live Model Training
summary: Experiment trackers show how training is progressing, but changing a live run still usually requires trainer-specific code. We present Interactive Training 2, an open-source control plane for steering training through a shared protocol. Training applications declare which settings and actions they expose, humans and automated controllers submit requests through the same interface, and the training loop validates and applies them at safe control points. A customized Aim workspace combines live metrics and controls with a chronological record of requests and outcomes. We demonstrate the system across five NLP and reinforcement-learning workflows. The released code and traces provide a reusable foundation for auditable human- and agent-guided training.

AI.tldr: IT2 is an open-source control plane that unifies training control via a shared protocol, enabling auditable, human- and agent-guided training across NLP and RL workflows.
AI.motivation: To move beyond trainer-specific code for live experiments by providing a reusable, auditable interface that supports both human and automated requests.
AI.method: Introduce Interactive Training 2 (IT2) with a shared protocol; training apps declare exposed settings/actions; requests from humans and controllers go through the same interface and are validated/ applied at safe control points; an Aim workspace integrates live metrics, controls, and a chronological log; demonstrated on five NLP/RL workflows.
AI.result: Demonstrated across five NLP and RL workflows; released code and traces as a reusable foundation for auditable human- and agent-guided training.
AI.conclusion: IT2 provides a scalable, auditable control plane for steering training via a unified protocol, enabling collaborative, safe, and reproducible training workflows.

title: SkyEV: RGB-Event UAV detection and tracking dataset and baseline
summary: Detecting UAVs in air spaces has become increasingly important due to UAVs widespread availability and easy usage. However, due to their small size, they are typically difficult to detect at a sufficient range. For the training of optimized detection algorithms, datasets have been published, covering optical sensing methods ranging from infrared to regular RGB to event-sensor-based. However, these datasets often fail to reflect realistic counter-UAV scenarios, lacking critical factors such as camera ego-motion, extremely small target scales, and diverse lens configurations, and introduce compression artefacts on the frame images. To address this gap, we introduce SkyEV, an open-source dataset featuring highly synchronized uncompressed RGB and event-based data. SkyEV distinguishes itself by capturing complex real-world conditions, including significant camera motion and varied optical setups, which are essential for testing the fundamental trade-off between Field of View and detection range. Furthermore, we provide a unified data loader and establish an experimental baseline using a multi-modal architecture, demonstrating the dataset's efficacy in detecting challenging, small-scale targets.

AI.tldr: SkyEV is an open-source dataset with synchronized uncompressed RGB and event data for UAV detection under realistic conditions, enabling assessment of the field-of-view vs. detection-range trade-off with camera ego-motion and diverse optics; includes a unified loader and a baseline multi-modal detector.
AI.motivation: UAV detection is challenged by small object size, motion, and variable optics; existing datasets often omit realistic factors (ego-motion, extreme small scales, diverse lens configurations, compression artefacts), hindering robust algorithm development.
AI.method: Collect synchronized, uncompressed RGB and event streams in real-world scenarios featuring significant camera motion and varied optical setups; develop a unified data loader; establish a baseline using a multi-modal detector to evaluate small, hard targets.
AI.result: SkyEV offers challenging, small-scale UAV targets under realistic conditions and demonstrates the dataset’s utility for testing FOV–detection-range trade-offs, with a baseline validating multi-modal detection.
AI.conclusion: SkyEV advances UAV detection research by providing uncompressed, multi-modal data with realistic conditions, enabling more robust evaluation and development of large-scale detectors that operate across diverse lens configurations.

title: Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
summary: The wisdom of crowds -- the finding that aggregating judgments across individuals often outperforms the best individual -- has been extensively studied with human forecasters. Whether the same phenomenon emerges when the ``crowd'' consists of large language models (LLMs) is an open question with both theoretical and practical implications. We elicited probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction market questions and evaluated classical and learned aggregation methods. Learned aggregators -- a multilayer perceptron and a logistic regression -- outperformed all individual models and classical methods. The logistic regression was found to match the neural network, suggesting that the benefit of learned aggregation derives from learning a linear combination of diverse model outputs rather than from nonlinear interactions. Symbolic regression applied to the neural network's learned mapping recovered a pure model-disagreement signal as the lowest-complexity useful formula on the Pareto frontier, further supporting this interpretation. Training cutoff contamination proved a pervasive confound: the apparent capability gap between frontier cloud models and smaller local models collapsed from 35.8% to 8.9% on a clean subset of questions resolving after all models' training cutoffs, and individual model rankings showed only moderate stability. Even when the prediction market is evaluated at each model's training cutoff, LLMs remained substantially less accurate, indicating a genuine gap in collective information aggregation. These findings suggest that LLM crowds can exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects, but that contamination-free evaluation is essential for reliable assessment.

AI.tldr: Learned aggregators (MLP and logistic regression) that combine outputs from 15 LLMs improve binary-forecast accuracy on 254 questions, outperforming individuals and classical averaging; linear combinations suffice, and a simple model-disagreement signal emerges via symbolic regression. Training-cutoff contamination significantly biases results, but clean evaluation shows a genuine, though not complete, wisdom-of-crowds effect for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Assess whether the wisdom-of-crowds phenomenon extends to ensembles of large language models and quantify how aggregation methods and data contamination affect the reliability of such crowds.
AI.method: Collect probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction-market questions; evaluate classical aggregators (e.g., majority, weighted averages) and learned aggregators (a multilayer perceptron and logistic regression); apply symbolic regression to the neural network mapping; analyze training-cutoff contamination by comparing frontier vs smaller local models and by re-evaluating at model training cutoffs.
AI.result: learned aggregators outperformed all individuals and classical methods; logistic regression performed as well as the neural network, implying linear combination of diverse model outputs drives gains; symbolic regression recovered a low-complexity model-disagreement signal as the most useful formula; training-cutoff contamination inflated frontier-model performance (gap reduced from 35.8% to 8.9%), and model rankings showed limited stability; even at training cutoffs, LLMs were less accurate, indicating a genuine gap in collective information aggregation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects when aggregated, but rigorous, contamination-free evaluation is essential to obtain reliable estimates of their collective accuracy; the benefits arise from effectively weighting diverse model outputs rather than complex nonlinear interactions, and simple disagreement signals provide interpretable insights; researchers should guard against data leakage and examine calibration and stability across model families.

title: Design and stability analysis of an underactuated hand with passively rotating fingers
summary: This paper presents an innovative design and stability analysis of an underactuated robotic finger with spatial mobility, designed to enhance gripping dexterity in robotic hands. The finger architecture incorporates a revolute joint at its base, enabling passive spatial rotation that facilitates both cylindrical and spherical grasping. With only two phalanges per finger, the design simplifies kinematic complexity while supporting precision and enveloping grasps. Stability criteria, based on the moment at the finger base joint induced by contact forces, are introduced to ensure reliable object gripping and prevent ejection during manipulation. The study also examines a differential mechanism that distributes a single actuation torque across multiple fingers, allowing adaptive and coordinated motion. This mechanism enhances the hand's ability to grasp diverse object shapes with minimal pre-grasp adjustments, leveraging passivity for autonomous adaptation. Theoretical findings are experimentally validated using a fully mechanical prototype, demonstrating versatility in performing cylindrical, spherical, parallel, and enveloping grasps. The integration of underactuation-both within individual fingers and among multiple fingers-reduces mechanical complexity, cost, and control demands while preserving functional adaptability. This work advances the development of compliant robotic hands suitable for applications requiring dexterity and robustness, such as agricultural robotics, logistics, assistive technologies, and waste sorting. Future research will focus on automating actuation and refining control strategies to further improve grasp stability and precision, paving the way for autonomous manipulation in unstructured environments.

AI.tldr: An underactuated, two-phalange robotic finger with a base rotation enables passive spatial mobility for cylindrical and spherical grasps. A differential mechanism distributes a single actuation torque across multiple fingers, reducing actuation complexity. Stability is analyzed via the moment at the base joint, and a fully mechanical prototype validates grasp versatility (cylindrical, spherical, parallel, enveloping). The approach lowers mechanical complexity and control demands while preserving dexterity, with applications in unstructured environments.
AI.motivation: To develop dexterous, robust, and compliant robotic hands that achieve versatile grasping with minimal actuation and control complexity, enabling reliable manipulation in unstructured settings for tasks such as handling diverse objects.
AI.method: Design and analysis of an underactuated finger with a base revolute joint for passive spatial rotation, two phalanges to simplify kinematics, a stability criterion based on base joint moment under contact forces, and a differential mechanism that shares one actuator torque among multiple fingers. A fully mechanical prototype is built, and experiments demonstrate cylindrical, spherical, parallel, and enveloping grasps.
AI.result: The finger achieves versatile grasp types and demonstrates stable gripping according to the proposed moment-based criteria. The differential actuation enables coordinated finger motion with reduced actuation effort. Experimental validation confirms practical feasibility and grasp versatility while maintaining low mechanical and control complexity.
AI.conclusion: Underactuation at both the finger level and among fingers, combined with passive spatial mobility and torque sharing, enhances dexterity and robustness of compliant robotic hands. The approach is suitable for applications requiring adaptable manipulation in unstructured environments, with future work focused on automating actuation and refining control for improved stability and precision.

title: Cost Accounting for Reactive Computational Graphs: Exhaustive Sweeps, Sequential Mutation, and the Backward-Locality Gap
comment: Companion paper: "Exact Network Surgery: Functional Invariance and Gradient Plasticity in Reactive Computational Graphs" (submitted concurrently)
summary: Exhaustive site-by-site interventions on a neural network's computational graph -- activation-patching sweeps, circuit-discovery searches, systematic ablation studies -- mutate the graph at every candidate site, and their cost is dominated by recomputation after each mutation. On a reactive graph engine whose invalidation provably touches exactly the downstream cone of a mutated node, we give a complete cost accounting for such workloads. First, the aggregate speedup of an exhaustive sweep over independent full recomputations is not a universal constant: if per-layer weight varies regularly with depth at Karamata index q, the ratio converges to (q+2)/(q+1) when weight concentrates near the output and to q+2 near the input, recovering 2 only in the depth-uniform case; a wall-clock corollary predicts a ceiling of about 1.79, below 2, until interpreter overhead is compiled away. Second, we prove the exact cost of a sequence of persistent mutations, never undone between insertions: the interleaved cost exceeds the isolated sum by an exact overcount summed over comparable site pairs, with closed-form extremes over insertion orders, while batched application is order-independent and sub-additive, costing exactly the union of the sites' cones plus the fresh nodes. Third, we prove the exact mirror of forward locality for the backward pass, showing it collapses the aggregate speedup to 1 under backpropagation on architectures without long skip connections. Every identity is validated on NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia: measured sweep ratios converge to the predicted limits under four cost profiles; the training-mode ratio collapses to 1 at the predicted rate; and all 18 per-graft sequential costs and the batched total match the closed forms at zero tolerance across three insertion orders.

AI.tldr: Exhaustive site-by-site perturbations on neural graphs yield non-universal speedups; the paper provides closed-form cost formulas, bounds, and validation on NeuroDSL.
AI.motivation: Quantify the cost and speedup tradeoffs of exhaustive perturbation experiments on reactive graph-based NN representations, covering forward and backward passes.
AI.method: Develop theoretical cost models for three regimes (independent full recomputation, sequences of persistent mutations, batched application), derive closed-form expressions and exact overcounts, prove forward/backward locality properties, and validate on NeuroDSL across multiple cost profiles and insertion orders.
AI.result: Found speedup bounds that depend on weight depth distribution (e.g., convergence to (q+2)/(q+1) or 2 in special cases, wall-clock ceiling ~1.79). Exact overcounts for interleaved mutations; batched application is order-independent and sub-additive; backward pass locality reduces speedup to 1 on architectures without long skip connections. Empirical validation on NeuroDSL shows measured ratios converging to predicted limits and exact-cost matches across three insertion orders.
AI.conclusion: The work provides precise cost accounting for exhaustive perturbation workloads on reactive graph engines, revealing non-universal speedups governed by weight-depth distributions, with practical guidance on experiment design and implications for forward/backward perturbations and batched mutation strategies.

title: Weakly Supervised Pathology-Informed Representation Learning for PET-Based Content Retrieval of Intra-Tumour Heterogeneity
summary: We propose a weakly supervised 18FFDG PET representation-learning framework for content based medical image retrieval, using H&E derived information during training while preserving PET-only inference. The proposed method was designed to use H&E derived information during training while maintaining PET only inference. A teacher student training strategy was used to learn the PET tumour derived voxel representations, from which global and hotspot conditioned embeddings were generated along with maps of intra tumour heterogeneity in our oesophegeal cancer test case. A progressive ablation strategy was used to evaluate the contribution of different supervision mechanisms. Retrieval performance was assessed across cross-validation folds using metrics including mean average precision, normalised discounted cumulative gain and mean reciprocal rank. Additional analyses evaluated ablation performance, hotspot faithfulness through perturbation/deletion experiments, prototype-specific PET uptake behaviour and indirect patient level concordance between learned PET prototype classes and selected histomic features. Progressive introduction of pathology informed supervision and hotspot modelling improved PET retrieval performance compared with global PET representations and conventional PET baselines. Across the ablation ladder, PET hotspot conditioned representations consistently provided stronger retrieval than global embeddings, indicating that focusing on informative tumour subregions improved sensitivity to intra tumour heterogeneity. Histopathology concordance further showed that the learned classes were not simply high uptake PET regions; instead, they demonstrated distinct heterogeneity in 18F FDG uptake.

AI.tldr: Weakly supervised 18F-FDG PET CBIR using H&E-derived supervision during training with PET-only inference; teacher-student learning yields hotspot-conditioned tumor representations that better capture intra-tumor heterogeneity than global PET embeddings, improving retrieval and showing histology concordance.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of global PET representations in capturing intra-tumor heterogeneity and retrieval performance; leverage pathology (H&E) information during training while preserving PET-only inference at test time.
AI.method: Teacher–student framework learning tumor-derived voxel representations from PET using H&E-derived supervision; generate global and hotspot-conditioned embeddings and maps of intra-tumor heterogeneity (oesophageal cancer); progressive ablation to assess contributions of supervision signals; evaluation via cross-validated retrieval metrics (MAP, nDCG, MRR); supplementary analyses include ablations, hotspot faithfulness (perturbation/deletion), prototype-specific PET uptake, and histomic feature concordance.
AI.result: Hotspot-conditioned PET representations consistently outperform global embeddings and conventional baselines in retrieval across ablations; progressive addition of pathology-informed supervision and hotspot modelling yields the best performance; learned PET classes reflect intra-tumor heterogeneity rather than merely high uptake, as evidenced by histopathology concordance.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on informative tumor subregions with pathology-informed supervision enhances PET CBIR by better capturing intra-tumor heterogeneity and aligning with histologic heterogeneity, without sacrificing PET-only inference.

title: Trajectory-Aware Clinical Risk Prediction via Severity-Grounded Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: While Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offer a wealth of clinical data, effectively augmenting a patient's records with heterogeneous external knowledge to predict the patient's clinical risk remains a significant challenge. Existing methods fail to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and nuanced clinical progression, due to data sparsity and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. To address these challenges, we propose TRACER (a trajectory-aware and clinically grounded prediction framework) that (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with severity information from medical literature, (2) retrieves clinically relevant, severity-weighted paths of a patient's progression from the knowledge graph, (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured clinical notes, and (4) augments patient context with similar peer cases. Experiments on the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets demonstrate large gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with up to 28.5% increase in Macro F1 score for the mortality prediction task, and 19.7% increase for the readmission prediction task.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a trajectory-aware, clinically grounded framework that enriches EHR-based predictions via a severity-enriched medical knowledge graph, severity-weighted progression paths, extraction of events from notes, and peer-case augmentation, achieving substantial gains on mortality and readmission predictions in MIMIC datasets.
AI.motivation: To address data sparsity and underutilization of unstructured notes in EHRs, and to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and clinical progression by leveraging external knowledge sources.
AI.method: 1) Build a medical knowledge graph with severity information from literature; 2) Retrieve severity-weighted patient progression paths from the KG; 3) Extract clinically relevant events from unstructured notes; 4) Augment patient context with similar peer cases.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, TRACER outperforms baselines with up to 28.5% Macro F1 improvement for mortality prediction and 19.7% for readmission prediction.
AI.conclusion: TRACER demonstrates that integrating structured external knowledge, trajectory-aware reasoning, and unstructured note signals enhances EHR-based clinical risk prediction, with strong performance gains and potential generalization to diverse tasks.

title: Bayesian Retraction Optimization for Tissue Attachment Mapping in Surgical Dissection
summary: With growing surgeon shortages, automating surgical sub-tasks such as tissue dissection offers a promising step toward reducing workload and expanding patient access. Prior work has relied on hand-crafted incision policies that cannot quantify uncertainty or has relied on simulation-based methods that require strong modeling assumptions. We instead view tissue attachment identification as an inherently probabilistic problem and propose a Bayesian approach that avoids explicit tissue modeling. Our method uses a Sequential Bayesian Hilbert Map (SBHM) to represent the likelihood that each tissue point is attached to the underlying resection surface. An ensemble of learned classifiers predicts attachment likelihoods from spatial data acquired during robotic tissue retraction, with each classifier serving as a noisy information source to update the SBHM. To plan the next retraction, we devise Bayesian Retraction Optimization (BRO) to select the most informative action under safety constraints. As the SBHM refines over time, regions with high attachment likelihood are selectively incised. We validate our method in simulation across diverse tissue geometries and acquisition strategies, and demonstrate zero-shot transfer to real robotic dissection experiments.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic framework using a Sequential Bayesian Hilbert Map and an ensemble of classifiers to identify tissue attachment during robotic dissection, with Bayesian Retraction Optimization for informative, safety-constrained action planning; shows simulation success and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Address surgeon shortages and the need to quantify uncertainty in tissue-attachment decisions; prior hand-crafted policies lack uncertainty quantification and simulation models rely on strong assumptions.
AI.method: SBHM models attachment likelihood; ensemble classifiers provide evidence; Bayesian updating; BRO selects the most informative next retraction under safety constraints; regions with high attachment likelihood are incised as SBHM refines; validated in simulation and zero-shot transfer to real experiments.
AI.result: Simulation validation across diverse tissue geometries and acquisition strategies; zero-shot transfer to real robotic dissection experiments.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a probabilistic, uncertainty-aware planning framework for robotic tissue dissection that improves upon prior methods by avoiding explicit tissue modeling and enabling safe, information-driven incisions with stealth sim-to-real applicability.

title: Dynamic Loss Balancing for Joint SOH and RUL Prediction of Lithium-Ion Batteries via a Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer
summary: The deployment of reliable lithium-ion battery management systems is crucial for accelerating electrification, yet the joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) remains severely hindered by task heteroscedasticity. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance the bounded, low-variance noise of SOH estimation with the unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty of long-term RUL predictions. Here, we present the Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer (RoSIP-Batt), a unified co-estimation framework that resolves these optimization conflicts. By formulating joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective, RoSIP-Batt introduces a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise levels. The architecture leverages decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism, secured by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from corrupting the stable SOH representation space. To capture electrochemical degradation patterns without relying on absolute cycle steps, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is incorporated into a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles. Crucially, the intermediate SOH estimate is directly injected into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior. Evaluations across the NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets show that RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing SOH estimation error to 1.994% MAE on NASA and restricting RUL prediction error to 62.85 cycles on Stanford. These findings establish RoSIP-Batt as a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian multi-task Transformer for joint SOH and RUL estimation with variance-based weighting and degradation priors, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Address the persistent challenge of joint SOH and RUL prognosis under task heteroscedasticity, where SOH noise is bounded and low-variance while long-term RUL uncertainty grows unboundedly, hindering unified learning and real-time embedded deployment.
AI.method: RoSIP-Batt uses a Bayesian multi-task objective with a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism. It features decoupled dual classification tokens, a per-dimension gated fusion, and a gradient-detachment operator to protect SOH stability. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) models translation-invariant temporal patterns in a shared Transformer backbone. The intermediate SOH estimate is injected into the RUL head as a physical degradation prior.
AI.result: Significant performance gains over baselines on NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets: SOH MAE ≈ 1.994% on NASA; RUL error ≈ 62.85 cycles on Stanford. Reported as a generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS.
AI.conclusion: RoSIP-Batt advances joint SOH–RUL prognostics by effectively balancing task-specific noise via uncertainty weighting, leveraging RoPE for degradation-aware temporal modeling, and injecting physical priors to the RUL head, yielding state-of-the-art accuracy and practical deployment viability.

title: Posterior Samplings are Missing Modalities Generators for Medical Image Translation
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging comes in various modality contrasts that provide complementary anatomical and pathological information. Complete multimodal acquisitions are often unavailable due to time and protocol constraints. This leads to real-world datasets with missing modalities, where conventional medical image translation methods are typically limited to fixed source-target settings or require retraining for each observed source-target pair. We propose a unified framework that formulates missing-modality generation as a linear inverse problem under a joint distribution and solves it via posterior sampling with a flow matching model. By learning a joint prior over the complete modality set, our method can reconstruct arbitrary missing modalities at inference time by guiding the sampling trajectory to enforce measurement consistency with observed modalities. We further mitigate inter-modality error propagation in multi-target generation by adopting a many-to-one sampling strategy. Experiments on BraTS and IXI datasets show that our method achieves the best performance over baselines across most missing-modality scenarios. In downstream tumor segmentation, synthesized images from our method result in higher segmentation performance, indicating better preservation of clinically relevant structures.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for missing-modality MRI generation using a joint prior and posterior sampling via flow matching, enabling inference-time reconstruction of arbitrary missing modalities and improved downstream segmentation.
AI.motivation: Real-world MRI datasets often lack one or more modalities due to time/protocol constraints; existing methods are limited to fixed source-target pairs or require retraining for each pair.
AI.method: Formulate missing-modality generation as a linear inverse problem under a learned joint prior over complete modalities. Train a flow-matching model to sample from the posterior, guiding sampling with observed modalities for measurement consistency. Employ many-to-one sampling to reduce inter-modality error propagation when generating multiple targets.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines across most missing-modality scenarios on BraTS and IXI datasets. Synthesized images improve downstream tumor segmentation performance, indicating better preservation of clinically relevant structures.
AI.conclusion: A joint-prior, flow-based posterior sampling approach provides a flexible, unified solution for universal missing-modality MRI generation, with tangible gains in reconstruction fidelity and clinical task performance without per-pair retraining.

title: Using LLMs for Explainable, Data-Driven Insight Generation from Time Series
summary:
Time series forecasts are widely used in decision-critical domains, where they are rarely consumed without accompanying explanations. Producing such explanations is usually a manual and costly process, and attempts to automate it using large language models often suffer from hallucination when applied to temporal data. We propose a domain-agnostic framework for grounded natural language explanation generation for time series forecasts, illustrated in Figure 1. The framework consists of three components: (i) extraction of structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations, (ii) evidence-conditioned explanation generation, and (iii) scalable evaluation for readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness. The design explicitly constrains generation to verifiable evidence, reducing unsupported claims.
  We evaluate the framework on a financial forecasting case study involving the NASDAQ-100 index and a freight pricing case study using data from Vortexa. Results show that generated explanations approached analyst-written explanations in terms of readability, consistency and persuasiveness. These findings demonstrate that grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be achieved at scale without domain-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A domain-agnostic framework for grounded natural language explanations of time series forecasts, using (1) extraction of explanatory factors from analyst explanations, (2) evidence-conditioned explanation generation, and (3) scalable evaluation; evaluated on NASDAQ-100 and Vortexa data; explanations near analyst-written in readability, consistency, and persuasiveness; achieves scalable, non-domain-specific explanations without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Forecast explanations are essential but costly to produce; LLM-based explanations for temporal data risk hallucinations. The work aims to provide grounded, verifiable explanations that accompany forecasts, in a domain-agnostic manner.
AI.method: A three-component framework: (i) extract structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations; (ii) generate explanations conditioned on verifiable evidence; (iii) scalable evaluation for readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness, with generation explicitly constrained to verifiable evidence.
AI.result: Applied to two case studies: NASDAQ-100 index forecasting and a freight pricing dataset from Vortexa. The generated explanations closely matched analyst-written explanations in readability, consistency, and persuasiveness.
AI.conclusion: Grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be scaled without domain-specific fine-tuning by constraining explanations to verifiable evidence and leveraging analyst-derived factors.

title: Agentic Real2Sim: Physics-based World Modeling with Vision-Language Agents
