summary: Real-to-sim conversion for robotic interaction with objects remains labor-intensive because it requires more than visual reconstruction: a streamlined real2sim process must recover scene geometries and object states, infer physical parameters, and assemble actors, objects, cameras, poses, and trajectories into a runnable physical simulation. Today this process still depends on manual tuning of visual foundation models, mesh cleanup, coordinate-frame alignment, and brittle workflow glue across visual perception tools and simulators. We introduce \textit{Agentic Real2Sim}, a framework for generalized physical world modeling with vision-language agents, converting a real-world recording of object-robot interaction into a simulatable episodic twin which preserves observations, geometries, robot interactions, and object states. We evaluate Agentic Real2Sim on rigid-object manipulation, deformable-object interaction, and humanoid motion scenes, spanning domains that are usually handled by separate Real2Sim pipelines, marking a first step toward scalable conversion. The framework's agentic decisions can be driven by an open-weight VLM backend at a small fraction of the cost of frontier models, while attaining comparable conversion success rate. We aim to use the resulting real-world-aligned twins for downstream robotics tasks, specifically policy learning and evaluation. The project site is available at https://ericchen321.github.io/agentic_real2sim.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Proposes Agentic Real2Sim, a framework leveraging vision-language agents to convert real-world object-robot interactions into runnable episodic twins, enabling scalable, cross-domain real-to-sim conversion with lower-cost backends.
AI.motivation: Labor-intensive, brittle real-to-sim pipelines require manual tuning, mesh cleanup, and glue logic across perception tools and simulators; a generalized, scalable solution is needed to recover geometries, states, and trajectories for simulatable scenes.
AI.method: Introduce Agentic Real2Sim; a framework using vision-language agents to process real-world recordings and construct episodic twins that preserve observations, geometries, robot interactions, and object states; supports rigid, deformable, and humanoid scenes; can leverage open-weight VLM backends to reduce cost; aims to streamline integration between perception and simulation.
AI.result: Evaluated on rigid-object manipulation, deformable-object interaction, and humanoid motion; demonstrates cross-domain applicability; shows comparable conversion success rate to frontier models at a fraction of the cost; a first step toward scalable real2sim conversion.
AI.conclusion: Real2Sim renders real-world-aligned twins suitable for downstream robotics tasks such as policy learning and evaluation; establishes a pathway for scalable real-to-sim conversion; project page provided for further exploration.

title: Physics-Guided Masked Multi-Task Network for Edge-Friendly Battery Health Diagnostics from Sto-chastically Fragmented Charging Profiles
summary: The deployment of reliable lithium-ion battery management systems is crucial for accelerating electrification, yet the joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) remains severely hindered by task heteroscedasticity. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance the bounded, low-variance noise of SOH estimation with the unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty of long-term RUL predictions. Here, we present the Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer (RoSIP-Batt), a unified co-estimation framework that resolves these optimization conflicts. By formulating joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective, RoSIP-Batt introduces a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise levels. The architecture leverages decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism, secured by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from corrupting the stable SOH representation space. To capture electrochemical degradation patterns without relying on absolute cycle steps, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is incorporated into a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles. Crucially, the intermediate SOH estimate is directly injected into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior. Evaluations across the NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets show that RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing SOH estimation error to 1.994% MAE on NASA and restricting RUL prediction error to 62.85 cycles on Stanford. These findings establish RoSIP-Batt as a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

AI.tldr: RoSIP-Batt is a Bayesian multi-task Transformer for joint SOH and RUL estimation in Li-ion batteries. It uses homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, decoupled dual tokens, gradient-detachment, RoPE-based relative temporal modeling, and injection of intermediate SOH into the RUL head, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and efficient real-time deployment.
AI.motivation: Joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) is hampered by task heteroscedasticity and the divergent noise characteristics of short-term SOH and long-term RUL predictions in battery management systems. A unified, efficient framework is needed for real-time embedded deployment.
AI.method: A unified Bayesian multi-task Transformer (RoSIP-Batt) with: (1) homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to scale task gradients by residual noise levels; (2) decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion, guarded by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from destabilizing SOH; (3) Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) in a shared Transformer backbone for translation-invariant temporal modeling; (4) direct injection of intermediate SOH estimate into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior; (5) evaluation on NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets.
AI.result: Significant performance gains over baselines: SOH MAE of 1.994% on NASA; RUL error of 62.85 cycles on Stanford; claimed generalizability and suitability for real-time embedded BMS due to computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: RoSIP-Batt offers a generalizable, computation-efficient solution for joint SOH–RUL prognosis in Li-ion batteries, addressing task heteroscedasticity and leveraging physics-informed prior injection to improve predictive reliability.

title: Bounding Boxes to Improve Small Language Model Performance on Vision-Based Grading Tasks
comment: Accepted for 1st Workshop on Small Language Models for Education (SLM4ED '26) at AIED 2026
summary: The deployment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in educational settings offers significant advantages in terms of privacy, cost, and scalability. However, SLMs often struggle with complex vision-based tasks, such as grading handwritten student exams, due to the high computational cost of processing large images and the visual distractions present on a full page. In this paper, we investigate whether cropping student responses using bounding boxes can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of SLMs on a short-answer grading task. Using a dataset of scanned handwritten responses from the 2025 Australian Physics Olympiad, we evaluate the performance of several models ranging from 4B to 72B parameters under varying conditions of Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting and image cropping. Our results demonstrate that using bounding boxes significantly improves grading accuracy and reduces computational cost (FLOPs) across models. We conclude that bounding boxes are a crucial pre-processing step for deploying SLMs in large-scale, vision-based educational assessments.

AI.tldr: Bounding box-based cropping markedly improves SLM-based short-answer grading on handwritten student work, increasing accuracy and cutting FLOPs across models (4B–72B) and CoT settings.
AI.motivation: To reduce computational cost and enhance accuracy for vision-based tasks in education, where full-page images contain distractions and high processing demands.
AI.method: Evaluate multiple SLMs (4B–72B) on a dataset of scanned handwritten responses from the 2025 Australian Physics Olympiad; compare full-page versus cropped responses using bounding boxes; test with/without Chain-of-Thought prompting; measure grading accuracy and computational cost (FLOPs).
AI.result: Bounding box cropping significantly improves grading accuracy and reduces FLOPs across models, indicating bounding boxes as a beneficial pre-processing step for large-scale vision-based educational assessments.
AI.conclusion: Bounding boxes are a crucial pre-processing step for deploying SLMs in large-scale, vision-based educational assessments.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning to Master the Asymmetric Strategy of Baghchal
summary: Baghchal is a two-player asymmetric board game with Nepali origins where four tigers are to capture goats and twenty goats desire to keep tigers in immobility. Although Baghchal has a complex structure which is strategic, has perfect information structure, and has cultural meaning, it has not been adequately covered in deep reinforcement learning (RL) literature. This paper gives a systematic exploration of four deep RL solutions Deep Q-Network (DQN), REINFORCE, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and MuZero that are trained on one side of the asymmetric gameplay of Baghchal and then evaluated on the other side. The algorithms are rated based on win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence and computational cost. It is experimentally found that MuZero generates the best performance in both tasks, achieving 86 percent win over these Tiger and 62 percent win over these Goat and the ability to do so is due to the model-based planning machine through the Monte Carlo Tree Search. PPO is the most realistic algorithm and is provided to be competitive over both asymmetric tasks with significantly reduced computational costs compared to MuZero. Emergent strategic behavior analysis shows that model-based strategies are optimal over long-horizon planning, whereas value-based counterparts like DQN are more biased up towards the Tiger role owing to the more substantial reward signal.

AI.tldr: MuZero-based deep RL achieves the strongest performance on Baghchal, leveraging model-based planning; PPO offers a realistic and computationally efficient competitor; DQN and REINFORCE underperform, with DQN biased toward Tiger signals.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in deep RL literature for Baghchal, a complex asymmetric board game with perfect information and cultural significance, by systematically evaluating four DL-RL methods trained on one side and tested on the opposite side.
AI.method: Train four DL-RL methods (DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, MuZero) on one side of Baghchal and evaluate on the opposing side. Assess via win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence, and computational cost. Also analyze emergent strategic behavior to contrast model-based vs value-based approaches.
AI.result: MuZero achieves the best performance in both tasks, with ~86% win against Tigers and ~62% win against Goats, attributed to its model-based planning via Monte Carlo Tree Search. PPO is the most realistic, offering competitive performance with significantly lower computational cost than MuZero. Value-based methods like DQN show a bias toward the Tiger role due to stronger reward signals, while emergent strategies indicate model-based approaches excel in long-horizon planning.
AI.conclusion: Model-based RL (MuZero) is superior for long-horizon, asymmetric, perfect-information games like Baghchal; PPO provides a practical, cost-efficient competitor; value-based methods exhibit role biases. The findings underline the importance of planning components in challenging strategic domains and offer guidance for applying DL-RL to similar games.

title: Cognitive Dual-Process Planning for Autonomous Driving with Structured Scene Knowledge and Verifiable Reasoning-Action Consistency
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Zhongyao Yang and Haoyu Li contributed equally to this work
summary: High-level planning for autonomous driving is a knowledge-intensive engineering decision task that requires accurate scene understanding, timely inference, and internally consistent action selection. Vision-language models (VLMs) can make intermediate reasoning explicit, but their use in deployed planners is constrained by costly structured supervision, unnecessary reasoning in routine scenes, and possible inconsistencies between generated rationales and driving actions. We present a cognitive dual-process planning framework that represents planning-relevant scene knowledge in a machine-parsable structured chain-of-thought (S-CoT) schema. An automated data engine integrates perception foundation models, critical-path filtering, and an expert VLM to generate S-CoT supervision without manual annotation of individual rationales. A lightweight visual Arbiter estimates scene complexity from multilevel vision-encoder features before language decoding and routes each input to either fast meta-action prediction or slow structured reasoning. For slow-path outputs, a deterministic rule-based validator checks whether the parsed S-CoT fields are consistent with the final meta-action and provides verifiable rewards for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). In a 195-scene manual audit, the generated annotations achieve 91.8\% CoT accuracy and a 98.5\% Logical Consistency Score (LCS). On 574 manually verified NAVSIM test samples, the planner achieves 80.14\% planning accuracy and 97.20\% LCS while reducing average latency by 17.39\% relative to applying slow reasoning to every scene. Evaluation on external long-tail subsets further identifies conditions under which routing and planning performance degrade. Together, these results show how explicit scene knowledge can be operationalized through adaptive reasoning and rule-based verification to support high-level VLM planning decisions.

AI.tldr: A cognitive dual-process planning framework for autonomous driving uses structured chain-of-thought (S-CoT) schemas, automated data generation, and a visual Arbiter to route between fast meta-action predictions and slow structured reasoning, with rule-based validation and GRPO-based optimization; achieving high CoT accuracy, strong planning accuracy, and reduced latency.
AI.motivation: To address the cost, inconsistency, and misalignment of vision-language model (VLM) reasoning in planners by explicitly representing planning knowledge in machine-parsable S-CoT, while avoiding unnecessary reasoning in routine scenes and ensuring consistency with actions.
AI.method: Propose a cognitive dual-process architecture: (1) an automated data engine that creates S-CoT supervision via perception models, critical-path filtering, and an expert VLM; (2) a lightweight visual Arbiter that estimates scene complexity from multilevel vision features to route inputs to fast meta-action prediction or slow structured reasoning; (3) a deterministic rule-based validator that checks S-CoT consistency with final actions and provides rewards for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
AI.result: In a 195-scene manual audit, generated annotations achieve 91.8% CoT accuracy and 98.5% Logical Consistency Score (LCS). On 574 NAVSIM test samples, planner achieves 80.14% planning accuracy and 97.20% LCS, with a 17.39% reduction in average latency relative to applying slow reasoning to all scenes. External long-tail subsets identify conditions where routing/planning degrades.
AI.conclusion: Explicit scene knowledge can be operationalized through adaptive reasoning and rule-based verification to support high-level VLM planning decisions, achieving strong accuracy and reduced latency while highlighting conditions that affect performance.

title: ChemHyperMag: Physics-informed magnetic hypergraph learning improves molecular ADMET prediction
comment: Accepted by Proceedings of the AI4Physics Workshop at the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning (AI4Physics@ICML 2026)
summary: Accurate prediction of ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) is important for drug discovery. Most predictors use undirected molecular graphs and pairwise edges. This choice misses asymmetric interactions, nonreversible dynamics, and motif level effects from functional groups and ring systems. We propose ChemHyperMag for multitask ADMET prediction under missing labels. ChemHyperMag builds a functional group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds. It also defines a potential driven nonreversible flow guided by electronegativity and Gasteiger partial charges. The resulting circulation is encoded by a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian and processed with a magnetic Chebyshev encoder. We perturb magnetic phases to form stochastic views and train with an InfoNCE objective. Experiments on multiple ADMET benchmarks show improvements over recent methods with fewer labeled samples and no conformers. ChemHyperMag is scalable and provides interpretable directional signals through its magnetic phases.

AI.tldr: ChemHyperMag introduces a functional-group hypergraph framework with a potential-driven nonreversible flow and magnetic Laplacian for multitask ADMET prediction with missing labels; uses magnetic Chebyshev encoding and InfoNCE supervision; achieves improved performance without conformers and with interpretable directional signals.
AI.motivation: Standard graph-based ADMET predictors rely on undirected graphs and pairwise edges, missing asymmetric interactions, nonreversible dynamics, and motif-level effects of functional groups and ring systems.
AI.method: Construct a functional-group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds; define a potential-driven nonreversible flow guided by electronegativity and Gasteiger charges; encode circulation via a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian and a magnetic Chebyshev encoder; create stochastic views by perturbing magnetic phases; train with an InfoNCE objective on multitask learning with missing labels.
AI.result: On multiple ADMET benchmarks, it shows improvements over recent methods with fewer labeled samples and no conformers.
AI.conclusion: The approach is scalable and provides interpretable directional signals through magnetic phases, improving multitask ADMET prediction under label scarcity.

title: Cross-Modal UAV Object Tracking: State-Aware Representation Learning and A Unified Benchmark
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) object tracking has emerged as a popular research field with broad practical applications. Modern UAVs are increasingly equipped with both visible light and thermal infrared sensors. However, due to constraints in communication bandwidth, computational resources and power consumption, current systems often activate one modality and switch between modalities to maintain robust tracking in complex scenarios. Such modality switch inevitably leads to significant appearance change and sudden spatial shift, posing great challenges for existing tracking algorithms. To handle this problem, we propose a novel State-Aware Representation Learning Approach called SARLA, which perceives the inconsistent modality states of current frame with template and last frame in the target representations to adapt to the sudden changes in both appearance and position, for robust cross-modal object tracking. In particular, we propose the Modality State Aware Representation Module (MSARM) and Spatial State Aware Representation Module (SSARM). MSARM guides the model to learn appearance correlation, bridging the modality gap, while SSARM models cross-frame spatial correlation to mitigate sudden spatial shift impacts. In addition, we design a spatial shift prediction loss to further handle the effects of spatial variation caused by modality switch. To promote the development of this research field, we establish a large-scale video benchmark called CM-UOT, which consists of 1079 cross-modal sequences with an average video length greater than 621 frames and encompasses over 671K frames in total. Extensive experiments on CM-UOT dataset demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed SARLA against 20 excellent tracking methods. The source code, datasets, and evaluation protocols associated with this work are publicly available at: https://github.com/hongsmile365/sarla-.

AI.tldr: Proposes SARLA, a state-aware representation learning framework for cross-modal UAV tracking, with MSARM and SSARM to handle modality switches and spatial shifts; introduces CM-UOT benchmark; reports superiority over 20 trackers and public release.
AI.motivation: Modality switching between visible and thermal IR in UAV tracking causes appearance and position changes, challenging traditional trackers; bandwidth/resource constraints necessitate modality switching; need representation learning that accounts for modality and spatial state.
AI.method: Introduces MSARM to learn cross-modality appearance correlation; SSARM to model cross-frame spatial correlation; adds spatial shift prediction loss; integrates into SARLA; builds CM-UOT benchmark (1079 sequences, >671k frames).
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on CM-UOT shows superior performance against 20 tracking baselines; shows robust cross-modal tracking; dataset and code released.
AI.conclusion: SARLA demonstrates improved robustness under modality switches; MSARM/SSARM effectively bridge modality gap and stabilize spatial alignment; CM-UOT provides a valuable resource for cross-modal UAV tracking research.

title: Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) serving as planners in tool-using autonomous agents introduce dynamic reliability risks in multi-turn execution. While single-turn safety mechanisms are relatively mature, extended interactions reveal structural vulnerabilities where initial alignment degrades over time. This paper empirically characterizes two observed failure modes across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs: Safety Drift, the gradual erosion of declared safety intent leading to constraint-violating actions (e.g., textual refusal followed by reconnaissance and unsafe execution), and Operational Hallucination, persistent repetitive tool calls indicative of flawed state perception (e.g., livelocks even in legitimate tasks). Through controlled multi-turn evaluation on high-stakes ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls, we quantify these phenomena using declaration-action gap and livelock metrics, demonstrating their cross-model prevalence under direct execution protocols. Root-cause analysis attributes the instabilities to the decoupling of reasoning context from execution state in current agent loops. We propose an Action-Aware Supervision Layer - a lightweight, plug-and-play architectural blueprint incorporating intent-action consistency checks, runtime state tracking, and forced termination primitives. Post-hoc simulation on captured failure trajectories shows the layer can intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases. This work advances agent reliability by shifting focus from linguistic safeguards to enforceable architectural mechanisms for responsible agentic AI.

AI.tldr: Two failure modes emerge when LLM planners operate over multiple turns: Safety Drift (declared safety erodes, leading to unsafe actions) and Operational Hallucination (repetitive tool calls and perception faults). Across models and tasks, these survive direct execution protocols; they are linked to decoupled reasoning and execution states. An Action-Aware Supervision Layer is proposed to enforce intent-action consistency with runtime state tracking and termination controls, intercepting violations post-hoc without harming benign cases.
AI.motivation: Ensure reliability of tool-using autonomous agents in multi-turn settings, where traditional single-turn safety measures fail to prevent emergent, architecture-level failures during extended interactions.
AI.method: Controlled multi-turn evaluations across state-of-the-art LLMs on high-stakes ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls; quantify failures using declaration-action gap and livelock metrics; perform root-cause analysis; design and test an Action-Aware Supervision Layer as a lightweight architectural addition; post-hoc simulation to assess interception capabilities and false positives.
AI.result: Identified two cross-model failure modes (Safety Drift and Operational Hallucination) and quantified their prevalence; demonstrated the proposed supervision layer can intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases, under direct execution protocols.
AI.conclusion: Reliability in autonomous agents hinges on architectural safeguards that enforce intent-action consistency and runtime state tracking, rather than relying solely on linguistic safeguards; the proposed Action-Aware Supervision Layer provides a practical, plug-and-play solution to improve accountability and safety in multi-turn agent systems.

title: Computing on the Fly: Navigating a Vision for the Future of Drone Computing
summary:
The report envisions a decade in which drones move goods, medical supplies, and information at a scale comparable to national infrastructure investments like highways and the electric grid. Potential applications include natural disaster detection drones that spot wildfire sources within minutes, medical supply chains that bypass ground congestion to reach rural hospitals, and nationwide fleets that continuously inspect bridges and power lines. Realizing this future, however, requires closing what report authors call a "capability gap," where hardware and aspirations are outpacing the software and systems needed to operate safely at scale.
  The report identifies twelve technical challenges that must be addressed to realize the transformative potential of drone technology: Scaling to millions of drones; AI intelligence and assurance; Edge-cloud continuum and real-time coordination; AI autonomy and agentic systems; Data, training, and validation infrastructure; Critical infrastructure protection; Building reliable fleets from non-deterministic agents; Trust, security, and distributed authentication; Next-generation drone networks; Human-AI partnership and scalable insight; Standards, certification, and regulation; and Workforce development and education.
  These twelve challenges and proposed approaches to them form the basis of the report, laying out a multifaceted path forward for the evolution of done technology.

AI.tldr: A forward-looking report envisions drones as national-scale infrastructure and identifies 12 technical challenges to achieve scalable, safe drone operations, outlining a roadmap spanning scaling, AI, edge-cloud integration, security, standards, and workforce development.
AI.motivation: To articulate a strategic path to close the 'capability gap' between hardware aspirations and the software/systems required for safe, large-scale drone deployments across disaster response, logistics, and infrastructure inspection.
AI.method: Qualitative roadmap deriving from the identification of key technical challenges and proposed approaches; the abstract suggests a policy/technology roadmap rather than empirical experiments (no explicit methods described).
AI.result: The twelve challenges are enumerated and tied to proposed approaches, forming the basis for a multifaceted path forward for drone technology evolution.
AI.conclusion: Advancing drone capability to scale safely and effectively requires coordinated efforts across technology, governance, standards, and workforce development, as outlined by the twelve-challenge framework.

title: Federated Lightweight Fine-Tuning
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Extended preprint with appendix. Under review at ACCV 2026
summary: Federated fine-tuning is bottlenecked by communication: FedAvg and pseudo-gradient schemes transmit a payload that scales with the model, and gradient compression shrinks it by only a constant factor. We take a different lever. Mapping networks generate a network's weights from a small trainable latent through a frozen affine projection; because the map is shared and affine, averaging latents is exactly averaging the generated weights. We turn this into a practical low-bandwidth federated channel with two changes: a low-rank, seed-regenerable factorisation of the projection (cutting generator memory from ~80 GB to ~10 MB), and a delta formulation $θ= θ^{\mathrm{pre}} + U V^{\top} z$ that learns an additive correction around a shared centrally-pretrained base -- federated fine-tuning, which is what makes the method work at scale. A frozen orthogonal classifier head further removes the head from the payload while improving accuracy. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm, our method (FLITE, Federated Low-rank Iterative Training Engine) communicates 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client per round -- an 8718x reduction -- and reaches 74.67%, within ~0.5 pp of full-weight FedAvg. The averaging identity holds to floating-point precision ($6 \times 10^{-8}$); the method sits one to two orders of magnitude below PowerSGD and top-k on the bandwidth-accuracy Pareto; it matches or exceeds full-weight FedAvg under strong non-IID skew. int4 latents reach 648 bytes per round at unchanged accuracy, whereas int4 full-weight FedAvg collapses to chance.

AI.tldr: FLITE introduces Federated Low-rank Iterative Training Engine that uses a shared latent-based generator with a low-rank, seed-regenerable projection and a delta correction to enable ultra-low-bandwidth federated fine-tuning, achieving ~5 KB per client per round on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm and near-FedAvg accuracy, with strong performance under non-IID and int4 latents.
AI.motivation: Reduce communication in federated fine-tuning beyond traditional gradient compression by exploiting a shared, affine generator map where averaging latents exactly corresponds to averaging generated weights, enabling low-bandwidth federation at scale.
AI.method: Leverage mapping networks that generate a network's weights from a small trainable latent via a frozen affine projection. Introduce a low-rank factorization of the projection (seed-regenerable) and a delta formulation θ = θ^pre + U V^T z that learns an additive correction around a centrally-pretrained base. Freeze an orthogonal classifier head to further reduce payload. Evaluate on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm, comparing to FedAvg, PowerSGD, and top-k baselines.
AI.result: Per-round communication: 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client, ~8718x reduction. Accuracy 74.67%, within ~0.5 percentage points of full-weight FedAvg. Averaging identity holds to floating-point precision (6×10^-8). Outperforms PowerSGD and top-k on bandwidth-accuracy Pareto; matches or exceeds FedAvg under strong non-IID skew. int4 latents reduce per-round payload to 648 bytes with unchanged accuracy; int4 full-weight FedAvg collapses to chance.
AI.conclusion: FLITE achieves extreme bandwidth efficiency in federated fine-tuning with negligible accuracy loss, leveraging exact averaging of a shared latent generator and a central pretrained base. It offers substantial memory and communication savings and shows promise for scalable deployment in non-IID federations; potential for broader applicability with int4 compression.

title: Privileged Lesion-Context Relational Distillation for Mask-Free Skin Lesion Classification
comment: Manuscript submitted for consideration. The paper presents a mask-free skin lesion classification framework evaluated on HAM10000 and externally validated on ISIC 2018
summary: Accurate skin lesion classification can benefit from lesion segmentation masks, but requiring masks or an auxiliary segmentation model during inference reduces clinical practicality and increases computational complexity. This work introduces Privileged Lesion-Context Relational Distillation (PLCRD), a teacher-student framework that exploits lesion masks exclusively during training while preserving image-only inference. The privileged teacher jointly analyzes the original dermoscopic image and its mask-guided lesion region to learn lesion-specific and contextual diagnostic representations. An image-only student is then trained through complementary knowledge-transfer mechanisms that convey the teacher's diagnostic distribution, lesion-focused attention, inter-lesion relational geometry, and lesion-context structure. PLCRD decomposes deep representations into lesion and contextual embeddings and transfers their relational organization through inter-lesion similarity alignment, lesion-context affinity matching, separation regularization, and class-aware relational learning. This formulation avoids direct feature matching between heterogeneous teacher and student architectures and enables the student to internalize mask-informed diagnostic structure without accessing masks at deployment. The framework was evaluated on HAM10000 using lesion-disjoint data partitioning and externally validated on ISIC 2018 without retraining. PLCRD achieved a lesion-level macro-F1 of 0.773 +/- 0.018, balanced accuracy of 0.764 +/- 0.023, and macro-AUROC of 0.976 +/- 0.002 on HAM10000, together with a macro-F1 of 0.732 +/- 0.008 on ISIC 2018. The results indicate that privileged lesion annotations can be transformed into transferable relational knowledge, yielding a practical and interpretable approach to mask-free skin lesion classification.

AI.tldr: A teacher–student distillation framework that uses masks only during training to enable image-only skin lesion classification with privileged lesion-context relational knowledge.
AI.motivation: To retain the benefits of segmentation masks for lesion understanding while avoiding inference-time reliance on masks or extra segmentation models, thereby improving practicality and efficiency.
AI.method: PLCRD trains a privileged teacher on the original image and its mask-guided lesion region to learn lesion-specific and contextual representations. An image-only student is trained via transfers of diagnostic distribution, lesion-focused attention, inter-lesion relational geometry, and lesion-context structure. Representations are decomposed into lesion and contextual embeddings; relations are aligned via inter-lesion similarity, lesion-context affinity, separation regularization, and class-aware relational learning. No direct feature matching between heterogeneous architectures is required, enabling mask-informed knowledge to be internalized without masks at deployment.
AI.result: On HAM10000 (lesion-disjoint partition): macro-F1 0.773 ± 0.018, balanced accuracy 0.764 ± 0.023, macro-AUROC 0.976 ± 0.002. On ISIC 2018 (external validation): macro-F1 0.732 ± 0.008. The approach demonstrates transferable relational knowledge from privileged annotations to an image-only classifier.
AI.conclusion: Privileged lesion annotations can be transformed into transferable relational knowledge, yielding a practical, interpretable, mask-free framework for skin lesion classification.

title: AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling -- Full Technical Report
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by the first name and their role. See the contribution section for details
summary: Unlike conventional video game development, which relies on labor-intensive pipelines for asset production, animation, physics, and programming, video world models generate interactive environments from user inputs instantly. It enable us to create customized, explorable, and continuously evolving virtual world from text, an image, or video. Realizing this vision requires four tightly coupled capabilities: interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response. We present AlayaWorld, an interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24-fps video at 540p and 720p. Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, AlayaWorld generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. Its bounded visual context combines a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. To reduce long-term drift, the model is trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from its own roll-outs. We further introduce a discrete autoregressive distillation formulation that combines distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation, reducing inference from approximately 30 sampling steps to four steps per chunk. On iWorld-Bench, AlayaWorld achieves the best performance over long-horizon generation. Conceived as a full-stack, open-source, and long-term project, AlayaWorld is intended to provide an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

AI.tldr: AlayaWorld is an open-source interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24fps video from user inputs using a 15B diffusion transformer, via autoregressive latent chunks with a bounded context and a novel distillation pipeline, achieving strong long-horizon performance on iWorld-Bench and enabling extensible research.
AI.motivation: To enable interactive, customizable, persistent virtual worlds generated from text, image, or video, addressing labor-intensive asset pipelines and persistent consistency challenges in long-horizon video generation.
AI.method: A 15B video diffusion transformer generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. It uses a bounded visual context consisting of a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. Long-term drift is mitigated by training on corrupted histories and prediction residuals from its own roll-outs. Introduces a discrete autoregressive distillation combining distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation to reduce inference from ~30 steps to 4 steps per chunk.
AI.result: On iWorld-Bench, AlayaWorld achieves the best performance for long-horizon generation, producing 24fps video at 540p/720p. It is conceived as a full-stack, open-source project intended as an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.
AI.conclusion: AlayaWorld proposes a comprehensive, scalable framework for interactive, long-horizon video world modeling, integrating an ultra-large diffusion backbone, persistent context, drift-mitigating training, and a compact distillation-based inference pipeline, with demonstrated gains on iWorld-Bench and a goal of broad community adoption.

title: Eversion-based robots can enable safe access,steering and endoscopic imaging within the spinal subarachnoid space
summary: Safe navigation within the spinal subarachnoid space is constrained by its narrow, compliant, and delicate anatomy. Conventional catheters and continuum robots rely on proximal pushing, generating friction and shear along the tissue device interface that limit distal controllability and increase the risk of neural injury. Here, we present a 2 mm diameter eversion-growing robotic platform that enables friction minimised extension and steering within the human spinal subarachnoid space, validated through computational modelling, phantom experiments, and intact human cadaver studies. The robot integrates a miniature endoscope for real time intrathecal visualisation and advances by pressure driven tip eversion, localising motion to the distal tip while minimising translational sliding of the deployed body. Phantom experiments demonstrated reductions of 65.2% in mean interaction force and 48.0% in peak interaction force compared with matched push-based insertion. Physics based modelling showed that eversion based growth redistributed tissue loading, reducing local stress concentrations and interfacial shear relative to conventional insertion. In an intact human cadaver, the system achieved 150 mm of controlled intrathecal extension with concurrent fluoroscopic and endoscopic visualisation, providing access across multiple vertebral levels from a standard lumbar entry point. Postprocedural laminectomy and durotomy revealed no observable macroscopic disruption of the dura mater or surrounding neural structures. These results provide the first mechanically characterised and multimodally validated demonstration of eversion-based robotic navigation in intact human spinal anatomy, establishing a quantitative and procedural foundation for future intrathecal interventions. Further validation in larger anatomical cohorts and under physiological conditions will be required before clinical translation.

AI.tldr: Eversion-based 2 mm robotic catheter enables friction-minimized intrathecal navigation with real-time endoscopic visualization; validated in phantoms and cadavers, showing reduced tissue loading and 150 mm extension, but requires larger, physiology-relevant validation before clinical translation.
AI.motivation: Safe navigation in the spinal subarachnoid space is constrained by narrow, compliant anatomy; conventional push-based catheters cause friction, shear, and potential neural injury. A friction-minimized, distributed-tip eversion approach aims to reduce tissue loading while enabling distal control.
AI.method: A 2 mm diameter eversion-growing robot uses pressure-driven tip eversion to localize motion at the distal tip with minimal body sliding, integrated miniature endoscope for intrathecal visualization, and multimodal validation including computational modeling, phantom experiments, and intact human cadaver studies. Comparative metrics include interaction force reductions versus push-based insertion; stress redistribution predicted by physics-based modeling; fluoroscopic and endoscopic visualization during extended intrathecal navigation.
AI.result: Phantom experiments show 65.2% reductions in mean interaction force and 48.0% reductions in peak interaction force compared with push-based insertion. Physics-based modeling indicates redistributed tissue loading with lower local stress concentrations and interfacial shear. In an intact cadaver, 150 mm of controlled intrathecal extension achieved with concurrent imaging; no observable macroscopic dura or neural disruption post-procedure.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanically characterized, multimodally validated demonstration of eversion-based intrathecal navigation in intact human spinal anatomy and establishes a quantitative foundation for future intrathecal interventions. Further validation in larger anatomical cohorts and under physiological conditions is required before clinical translation.

title: An Analysis of Residual-Stream Geometry Across Transformer Depth
summary: We propose a transition-centred geometric analysis of transformer residual streams. Relative displacement measures how \emph{far} representations move between consecutive layers, and orthogonal Procrustes analysis separates each transition into a rigid rotation and a non-rigid residual. Across six instruction-tuned models, on code generation and cross-lingual translation, these measurements reveal reproducible depth regularities. Relative displacement is strongly layer-dependent; typically larger early and late, with a quieter middle third; and nearly invariant across conditions within each model. Rotation magnitude is nearly constant across depth, while Procrustes residual and angle concentration remain depth-modulated, with residual peaking at the final transition. During generation, non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement and residual than English targets. We present these as descriptive geometric regularities, not as measures of computational effort or causal explanations. The contribution is a measurement framework for residual-stream transitions and evidence that, in the settings studied here, depth curves are model-dependent and largely condition-stable.

AI.tldr: A geometry-based analysis of transformer residual streams using relative displacement and Procrustes decomposition to reveal depth- and condition-dependent regularities across six instruction-tuned models during code generation and translation.
AI.motivation: To characterize how representations evolve across layers in transformers and whether geometric regularities emerge that are consistent across models and tasks, without attributing causal efficacy.
AI.method: Compute relative displacement between consecutive layer representations and apply orthogonal Procrustes analysis to decompose transitions into rigid rotation and non-rigid residual. Analyze six instruction-tuned models on code generation and cross-lingual translation, examining depth-dependence and condition-stability of metrics (rotation magnitude, residual, and angle concentration).
AI.result: Relative displacement is strongly layer-dependent and largely invariant across conditions within a model; rotation magnitude is nearly constant with depth; Procrustes residual and angle concentration vary with depth, with residual peaking at the final transition; during generation, non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement and residual.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a descriptive measurement framework for residual-stream transitions, showing depth curves are model-dependent and largely condition-stable, and cautions against interpreting these metrics as causally explanatory or reflective of computational effort.

title: CGMap: A Geospatially Aware Deep Learning Framework for Crop Gap Mapping Using UAV
summary: In India, crop germination is primarily monitored by visual inspection and manual counting, which are prone to errors, despite their crucial role in determining eventual yield potential. This paper highlights a deep learning based pipeline which uses object detection methods and drone imagery to assess and provide a precise count of sugarcane germination in fields. The approch uses a pre-trained AI model to find germinated plant sampling and identify gaps, also known as ``bald spots'', which restricts field productivity. The techniques used here relies on the YOLOV8 architecture, which was trained on a carefully selected dataset of UAV photos taken in various agroclimatic zones of India. Here, we bring upon a novel orientation-normalization technique that uses minimum Spanning Trees (MST) to account for variations in planting geometry, allowing for dependable row and column extraction across a variety of field layouts. By converting detected seedlings into spatial point clouds, emergence gaps can be inferred from the anticipated spacing between plants. A geospatial germination map exported in Well-Known Text (WKT) format is the end result, and it can be easily incorporated into GIS platforms used by sugar mills and agronomists to direct transplant initiatives. Timely interventions based on the insights provided by the algorithm can significantly increase yield, resulting in higher profits. Hence, support proper allocation of resources, avoid wastage, and enhance long-term sustainability.

AI.tldr: YOLOv8-based UAV pipeline for sugarcane germination counting and gap mapping, with MST-based orientation normalization and WKT geospatial outputs.
AI.motivation: Manual germination counting is error-prone and labor-intensive; precise germination assessment directly informs transplant planning and yield potential in sugarcane across India's diverse agroclimates.
AI.method: Fine-tuned/pre-trained YOLOv8 detector on UAV imagery from multiple agroclimatic zones; orientation normalization via minimum spanning trees to align planting geometry; extract row/column structures; convert detections to spatial point clouds; infer emergence gaps from expected plant spacing; output geospatial germination map in Well-Known Text (WKT) for GIS integration.
AI.result: Accurate counting of germinated seedlings; identification of bald spots; robust row/column extraction across variable field layouts; GIS-ready geospatial map enabling informed transplant planning and resource allocation.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides timely, GIS-compatible insights to guide transplant initiatives, enhance yield, reduce waste, and promote sustainability in sugarcane cultivation, with practical applicability for sugar mills and agronomists.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Meta-Policies for Temporal Knowledge-Graph Memory under Partial Observability
summary: Partially observable reinforcement learning requires deciding what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time. We introduce a neuro-symbolic meta-policy that learns which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each decision point while keeping execution symbolic. Our setting uses temporal knowledge-graph memory in RoomKG, where hidden state and observations are represented as Resource Description Framework (RDF) graphs and memory is augmented with temporal RDF triple annotations. The model combines knowledge-graph encoding of memory contents with value heads for question answering, exploration, and forgetting, yielding a controller that is both adaptive and inspectable. This gives the work a direct Semantic Web grounding through RDF-based representation, annotation-compatible graph semantics, and graph-based symbolic operations over explicit memory state. On train/test room splits at long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance among the compared symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic systems while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic meta-policy for partially observable RL uses temporal RDF-based memory (RoomKG) to decide memory retention, retrieval, and forgetting; achieves state-of-the-art held-out performance with StarE-GNN at memory capacity 512 and retains step-level traceability.
AI.motivation: Enable adaptive, interpretable memory management in POMDPs by integrating symbolic memory heuristics with neural decision-making, grounded in Semantic Web representations (RDF/Knowledge Graphs).
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic controller learns which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each decision point while maintaining execution in symbolic form. Memory is a temporal knowledge-graph with RDF annotations; uses KG encoding of memory plus value heads for QA, exploration, and forgetting. The system yields a train/test setup (RoomKG) where a StarE-GNN-based configuration is evaluated for memory capacity 512 and is shown to be best among symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic baselines; memory-management decisions are traceable.
AI.result: Qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance on RoomKG under long-term memory capacity 512, outperforming symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic baselines while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.
AI.conclusion: Issues a Semantic Web-grounded, graph-based symbolic operation framework for memory management in POMDPs, delivering adaptive, inspectable control and strong performance; highlights the value of neuro-symbolic integration with explicit memory state and RDF-based representation, with potential limitations related to scalability and dataset specificity.

title: Stochastic Multi-Objective Kinodynamic Planning Against Adversaries
summary: This paper addresses multi-objective kinodynamic planning in environments with stochastic hybrid adversaries that probabilistically transition to adversarial modes based on the ego state. The goal is to construct the Pareto-front of paths that trade off execution cost and the probability of safety constraint violation (risk). Existing chance-constrained planners evaluate risk over open-loop trajectories, yielding overly conservative solutions that fail to account for ego-agent reactivity. To address this limitation, we shift the planning space to sequences of closed-loop policies, and integrate sample-based risk evaluation directly into tree construction via Monte-Carlo particle rollouts. We first introduce Stochastic Multi-Objective RRT (SMO-RRT), for which we prove probabilistic completeness, followed by Stochastic Multi-Objective Stable Sparse RRT (SMO-SST), which leverages selective pruning to improve numerical performance at the cost of completeness. For both algorithms, we derive a finite-sample bound on the probability of chance constraint violation for systems with non-Gaussian, state-dependent uncertainty, enabling probabilistically safe planning in a broad class of environments applicable to multi-agent systems, social navigation, and autonomous driving.

AI.tldr: Presents SMO-RRT/SMO-SST for multi-objective kinodynamic planning under stochastic adversaries, using closed-loop policies and Monte-Carlo risk evaluation; provides probabilistic completeness and finite-sample risk bounds for non-Gaussian, state-dependent uncertainty to construct Pareto-fronts of cost vs safety risk.
AI.motivation: Existing chance-constrained planners evaluate risk on open-loop trajectories, which yields overly conservative solutions and ignores ego-agent reactivity. There is a need to account for closed-loop policy sequences and state-dependent stochastic adversaries to safely and efficiently trade off performance and safety.
AI.method: Shift planning space from open-loop trajectories to sequences of closed-loop policies. Integrate Monte-Carlo particle rollouts for risk evaluation directly into tree construction. Develop SMO-RRT with probabilistic completeness, and SMO-SST with selective pruning to improve numerical performance at the expense of completeness. Derive finite-sample bounds on the probability of chance constraint violation for non-Gaussian, state-dependent uncertainty.
AI.result: Two algorithms with formal guarantees: SMO-RRT is probabilistically complete; SMO-SST offers computational efficiency via pruning while sacrificing completeness. For both, finite-sample bounds on chance-constraint violation are derived, enabling probabilistically safe planning under broad, non-Gaussian uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled framework for multi-objective, risk-aware planning under stochastic hybrid adversaries, enabling Pareto-front computation of cost versus safety risk. Applicable to multi-agent systems, social navigation, and autonomous driving, with a general approach to risk evaluation using closed-loop policies and Monte-Carlo rollouts.

title: MambaLSTM: A Spatio-Temporal Framework for Enhanced Traffic Accident Risk Prediction
summary: In traffic accident risk prediction, most studies overlook the extra noise that could be incorporated when fusing temporal features into spatial features, and some models struggle to capture global correlations among spatial regions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel traffic accident risk prediction framework named MambaLSTM. First, we develop a squeeze-and-excitation temporal feature fusion module to integrate temporal information without compromising spatio-temporal integrity. Second, we introduce a new patch embedding module for effectively capturing semantic relationships among spatially adjacent regions. Additionally, we introduce a Mamba block based on state-space models to model global spatial semantics in urban regions. Finally, we propose a MambaLSTM unit to efficiently capture long- and short-term temporal dependencies for identifying dynamic risk patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed model's superiority over state-of-the-art methods. The code is released at https://github.com/Zhenzovo/MambaLSTM.

AI.tldr: MambaLSTM: a new traffic accident risk-prediction framework that fuses temporal and spatial information with four components (SE temporal fusion, patch embedding, Mamba block via state-space models for global spatial semantics, and MambaLSTM unit) to capture dynamic risk patterns and outperform SOTA on real-world data; code available.
AI.motivation: Addresses noise and loss of global spatial correlations when fusing temporal and spatial features in accident risk prediction, and the need to capture both long- and short-term temporal dynamics and global spatial semantics.
AI.method: 1) Squeeze-and-Excitation temporal feature fusion to integrate temporal information without harming spatio-temporal integrity. 2) Patch embedding to capture semantic relationships among neighboring regions. 3) Mamba block based on state-space models for global spatial semantics in urban areas. 4) MambaLSTM unit to model long and short-term temporal dependencies.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: MambaLSTM effectively captures dynamic risk patterns in traffic accident data and offers superior performance; code is released on GitHub.

title: Image Editing Models are Numerical Solvers
summary: We investigate whether a pretrained generative image-editing model can provide a common interface for numerical simulation. Physical inputs and solutions are rendered as images, while scalar quantities such as material properties, diffusivity, and loading parameters enter through lightweight adapters. Using established numerical and analytic solvers for supervision, we apply the same architecture and training protocol to heterogeneous elliptic equations, forced heat and Burgers evolution, complex Ginzburg-Landau dynamics, two-dimensional Navier-Stokes prediction, potential flow, elasticity, eikonal travel time, phase-field fracture, and entropic optimal transport. The results show that a pretrained image model can represent diverse static and time-dependent physical mappings, including unstable and shock-like behavior, when each task is expressed through a suitable visual encoding. This work is a capability study rather than an attempt to surpass specialized solvers. It also identifies fundamental constraints: image and latent representations complicate numerical range selection and direct enforcement of governing equations or invariants, while a failed Kuramoto-Sivashinsky experiment indicates that representation errors prevent meaningful long-horizon simulation of chaotic systems.

AI.tldr: Pretrained image-editing models can serve as a common interface for diverse numerical simulations by encoding physics as images and using adapters for scalar inputs; demonstrated across elliptic equations, heat/Burgers, complex dynamics, Navier–Stokes, elasticity, wave travel, phase-field fracture, and entropic OT; not a replacement for solvers; limitations include representation-range and equation enforcement challenges, with a failed chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky run showing limits for long-horizon predictions.
AI.motivation: Explore whether a single pretrained image-based model can act as a universal interface for numerical simulation, reducing reliance on bespoke solvers and architectures while preserving performance across a broad class of physical problems.
AI.method: Use a pretrained generative image-editing model. Represent physical inputs and solutions as images; parameters (material properties, diffusivity, loading) enter via lightweight adapters. Supervise with established numerical/analytic solvers and apply the same architecture/training protocol to a broad set of problems (elliptic equations, forced heat and Burgers, complex Ginzburg–Landau, 2D Navier–Stokes, potential flow, elasticity, eikonal travel time, phase-field fracture, entropic OT).
AI.result: The pretrained image model can represent a wide range of static and time-dependent physical mappings, including unstable and shock-like behavior, when each task is expressed with appropriate visual encoding; the work is a capability study, not a solver competitor.
AI.conclusion: Represents a capability rather than a solver; key constraints include difficulties in selecting numerical ranges and enforcing governing equations/invariants via image/latent representations; a Kuramoto–Sivashinsky failure highlights that representation errors hinder meaningful long-horizon chaotic simulations; further work is needed to mitigate these representation-driven limitations.

title: MAGE: Human-Like Macro Placement via Agentic Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Macro placement still requires substantial manual refinement in industrial physical design flows. We present MAGE (Macro Placement Agentic Engine), a multimodal multi-agent framework for macro placement refinement. MAGE decomposes the macro placement task into a six-phase workflow that combines structured floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement. Expert floorplanning knowledge is encoded through natural-language directives and validation criteria, rather than learned from labeled placement data. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements and propagates feedback from higher-quality solutions. We also introduce four metrics for quantifying human-likeness in macro placement: notch score, whitespace score, pocket score, and alignment score. These metrics capture structural properties used by expert designers but not directly measured by conventional PPA metrics. Across nine designs in NanGate45 and GlobalFoundries 12nm enablements, MAGE achieves geometric-mean improvements of 11.1%-19.3% in WNS and 70.0%-74.0% in TNS over commercial macro placers. On the three NanGate45 designs, for which human-expert and Hier-RTLMP baselines are available, MAGE improves WNS and TNS by 18.3% and 72.5% over the human expert, and by 47.0% and 80.4% over Hier-RTLMP, with comparable wirelength and power. On human-likeness metrics, MAGE improves the overall score by 6%-48% over all baselines. Additional case studies on anonymized netlists, unseen designs, dense rectilinear floorplans, and high-utilization settings show that the framework transfers to new placement settings without design-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: MAGE is a NL-guided multimodal macro placement refinement framework with a six-phase workflow and tournament-style refinement, plus four human-likeness metrics, achieving strong WNS/TNS gains and transferability without retraining.
AI.motivation: Industrial macro placement requires substantial manual refinement based on expert knowledge; current data-driven methods rely on labeled data. This work encodes expert floorplanning knowledge via natural-language directives and validation criteria and introduces metrics to quantify human-likeness.
AI.method: Six-phase macro placement workflow combining structured floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement. Expert knowledge is encoded through natural-language directives and validation criteria rather than learned from data. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements and propagates feedback from higher-quality solutions. Introduces four human-likeness metrics: notch score, whitespace score, pocket score, and alignment score.
AI.result: Across nine designs in NanGate45 and GlobalFoundries 12nm enablements, MAGE achieves geometric-mean improvements of 11.1%-19.3% in WNS and 70.0%-74.0% in TNS over commercial macro placers. On NanGate45 designs, MAGE improves WNS by 18.3% and TNS by 72.5% over a human expert, and by 47.0% WNS and 80.4% TNS over Hier-RTLMP, with comparable wirelength and power. Human-likeness metrics show 6%-48% improvement over baselines. Additional case studies show transfer to unseen designs and settings without retraining.
AI.conclusion: MAGE demonstrates effective integration of expert knowledge, yielding substantial placement quality gains and improved human-likeness, while generalizing to new, unseen designs without dataset-specific retraining.

title: From Distances to Trajectories: Real-Time Signed Distance Function Mapping and Distance-Accelerated Motion Planning for UAVs
summary: Autonomous flight in cluttered environments requires a robot to build a geometric map of its surroundings and plan safe, dynamically feasible trajectories, all onboard and in real time. Conventional approaches treat mapping and planning as separate stages and often rely on binary occupancy for collision checking. We argue that these two stages should be co-designed around a single representation: a signed distance function (SDF). By encoding distance to the nearest obstacle, an SDF provides richer information for planning and trajectory optimization than occupancy alone. We develop an Octree REsidual Network (OREN) that pairs an explicit octree prior with an implicit neural residual to reconstruct SDFs online from point cloud observations with the efficiency of volumetric methods and the accuracy and differentiability of neural methods. In tandem, we develop Bubble$^\star$, a search-based planner that exploits the distance information to grow maximal collision-free balls, which we call bubbles, with formal guarantees of termination, completeness, and failure detection. Planning over a graph of bubbles significantly reduces collision checks compared to a grid-based A$^\star$ search and returns a bubble sequence that forms a safe corridor for trajectory optimization. We demonstrate the integrated OREN-Bubble$^\star$ approach onboard a quadrotor, navigating unseen indoor environments in real time under tight compute constraints. OREN improves SDF estimation by $22$% compared to baselines, while Bubble$^\star$ finds trajectories spanning $\approx 90$ m through a cluttered environment in $1$-$3$ sec., whereas baselines take up to $10$ sec. in the same environment.

AI.tldr: Co-design of mapping and planning around a signed distance function (SDF); introduces OREN for online SDF estimation from point clouds and Bubble* for a bubble-based planner with formal guarantees, enabling real-time onboard autonomous flight in cluttered environments.
AI.motivation: Conventional robotics pipelines treat mapping and planning separately and rely on binary occupancy for collision checking, which limits planning quality and onboard real-time performance; an SDF provides richer geometric information (distance to obstacles) for planning and trajectory optimization.
AI.method: OREN combines an explicit octree prior with an implicit neural residual to reconstruct SDFs online from point cloud observations, achieving efficient, differentiable estimates; Bubble* is a search-based planner that grows maximal collision-free balls (bubbles) to form a graph that yields safe corridors while providing termination, completeness, and failure detection guarantees. Planning over the bubble graph reduces collision checks vs grid-based A* and yields a bubble sequence for trajectory optimization.
AI.result: Onboard quadrotor demonstration navigating unseen indoor environments in real time under tight compute constraints; OREN improves SDF estimation by 22% over baselines; Bubble* finds trajectories spanning ~90 meters in 1–3 seconds in cluttered environments, while baselines take up to 10 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Integrating SDF-based mapping with bubble-based planning yields a real-time, complete, and robust autonomous flight pipeline in cluttered environments, with improved map accuracy and faster trajectory generation.

title: Multi-layer MIMO Relay as Deep Physical Neural Networks: Power Amplifiers as Activation Functions
summary: Wireless physical neural networks (WPNNs) embed neural computation directly into analog hardware, offering lower energy consumption and latency than conventional digital implementations. In this paper, we propose a deep WPNN in which nonlinear activations are realized by a multi-hop multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) relay network, in which each relay implements a trainable complex linear gain and bias, followed by the power amplifier's intrinsic nonlinearity acting as an activation function. The cascade of multiple relays therefore realizes an over-the-air fully connected network whose parameters can be trained end-to-end. We develop two transceiver designs for different channel state information (CSI) availability scenarios: a least squares (LS)-based scheme requiring only receiver-side CSI, and a singular-value-decomposition (SVD)-based scheme requiring both transmitter-side and receiver-side CSI. Simulation results show that the proposed architecture enables accurate over-the-air inference for image classification. In particular, the results highlight the advantage of exploiting hardware nonlinearity for enhanced inference capability.

AI.tldr: A deep Wireless Physical Neural Network (WPNN) is proposed, where nonlinear activations are realized by the intrinsic nonlinearity of power amplifiers in a cascade of trainable MIMO relays, enabling an over-the-air fully connected network trained end-to-end. Two CSI-aware transceiver designs (LS-based with receiver CSI only; SVD-based with full CSI) are developed. Simulations demonstrate accurate over-the-air image classification and show hardware nonlinearity can enhance inference performance.
AI.motivation: Reduce energy consumption and latency of neural computation by embedding it in analog wireless hardware; leverage over-the-air computation through a trainable multi-hop MIMO relay chain to realize fully connected networks.
AI.method: A deep WPNN is built as a cascade of relay nodes, each implementing a trainable complex linear gain and bias. The power amplifier nonlinearity serves as the activation function. End-to-end training is performed. Two transceiver designs are provided: LS-based requiring only receiver-side CSI, and SVD-based requiring both transmitter and receiver CSI.
AI.result: Simulation results show accurate over-the-air inference for image classification using the proposed architecture. Exploiting hardware nonlinearity can enhance inference capability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed WPNN architecture is feasible for over-the-air neural inference, enabling energy-efficient analog computation with trainable nonlinearities, and performing well for image classification under the considered CSI scenarios.

title: Moving Alphabet: A Controlled Study of Training Data for Text-to-Video Generation
summary: Text-to-video generation has advanced significantly over the past five years through scaling of model size, data, and compute. Unlike model architecture, training data is often underexplored. Real-world data curation is complex and non-trivial, involving clip selection from raw videos and captioning to create video-text pairs for learning text-to-video mappings. We study how data distribution and caption quality impact text-to-video models. To enable controlled experiments, we introduce Moving Alphabet, a procedural testbed that renders letters with varying fonts, colors, sizes, and positions, moving in different directions and speeds against a black background. This design allows precise control over data distribution and caption quality by corrupting ground-truth metadata. Our experiments yield three findings: a) a diverse and balanced distribution of video content and duration is critical for generalization; b) caption quality significantly affects both model performance and training efficiency, suggesting that text-to-video models are bounded by video understanding capabilities; and c) classifier-free guidance and fine-tuning on high-quality data provide partial recovery from models trained on corrupted captions, but cannot fully compensate for poor pre-training data. We believe these insights can inform the development of large-scale text-to-video models, and we advocate for greater attention to the science of pre-training data.

AI.tldr: A study on data distribution and caption quality in text-to-video models, using a controlled testbed called Moving Alphabet; shows diversity and caption quality critically shape generalization and training efficiency; partial recovery from poor data via classifier-free guidance and fine-tuning, but not full compensation.
AI.motivation: To understand how training data properties—distribution and caption quality—limit or enable text-to-video learning, addressing the underexplored role of data curation in real-world datasets.
AI.method: Introduce Moving Alphabet, a procedural testbed rendering letters with varying fonts, colors, sizes, and motions to control data distribution; generate corrupted ground-truth captions to vary caption quality; perform controlled experiments on text-to-video models examining effects on generalization, training efficiency, and response to guidance/fine-tuning.
AI.result: Findings: (a) diverse and balanced content/duration distributions are essential for generalization; (b) caption quality strongly affects model performance and training efficiency, indicating a bound set by video understanding; (c) classifier-free guidance and high-quality fine-tuning offer partial recovery from corrupted captions but cannot fully offset poor pre-training data.
AI.conclusion: Highlights the importance of pre-training data science for large-scale text-to-video models and suggests the Moving Alphabet framework as a controlled means to study data-related effects, urging more attention to data curation and quality in future work.

title: Engineering Trustworthy Agentic AI for Critical Systems
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems, capable of autonomous perception, planning, tool use, and multi-step action, are increasingly proposed for critical engineering domains where decisions carry physical, operational, or economic consequences. This survey addresses a gap in current literature by treating trustworthiness, whether agentic behavior can be verified, audited, and trusted under the constraints that engineering practice actually requires, as a first-class engineering property, rather than evaluating agentic AI by task capability alone. The study adopts a trustworthiness model organized around five cross-cutting dimensions: safety and constraint satisfaction; robustness and reliability; transparency and interpretability; accountability and auditability; and privacy and security. This is mapped onto an agentic assurance workflow spanning perception through audit. Building on this foundation, agentic systems architectures, threats, concrete trust mechanisms, and quantitative metrics are surveyed for direct application in agentic systems development and evaluation. These principles are then examined across four constraint-bound engineering domains: power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, high-performance computing, and communication networks, identifying recurring design patterns, shared failure modes, and domain-specific gaps. Synthesizing across those domains, agentic AI trustworthiness is shown to be a single problem, with a path outlined toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework analogous to the graded certification regimes used by mature safety-critical engineering fields.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys trustworthiness of agentic AI in engineering, integrating five cross-cutting dimensions into an agentic assurance workflow, and argues for a cross-domain, reusable certification-like framework across four domains.
AI.motivation: Current literature emphasizes capability and performance; there is a gap where trustworthiness must be treated as a first-class engineering property—verifiable, auditable, and trustworthy under real-world engineering constraints.
AI.method: Proposes a trustworthiness model with five dimensions (safety & constraint satisfaction; robustness & reliability; transparency & interpretability; accountability & auditability; privacy & security), maps this onto an agentic assurance workflow from perception to audit, surveys agentic architectures, threats, trust mechanisms, and quantitative metrics, and applies the framework across four constraint-bound domains (power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, high-performance computing, and communication networks).
AI.result: Synthesizes cross-domain patterns: trustworthiness is a single, unified problem; identifies recurring design patterns and shared failure modes, plus domain-specific gaps; demonstrates the potential for a reusable cross-domain assurance framework analogous to graded certification in safety-critical engineering.
AI.conclusion: Advocates treating agentic AI trustworthiness as a core engineering property and outlines a path toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework that could underpin graded certification for agentic systems.

title: Physical Self-Supervised Learning: IMU Sensing without Manual Labels
comment: 15 pages, 20 figures. Published in ACM MobiSys 2026
summary: Deep neural networks have become a promising approach for IMU-based sensing, but their scalability is fundamentally limited by costly labeled data and poor robustness to heterogeneous devices, placements, and users. Existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods reduce but do not remove this dependence, still requiring labeled data for domain adaptation and largely ignoring known physical structure. We propose physical self-supervised learning, an autoencoder-style paradigm for label-free IMU sensing. We replace the conventional neural decoder with an auto-adaptive physics decoder, a learnable family of kinematic equations that enforces explicit physical structure while adapting across environments, and adopt a hybrid two-stage IMU encoder with reconstruction in a structured latent space to mitigate sensor noise. Our framework further introduces probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor and object motion, a multi-view kinematic tree to exploit sparse physical self-supervised signals, and an uncertainty-aware formulation to handle the inherent ambiguity of IMU inference. Evaluated on inertial tracking and full-body motion capture over public datasets and realistic deployments, physical self-supervised learning reduces errors by up to 5x for tracking and 4x for motion capture in challenging generalization scenarios, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without any labels.

AI.tldr: Physical self-supervised learning for IMU sensing combines an auto-adaptive physics decoder with a structured latent space and probabilistic, frequency-spatial constraints to enable label-free tracking and motion capture with strong generalization across devices and deployments.
AI.motivation: Address the data-label bottleneck and robustness gaps in IMU-based learning by embedding explicit physical structure into self-supervised learning, enabling cross-device/environment generalization without labeled data.
AI.method: An autoencoder-style architecture where the decoder is an auto-adaptive physics decoder (learnable kinematic equations) enforcing explicit physical structure; a two-stage IMU encoder with reconstruction in a structured latent space to mitigate sensor noise; probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor vs. object motion; a multi-view kinematic tree to exploit sparse physical self-supervision signals; and an uncertainty-aware formulation to handle inherent IMU ambiguity.
