AI.result: On inertial tracking and full-body motion capture across public datasets and real deployments, the method yields up to 5x error reduction for tracking and 4x for motion capture, outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without any labels.
AI.conclusion: Infusing physical structure via a learnable physics decoder and structured latent representations enables robust, label-free generalization in IMU sensing, reducing reliance on labeled data and improving robustness to heterogeneity.

title: STS-NET: Spatio-Temporal Stress Network for Self-Supervised Crop Stress Detection using Satellite Image Time Series
summary: Early and accurate detection of crop stress is essential to improve agricultural productivity and ensure global food security. However, collecting a large labeled crop stress dataset is a challenging task. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel spatial-temporal stress network (STS-NET), built on a self-supervised 3D-convolutional autoencoder (3D-CAE), designed to utilize Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) data for crop stress detection. STS-NET exploits four vegetation indices: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), Red-Edge Chlorophyll Index (RECI) and Normalized Difference Red-Edge Index (NDRE) obtained from high resolution Planetscope imagery to capture spatiotemporal stress patterns. The model is trained on our BSPT (Barnala Spatial-Temporal) dataset and evaluated on a real-world sugarcane dataset collected over a year from a 2.5-acre test plot located in Lakhimpur-Kheri (LK) district in Uttar Pradesh in India. STS-NET achieved a precision of 97. 98\% for water stress, 85.08\% for nitrogen stress, and 83.47\% for combined stress. The results demonstrate the potential of STS-NET in effectively detecting stress in sugarcane crops with minimal reliance on labeled data. Furthermore, STS-NET can serve as a robust feature extractor for simpler models.

AI.tldr: STS-NET: a self-supervised 3D-CAE framework using Satellite Image Time Series and four vegetation indices to detect crop stress with high precision under limited labeled data; validated on sugarcane data.
AI.motivation: Address scarcity of labeled crop-stress data; leverage spatiotemporal patterns in SITS via self-supervised learning to enable early and accurate stress detection.
AI.method: Develop STS-NET built on a self-supervised 3D convolutional autoencoder; inputs four vegetation indices (NDVI, GNDVI, RECI, NDRE) from Planetscope; trained on BSPT dataset; STS-NET serves as robust feature extractor for downstream models; evaluated on real-world sugarcane data over a year.
AI.result: Precision results: water stress 97.98%; nitrogen stress 85.08%; combined stress 83.47% on the sugarcane dataset; demonstrates efficacy with minimal labeled data.
AI.conclusion: STS-NET demonstrates strong potential for early crop-stress detection and can function as a versatile feature extractor for simpler models in agritech pipelines.

title: Attacking Graph Foundation Models Through Their Shared Representation
summary: A graph foundation model generalizes across graph domains by mapping every input into one shared representation before any task reasoning. We call this map the alignment layer, the component that separates a graph foundation model from a graph neural network, and we show it is a distinct attack surface that prior work has not studied. We attack it at inference time, with no access to training, on six public models spanning spectral tokenizers, text embedding spaces, and a discrete codebook. A directed representation-space perturbation collapses every model, but at a budget comparable to the representation norm a plain graph network also needs, with one exception: OpenGraph, whose spectral tokenizer collapses at a fifth of that budget, an alignment-specific fragility a plain network does not share and which a same-representation control traces to the tokenizer rather than the decoder. A realizable input-space attack that edits edges, features, or text removes at least half the correct predictions on three of the six models at peak. How much of this fragility an input-access attacker realizes tracks how directly the decoder reads the representation, and not the clean accuracy a task leaves; we measure this carrier gain structurally from the decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity, and report clean-accuracy headroom as a within-model ordering heuristic that does not survive on realizable attacks.

AI.tldr: Alignment-layer fragility in graph foundation models enables both representation-space and input-space attacks, with OpenGraph showing stronger tokenizer-linked vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Identify the alignment layer as a distinct, empirically attackable surface in graph foundation models and understand how its fragility affects robustness across diverse graph architectures.
AI.method: Evaluate six public models spanning spectral tokenizers, text embedding spaces, and a discrete codebook; perform inference-time representation-space perturbations; execute realizable input-space attacks editing edges, features, or text; quantify attacker impact via the decoder’s local Lipschitz sensitivity and a same-representation control; derive a clean-accuracy headroom ordering as an inner-model heuristic.
AI.result: A directed representation-space perturbation collapses all models within a budget comparable to the representation norm; OpenGraph’s spectral tokenizer collapses at about one-fifth that budget; an alignment-specific fragility appears that a plain network does not share, linked to the tokenizer rather than the decoder; input-space attacks editing edges/features/text remove at least half the correct predictions on three of six models at peak.
AI.conclusion: The fragility is tied to how directly the decoder reads the representation; the decoder’s local Lipschitz sensitivity captures the attacker’s effectiveness (carrier gain); clean-accuracy headroom is a within-model heuristic that fails under realizable attacks, highlighting the alignment layer as a critical attack surface needing defense.

title: A Controlled Study of Attention-Only Transformers
summary: Feed-forward networks hold two thirds of a transformer's non-embedding parameters, yet the architecture has not received a necessity test that controls parameters, compute, and depth at once. We pretrain attention-only decoder transformers (Simple Attention Networks, SANs) against standard transformers matched separately for parameter count, training FLOPs, and depth (2 to 48 layers), for up to 105B tokens at 6M to 87M parameters. Deleting feed-forward layers in place is costly: the standard transformer leads by 0.47 nats at matched depth and 0.26 nats at matched FLOPs. Reallocating the freed budget into attention depth closes the gap: at matched parameters the difference is 0.006 nats (0.27 percent of loss), reproducible to one part in ten thousand across seed pairs, shrinking across 5B, 30B, and 105B budgets, and holding near 0.02 nats across a 29x size range. Three measurements localize the remaining gap to parametric recall: attention-only models are better on context-grounded answers and worse where knowledge must come from weights. Weight spectra show why: routing matrices (Q/K) crystallize early, content matrices accumulate rank slowly, and removing feed-forward layers relocates this accumulation to the attention output projection. QK-normalization, not feed-forward layers or residual gating, keeps 48-layer attention-only stacks trainable. The deficit concentrates on low-context query prediction and localizes there entirely by the largest budget. A pre-registered test confirms the account: it predicts a 0.02 to 0.05 nat gap on knowledge-dense web text; a matched pair trained on fineweb-edu measures 0.040. Within the tested regime, attention does the rest.

AI.tldr: Attention-only decoders (SANs) can nearly match standard transformers when matched for parameters, compute, and depth; the remaining gap is due to parametric recall and knowledge encoded in weights, not architectural necessity of feed-forward layers.
AI.motivation: FFN-heavy transformers account for most parameters; it remains unclear whether FF layers are necessary once parameter, compute, and depth are controlled. This study tests this by comparing attention-only decoders to standard transformers across budgets and depths to isolate the true architectural necessity of FF components.
AI.method: Pretrain attention-only decoders (SANs) and standard transformers under matched conditions: equal parameter counts, training FLOPs, and depth ranging from 2 to 48 layers; evaluate up to 105B tokens with 6M–87M parameter models. Investigate deleting FF layers, reallocating budget to attention depth, and enforce QK normalization; analyze weight spectra to trace where learning accumulates; include pre-registered tests on knowledge-dense tasks.
AI.result: With FF layers removed and budget reallocated to attention depth, the performance gap closes markedly: at matched parameters the gap is ~0.006 nats (0.27%) of loss and reproducible across seeds; the remaining gap localizes to parametric recall (knowledge from weights). Weight analysis shows early Q/K routing crystallization, slow development of content matrices, and shift of rank accumulation to the attention output projection after removing FF layers. QK-normalization is crucial for training 48-layer SANs. The deficit is most pronounced on low-context query prediction and entirely relocates to knowledge-dense tasks at large budgets; pre-registered tests predict a gap of 0.02–0.05 nats on web text, e.g., 0.040 in a fineweb-edu setting.
AI.conclusion: Attention-only architectures with proper QK normalization can nearly match standard transformers under controlled budgets, implying FF layers are not strictly necessary for performance within the tested regime. Remaining gaps are primarily due to how knowledge is stored (weights) rather than architectural deficits, guiding future work toward improving parametric recall and weight-based knowledge representation.

title: UVFaceFusion: Fast Multi-view Topologically Consistent Face Reconstruction in the Wild via UV-space Neural Fusion
summary: Reconstructing high-fidelity facial geometry with an assigned topology is essential for digital avatar creation and animation, yet existing automated methods often trade off geometric fidelity and in-the-wild generalization. We present UVFaceFusion, a feed-forward framework for multi-view, fixed-topology face reconstruction from daily images. Our key idea is to replace heuristic topological optimization with learnable neural fusion in a canonical UV space. Given multi-view images, we first obtain dense point maps and facial UV correspondences of each view using VGGT and Pixel3DMM, respectively. Then, the view-specific point maps are lifted into the canonical UV domain and fused with a novel mask-aware neural fusion network. The network predicts a complete UV-space point map, from which a fixed-topology mesh is directly sampled. Although trained only on Ava-256, UVFaceFusion generalizes well to multiple public benchmarks and in-the-wild captures, benefiting from its canonical UV-space geometry-to-geometry fusion that reduces dependence on dataset-specific appearance and capture conditions. Experiments on various benchmarks show that UVFaceFusion achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy while reconstructing a mesh from 16 input views in less than 3 seconds on a single RTX 4090. Code is available at https://github.com/grignarder/UVFaceFusion.

AI.tldr: UVFaceFusion is a feed-forward, multi-view, fixed-topology facial reconstruction method that operates in a canonical UV space with a mask-aware neural fusion network, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and fast inference.
AI.motivation: To achieve high-fidelity, fixed-topology facial geometry with strong generalization to in-the-wild images. Existing methods trade geometric fidelity against generalization; a canonical UV-space fusion approach aims to unify geometry while reducing dataset-specific biases.
AI.method: From multi-view images, obtain dense point maps via VGGT and facial UV correspondences via Pixel3DMM. Lift view-specific point maps into a canonical UV domain and fuse with a mask-aware neural fusion network to predict a complete UV-space point map, enabling direct sampling of a fixed-topology mesh. Trained on Ava-256, then tested across multiple public benchmarks and in-the-wild data.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy on benchmarks; reconstructs a 3D mesh from 16 views in under 3 seconds on a single RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: Canonical UV-space geometry-to-geometry fusion reduces dependence on dataset-specific appearance and capture conditions, enabling fast, generalizable high-fidelity fixed-topology face reconstruction.

title: When Does Machine Learning Beat Value Sorting? A Three-Dataset Diagnostic of Exposure-Weighted Shipment Prioritization
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables, accepted for presentation at AIIIP 2026
summary: Delay-risk models are usually judged by predictive accuracy. What matters in practice is narrower: with capacity to review only a few shipments, which ones should a manager check first? We evaluate whether machine learning clears a demanding no-model baseline: inspect the highest-value shipments first. Across three real supply-chain contexts: SCMS procurement, DataCo logistics, and Olist e-commerce, we use leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation and 1000-sample paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking by predicted delay severity times known value (M1) beats severity-only ranking in all three datasets, yet it does not generally beat value sorting. At a 10% review budget, M1 minus VALUE_ONLY is -5.5 percentage points (pp) for SCMS, +10.1 pp for DataCo, and -4.9 pp for Olist. The divide is consistent with severity learnability: DataCo has R^2 = 0.27 and calibration bias of +0.01 days, whereas SCMS and Olist have R^2 of approximately -0.02 and negative calibration bias. Nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining does not deliver a stable improvement over M1. Rather than proposing a new learning algorithm, this paper presents a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol. Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark, and ML should be deployed only after severity learnability and calibration have been audited and the model clears that gate under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation.

AI.tldr: Value-based shipment ranking (VALUE_ONLY) is a robust benchmark; ML severity-based ranking (M1) often helps but rarely beats value-sorted selection. Across three real datasets, M1 underperforms VALUE_ONLY in most cases and gains are inconsistent. Leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation and calibration/learnability checks are essential before deployment; nested-CV retraining offers no stable improvement.
AI.motivation: To test whether ML delay-risk models add value beyond a simple high-value-first policy under realistic review budgets and leakage constraints.
AI.method: Three real contexts (SCMS procurement, DataCo logistics, Olist e-commerce). Compare ranking rules: M1 (predicted delay severity × known value) vs VALUE_ONLY (value sorting) vs severity-only. Use leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation with 1000-sample bootstrap CIs. Evaluate at fixed budget (e.g., 10%). Also test nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining.
AI.result: M1 beats severity-only ranking in all datasets but does not generally beat VALUE_ONLY. At 10% budget, M1−VALUE_ONLY differences: SCMS −5.5 pp, DataCo +10.1 pp, Olist −4.9 pp. DataCo shows moderate severity learnability (R^2=0.27; calibration bias +0.01 days); SCMS and Olist show poor learnability (R^2≈−0.02; negative calibration bias). Nested-CV retraining yields no stable improvement over M1.
AI.conclusion: Deploy ML only after auditing severity learnability and calibration under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation. Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark; ML adds value only if severity is learnable and well-calibrated.

title: Scalable and Efficient Joint Spiking Embedding Predictive Architecture for Large-Scale Dynamic Graphs
summary: Dynamic graph learning aims to capture evolving structural and semantic patterns in real-world systems, such as fraud detection and recommender systems. Due to the scarcity of labeled data in real-world dynamic graphs, recent studies have introduced generative or contrastive paradigms (e.g., masked graph autoencoders or graph contrastive learning) to generate task-agnostic graph embeddings. However, these methods typically rely on complex edge-level reconstruction objectives and tailored graph augmentation strategies. This incurs substantial computational overhead when scaling to large-scale dynamic graphs. In this paper, we propose SG-JEPA, a joint spiking embedding predictive architecture for large-scale dynamic graphs. In contrast to existing self-supervised methods, SG-JEPA partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension to learn embeddings that are predictive of each other via additional spatial-temporal information. Furthermore, through encoding sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings, spiking neurons enable SG-JEPA to adapt to the varying computational constraints of downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SG-JEPA achieves competitive or even superior performance over discriminative baselines on node classification, while effectively scaling to the dynamic graph with 13 million edges. SG-JEPA avoids the complex machinery (negative sampling, graph augmentations, edge-level reconstruction, etc.), resulting in superior training efficiency and memory scalability compared with prior self-supervised dynamic graph baselines.

AI.tldr: SG-JEPA is a scalable self-supervised dynamic graph learning method that uses joint spiking embeddings and temporal context-target partitioning to predict embeddings, achieving competitive accuracy with high efficiency on large graphs.
AI.motivation: Dynamic graphs often lack labeled data and current self-supervised methods rely on expensive edge-level reconstructions and graph augmentations, hindering scalability to large-scale dynamic graphs.
AI.method: SG-JEPA introduces a joint spiking embedding predictive architecture. It partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension, uses spatial-temporal information to make embeddings predictive of each other, and encodes sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings via spiking neurons to adapt to downstream computational constraints. It avoids negative sampling, heavy graph augmentations, and edge-level reconstructions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows SG-JEPA achieves competitive or superior performance compared with discriminative baselines on node classification and scales to dynamic graphs with about 13 million edges, with improved training efficiency and memory scalability over prior self-supervised dynamic graph baselines.
AI.conclusion: SG-JEPA provides a scalable, efficient self-supervised framework for dynamic graphs, achieving strong node-classification performance without the heavy machinery typical of earlier methods and demonstrating good scalability to large graphs.

title: ZeroSplat: Generalized Referring Segmentation in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Recent advancements in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled language-guided scene understanding. However, existing Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting (R3DGS) methods are fundamentally restricted to single-target queries. To reflect the ambiguity of real-world instructions, we introduce the Generalized Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting Segmentation (GR3DGS) task, which requires dynamically segmenting an arbitrary number of targets (0, 1, or $N$). To facilitate comprehensive evaluation of this new task, we construct two new benchmarks: GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet. Crucially, existing R3DGS paradigms exhibit fundamental technical bottlenecks that severely limit their performance on the GR3DGS task: they lack intrinsic 3D point-level understanding by operating merely on 2D rendered pixels, and they incur prohibitive computational overhead by requiring per-scene optimization to embed heavy semantic features. To dismantle these bottlenecks, we propose ZeroSplat, a novel training-free and zero-feature framework. ZeroSplat lifts 2D Vision-Language Model (VLM) priors into 3D space through robust multi-view geometric constraints. This strategy enables intrinsic point-level understanding without incurring any additional feature storage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZeroSplat significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across generalized and single-target scenarios while maintaining exceptional efficiency. Project Page: https://inkmind-ai.github.io/ZeroSplat

AI.tldr: A training-free 3D segmentation framework for generalized referring Gaussian splatting, called ZeroSplat, that lifts 2D VLM priors to 3D via multi-view geometry; introduces GR3DGS task and benchmarks GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet; outperforms prior methods with high efficiency.
AI.motivation: Real-world instructions are often ambiguous and require segmenting an arbitrary number of targets (0, 1, or N). Existing Referring 3D Gaussian Splatting (R3DGS) methods are limited to single-target queries and rely on 2D pixel-level processing plus per-scene optimization, which yields poor intrinsic 3D understanding and high computational cost.
AI.method: ZeroSplat is a training-free, zero-feature framework that lifts 2D Vision-Language Model priors into 3D space using robust multi-view geometric constraints. It achieves intrinsic point-level understanding without additional feature storage and avoids per-scene optimization.
AI.result: ZeroSplat significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both generalized and single-target GR3DGS scenarios, while maintaining exceptional efficiency across benchmarks GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet.
AI.conclusion: ZeroSplat addresses core bottlenecks in GR3DGS by providing a training-free, zero-feature 3D segmentation framework that leverages 2D VLM priors through multi-view geometry, enabling accurate, efficient generalized referring segmentation and facilitating robust evaluation via new benchmarks GR-LERF and GR-ScanNet.

title: SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance. Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding. To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness. SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios. To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk. For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification. An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline. We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation. Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses. Code and dataset are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeharmScore-7B55.

AI.tldr: A real-world-grounded benchmark (SciHazard) assesses harmful guidance in science; introduces DeHarm-Score to decompose harm into hazard severity, refusal, executability, and net-new risk; benchmarks 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents, showing agents pose higher risk; dataset/code available.
AI.motivation: Fill gaps in realistic, domain-grounded evaluation of harmful scientific guidance, addressing templated queries and LLM-as-Judge limitations by grounding in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios.
AI.method: Define DeHarm-Score: 1) hazard severity and refusal behavior; 2) for non-refused responses, decompose harm into executability (dynamic checklists with weighting) and net-new risk (retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification); expert validation; 2400 hazardous questions + 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines with real-world grounding.
AI.result: Expert validation shows DeHarm-Score increases agreement with experts by 90.17% over strongest baseline; 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents evaluated; deep research agents have 32.3% higher mean DeHarm-Score than standard LLMs.
AI.conclusion: SciHazard offers a realistic, dataset-agnostic framework for measuring harmfulness of scientific guidance; highlights autonomous agents as a blind spot in safety defenses; code and data available.

title: No Training, Better Flights: Test-Time Scaled VLMs for UAV Navigation
summary: Test-time scaling offers a promising method to improve the inference performance of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) without additional training. Existing approaches to vision-language navigation (VLN) for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) typically relies on a single inference pass, which can falter in complex environments by producing suboptimal or unsafe trajectories. In this paper, we explore a simple and effective approach to apply test-time scaling to VLN for UAV. We enhance navigation reasoning through an iterative refinement process that requires no extra model training, guiding the model to re-evaluate its initial navigation plan for better accuracy and safety. Our method first prompts the model to generate multiple parallel candidates and then performs a self-correction step, achieving deeper and more robust planning without changing the underlying model. To further strengthen decision-making, we design a multi-criteria scoring function to evaluate the refined candidates based on safety, goal alignment, and forward-progress. This simple yet powerful combination enables a frozen UAV navigation VLMs to self-correct and generate more accurate and reliable flight plans, achieving SOTA performance in this task.

AI.tldr: Proposes test-time scaling via iterative refinement for UAV vision-language navigation (VLN) using a frozen model: generate multiple candidate plans, self-correct, and score with a multi-criteria function (safety, goal alignment, forward progress) to improve planning without retraining, claiming SOTA performance.
AI.motivation: Single-pass inference often yields suboptimal or unsafe trajectories in complex UAV environments; a training-free enhancement is desirable to improve inference-time planning.
AI.method: At inference, generate several parallel navigation candidates with the frozen VLM, apply a self-correction step to refine plans, and use a multi-criteria scoring function combining safety, goal alignment, and forward progress to select the best refined plan.
AI.result: Reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance on the UAV VLN task by enabling the model to self-correct and produce more accurate and reliable flight plans without additional training.
AI.conclusion: Test-time scaling through iterative refinement and multi-criteria evaluation is a simple, effective strategy to boost UAV VLN performance with frozen models, balancing safety and progress while maintaining model simplicity.

title: PAC--Bayes Bounds on Quotient Parameter Spaces: Geometry-induced Implicit-Bias Priors
summary:
Overparameterized models often have continuous parameter symmetries, so different parameters define the same predictor. We show that PAC--Bayesian analysis should be performed on the quotient predictor space: pushing a prior and posterior to the quotient preserves the empirical and population Gibbs risks while removing the nonnegative KL contribution caused solely by how the two distributions differ among parameterizations of the same predictor.
  Quotienting alone does not determine which prior to use. We construct a canonical choice of one parameterization for each predictor and account for the geometric volume of its equivalent parameterizations. This transforms a neutral reference prior into a data-independent prior that reflects the model's implicit bias. It approximates the ideal but inadmissible posterior-matched prior, which would minimize the KL term by depending on the training data. The resulting certificate is tighter exactly when this geometry-induced prior has smaller KL divergence from the learned quotient posterior than the neutral prior.
  We test this prediction in Fourier regression with a Hadamard parameterization and in Query-Key attention, using ordinary SGD without an explicit regularizer. The implicit-bias prior reduces the mean quotient-space KL by \(40.69\%\) and the mean PAC--Bayes certificate by \(21.40\%\) in the Fourier-Hadamard experiment. The smaller, prior-scale-dependent improvement in Query-Key attention confirms the predicted conditional nature of the effect.

AI.tldr: PAC-Bayes should operate on quotient predictor space to remove parameterization-induced KL; a geometry-aware canonical prior tightens the bound and reflects model bias; experiments show substantial reductions in KL and certificate, modulated by prior geometry.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized models have continuous parameter symmetries leading to multiple parameterizations for the same predictor. Standard PAC-Bayes incurs nonnegative KL due to reparameterization; analyzing on the quotient space eliminates this artifact and clarifies the role of the prior.
AI.method: Push priors and posteriors to the quotient predictor space; construct a canonical parameterization for each predictor; account for the geometric volume of equivalent parameterizations; derive a data-independent prior that reflects implicit bias; compare to the ideal posterior-matched prior; evaluate via PAC-Bayes certificates.
AI.result: Quotienting removes the nonnegative KL from reparameterizations; a geometry-aware prior reduces the KL term and tightens the PAC-Bayes certificate. In Fourier-Hadamard experiments, the mean quotient-space KL decreases by 40.69% and the mean certificate by 21.40%; in Query-Key attention the improvement is smaller and depends on prior scale.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing PAC-Bayes bounds in quotient space with a geometry-aware canonical prior yields tighter certificates and reveals that the gain is data-independent and contingent on the geometry of the parameterization. The approach is effective in symmetry-rich models and exposes the conditional nature of improvements across tasks.

title: In-Context Learning for Wound Classification with Small Multimodal Language Models
summary: Wound image classification is often treated as a task-specific supervised learning problem, requiring substantial amounts of manually labelled data and retraining when the label space or deployment setting changes. This study evaluated whether small multimodal language models (SMLMs) can provide a training-free alternative for wound classification through retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL). Experiments used two public wound-image datasets: the Kaggle wound dataset (1469 images, 10 classes) and the Medetec dataset (560 images, 9 classes). Eleven SMLMs from the Qwen 3.5, Ministral 3, and Gemma 4 families were evaluated under zero-shot prompting and few-shot prompting with random support examples, embedding-based k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) retrieval, and kNN retrieval followed by maximal marginal relevance reranking (MMR). Retrieval-only weighted-kNN controls, support-set reduction experiments, and support-context size sweeps were used to assess the effects of retrieval, model scale, and prompt length. Query-conditioned ICL consistently outperformed zero-shot and random few-shot prompting. On the Kaggle dataset, the best result was achieved by Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR, reaching 0.872 accuracy and 0.871 F1 score. On Medetec, Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.670 F1. Larger models exceeded matched weighted-kNN controls, indicating use of retrieved examples beyond nearest-neighbour voting. Retrieval-based ICL degraded modestly under support-set reduction, and most gains saturated with 8-10 support images. Retrieval-based ICL allows SMLMs to perform adaptable wound image classification without task-specific retraining. Compact retrieved contexts may support practical and privacy-conscious deployment, although performance remains dependent on model scale, retrieval strategy, and dataset difficulty.

AI.tldr: SMLMs with retrieval-based in-context learning enable training-free wound image classification; performance improves with model scale and retrieval strategy; best Kaggle result 0.872 accuracy (Qwen 3.5 27B + kNN+MMR); Medetec is lower (0.678).
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether small multimodal language models can perform wound classification without task-specific retraining by leveraging retrieved in-context exemplars.
AI.method: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting; embedding-based kNN retrieval; kNN with maximal marginal relevance reranking (MMR); retrieval-only weighted-kNN controls; support-set reduction and prompt-length analyses; datasets: Kaggle wound dataset (1469 images, 10 classes) and Medetec dataset (560 images, 9 classes); 11 models from Qwen 3.5, Ministral 3, and Gemma 4 families.
AI.result: Query-conditioned in-context learning consistently outperforms zero-shot and random few-shot prompts. Kaggle best: Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR achieved 0.872 accuracy and 0.871 F1. Medetec: Qwen 3.5 27B with kNN+MMR achieved 0.678 accuracy and 0.670 F1. Larger models outperform baseline weighted-kNN controls, indicating utilization of retrieved examples beyond simple nearest-neighbour voting. Retrieval-based ICL degrades modestly with reduced support sets; gains saturate around 8–10 support images. Overall, it enables adaptable wound classification without retraining, with privacy-friendly compact contexts.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-based in-context learning with small multimodal models provides a training-free, adaptable pathway for wound image classification. Performance depends on model scale, retrieval strategy (kNN with MMR), and dataset difficulty; practical deployment is feasible with privacy-preserving retrieved contexts, though benefits are scale- and data-dependent.

title: Semantic Primes as Explanans for Emotion in Large Language Models
summary: Progresses have been made on understanding emotion mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to explain emotion in LLMs, or even what constitutes good explanations, are less clear. Emotion representations, components, circuits are widely recoverable, but as explanations of a model's own computation they are circular; the emotion space dimensions tend to be arbitrary and non-terminating. A pressing question to ask is whether a more primitive set of internal variables does the work: the semantic primes of the Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM). Across four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B), experiments show that the NSM primes are (1) recoverable internal elements; and (2) on the reference model, intervening with a prime based direction controls emotion about three times as strongly, and twice as selectively, as the best appraisal based direction; and (3) the model treats a prime based explication as interchangeable with the corresponding emotion. These evidences suggest that NSM primes seem to be better explanans for emotion in LLMs than many alternative options according to scientific explanations criteria.

AI.tldr: NSM primes function as primitive internal variables that explain emotion in LLMs; across four instruction-tuned models, these primes are recoverable; prime-based prompts modulate emotion more strongly and selectively than appraisal-based methods; and explications based on primes are interchangeable with the corresponding emotion. This suggests NSM primes are a superior explanans for LLM emotion.
AI.motivation: Explain emotion in LLMs with interpretable, primitive internal substrates. Current emotion representations in models are circular and arbitrary; NSM primes may provide a principled basis for explaining the model's affective outputs.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation across four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B). The study tests (1) recoverability of NSM primes as internal elements, (2) whether a prime-based directional intervention modulates the model's emotion more strongly and selectively than the best appraisal-based direction, and (3) whether a prime-based explication is interchangeable with the corresponding emotion.
AI.result: NSM primes are recoverable internal elements. A prime-based direction modulates emotion about three times as strongly and twice as selectively as the best appraisal-based direction. Prime-based explication is interchangeable with the corresponding emotion.
AI.conclusion: NSM primes appear to be a better explanans for emotion in LLMs than many alternatives, according to scientific explanations criteria; NSM primes may provide a more principled, interpretable basis for understanding and controlling model emotion.

title: Masked Visual Actions for Unified World Modeling
summary: Video models absorb rich priors over how the visual world moves, interacts, and responds to contact, making them promising substrates for robotic world modeling. The central challenge is how to communicate action to such models in a form aligned with the visual space in which they learned these interaction priors, yet still grounded in physical manipulation. We introduce Masked Visual Actions, a pixel-space control interface that expresses action as a partially revealed trajectory of an arbitrary entity in a video. Revealing robot motion makes the model act as a forward dynamics model that predicts the scene's response to low-level robot actions, while revealing desired object motion makes the same model recover robot behavior consistent with that outcome. Finetuned with only 15 hours of masked examples from real videos and simulation, a single checkpoint achieves strong visual fidelity and controllability across diverse scenes and multiple embodiments. In downstream manipulation settings, the model produces imagined rollouts whose outcomes correlate with real-world execution for policy evaluation, improves decision making by ranking candidate futures in model-based planning, and supports inverse modeling by synthesizing robot motion from desired object motion.

AI.tldr: Masked Visual Actions introduces a pixel-space control interface for video-based world models, enabling controllable robot manipulation by partially revealing trajectories in video. Finetuned from only 15 hours of masked data, a single model achieves strong visual fidelity, forward dynamics for action execution, and applicability to planning and inverse modeling across diverse scenes and embodiments.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between rich visual priors learned by video models and physical manipulation actions; align action signaling with visual space while remaining grounded in low-level robot control; enable model-based planning, evaluation, and inverse control with limited data.
AI.method: Introduce Masked Visual Actions: a pixel-space control interface that expresses action as a partially revealed trajectory of an arbitrary entity in a video. Revealing robot motion enables the model to act as a forward dynamics predictor of scene responses to low-level actions; revealing desired object motion makes the model produce robot behavior consistent with that outcome. Finetuned with ~15 hours of masked real/simulated video data on a single checkpoint, achieving cross-scene and cross-embodiment controllability and fidelity.
AI.result: In downstream tasks, the model yields imagined rollouts that correlate with real execution, improves model-based planning by ranking futures, and supports inverse modeling by synthesizing robot motion from desired object motion.
AI.conclusion: Masked Visual Actions show that pixel-space interfaces can render video-based world models usable for robotics, enabling forward dynamics, planning, and inverse control with limited labeled data and generalization across scenes and embodiments.

title: Intelligence from Learnable Novelty
summary: Intelligence appears under different names in different fields: as data compression in statistics and machine learning, as universal computation in dynamical systems, and as adaptive behavior in agents. Each field carries its own objective, and the two most influential drives often fail in mirror image: novelty search, which seeks surprise, is transfixed by a noisy television screen, while the free-energy principle, which avoids surprise, is most content in a dark room. Both failures have a single cause: each objective treats as one quantity the surprise a learner can convert into knowledge and the surprise it never can. Here we show that the learnable part of that information, which we call learnable novelty, yields the seemingly disparate projections of intelligence, and we give a closed-form estimator of it built on a cheap and differentiable reservoir computer. Used as a measure, with no supervision of any kind, the estimator recovers decades of complexity classification, ranking the Turing-complete rule~110 highest among the elementary cellular automata. Used as an objective, its gradient carries a neural cellular automaton from simple dynamics into a regime of solitons, the traveling, colliding structures by which rule~110 computes, as well as organizes the representation of an image encoder around the ten digit classes of MNIST, fully unsupervised: no label ever enters training. Handed to a reinforcement-learning agent as an intrinsic reward, it supplies the exploration that task rewards lack, improving on the task baseline in nine of ten environments and collapsing in none. Complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration, ordinarily pursued with unrelated objectives in separate fields, thus emerge from ascent on one differentiable quantity, and the projections of intelligence gain a common quantitative footing.

AI.tldr: A single differentiable quantity, learnable novelty, unifies complexity, representation, and exploration by estimating the learnable portion of information; a differentiable reservoir-based estimator serves as a measure and an objective, yielding robust results across cellular automata, unsupervised MNIST encoding, and intrinsic RL rewards.
AI.motivation: To reconcile contrasting objectives across fields (surprise-based novelty search, free-energy minimization) by isolating the learnable part of surprise and providing a practical, differentiable quantity that can be used both as a measure and as a learning signal.
AI.method: Introduce a closed-form estimator of learnable novelty built on a cheap, differentiable reservoir computer. Demonstrate its utility as a measurement (ranking complexity of systems like Rule 110 among elementary CA), as an unsupervised objective (training a neural cellular automaton to form solitons and organize an MNIST encoder) and as an intrinsic reward in reinforcement learning (improving exploration across environments).
AI.result: The estimator recovers decades of complexity classifications (Rule 110 ranked highest among elementary CA). Its gradient drives a neural cellular automaton to exhibit solitons and to structure an image encoder for MNIST without labels. When used as an intrinsic reward, it enhances exploration in 9 of 10 tasks without worsening any.
AI.conclusion: A single differentiable quantity—learnable novelty—bridges complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration, providing a common quantitative footing for projections of intelligence across disparate domains.

title: Open-Vocabulary Gaze Object Prediction: Benchmark and Method
summary: Gaze Object Prediction (GOP) aims to localize and recognize the objects humans attend to, a task crucial for understanding human-centric interactions. However, existing methods are typically trained under a closed-vocabulary paradigm with a fixed label space and evaluated on scene-specific datasets, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios where gaze targets often follow a long-tail distribution or belong to unseen categories. To address this gap, we introduce Diverse Scenes for Gaze object prediction (DiSG), a benchmark containing 86 in-the-wild categories that facilitates the evaluation of Open-Vocabulary GOP (OVGOP). Building on DiSG, we propose a framework that leverages text-driven object discovery to localize potential gaze candidates, with a gaze-guided selection module to pinpoint the intended target from the candidate objects. Furthermore, to better capture semantic knowledge across diverse in-the-wild categories, we introduce Gradient-Informed Selection Tuning (GIST) to selectively update parameters most relevant to a given class vocabulary. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed model performs effectively in open-vocabulary settings and also outperforms existing methods in the conventional closed-vocabulary setting. The benchmark and code is available at https://github.com/sensniu/ovgop.

AI.tldr: Introduces DiSG benchmark for Open-Vocabulary GOP and a text-driven discovery framework with gaze-guided target selection, augmented by Gradient-Informed Selection Tuning (GIST); achieves strong open-vocabulary results and improves closed-vocabulary performance.
AI.motivation: GOP models are restricted to fixed label spaces and scene-specific datasets, limiting applicability to real-world gaze understanding with long-tail or unseen categories.
AI.method: (1) Propose DiSG, a benchmark with 86 in-the-wild categories for Open-Vocabulary GOP (OVGOP). (2) Develop a framework that uses text-driven object discovery to generate gaze candidates and a gaze-guided selection module to identify the intended target. (3) Introduce Gradient-Informed Selection Tuning (GIST) to selectively update parameters most relevant to the current class vocabulary.
AI.result: Experiments show strong performance in open-vocabulary settings and improved performance over existing methods in closed-vocabulary settings; benchmark and code are released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: The work advances Open-Vocabulary GOP by supplying a challenging benchmark and a semantically informed framework that leverages diverse in-the-wild categories and targeted parameter updates to improve gaze object prediction across settings.

title: Do AI-Native Biotechs Need Departments? Benchmarking Company World Models for AI-Driven Drug Development
comment: Working paper. Includes public no-label benchmark cases and dry-lab evaluation artifacts. No wet-lab, patient-level, clinical, regulatory, or investment validation is claimed
summary: AI-native biotechnology companies are often designed by copying human biotech org charts into agent roles. We argue for a different abstraction: a Company World Model, defined as a persistent asset-to-value state representation with transition models, explicit value functions, planning, and updating across scientific, regulatory, BD, commercial, financial, and execution constraints. We introduce a dry-lab benchmark for testing whether AI-agent organizations should mimic departments or operate around such a world model. The benchmark contains 45 retrospective public-information decision cases with strict time cutoffs, hidden outcomes, common schemas, automatic scoring, and blinded pairwise judging. We compare human-org-mimic, stronger human-org-mimic-plus, AI-native asset-centric, and AI-native value-conversion architectures. The value-conversion architecture is a prompt-level approximation of a Company World Model: a Live Asset Value Record updated by Deal, Approval, Revenue, and Investment Arbiter loops. Under a success function defined by external BD, regulatory approval and launch, and revenue discipline, it achieved the highest automatic value-conversion score and was strongly preferred over the original baselines by value-specific blinded judges. Stress tests narrowed the claim: a stronger human baseline remained competitive, and a neutral judge did not show robust value-conversion dominance. Codex-only mechanistic ablations suggest that Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room carry useful work under the target objective. The central finding is objective-sensitive: departments may remain useful governance views, but the core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart. The study is dry-lab only and does not establish real-world drug success, clinical benefit, or revenue prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: AI-native asset-to-value state (Company World Model) outperforms human-org-mimic baselines on a dry-lab benchmark, but robust dominance is not demonstrated; departments are useful as governance views, and the study is exploratory/dry-lab only.
AI.motivation: To redesign AI-enabled biotech org design around a persistent asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart, enabling cross-domain planning, execution, and value updates.
AI.method: Define a Company World Model (asset-to-value state with transition models, value functions, planning, and updates across scientific, regulatory, BD, commercial, financial, and execution constraints). Develop a dry-lab benchmark with 45 retrospective public-information decision cases (time cutoffs, hidden outcomes, common schemas, automatic scoring, blinded pairwise judging). Compare four architectures: human-org-mimic, stronger human-org-mimic-plus, AI-native asset-centric, and AI-native value-conversion (Live Asset Value Record updated via Deal, Approval, Revenue, Investment Arbiter loops). Evaluate with external BD/regulatory/launch/revenue success as success function; include stress tests and ablations (Codex-only) for Revenue Room/Deal Room/Approval Room.
AI.result: The AI-native value-conversion architecture achieved the highest automatic score and was strongly preferred by value-focused blinded judges. Stress tests show a stronger human baseline remains competitive and a neutral judge lacks robust value-conversion dominance. Codex ablations indicate Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room contribute useful work. The central finding is that a shared asset-to-value state can outperform static org-chart mimics, though departments may still be useful governance views.
AI.conclusion: Asset-to-value state should be the core operating primitive for AI-native biotech organizations rather than a static human org chart; however, the evidence is dry-lab-based and does not validate real-world drug success or revenue prediction accuracy.

title: CANDOR: Chance-Calibrated Discordance in Frozen Foundation Encoders
summary: Frozen encoders are chosen by how well a lightweight head reads a finding from their features, not whether the geometry separates it. Nearest-neighbor discordance does, but with unequal banks the opposite-label neighbor wins on density, not geometry, so prevalence alone makes an uninformed encoder look blind. We introduce CANDOR, a discordance measure whose equal-size banks are symmetric under a label swap, fixing its chance level at exactly one half. Across 22 encoders, 20 datasets from 7 domains, and 605,443 images, this correction reverses the conclusion. Collapse falls below chance almost everywhere, so no encoder is blind, yet all are weak: the best chest model reads pneumothorax at 84.5 AUROC and still places 18.4% of those positives nearer an opposite-label film than its own kind in the same hospital. The same encoder that resolves bird species at 4.5 leaves chest findings at 42.8 and glaucoma at 49.8, at chance and worse than random weights. Such a case caps the normalized margin of any Lipschitz head, yet some head among eleven is correct on all but 2.8% of cases where one head misses 35.9%: the deficit is selection, not information. Erasure retention is associated with collapse; we detect no association with the objective, scale, recency, or size of the finding. Because the chance level is fixed, CANDOR can be read before any head is trained, flagging which findings a frozen encoder supports poorly.

AI.tldr: CANDOR introduces an equal-size-bank, label-symmetric discordance measure that fixes chance at 0.5, revealing that frozen encoders are not universally blind but yield weak performance; prior inferences biased by label prevalence are overturned.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether frozen encoders meaningfully support downstream heads by reading findings from features, independent of geometric separability, and to correct biases in existing discordance metrics.
AI.method: Define CANDOR with symmetric, equal-size banks to enforce a fixed chance level; apply across 22 encoders, 20 datasets from 7 domains, ~605k images; compare against existing discordance notions; analyze encoder-head performance, erasure retention, and selection effects.
AI.result: CANDOR reverses prior conclusions: collapse is near or below chance in most cases; no encoder is truly blind, but performance is weak (best chest model at 84.5 AUROC, yet 18.4% of positives are nearest to opposite-label films in the same hospital); domain-specific readings vary (bird 4.5, chest 42.8, glaucoma 49.8, at or near chance or worse than random); erasure retention correlates with collapse, not objective/scale/recency/size; deficits are due to selection, not information; the fixed chance level enables pre-training screening of which findings an encoder can support.
AI.conclusion: With a fixed chance baseline, CANDOR provides a reliable pre-training diagnostic to flag which findings a frozen encoder can support, clarifying that downstream performance is constrained by selection mechanics rather than information content.

title: OPD-IAD: From Language Judgment to Industrial Anomaly Detection via On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently shown strong potential for industrial anomaly detection (IAD) by providing image-level anomaly judgments and interpretable defect reasoning. However, current LVLM-based IAD methods still struggle to produce precise pixel-level anomaly maps from generated language judgments. We aim to achieve precise pixel-level localization while using language as guidance rather than letting it dominate the visual response. Specifically, we propose \textbf{OPD-IAD}, an evidence-privileged dense on-policy self-distillation framework for LVLM-based IAD. OPD-IAD distills privileged defect evidence onto the model's own on-policy judgment trajectory, enabling the final generated judgment to be learned under dense supervision rather than treated only as a textual answer. The resulting judgment serves as a semantic condition for dense anomaly perception. To turn this condition into dense visual evidence, we introduce \textbf{Language-guided Visual Anchoring}, which uses a judgment reforward to re-encode the image and question under the final-judgment condition into semantic anchors and contrasts them with dense visual features through a contrastive heatmap head to generate anomaly maps. The language judgment therefore provides compact semantic guidance, while dense visual features remain the basis for pixel-level scoring, allowing language to guide anomaly localization without letting language quality directly dictate the pixel-level response. Extensive experiments show that OPD-IAD achieves the best overall performance among LVLM-based IAD methods, leading on most image-level, pixel-level, and QA metrics.

AI.tldr: OPD-IAD introduces an evidence-privileged dense on-policy self-distillation framework for LVLM-based industrial anomaly detection, combining language-guided semantic conditioning with a contrastive heatmap for pixel-level anomaly maps, achieving state-of-the-art results across image-level, pixel-level, and QA metrics.
AI.motivation: Current LVLM-based IAD yields image-level judgments but struggles with precise pixel-level localization; language should guide localization without dominating the visual response, necessitating dense supervision and semantic anchors.
AI.method: 1) On-policy self-distillation of privileged defect evidence onto the model's judgment trajectory (OPD). 2) Language-guided Visual Anchoring: re-forward the image and question under the final judgment condition to create semantic anchors and contrast them with dense visual features via a contrastive heatmap head to generate anomaly maps.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show OPD-IAD achieves the best overall performance among LVLM-based IAD methods, leading on image-level, pixel-level, and QA metrics.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables language-guided dense anomaly localization while preserving pixel-level scoring, demonstrating the value of evidence-privileged distillation and semantic anchors for LVLM-based IAD.

title: DWM: Separating World Effects from Actions in Latent World Models
summary:
Latent world models underpin much of modern model-based control, yet current action-conditioned formulations supervise
  the next-latent transition with a single, undifferentiated target, forcing a monolithic learning signal to absorb every
  source of state change. In real world, however, transitions arise from two heterogeneous sources: an action-driven
  component induced by the agent, and an action-invariant world effect -- the change that would still occur under a null
  action, dictated by the environment's intrinsic dynamics (e.g., gravity-driven sliding, inertia, contact rebound, and
  persistent drift). Fusing them into a single target entangles the two inside the latent transition, prevents the model
  from attributing observed changes to their underlying causes, and undermines the transferability of the learned
  dynamics. We introduce DWM (Decomposed World Model), a supervision-level framework that operationalizes this
  decomposition. DWM augments the predictor of a latent world model with an auxiliary world head, regularized by a
  normalized world-contrastive objective to be action-invariant, while the original pred head is coupled to it via an
  orthogonality constraint; together, the two signals induce an explicit additive decomposition of the predicted
  transition into an action-invariant and a complementary action-driven component, without altering the underlying
  architecture or inference pipeline. To evaluate DWM under persistent world effects, we construct W-variants of three
  standard control benchmarks -- PushT-W, Reacher-W, and TwoRoom-W -- each instantiating a distinct action-invariant
  dynamic. DWM matches strong baselines on the flat counterparts and delivers a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM
  planning success across the W-variants.

AI.tldr: Decomposes latent world-model transition into action-driven and action-invariant parts with an auxiliary head and world-contrastive objective, improving planning on W-variants.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned models conflate heterogeneous sources of state change into a single target, hindering attribution to causes and transferability; real-world dynamics include action-invariant effects (gravity, inertia, etc.).
AI.method: Add an auxiliary world head to predict an action-invariant component, regularized by a normalized world-contrastive objective; keep the original prediction head and enforce an orthogonality constraint between the two, yielding an additive decomposition of the transition without changing the base architecture.
AI.result: On W-variants of PushT, Reacher, and TwoRoom, DWM matches strong baselines on flat variants and achieves a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM planning success across the W-variants.
AI.conclusion: DWM provides a supervision-level, explicit decomposition of latent transitions into action-driven and action-invariant components, improving transferability and planning under persistent world effects without altering the underlying model.

title: Estimating Rare Events in Language Models with Proper Evaluation
summary: Quantifying the risk of rare failures in language models, such as those triggered by adversarial distribution shifts or very large-scale deployments, requires estimating probabilities far too small for random sampling. While recent work has formalized Low Probability Estimation, existing pipelines remain fragile in the rarest regimes: estimators can suffer zero-estimate collapse or systematic bias, and standard evaluation losses can become unstable or poorly matched to asymmetric safety costs. In this work, we introduce Gradient Activation Adaptive Multi-Level Splitting (GA-AMLS), which adapts rare-event Monte Carlo methods to the continuous activation space of language models. Specifically, GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to navigate activation space, eliminating the zero-estimate collapse of input-space search and replacing the independence assumptions of prior activation-space estimators with conditional sampling under an explicit, heavier-tailed activation prior. We also propose the Shifted-Power Bregman (SPB) Loss, a proper scoring rule that remains finite for zero-estimates and offers tunable asymmetry between underestimation and overestimation penalties. Experiments on small transformer models reveal a bias-variance tradeoff: GA-AMLS achieves the lowest loss under symmetric evaluation, reducing average log-space squared error relative to the strongest baseline across model sizes, while methods with overestimation bias prevail under asymmetric penalties. Our findings highlight that estimator choice should be matched to deployment context. More broadly, our work establishes activation space as a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in language models, circumventing the brittleness of discrete input-space search.

AI.tldr: Introduces GA-AMLS, a gradient-based multi-level splitting method to estimate extremely rare failures in language models by exploring activation space; paired with Shifted-Power Bregman loss; shows favorable symmetric performance and highlights bias-variance tradeoffs under asymmetry.
AI.motivation: Rare failures in LMs under adversarial shifts or large deployments require accurate probability estimates beyond conventional sampling; existing pipelines inoperative due to zero-estimate collapse, bias, and unstable losses.
AI.method: GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to traverse continuous activation space; performs multi-level splitting with adaptive level selection; uses a heavier-tailed activation prior and conditional sampling to avoid independence assumptions; SPB Loss provides a finite, tunable-asymmetry proper scoring rule for evaluation.
AI.result: On small transformer models, GA-AMLS achieves the lowest symmetric evaluation error (log-space squared error) vs baselines, across model sizes; under asymmetric penalties, methods with overestimation bias perform better; demonstrates a bias-variance tradeoff and improved activation-space rare-event estimation.
AI.conclusion: Activation space is a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in LMs, improving robustness over input-space search; estimator choice should be aligned with deployment context.

title: Think Sparse, Predict Dense: Continuous Thought Machines for Image Super-Resolution
summary: Continuous Thought Machines introduce an internal temporal dimension in which neuron-level histories and synchronization-derived representations evolve over a sequence of thought ticks. Extending this mechanism to dense visual prediction is non-trivial, because tasks such as image super-resolution require spatial evidence to remain available at every output location rather than being compressed into a single global representation. In the proposed window-level use of CTM, the thought dynamics produce a compact summary representation for each local window. DQ-CTM transforms this compact thought representation into window-aligned dense queries through a structured low-rank, parameter-efficient compact-to-dense query mechanism. Each position within a window receives its own query, while shared thought dynamics progressively refine the dense representation across ticks. In its super-resolution instantiation, termed ThinkSR, encoded feature maps are partitioned into local visual windows without token pooling, restored to the original feature field after shared refinement, and decoded into a high-resolution image. Preliminary experiments under a fixed four-tick training horizon reveal a progressive reconstruction trajectory. PSNR-Y increases from 28.1045 dB at $T=0$ to 30.2817 dB at $T=4$, while PSNR-RGB increases from 26.6271 dB to 28.7781 dB and the mean $\ell_1$ error decreases from 0.034602 to 0.023545. All 100 evaluated images improve from $T=1$ to $T=4$. These initial results establish the feasibility of sparse latent thought for dense spatial reconstruction and motivate broader continuous-thought architectures for dense vision.

AI.tldr: CTM-based continuous thought introduces an internal temporal dimension to support dense visual prediction; a window-level CTM with a compact-to-dense query mechanism (DQ-CTM) enables per-window queries and iterative refinement; ThinkSR demonstrates preliminary, tick-based improvements in super-resolution.
AI.motivation: To bring internal thought dynamics to dense vision tasks without collapsing spatial information into a single global representation; enables maintaining spatial evidence at every output location.
AI.method: Partition encoded feature maps into local windows; generate compact thought representations via CTM; use structured low-rank compact-to-dense query mechanism (DQ-CTM) to produce window-aligned dense queries; perform shared refinement across ticks; decode to high-resolution image without token pooling.
AI.result: In 4-tick horizon training, PSNR-Y rises 28.1045→30.2817 dB; PSNR-RGB 26.6271→28.7781; mean L1 error 0.034602→0.023545; all 100 images improve from T=1 to T=4.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of sparse latent thought for dense spatial reconstruction and motivates broader continuous-thought architectures for dense vision.

title: One Rewrite to Fix Them All? Type-Aware Repair Allocation for Text-to-Image Prompt Optimization
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) generators often fail to follow their prompts faithfully, producing wrong counts, swapped attributes, ambiguous relations, and illegible text. Prompt optimization repairs such failures by rewriting the user prompt, requiring no generator retraining, and has yielded promising results. However, existing optimizers absorb heterogeneous failures into one uniform prompt expansion, even though each calls for different repair language. We formulate semantic prompt optimization as atomic repair allocation: each failed proposition is routed to a type-conditioned repair operator before the resulting local constraints are compiled into one executable prompt. We instantiate this formulation in the training-free Type-Aware Repair Allocation (TARA) framework, which separates diagnosis, allocation, compilation, and a semantic repair gate, an accept-or-revert controller over exactly one prescribed repair that prevents semantic regressions. Extensive experiments on DSG and TIFA across four frozen generators demonstrate that TARA achieves the best semantic accuracy in all eight benchmark-generator cells, improving over VisualPrompter by 5.6 and 2.6 points on DSG and TIFA, respectively, while maintaining image quality and running fastest in our matched local setting at 16.0 seconds versus 20.0 seconds per prompt.

AI.tldr: Semantic prompt optimization via atomic repair allocation improves prompt fidelity in text-to-image generation with training-free, type-aware repairs.
AI.motivation: T2I prompts often fail to be followed faithfully, with issues like counts, attribute swaps, relationships, and illegible text. Existing optimizers merge failures into a single prompt expansion, which is suboptimal. There is a need for per-failure, type-conditioned repair strategies to maximize semantic fidelity without retraining generators.
AI.method: Introduce Type-Aware Repair Allocation (TARA): a training-free framework that segments the process into diagnosis, allocation, compilation, and a semantic repair gate. Each failed proposition is routed to a type-conditioned repair operator; exactly one prescribed repair is applied via an accept-or-revert controller to avoid semantic regressions. Evaluates semantic repair across DSG and TIFA using four frozen generators.
AI.result: TARA achieves the best semantic accuracy across all eight benchmark-generator cells, outperforming VisualPrompter by 5.6 points on DSG and 2.6 points on TIFA. It preserves image quality and is faster in the matched local setting (16.0s per prompt versus 20.0s).
AI.conclusion: Semantic failure repair via atomic, type-aware allocation yields superior semantic fidelity for T2I prompts while maintaining quality and speed, outperforming prior prompt optimization methods like VisualPrompter.

title: AHEAD: Advancing Multi-Class Label Aggregation with Interpretable Cross-Annotator Modeling
summary: Crowdsourced labeling provides valuable labeled data for domains across natural language processing, computer vision, and video. Label aggregation aims to infer latent true labels from noisy and biased annotations, with the key lying in annotator reliability estimation. Despite promising progress, existing approaches struggle with one real-world bottleneck: most individual annotators label only a small subset of tasks, making accurate annotator estimation highly intractable. In this paper, we focus on the considerably more challenging multi-class label aggregation and propose AHEAD (cross-Annotator learning and High-confidEnce Annotator-guideD label aggregation), a cross-annotator learning framework that advances annotator reliability estimation by leveraging the population-level data. Specifically, AHEAD first learns high-dimensional cross-annotator contexts via a graph neural network, deriving multi-view, complementary annotator embeddings by aggregating individual-level annotator features with contextual information. These embeddings are then decoded into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices to fit the observed labels. We formulate a composite objective incorporating high-confidence annotators to alleviate the unsupervised training issues faced by prior models. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, CV, Video, and Audio show that AHEAD substantially improves label accuracy, increasing average accuracy from 68.75% to 73.23%, with gains of up to 14.9% in the best case. Meanwhile, scalability experiments on the largest dataset further demonstrate the overall superiority of our method.

AI.tldr: AHEAD is a cross-annotator learning framework that uses a graph neural network to estimate annotator reliability across tasks, producing annotator-specific confusion matrices, and thereby improves multi-class label aggregation; demonstrated average accuracy gains (68.75% to 73.23%) across 10 real-world datasets, with up to 14.9% improvement in the best case, and scalable to large datasets.
AI.motivation: Annotator sparsity: most annotators label only a small subset of tasks, making reliability estimation hard. There is a need to leverage population-level information and high-confidence annotators to improve multi-class label aggregation.
AI.method: Cross-annotator learning via a graph neural network that learns high-dimensional annotator contexts and derives multi-view, complementary annotator embeddings by aggregating individual features with contextual information; embeddings are decoded into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices; a composite objective incorporating high-confidence annotators alleviates unsupervised training issues seen in prior models.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, computer vision, video, and audio shows an average accuracy increase from 68.75% to 73.23%, with gains up to 14.9% in the best case; scalability experiments on the largest dataset demonstrate overall superiority of the method.
AI.conclusion: AHEAD effectively exploits population-level data and high-confidence annotators to improve annotator reliability estimation for multi-class label aggregation, achieving substantial accuracy gains and demonstrating scalability across diverse domains.

title: Reliability-Aware 3D Geometric Injection for Universal Person Re-identification
summary: Universal person re-identification (ReID) aims to retrieve pedestrian identities across diverse real-world scenarios, including severe occlusions, clothing changes, and cross-modality shifts, within a unified model. However, existing 2D representations fundamentally struggle with spatial ambiguities due to a lack of depth and topological awareness, while naively introducing monocular 3D priors often causes severe negative transfer due to geometric estimation noise under extreme visual degradation. To safely harness the clothing-invariant and canonical structural properties of 3D geometry, we propose UniGeo, a Universal Monocular 3D-Enhanced ReID framework driven by a Consistency-Aware Reliability Gate and Dual-Stream Residual Fusion. Specifically, the processing of 3D information is strategically decoupled into geometric extraction and dynamic utilization. To provide pure structural compensation, we project monocular 3D parameters into kinematic joint representations, explicitly capturing instance-level geometric topology to resolve appearance-based ambiguities. To robustly incorporate these cues without perturbing the reliable 2D feature space, we isolate the 3D prior as a late-stage structural residual; modulated by the consistency-aware gate, this mechanism adaptively filters geometric noise and enables controlled fallback to the pure 2D baseline. Extensive experiments show that our method improves challenging, structure-sensitive scenarios while preserving competitive performance on clean domains. Code is available at https://github.com/BohanSu/UniGeo.

AI.tldr: UniGeo is a universal monocular 3D-enhanced ReID framework that safely leverages monocular 3D priors by decoupling geometric extraction from dynamic usage, using a consistency-aware gate to gate 3D residuals, improving structure-sensitive cases while preserving 2D performance.
AI.motivation: 2D ReID is hampered by spatial ambiguities and lacks depth/topology; naive monocular 3D priors can cause negative transfer due to geometric noise in degraded scenes; a mechanism is needed to exploit 3D geometry without harming 2D features.
AI.method: Decouple 3D processing into geometric extraction and dynamic utilization; project monocular 3D parameters into kinematic joint representations to capture instance-level topology; introduce 3D priors as a late-stage structural residual modulated by a consistency-aware gate; employ dual-stream residual fusion to integrate with a pure 2D baseline and enable controlled fallback to 2D.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show improvements in structure-sensitive scenarios (e.g., occlusions, clothing changes, cross-modality) while maintaining competitive performance on clean domains; code is released at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: Safe, adaptive integration of 3D geometry can harness canonical structure for ReID without perturbing 2D features; the consistency gate suppresses geometric noise and enables robust fallback to 2D when needed.

title: AgentDebugX: An Open-Source Toolkit for Failure Observability, Attribution, and Recovery in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agent failures are difficult to debug because the step where an error surfaces is often not the one that caused it. Existing observability tools replay execution traces but provide little support for identifying the root cause or translating diagnosis into recovery. We present AgentDebugX, an open-source debugging framework that organizes debugging as a closed loop of Detect, Attribute, Recover, and Rerun. At its core, DeepDebug performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis through global trajectory understanding, structure-guided investigation, and cross-examination. On the Who and When benchmark, DeepDebug achieves the best strict attribution accuracy among the evaluated methods on both tested open-weight backbones, reaching 28.8 percent exact agent-and-step accuracy on qwen3.5-9b versus 21.7 percent for the strongest single-pass baseline. On GAIA, DeepDebug repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun, compared with 4 to 6 for three decoupled self-correction baselines, improving overall accuracy from 55.8 percent to 63.6 percent. AgentDebugX exposes this workflow through a Python library, CLI, web console, and installable agentic skill, and provides an opt-in Error Hub for sharing scrubbed failure-diagnosis-repair bundles and reusing them as debugging memory.

AI.tldr: AgentDebugX and DeepDebug offer a structured LLM agent debugging framework that closes the loop (Detect, Attribute, Recover, Rerun) and performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis, achieving state-of-the-art attribution and repair performance on standard benchmarks, with open-source tooling and an Error Hub for shared debugging memory.
AI.motivation: LLM agent failures are hard to debug because error surfaces do not point to root causes, and existing observability tools mainly replay traces without aiding diagnosis or actionable recovery.
AI.method: Propose AgentDebugX with DeepDebug for global trajectory understanding, structure-guided investigation, and cross-examination to perform multi-turn root-cause diagnosis. Evaluated on Who and GAIA benchmarks. Provided via Python library, CLI, web console, installable agentic skill, and an opt-in Error Hub for scrubbed failure-diagnosis-repair bundles.
AI.result: On Who: DeepDebug achieves best strict attribution accuracy among evaluated methods on two tested open-weight backbones, with 28.8% exact agent-and-step accuracy on qwen3.5-9b (vs 21.7% baseline). On GAIA: repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun (vs 4–6 for three baselines), increasing overall accuracy from 55.8% to 63.6%.
AI.conclusion: AgentDebugX provides a practical, open-source end-to-end debugging workflow for LLM agents, enabling structured diagnosis, guided recovery actions, and reuse of past failures via an Error Hub, thereby improving attribution and repair success in real-world tasks.

title: Weak-to-Strong Learning in Decision Making
summary: Many operational decisions rely on predictive models that estimate uncertain outcomes conditional on observable contexts. Training such models, however, often faces a fundamental data asymmetry: labeled outcomes are scarce or costly to obtain, while contextual covariates are abundant. Motivated by this data asymmetry, we develop a decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve contextual stochastic optimization.
