Specifically, we first train a weak model using limited labeled data and then use it to generate predicted outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts. These distributions provide soft supervision for training a strong model. We establish a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess decision risk of W2S and a complementary lower bound for a strong-only benchmark. Their comparison yields explicit sufficient conditions under which W2S improves downstream decision performance. The key quantity is the correlation dimension between the weak and strong feature representations: when it is small, abundant unlabeled data reduce the effect of teacher errors along non-overlapping directions. A synthetic newsvendor experiment and a comment moderation experiment based on real-world data provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory.

AI.tldr: A decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework uses scarce labeled data to train a weak model, which then predicts outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts to provide soft supervision for a stronger model in contextual stochastic optimization.
AI.motivation: Address data asymmetry where labeled outcomes are costly while contextual covariates are abundant, aiming to improve downstream decisions by leveraging unlabeled data.
AI.method: Two-stage training: train a weak model on labeled data; generate predicted outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts; use these soft predictions to supervise training of a stronger model. Theoretical analysis yields non-asymptotic upper bounds on excess decision risk for W2S and a lower bound for a strong-only benchmark; analysis centers on the correlation dimension between weak and strong representations.
AI.result: W2S improves downstream decision performance when the correlation dimension is small, supported by non-asymptotic bounds and experiments (synthetic newsvendor and real-world comment moderation) that align with theory.
AI.conclusion: W2S provides a principled way to exploit abundant unlabeled data to enhance contextual stochastic optimization; its benefits hinge on low correlation-dimension between weak and strong representations, suggesting practical guidelines for model design and data collection.

title: Wave2Body: Rethinking mmWave Human Pose Estimation as Radar-to-Body Token Translation
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-friendly human sensing, but its sparse point clouds are physical measurements of view-dependent electromagnetic reflections and only indirectly characterize body articulation. Recovering a complete 3D pose from such partial, geometry-dependent observations is therefore under-constrained. Existing methods directly regress joint coordinates from paired radar-pose data, relying on the same limited paired supervision to learn radar perception, human-body structure, and their alignment. This coupling can encourage dataset-specific shortcuts under ambiguous radar observations. We propose Wave2Body, a radar-to-body token translation framework that decouples these learning targets using a self-supervised mmWave tokenizer, a pretrained compositional body tokenizer that defines the output space, and a lightweight translator between them. Experiments on M4Human and mmBody show that Wave2Body achieves stronger cross-domain generalization than previous methods while incurring much lower computational costs for training and inference. All the code and experiment results are publicly available at https://github.com/Galaxywalk/Wave2Body.

AI.tldr: Wave2Body introduces a decoupled, self-supervised radar-to-body translation framework for mmWave pose estimation, using a self-supervised tokenizer and a pretrained body tokenizer to improve cross-domain generalization and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Radar-based human pose estimation with mmWave is inherently under-constrained due to view-dependent, sparse measurements. Coupled learning of radar perception and human body structure risks dataset-specific shortcuts; a decoupled, principled representation can improve generalization.
AI.method: A three-component framework: (1) a self-supervised mmWave tokenizer to extract robust radar tokens, (2) a pretrained compositional body tokenizer as the target output space, and (3) a lightweight translator that maps radar tokens to body tokens.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on M4Human and mmBody shows Wave2Body achieves stronger cross-domain generalization than prior methods and requires significantly less computation for training and inference.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling radar-to-body learning with tokenizers yields better cross-domain generalization and efficiency in mmWave pose estimation, with publicly available code and results.

title: SkillSight: Seeing Through Shared Descriptions for Accurate Skill Retrieval
summary: As large language model agents gain access to increasingly large skill libraries, retrieving the right skill becomes critical to reliable capability selection and execution. Existing retrievers often treat skill descriptions as ordinary documents, overlooking their highly regular structure: shared descriptive patterns recur across many skills while providing little evidence for distinguishing the required capability. We show that this shared descriptive background systematically contributes to dense relevance scores, induces a pronounced energy gap between queries and skill documents, and obscures task-relevant signals. Based on this observation, we propose SkillSight, a training-free retrieval framework that calibrates shared background in both semantic and lexical spaces. Semantic Background Calibration estimates a background subspace from generic tokens identified by IDF, reducing similarity induced by shared descriptive patterns, while Lexical Evidence Calibration downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence. Experiments on SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp demonstrate consistent improvements across retrieval metrics, with SkillSight improving Recall@10 by up to 20.21 percentage points over the original dense retriever. In end-to-end evaluation, SkillSight achieves the best overall performance across three agent models and outperforms LLM Selection by up to 4.97 percentage points. It is also up to 1,248 times faster than the Dense + Reranker baseline. These results identify shared descriptive background as a key source of bias in skill retrieval and demonstrate that explicitly calibrating it enables accurate and efficient skill selection without additional training. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaojinying/SkillSight.

AI.tldr: SkillSight is a training-free retrieval framework that calibrates shared descriptive background in skill descriptions in both semantic and lexical spaces to improve skill retrieval, yielding notable gains in Recall@10 and end-to-end performance while being substantially faster than baselines.
AI.motivation: Skill descriptions exhibit common descriptive patterns that inflate dense relevance scores, creating an energy gap between queries and skill documents and obscuring task-relevant signals; this background bias can hinder accurate skill selection.
AI.method: Two-calibration, training-free approach: (1) Semantic Background Calibration (SBC) extracts a background subspace from generic tokens identified via IDF to reduce background-driven similarity; (2) Lexical Evidence Calibration (LEC) downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp shows consistent improvements; Recall@10 improves by up to 20.21 percentage points over the original dense retriever. End-to-end, SkillSight yields best overall performance across three agent models and surpasses LLM Selection by up to 4.97 percentage points; speed gains up to 1,248× over Dense+Reranker baseline.
AI.conclusion: Shared descriptive background is a key bias source in skill retrieval. Explicit calibration in semantic and lexical spaces enables accurate, efficient skill selection without additional training; code available.

title: RRPO: Reference-Relative Policy Optimization with Stratified Conditional Rollouts
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has shown strong effectiveness in reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback, where sampled rollouts can be compared within a group using task-provided correctness signals. However, extending group-relative optimization beyond verifiable settings is challenging because success in many tasks is not captured by a single correctness criterion. We propose \textbf{Reference-Relative Policy Optimization (RRPO)}, which generalizes GRPO by replacing direct correctness-based advantage construction with reference-relative contrastive comparisons. RRPO first uses \emph{stratified conditional rollouts} to construct positive and negative anchor sets, and then trains a metric projection head with a set-contrastive objective to compare candidate rollouts against these anchors. The resulting alignment scores directly define contrastive advantages: during policy optimization, the projection head is frozen, and the scores are centered within each rollout group in a standard group-relative objective. We evaluate RRPO using anchor-based contrastive advantages throughout policy optimization, without relying on task ground-truth verifiers. Across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings, RRPO remains competitive with verifier-based optimization, improves over weakly supervised baselines, and provides additional gains after supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: RRPO generalizes Group Relative Policy Optimization by replacing direct correctness-based advantages with reference-relative, contrastive comparisons. It uses stratified conditional rollouts to form anchor sets, trains a fixed metric projection head via set-contrastive objectives to score candidate rollouts against anchors, and centers scores within groups to form contrastive advantages for policy optimization. It performs well without verifiable ground-truth signals, competitive with verifier-based methods, and gains are observed after supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Extend GRPO to non-verifiable settings where success is not captured by a single correctness criterion by using reference-relative, contrastive comparisons instead of direct correctness signals.
AI.method: RRPO constructs positive and negative anchor sets via stratified conditional rollouts, trains a metric projection head with a set-contrastive objective to map rollouts to alignment scores against anchors, freezes the projection head during policy optimization, and uses the centered alignment scores as contrastive advantages within a group-relative objective.
AI.result: RRPO achieves competitive performance with verifier-based optimization across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings; it improves weakly supervised baselines and yields additional gains after supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Reference-relative contrastive optimization provides effective guidance in non-verifiable tasks, enabling competitive performance without ground-truth verifiers and offering additional benefits after supervised fine-tuning.

title: Local Label-Informed Feature Transfer for Generating Ground-Truth Medical Images: A Comparison of GAN- and Diffusion-Based Approaches
summary: Validating Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in medical imaging requires ground-truth data with known locations of informative features. However, current approaches rely on expert annotations, which are prone to labeling errors, or on hand-crafted artificial perturbations superimposed onto healthy images to mimic lesions or malignant features, which lack clinical realism. We present Local Label-Informed Feature Transfer (LLIFT), a framework for generating semi-synthetic brain magnetic resonance images with realistic lesions placed in user-controlled regions, which does not require pixel-level lesion annotations during training. We implement LLIFT with two generative paradigms: LLIFT-GAN, a custom GAN that learns pathological features from binary class labels alone, and LLIFT-DM, a diffusion-based inpainting pipeline conditioned on bounding-box masks via ControlNet. Both approaches are evaluated on brain magnetic resonance imaging data derived from the Human Connectome Project. In evaluations, both achieve Fréchet Inception Distance scores, with respect to the real pathological distribution, that are comparable to the inter-class reference between healthy and pathological images in the given dataset. Furthermore, qualitative inspection confirms the realism of lesion structures. The resulting benchmark datasets provide spatially controlled ground truth data for evaluating XAI methods in medical imaging.

AI.tldr: LLIFT generates semi-synthetic brain MRI with controllable lesions to benchmark XAI; two pipelines LLIFT-GAN and LLIFT-DM; yields realistic lesions and competitive FID results; outputs datasets for XAI ground truth.
AI.motivation: Need ground-truth lesion localization for XAI evaluation; current labeled or artificial perturbations are inadequate; create realistic, region-controllable synthetic data without requiring pixel-level annotations.
AI.method: LLIFT framework; LLIFT-GAN learns pathological features from binary labels; LLIFT-DM uses diffusion-based inpainting with ControlNet conditioned on bounding boxes; training on HCP data; generate lesions in user-specified regions; evaluate using FID against real pathology distribution.
AI.result: FID scores comparable to inter-class healthy/pathological separation; qualitative inspection shows realism; datasets provide spatial ground truth for XAI evaluation.
AI.conclusion: LLIFT provides practical, annotation-free semi-synthetic data for XAI benchmarking in medical imaging with two viable generative approaches; opens groundwork for standardized XAI evaluation benchmarks; potential for extension to other modalities and annotations.

title: AI Tour Meeting: Group Travel Planning by LLM Agents
summary: This paper proposes AI Tour Meeting, a group travel planning framework powered by multiple Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents. The agents are instantiated with distinct personas and collaboratively seek an itinerary that satisfies their constraints and preferences through natural language discussion. The framework enables easy and flexible orchestration of such discussions by providing interfaces for configuring agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment. Its primary use case is a simulation tool for analyzing the behavior of multiple LLM agents during tour planning discussions. This paper demonstrates the utility of the framework by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained by the framework.

AI.tldr: A framework named AI Tour Meeting enables multi-agent, persona-based LLM collaboration to plan group travel itineraries; it serves as a simulation tool to study agent interactions, with configurable workflows and deployment interfaces.
AI.motivation: To study and understand the behavior and coordination of multiple LLM agents in a constrained, preference-driven tour-planning task, and to provide an extensible orchestration platform for experimentation.
AI.method: A scalable framework where multiple LLM-based agents, each instantiated with distinct personas, interact via structured discussion workflows to generate itineraries. The framework offers configurable agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment abstractions, enabling flexible simulation and evaluation.
AI.result: Demonstrated utility through system validation and analytical results derived from simulations of agent discussions, illustrating coordination dynamics and framework capabilities.
AI.conclusion: AI Tour Meeting provides a versatile, extensible tool for analyzing multi-agent LLM collaboration in tour planning, enabling researchers to study coordination, constraints satisfaction, and preference handling in a controlled environment.

title: Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF) for Cyber Anomaly Detection
summary: Malicious anomalous activity detection is a fundamental challenge for cyber security systems. Both tensor decomposition under statistical framework with CANDECOMP-PARAFAC alternating Poisson regression (CP-APR) and normalizing flows have proven to be powerful unsupervised machine learning methods that model multi-dimensional data and capture complex and multi-faceted details of behavior profiles in cyber security applications. In this study, we propose Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework integrating CP-APR structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores derived from normalizing flows. In our experiments, we show that the HLSF framework improves anomaly detection performance on a dataset of real-world compromised user credentials collected from the large enterprise network of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) during a red-teaming exercise, compared with using CP-APR or normalizing flows alone.

AI.tldr: HLSF: a weighted fusion framework that combines CP-APR tensor-based structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores from normalizing flows, improving malicious anomaly detection on LANL red-team data versus CP-APR or NF alone.
AI.motivation: To leverage complementary strengths of CP-APR (structure-focused, tensor-based) and normalizing flows (distribution-focused) to detect complex, multi-dimensional cyber anomalies; existing single-method approaches may miss cross-domain cues.
AI.method: Propose Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted fusion framework that integrates CP-APR structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores derived from normalizing flows. Unsupervised training on multi-dimensional cyber data; final anomaly score is a weighted combination of the two sources. Evaluated against CP-APR alone and normalizing flows alone on a real-world LANL red-team credential dataset.
AI.result: HLSF improves anomaly detection performance compared with using CP-APR or normalizing flows in isolation on the LANL red-team dataset.
AI.conclusion: Integrating structural (tensor-based) and latent-density (flow-based) cues yields superior anomaly detection in cyber security contexts; the approach can generalize to other multi-dimensional data scenarios and motivates further exploration of weighted, multi-view fusion for unsupervised cyber anomaly detection.

title: SynGallery: A Synthetic Gallery of Real Paintings for Instance-Level Artwork Recognition
summary: Instance-level artwork recognition requires matching a handheld visitor photograph to a specific work in a large museum collection. This is challenging because painting datasets typically provide clean catalog images for training, while test queries are captured under oblique viewpoints, gallery lighting, reflections, frames, and other scene-level variations. We present SynGallery, a synthetic gallery dataset for artwork retrieval that addresses this gap without collecting additional real photographs. Starting from catalog images of real paintings, we place each artwork into a procedurally generated 3D gallery scene and render it from multiple viewpoints under varied geometric and appearance conditions, while preserving the exact identity of the original work. The resulting dataset contains 24,490 rendered views of 4,898 paintings from the Met benchmark. We show that these synthetic views provide a stronger training signal than the corresponding studio photographs. At the same number of training data points, training only on SynGallery improves art painting recognition from 67.18 to 73.47 GAP$^-$. When added to the full Met training set, SynGallery improves the published benchmark protocol from 35.97 to 38.48 GAP. Ablation experiments show that the gain comes primarily from geometric viewpoint variation rather than photographic realism: blur, sensor noise, and image compression consistently reduce performance.

AI.tldr: A synthetic gallery dataset (SynGallery) renders Met paintings in procedurally generated 3D gallery scenes to bridge training-test gaps, yielding strong performance gains for artwork retrieval by emphasizing viewpoint variation.
AI.motivation: Instance-level artwork recognition suffers when test queries are oblique photographs vs clean catalog images; current datasets lack training data that reflect real-world gallery viewpoints.
AI.method: Create SynGallery by placing each painting into a procedurally generated 3D gallery scene and rendering from multiple viewpoints under varied geometric and appearance conditions, preserving artwork identity; yields 24,490 rendered views of 4,898 paintings from the Met benchmark.
AI.result: Training on SynGallery provides stronger signals than studio photos; at the same data size, GAP^− improves from 67.18 to 73.47; adding SynGallery to the full Met set raises GAP from 35.97 to 38.48; ablations show gains mainly from viewpoint variation; realism factors like blur/noise reduce performance.
AI.conclusion: Geometric viewpoint variation in synthetic data is the primary source of improvement for artwork retrieval; synthetic data can be a cost-effective substitute or supplement to real data, though realism factors may have a negative effect if not aligned with training objectives.

title: Evaluating medical AI under missing information: same-provider judges and human raters change apparent safety
summary: Readiness stress-testing of medical AI has focused on closed-ended and multimodal benchmarks. We extend it to open-ended clinical conversation under missing information, where safe behavior means recognizing absent information and qualifying, clarifying, or not over-committing - and where the evaluator becomes part of the measurement. We stress-test four models - three flagships (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3) and one mid-tier model (Gemini 3.5 Flash) - by deleting the latter half of the final user turn in HealthBench conversations, grading responses with a four-provider LLM-judge panel and a blinded clinician-anchored reference. Two evaluator-facing results are robust. First, judge choice materially changes apparent safety: inter-judge agreement is only moderate (Fleiss' kappa = 0.65), and after adjusting for each judge's general leniency (vote-level logistic regression), a positive same-provider association remains (exact permutation p = 0.04; GPT-5.5 ~ +0.10 on the probability scale) - large enough to change which model appears to over-commit least once its own-provider judge is excluded. Second, LLM judges are more permissive than clinicians on a blinded 50-item subsample: all four are significantly more lenient than the stricter independent clinician (crediting appropriate uncertainty on 66-84% of items vs 52%), and three of four than the author-influenced consensus (Grok directional only; judge-vs-consensus kappa = 0.20-0.43). On the author-audited clinical-underdetermined subset the permissiveness gap widened and the point-estimate model ordering held. A closed-ended MedQA anchor confirms accuracy is high and option-order effects are within a +/-5-point equivalence region for three of four models, so the safety gap is about calibration, not knowledge. We release the harness, prompts, per-item outputs, judge panel, perturbation audit, and human-annotation protocol.

AI.tldr: Open-ended clinical safety stress-testing by truncating user turns; evaluates four models using LLM judges and clinician anchors; judge variability and leniency impact safety rankings; results suggest calibration gaps rather than knowledge gaps; release dataset and evaluation harness.
AI.motivation: Extend readiness stress-testing from closed-ended benchmarks to open-ended clinical conversations with missing information, where safe behavior is recognizing absence and clarifying rather than over-committing; examine how evaluator design affects measurement.
AI.method: Modify HealthBench conversations by deleting the second half of the final user turn; evaluate four models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, Gemini 3.5 Flash) using a four-provider LLM-judge panel and a blinded clinician-anchored reference; two evaluator-facing results include inter-judge agreement (Fleiss' kappa = 0.65) and judge leniency adjusted via vote-level logistic regression; analyze same-provider associations, a 50-item blinded subsample, and a closed-ended MedQA anchor; assess safety vs knowledge.
AI.result: Two evaluator-facing results are robust: inter-judge agreement is moderate; judge leniency materially shifts safety rankings, with a positive same-provider association (p=0.04; GPT-5.5 ~ +0.10). LLM judges are more permissive than clinicians on a 50-item subsample; three models maintain ordering when excluding author- or judge-derived consensus; a closed-ended MedQA anchor shows high accuracy and small option-order effects (within +/-5 points for three models). The safety gap appears due to calibration rather than knowledge gaps.
AI.conclusion: The authors release the evaluation harness, prompts, per-item outputs, judge panel, perturbation audit, and human-annotation protocol, enabling further study of open-ended AI safety in clinical settings.

title: Attractor Geometry Determines the Identifiability Limits of System Discovery
summary: Symbolic discovery of governing equations from data is limited not only by algorithm design and data volume, but by the geometry of the attractor: what the long-run dynamics allow to be recovered. Using a within-system design on Lorenz-84, where one forcing parameter drives fixed-point, limit-cycle, and chaotic regimes while the governing equations and library stay fixed, we show that a single number, $λ_{\min}(M)$, the smallest eigenvalue of the invariant-measure moment matrix, sets the identifiability ceiling for both sparse regression (SINDy) and evolutionary symbolic regression (PySR). Derived from the Birkhoff ergodic theorem and obtained from a short reference trajectory before any run, $λ_{\min}(M)$ measures how fully the attractor covers function space: where it vanishes, recovery is impossible for any algorithm, sparse or combinatorial alike; as it grows, both algorithms improve. Chaos raises $λ_{\min}(M)$ by spreading the attractor, but also enlarges it and amplifies noise; because noise enters SINDy's regression bottleneck linearly and PySR's discrimination channel superlinearly, the same transition can push the two methods in opposite directions, so deeper chaos is not uniformly better. Parameter-free mechanistic scores from this framework transfer without refitting to a held-out Lorenz-96 system, confirming mechanism rather than curve-fitting; a criterion read from the equations predicts when added chaos will not improve conditioning. We also introduce Soft F1, a coefficient-weighted structural metric that resolves performance differences invisible to binary-success and predictive scores. The first question of discovery is then not which algorithm, but what the attractor permits.

AI.tldr: A single invariant-measure moment matrix eigenvalue λ_min(M) bounds identifiability of symbolic discovery for Lorenz-84; chaos and noise shape performance of SINDy and PySR; framework yields transferable, mechanism-based scores and a Soft F1 metric; attractor geometry governs discovery potential.
AI.motivation: Quantify how attractor geometry limits data-driven discovery of governing equations and provide a scalable, mechanism-based criterion for algorithmic success.
AI.method: Within-system Lorenz-84 with a single forcing parameter traversing fixed-point, limit-cycle, and chaotic regimes; compute λ_min(M) from a short reference trajectory via the Birkhoff ergodic theorem; assess identifiability of SINDy and PySR; test transfer to Lorenz-96; introduce Soft F1 as a coefficient-weighted structural metric.
AI.result: λ_min(M) sets the identifiability ceiling: as it grows, both SINDy and PySR improve; chaos spreads and enlarges the attractor, increasing λ_min(M) but also amplifying noise, causing nonuniform effects where SINDy and PySR can diverge in performance; parameter-free mechanistic scores transfer to Lorenz-96 without refitting; a criterion predicts when added chaos no longer improves conditioning; Soft F1 reveals performance differences invisible to binary success metrics.
AI.conclusion: The attractor’s geometry governs discovery potential; λ_min(M) provides a principled, data-driven bound on recoverability; the framework shifts focus from algorithm choice to attractor-permissible function-space coverage, with Soft F1 offering a finer diagnostic.

title: TAP-RAG: Task-Aware Policy Control for Long-Document Multimodal Question Answering
summary: Long-document multimodal question answering requires more than retrieving relevant chunks from a large document. Different queries require different evidence behavior. Existing multimodal RAG systems improve evidence access through text chunks, page images, graph links, or heterogeneous document elements, but they often apply a largely query-agnostic evidence-use strategy. We present TAP-RAG, a task-aware policy-controlled RAG framework for long-document multimodal QA. TAP-RAG contains a main controller, the Task-Aware Policy Controller (TAPC), and two policy-guided evidence executors: Task-Aware Query-Guided Flow Diffusion (TA-QFD) and Task-Aware Visual Enhancement (TAVE). For each query, TAPC predicts the task prior, estimates visual/local/global evidence signals, and produces an executable policy. TA-QFD then expands textual and structural evidence over the multimodal document graph, while TAVE selectively inspects page images when visual or layout evidence is needed. A guarded synthesis stage fuses text, visual, and structural evidence and abstains when support is insufficient. On DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc, TAP-RAG achieves the best overall accuracy among the compared systems, improving over a matched multimodal-RAG baseline by +9.1 points (61.1 to 70.2) and +4.5 points (42.2 to 46.7), respectively.

AI.tldr: TAP-RAG is a task-aware policy-controlled RAG framework for long-document multimodal QA. It uses a Task-Aware Policy Controller to predict task priors and signals and to output an executable policy for evidence use. Two policy-guided executors—TA-QFD and TAVE—expand textual/structural evidence and selectively inspect visuals. A guarded synthesis stage fuses multimodal evidence and abstains when insufficient support. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc relative to a matched multimodal-RAG baseline (+9.1 and +4.5 points).
AI.motivation: Long-document multimodal QA requires dynamic, task-specific evidence use. Existing multimodal RAG systems often apply a largely query-agnostic evidence-use strategy, potentially misallocating attention to text, images, or graph structure. A task-aware policy could tailor evidence gathering to the query.
AI.method: Propose TAP-RAG with: (1) Task-Aware Policy Controller (TAPC) that predicts a task prior, estimates visual/local/global evidence signals, and outputs an executable policy; (2) Task-Aware Query-Guided Flow Diffusion (TA-QFD) that expands textual and structural evidence over a multimodal document graph; (3) Task-Aware Visual Enhancement (TAVE) that selectively inspects page images when visual or layout evidence is needed; (4) a guarded synthesis stage that fuses text, visual, and structural evidence and abstains if support is insufficient.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc shows TAP-RAG achieves the best overall accuracy among compared systems, with improvements of +9.1 points (61.1->70.2) and +4.5 points (42.2->46.7) over matched multimodal-RAG baselines.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware policy control over evidence usage yields stronger long-document multimodal QA performance. The combination of policy-guided evidence expansion (text/structure) and selective visual processing, followed by guarded fusion, enables robust answers and abstention when evidence is lacking.

title: PhoenixRepair: Rethinking Repair Strategy Exploration in Software Agents
summary: While Large Language Models have greatly advanced automated issue resolution, existing agent-based methods exhibit a fundamental limitation in their insufficient exploration of repair strategies. This insufficiency manifests in two key aspects. First, the exploration of multiple potential edit locations is limited. Second, the exploration of repair attempts at each location is also insufficient. To address these challenges, we present PhoenixRepair, a multi-agent framework that systematically explores multiple candidate edit locations and performs iterative reflection and refinement on patch generation, thereby expanding the search space of repair strategies. Our framework begins with multi-location sampling, optionally augmented with graph-based localization information for difficult tasks, followed by iterative reflection and refinement to generate better patches, culminating in final-round generation guided by distilled insights from all historical attempts. Experiments on SWE-bench-Verified demonstrate that PhoenixRepair achieves the largest relative improvement of 7.8\% over SWE-agent under DeepSeek-V3.1, and attains the highest resolved rate of 76.0\% Pass@1 under MiniMax-M2.5. Meanwhile, it achieves higher fault localization accuracy than existing approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/PhoenixRepair.

AI.tldr: PhoenixRepair introduces a multi-agent program repair framework that jointly explores multiple edit locations and iteratively refines patches through reflection, culminating in a final generation guided by historical attempts; it yields state-of-the-art repair performance on SWE-bench-Verified and competitive results, with code released.
AI.motivation: Existing agent-based repair methods underexplore repair strategies: limited search across edit locations and insufficient attempts per location, impairing repair success. A more expansive search with collaborative multi-agent exploration and iterative refinement is proposed.
AI.method: Multi-location sampling (with optional graph-based localization) followed by iterative reflection and refinement on patch generation, and final-round generation guided by insights distilled from all past attempts; architecture called PhoenixRepair.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines on SWE-bench-Verified: up to 7.8% relative improvement over SWE-agent under DeepSeek-V3.1; achieves Pass@1 of 76.0% on MiniMax-M2.5; higher fault localization accuracy; code released at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Expands the repair search space and improves effectiveness; demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on benchmark; provides reproducible results via public code.

title: Now We Know? A Systematic Comparison of TerraMind and THOR
summary: Benchmarks for Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) increasingly rank models by aggregate score, but such rankings obscure why models differ: how much of the gap is architecture, how much is decoder capacity, and how much is a use-case-specific artefact? This study addresses that gap through a controlled comparison of two GFMs developed under European Space Agency's $Φ$-lab with contrasting design philosophies: THOR, which introduces a compute-adaptive architecture supporting variable patch sizes and unifies Sentinel-1, -2, and -3 data at their native resolutions; and TerraMind, a multimodal generative GFM pretrained with a dual-scale token/pixel objective that enables any-to-any cross-modal generation (Thinking-in-Modalities) to infer missing sensors at inference time. Rather than reporting a single leaderboard, we investigate the axes along which the two architectures actually differ - patch size, decoder complexity, finetuning regime, input modality, and model scale - across ten use cases spanning segmentation and regression in diverse domains, including climate disaster response, methane leak detection, snow monitoring, or sea ice mapping. We find that architectural design choices - patch size and decoder type in particular - explain more performance variance than model identity itself, that the two models embody complementary investment strategies (pretraining-time scale for TerraMind versus inference-time tokenisation for THOR), and that correctly interpreting results requires dataset-level characterisation. The resulting picture is not a single winner but a set of hypotheses and a diagnostic ablation methodology that we expect to generalise to future GFMs beyond THOR and TerraMind.

AI.tldr: Architectural choices (patch size and decoder type) explain more performance variance in GFMs than model identity; THOR and TerraMind show complementary strategies (inference-time tokenisation vs pretraining-time scale); a diagnostic ablation framework with dataset-level characterization is needed; no single winner, but hypotheses and generalizable methodology.
AI.motivation: Disentangle sources of performance gains in geospatial foundation models beyond leaderboard scores by comparing two contrasting GFMs with different design philosophies to understand where improvements come from.
AI.method: Controlled, multi-axis comparison across ten use cases (segmentation and regression) spanning climate, disaster response, methane detection, snow monitoring, sea ice mapping, etc. Axes include patch size, decoder complexity, finetuning regime, input modality, and model scale; compare THOR (compute-adaptive architecture with variable patch sizes and unified sensors) and TerraMind (multimodal generative GFM with dual-scale token/pixel objective).
AI.result: Architectural design choices account for more performance variance than model identity; TerraMind emphasizes pretraining-scale investment while THOR emphasizes inference-time tokenisation; models are complementary; results require dataset-level characterization; proposes a diagnostic ablation methodology and hypotheses that generalize to future GFMs.
AI.conclusion: The study offers a diagnostic framework rather than a single winner, with results expected to generalize to future GFMs and inform more nuanced benchmarking beyond aggregate leaderboard rankings.

title: Learning Explicit Physical Parameter Control and Benchmarking for Video Generation
summary:
Recent advances in image-to-video generation have improved visual realism, making physically grounded and controllable dynamics an important step toward future world simulation.
  Current models often generate plausible motion, but it is not reliably governed by explicit physical causes, and instance-level constraints can leak or become entangled in multi-object interactions.
  We attribute this gap to two missing pieces: large-scale, fine-grained physical parameterization, and model designs that correctly bind physical attributes to instances and emphasize dynamics over appearance.
  To bridge this gap, we introduce PhyParam-Dataset, an interaction-centric collection of 130K physically simulated videos with dense physical parameterization, including force vectors, object material properties, and environmental constants across five representative rigid-body motion types.
  Built on this data, we present PhyParam, a physics-guided image-to-video diffusion model that conditions on object-level forces, masses, friction, restitution, and scene-level gravity via a lightweight physical-attention routing mechanism, and further improves motion learning with semantic-structural feature-space supervision.
  We also establish PhyParam-Bench, a benchmark for physical-law consistency in image-to-video generation, with a multi-level protocol evaluating temporal dynamics, spatial stability, and semantic--physical alignment. Experiments show that PhyParam improves physical consistency while maintaining high visual fidelity, advancing explicit rigid-body physical-parameter control for image-to-video generation.
  We will publicly release the dataset, benchmark, and code to support future research.

AI.tldr: Proposes PhyParam: a physics-guided image-to-video framework with a large, parameterized dataset and a benchmark to enforce explicit rigid-body physics in generated videos, achieving better physical consistency without sacrificing visual fidelity.
AI.motivation: Current image-to-video models produce plausible motion but lack explicit physical causality and robust instance-level disentanglement. There is a need for large-scale, fine-grained physical parameterization and architectures that correctly bind physical attributes to instances and emphasize dynamics over appearance.
AI.method: Introduce PhyParam-Dataset (130K physically simulated videos with dense parameterization: forces, masses, friction, restitution, gravity across five rigid-body motion types). Develop PhyParam, a physics-guided image-to-video diffusion model conditioned on object-level forces, masses, friction, restitution, and gravity via a lightweight physical-attention routing mechanism, plus semantic-structural feature-space supervision. Establish PhyParam-Bench, a benchmark with a multi-level protocol to evaluate temporal dynamics, spatial stability, and semantic-physical alignment.
AI.result: Experiment results indicate PhyParam improves physical consistency while maintaining high visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The work advances explicit rigid-body physical-parameter control for image-to-video generation and provides datasets, benchmark, and code to support future research.

title: NaviAIS: A Scenario-Level Vessel Trajectory Prediction Dataset withVectorized Lane Priors and the NaviLane Forecasting Framework
summary: Vessel trajectory prediction in complex maritime environments is essential for traffic management, collision warning, route planning, and autonomous navigation. Although AIS-based learning methods have progressed rapidly, existing datasets are often released as raw message streams or irregular time series, with inconsistent sampling rates, noisy observations, heterogeneous coordinate systems, and non-unified scenario protocols. Most public AIS resources also lack structured representations of navigational lanes, waterway geometry, and navigable-region constraints, limiting reproducible, environment-aware forecasting. To address this, we introduce NaviAIS, a standardized scenario-level AIS dataset for vessel trajectory prediction. It organizes multi-vessel historical-future trajectories within unified temporal windows and local coordinate systems, and provides rasterized navigable maps, vectorized lane priors, lane graphs, and structured map representations. Compared with existing datasets, it jointly supports vectorized lanes, multi-scenario coverage, vectorized maps, open accessibility, and processed trajectories. Built on this dataset, we propose NaviLane, a hierarchical macro-action framework for map-aware prediction. NaviLane first performs trajectory-map joint encoding for a unified scene representation, then uses a discrete macro-action codebook to generate multimodal candidates coarse-to-refined. A residual refinement module improves local geometric and dynamical consistency, and a world-model-based consequence-aware evaluator ranks candidates by interaction risk and environmental feasibility. Experiments show NaviLane outperforms representative baselines in both single-modal and multimodal settings, confirming the value of structured navigational priors, hierarchical multimodal generation, and consequence-aware evaluation.

AI.tldr: NaviAIS introduces a dataset and NaviLane a map-aware, hierarchical predictor for vessel trajectories. It standardizes AIS data with scenario-level windows and provides navigational maps and lanes; NaviLane uses joint trajectory-map encoding, a macro-action codebook for multimodal predictions, residual refinement, and a consequence-aware evaluator, achieving superior results over baselines.
AI.motivation: AIS datasets are fragmented, irregular, and lack unified navigational priors (lanes, maps, constraints). A standardized, environment-aware dataset and a map-aware prediction framework are needed to improve reproducibility and forecasting quality.
AI.method: NaviAIS provides scenario-level, unified-window AIS trajectories with local coordinates, rasterized maps, vectorized lanes/graphs, and structured map representations. NaviLane encodes trajectories with the map jointly, uses a discrete macro-action codebook to generate multimodal predictions in a coarse-to-refined process, applies a residual refinement module for local geometric/dynamical consistency, and employs a world-model-based consequence-aware evaluator to rank candidates by interaction risk and feasibility.
AI.result: Experiments show NaviLane outperforms representative baselines in single-modal and multimodal settings, validating the value of structured navigational priors, hierarchical multimodal generation, and consequence-aware evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A standardized AIS dataset with integrated navigational priors enables reproducible, environment-aware vessel trajectory forecasting; the proposed NaviLane framework demonstrates how map-aware, hierarchical multimodal generation plus consequence-aware ranking improves performance.

title: Automated Data Engineering and Feature Selection for the Case Study of Warpage Detection in Fused Deposition Modeling
summary: This study contributes toward development of an Automated Data Processing (ADP) framework designed to evaluate and reinforce optimal machine learning model-feature combinations for predictive tasks in fused deposition modeling (FDM) process datasets. The methodology is centered around a reinforcement learning-inspired policy updating mechanism, where multiple machine learning models are trained on both full feature sets and feature subsets selected through Shapley-based Explainable AI (SHAP XAI) across 217 datasets. At each episode, the framework assesses the predictive accuracy and F1-scores of each model-feature pair, computes a scalar reward, and updates $Q$ values to guide future model selection. SHAP XAI feature importance was employed to generate reduced yet informative feature subsets to enable the framework to explore performance with dimensionality. The policy was shown to evolve over multiple episodes, with reward distributions used to visualize performance stability. Overall, results indicate that leveraging the ADP framework through XAI algorithms successfully converges toward optimal model-feature configurations with improved accuracy and stability. Specifically, the proposed framework improves the test-set AUC from 0.9248 to 0.9731 and increases the mean reward value by more than fifty percent compared with the baseline full-feature configuration.

AI.tldr: An ADP framework uses reinforcement-learning-inspired policy updates and SHAP-derived feature subsets to optimize model-feature combinations for predictive tasks across 217 FDM datasets; achieves higher AUC and stability.
AI.motivation: Improve predictive performance and stability by automatically selecting informative feature subsets and model-feature pairings across diverse datasets using an RL-like policy.
AI.method: Train multiple models on full and SHAP-subset features across 217 datasets; at each episode evaluate accuracy and F1, compute a scalar reward, update Q-values; SHAP-based feature importance used to generate reduced feature subsets; analyze reward distributions across episodes.
AI.result: Policy converges toward optimal configurations; test-set AUC improved from 0.9248 to 0.9731; mean reward increased by >50% relative to baseline full-feature config.
AI.conclusion: The ADP framework integrated with XAI achieves higher accuracy and stability, demonstrating effective cross-dataset optimization of model-feature choices in FDM processes.

title: Dual Adversarial Fine-tuning for Enhancing Robustness of Large Vision Language Model
summary: While Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), represented by LLaVA and GPT-4V, have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their visual inputs remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, posing significant security risks. Existing defense methods predominantly target single-task scenarios (e.g., zero-shot classification) and consequently lack generalizability across various multimodal tasks. To address this limitation, we propose a dual adversarial fine-tuning framework that jointly optimizes visual and semantic supervision signals from two modalities, enhancing model robustness while generalizing across multiple downstream tasks. The proposed framework comprises two core components, i.e., $\textbf{Visual}$ supervision branch and $\textbf{Semantic}$ supervision branch. The former branch leverages features from clean images, extracted via a frozen original vision encoder, to guide adversarial robustness while the latter incorporates caption-image alignment as a contextual signal to preserve semantic coherence under attack. Moreover, our method achieves cross-task robustness by simply replacing the CLIP vision encoder in the original model, with no need of separate task-specific retraining or architecture modifications.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art method in adversarial robustness evaluation across zero-shot classification, image captioning, and visual question answering (VQA) tasks.

AI.tldr: A dual-adversarial fine-tuning framework improves LVLM robustness against adversarial attacks across multimodal tasks (zero-shot classification, image captioning, VQA) by jointly leveraging visual supervision from clean images and semantic supervision via caption-image alignment, with cross-task robustness achieved by swapping the CLIP vision encoder—no task-specific retraining required.
AI.motivation: LVLMs (e.g., LLaVA, GPT-4V) are vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Existing defenses are mostly single-task and do not generalize well to diverse multimodal tasks; a generalizable, cross-task defense is needed.
AI.method: Two branches: Visual supervision using a frozen original vision encoder to guide robustness on clean-image features; Semantic supervision incorporating caption-image alignment as contextual signal to preserve semantics under attack. Cross-task robustness is enabled by replacing the CLIP vision encoder in the original model without task-specific retraining or architecture changes.
AI.result: Experimental results show the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art in adversarial robustness across zero-shot classification, image captioning, and Visual Question Answering (VQA).
AI.conclusion: The dual-adversarial fine-tuning framework yields improved cross-task robustness by jointly optimizing visual and semantic signals, enabling generalization across multiple downstream tasks without additional architectural changes.

title: Black-Mamba: Biologically-Inspired Leaky Accumulation for Conceptual Knowledge under Distribution Drift
summary: Forecasting under real-world conditions is inherently non-stationary, as the conditional distribution of future observations evolves over time. Recent test-time adaptive sequence models address this challenge by updating internal states during inference, but tie adaptation to instantaneous prediction errors or surprise. This coupling can conflate persistent distribution shift with stochastic innovations, leading to unnecessary updates and inefficient adaptation. We introduce Black-Mamba, a test-time adaptive forecasting architecture that formulates online adaptation as evidence-gated state tracking under distribution drift. The model augments a base predictor with a dynamic memory updated when temporally accumulated surprisal provides sufficient evidence of a regime change. This turns adaptation into a selective, event-driven process rather than a continuous one. Across multiple forecasting benchmarks with non-stationary dynamics, Black-Mamba achieves competitive or improved predictive performance compared to existing test-time adaptation methods while significantly reducing the number of memory updates during inference. Together with mathematical analysis and biological evidence, these results suggest that accumulated surprisal provides a principled signal for distinguishing persistent drift from transient noise, yielding more efficient and robust adaptation.

AI.tldr: A test-time adaptive forecasting method (Black-Mamba) uses evidence-gated, event-driven memory updates to handle non-stationary distributions, improving efficiency while maintaining or boosting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Forecasting under non-stationarity is challenged by drifting distributions. Existing test-time adapters tie adaptation to instantaneous errors, conflating persistent drift with noise and causing unnecessary updates. A selective, evidence-based approach aims to improve robustness and efficiency.
AI.method: Augment a base predictor with a dynamic memory that updates only when temporally accumulated surprisal indicates a regime change. Adaptation is framed as evidence-gated state tracking under distribution drift, enabling selective, event-driven updates rather than continuous adjustment. The work includes mathematical analysis and references biological evidence to justify the approach.
AI.result: On several non-stationary forecasting benchmarks, Black-Mamba achieves competitive or improved predictive performance relative to existing test-time adaptation methods while substantially reducing the number of memory updates during inference.
AI.conclusion: Accumulated surprisal provides a principled signal to distinguish persistent distribution drift from transient noise, yielding more efficient and robust test-time adaptation, as supported by theory and biological evidence.

title: Signed Rectified Flow: Negativity-Controlled Generation
summary: We introduce Signed Rectified Flow (Signed RF), a generalization of Rectified Flow that targets the signed measure $π^{sign} = (1+α)π^+ - απ^-$, where $α>0$, $π^+$ is the distribution to promote, and $π^-$ is the distribution to suppress. Although direct sampling from a signed measure is not well-defined, Signed RF induces a valid generative process that concentrates probability in regions where the signed measure is positive while provably excluding regions dominated by its negative component. It therefore provides a principled framework for incorporating negative information and exclusion constraints into generative modeling. We analyze the signed continuity equation underlying Signed RF and use a charged-particle interpretation to explain how negative mass forms exclusion barriers. This theory further motivates practical adaptive guidance algorithms. Across several applications, Signed RF improves the fidelity-diversity trade-off on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization experiments, and reduces nudity induced by adversarial prompts in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP and aesthetic scores.

AI.tldr: Generalizes Rectified Flow to signed measures to promote positive and suppress negative components, yielding a valid generative process that concentrates on positive regions and excludes negative regions; offers a framework to incorporate negative information and exclusion constraints into diffusion-type models; supported by theoretical 'charged-particle' interpretation and adaptive guidance, with empirical gains on ImageNet fidelity-diversity, anti-memorization, and nudity reduction in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP/aesthetics.
AI.motivation: Incorporate negative information and exclusion constraints into generative modeling and diffusion-like flows; overcome limitations of positive-only sampling by using signed measures to encode both promotion and suppression of regions.
AI.method: Define π^sign = (1+α)π^+ − α π^− with α>0; generalize Rectified Flow to operate on signed measures; analyze the signed continuity equation; use a charged-particle interpretation to produce exclusion barriers; develop adaptive guidance algorithms; ensure the resulting process concentrates where the signed measure is positive and excludes negative regions, despite sampling from a signed measure not being directly defined.
AI.result: The proposed Signed RF yields improved fidelity-diversity trade-offs on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization tests, and reduces nudity artifacts from adversarial prompts in Stable Diffusion 3.5, without sacrificing CLIP and aesthetic scores.
AI.conclusion: Signed RF provides a principled framework to integrate negative information into generative modeling via signed measures and exclusion constraints; it offers theoretical insights (signed continuity equation, charged-particle view) and practical gains across multiple tasks, with potential for broader adoption and extension.

title: DobicVLM: Aligning Chest X-Ray Report Generation with Clinically-Grounded Programmatic Rewards via Group Relative Policy Optimization
summary: Medical imaging is a cornerstone of diagnostics, yet automated chest X-ray report generation struggles with structural adherence, anatomical completeness, and semantic faithfulness. We introduce DobicVLM, a vision-language model combining supervised fine-tuning on MedGemma-4B with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and clinically-grounded programmatic rewards. Our approach uses interpretable, rule-based reward components; structural verification, anatomical checklist, semantic similarity, and length constraints to enforce clinical standards without neural reward models. Trained on 1,000 de-identified image-report pairs from a private clinical dataset (with ethics approval and compliance to local regulations), DobicVLM is evaluated via blinded expert review on 69 held-out cases. DobicVLM outperforms Gemini 2.5 Flash across the majority of criteria, achieving the highest impression accuracy (27.2%) and medical terminology (86.5%) compared to both Gemini 2.5 Flash and MedGemma 4B baselines, with minor trade-offs in completeness and referrals. This demonstrates GRPO's value for transparent alignment in resource-limited settings. Keywords: Vision-Language Models, Radiology Report Generation, Reinforcement Learning, Medical AI, GRPO

AI.tldr: DobicVLM is a vision-language model for chest X-ray report generation using GRPO with rule-based rewards, achieving improved impression accuracy and medical terminology over baselines, demonstrating transparent alignment in resource-limited settings.
AI.motivation: Automated chest X-ray reporting struggles with structural adherence, anatomical completeness, and semantic faithfulness; neural rewards may lack interpretability and clinical transparency. The paper motivates using interpretable, programmatic rewards via GRPO to ensure clinical standards.
AI.method: Fine-tune on MedGemma-4B; apply Group Relative Policy Optimization with rule-based rewards: structural verification, anatomical checklist, semantic similarity, length constraints; train on 1,000 de-identified image-report pairs with ethics approval; evaluate with blinded expert review on 69 held-out cases.
AI.result: DobicVLM outperforms Gemini 2.5 Flash across most criteria; highest impression accuracy 27.2%; medical terminology 86.5%; baselines other numbers not specified; minor trade-offs in completeness and referrals.
AI.conclusion: GRPO provides transparent alignment for medical V&L models, particularly beneficial in resource-limited settings.

title: Enhancing Transformer-based Routing by Encoding Distance via Relative Positional Encoding
comment: This work was accepted to be presented at the Graph Signal Processing Workshop 2026
summary: This paper explores Relative Positional Encoding (RPE) as an additive bias in Transformer architectures to solve the Team Orienteering Problem. By embedding in the attention mechanism pairwise spatial relationships among nodes of the graph that represents the routing problem, the transformer encoder can compute a richer spatial-aware graph embedding that allows the decoder to estimate better routes. Experimental results involving instances up to 100 nodes demonstrate consistent improvements in collected rewards and optimality gaps over vanilla Transformer architectures used by other state-of-the-art works. These findings highlight that explicit relational modeling significantly enhances scalability and generalization for complex combinatorial optimization.

AI.tldr: RPE as additive bias in Transformer attention improves Team Orienteering Problem solving.
AI.motivation: Capture explicit pairwise spatial relations to improve spatial-aware graph embeddings for combinatorial optimization.
AI.method: Incorporate Relative Positional Encoding as additive bias in Transformer attention to model pairwise node relationships; evaluate on TOP instances up to 100 nodes; compare to vanilla Transformer and SOTA methods.
AI.result: Achieves consistent improvements in rewards and lower optimality gaps over vanilla Transformers; demonstrates better scalability and generalization.
AI.conclusion: Explicit relational modeling via RPE enhances Transformer-based solvers for complex routing problems, suggesting broader applicability to graph-structured combinatorial optimization.

title: Adaptive Two-Stage Online Learning for Service-Affecting Failure Detection in Mobile Core Networks
summary: Mobile network operators monitor aggregated traffic volumes to assess the operational health of core network infrastructure. Reliable failure detection is challenging due to strong temporal structure, non-stationarity, measurement artefacts, and extreme class imbalance, which limit static threshold-based monitoring. This paper proposes a two-stage online learning framework for traffic-based failure detection in mobile core networks. Stage I incrementally models normal traffic dynamics using lightweight regression with time-aware features. Stage II analyses prediction residuals together with contextual indicators to detect genuine service-affecting network failures. The framework operates fully online under a prequential evaluation protocol, enabling continuous adaptation with low computational overhead. Across linear and non-linear models, the proposed two-stage architecture achieves the best precision-recall trade-off, attaining the highest recall, F1-score, and AUC at acceptable false positive rates. These results demonstrate the importance of explicit residual decomposition for reliable failure detection in streaming mobile core network data.

AI.tldr: Two-stage online learning framework for real-time traffic-based failure detection in mobile core networks: Stage I online regression models normal traffic with time-aware features; Stage II analyzes residuals with contextual indicators to detect genuine failures; evaluated in a fully online prequential setting, achieving superior precision-recall trade-offs across linear and nonlinear models and highlighting the value of residual decomposition.
AI.motivation: Challenges: strong temporal structure, non-stationarity, measurement artefacts, and extreme class imbalance hinder static threshold-based monitoring; need continuous adaptation and reliable detection of service-affecting events.
AI.method: Stage I incremental modeling of normal traffic dynamics with lightweight regression using time-aware features. Stage II uses prediction residuals plus contextual indicators to detect failures. Fully online prequential evaluation; tested across linear and nonlinear models; two-stage architecture.
AI.result: Best precision-recall trade-off; highest recall, F1-score, and AUC at acceptable false positive rates; explicit residual decomposition improves reliability in streaming network data.
AI.conclusion: Explicit residual decomposition in a two-stage online framework enhances reliable failure detection in streaming mobile core network data; method offers low computational overhead and continuous adaptation.

title: SWITi: Quantifying and Reducing Tiling Artifacts with Sliding Window Inner Tiling
summary: SWITi is a test-time method for reducing artifacts in tiled predictions, particularly for neural networks that learn posterior distributions from which solutions are sampled at inference time. Tiled predictions are unavoidable for large image data, and artifacts arise whenever tiles are smaller than a network's receptive field and when tiles are independent posterior samples. SWITi averages overlapping sliding-window predictions, so discrepancies between neighboring samples are spread across shifted tile positions rather than accumulating at fixed seam coordinates. For posterior models, SWITi uses no more tile samples than an MMSE estimate requires and therefore incurs no additional forward passes. Additionally, we introduce two reference-free metrics, the Fraction of Rejected Tests (FRT) and Artifact Severity (ASV), for detecting and quantifying tiling artifacts from a per-tile permutation test that compares the distribution of pixel gradients across tile seams against the surrounding image content. On pre-trained and published image splitting models across three fluorescence microscopy datasets in 2D and 3D, we show that SWITi substantially attenuates stitching seams while also improving reconstruction fidelity and resolution. Since tiling artifacts in posterior predictions can easily be mistaken for biological structures or for boundaries between biological structures, removing or reducing them using SWITi will improve the downstream processing of large image predictions, which is particularly relevant for biomedical data.

AI.tldr: SWITi reduces tiling artifacts in tiled predictions by averaging overlapping sliding-window outputs, with no extra forward passes for posterior models; introduces two reference-free metrics FRT and ASV to detect artifacts; improves fidelity and resolution on fluorescence microscopy data.
AI.motivation: Tiled processing is necessary for large images; artifacts arise when tiles are smaller than the network's receptive field or when samples are independent; need seam-robust inference and reliable, reference-free artifact detection for biomedical imaging.
AI.method: Compute predictions with overlapping sliding windows and average overlapping regions to spread seam discrepancies across shifted tile positions; for posterior models, reuse an MMSE-equivalent sampling to avoid extra forward passes; introduce two reference-free metrics (FRT and ASV) based on per-tile permutation tests comparing pixel-gradient distributions across seams with surrounding content.
AI.result: SWITi substantially attenuates stitching seams and improves reconstruction fidelity and resolution on pre-trained, published splitting models across three fluorescence microscopy datasets in 2D and 3D.
AI.conclusion: Reducing tiling artifacts improves reliability of large-scale biomedical image predictions by preventing artifacts from being mistaken for biological structures; SWITi is computationally efficient and practical for biomedical imaging pipelines.

title: OntoBook: Ontology-Grounded Synthetic Textbooks for Medical Encoder Pretraining
summary: We present OntoBook, a method that converts medical ontology structure into pretraining signal for encoder language models. Our approach has three stages: random walks through ontology graphs capture hierarchical and causal relations between medical codes, a large language model reformulates these walks into fluent textbook-style prose, and the resulting text is used to train ModernCamemBERT, a 149M-parameter French encoder, with two objectives on the same data: masked language modeling and relation prediction between code pairs. On three French medical coding benchmarks (FRACCO, Cantemist-FR, Distemist-FR), OntoBook achieves significant improvements over MLM-only pretraining, with +2.5 micro-F1 on FRACCO and +8.0 micro-F1 on Distemist. We find that alignment between objectives is necessary: misaligned training, where each task uses different data, causes a 30-point degradation. We release 1.3 million LLM-reformulated medical textbooks across three French ontologies (CIM-10, CCAM, ATC) and pretrained model checkpoints.

AI.tldr: OntoBook converts medical ontologies into pretraining signals for encoder language models via random walks, LLM reformulation into prose, and dual-objective pretraining, yielding improvements on French medical coding benchmarks and releasing reformulated textbooks and checkpoints.
AI.motivation: Inject structured ontology knowledge (hierarchical/causal relations among medical codes) into encoder pretraining to improve downstream medical coding tasks in French.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) random walks over ontology graphs to capture relations; (2) a large language model reformulates the walks into fluent textbook-style prose; (3) pretrain ModernCamemBERT (149M) with two objectives on the reformulated text: masked language modeling and relation prediction for code pairs; training data alignment is crucial.
AI.result: On FRACCO (+2.5 micro-F1) and Distemist (+8.0 micro-F1) benchmarks, OntoBook outperforms MLM-only pretraining. Misaligned training (different data per task) degrades performance by ~30 points. They release 1.3 million reformulated textbooks across CIM-10, CCAM, ATC and pretrained model checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Aligning pretraining objectives with shared data is essential for gains from ontology-informed signals; OntoBook demonstrates effective use of reformulated ontology content to boost French medical coding and provides resources for reproducibility.

title: Censoring-Aware In-Context Learning for Generalized Supplier Lead Time Estimation in Supply Chain Planning
summary: Supplier lead time forecasting is a central input to material requirements planning, inventory optimization, and supply chain risk management. However, many industrial lead time datasets are naturally right-censored: at the time forecasts are required, some orders have not yet arrived. Standard regression and classification approaches discard this information, while conventional survival models require task-specific modeling. We propose LeadTime-ICL (LT-ICL), a censoring-aware in-context learning model for probabilistic lead time forecasting. LT-ICL combines a transformer backbone with a conditional normalizing-flow head, producing a full predictive distribution over lead times. The model is pretrained on synthetic right-censored lead time tasks, enabling in-context adaptation to new industrial datasets without task-specific parameter updates. We provide theoretical support for this formulation by showing that excess CRPS is bounded by prior misspecification and amortized approximation errors, providing clear direction for improving forecasting performance. We evaluate LT-ICL on 24 proprietary supply-chain datasets spanning seven industries. LT-ICL achieves the lowest point-forecasting error on 15 of the 24 datasets, and the lowest probabilistic forecasting error on 14 datasets, yielding the best average rank across both. These results support right-censored probabilistic forecasting as a practical formulation for supplier lead time prediction and demonstrate that pretrained in-context models can provide accurate, low-adaptation-cost forecasting for industrial planning systems.

AI.tldr: LT-ICL is a censoring-aware in-context learning model for probabilistic supplier lead-time forecasting, combining a transformer backbone with a conditional normalizing-flow head to model full predictive distributions for right-censored data. It is pretrained on synthetic tasks and adapts to new datasets without task-specific parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Industrial lead time data are often right-censored when forecasts are required; standard regression and classification ignore censoring and conventional survival models require task-specific design. There is a need for accurate probabilistic forecasts with low adaptation cost in SCM.
AI.method: LT-ICL uses a transformer backbone with a conditional normalizing-flow head to produce a full predictive distribution. It is pretrained on synthetic right-censored lead time tasks and adapts to new industrial datasets via in-context learning without parameter updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on 24 proprietary datasets across seven industries, LT-ICL achieves the lowest point-forecasting error on 15/24 datasets and the lowest probabilistic forecasting error (CRPS) on 14/24 datasets, yielding the best average rank across both metrics.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained in-context models with censoring-aware probabilistic forecasting are practical and effective for supplier lead time prediction, enabling low-adaptation-cost deployment in industrial planning systems.

title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Approaches for AEC Engineering Drawing Layout Detection and Information Extraction
comment: 2026 European Conference of Computing in Construction (EC3 2026), 8 pages
summary: Information Extraction (IE) from Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) drawings remains hindered by manual inefficiency, while Layout Detection, a vital 'middleware' organizing graphical and textual hierarchies, is underexplored. General document layout models, optimized for text-centric content, lack validation on engineering drawings. This study constructs a custom AEC-specific layouts dataset and benchmarks five deep learning architectures. RF-DETR achieves state-of-the-art performance with an $mAP_{50}$ of 0.949, while the Vision-Language Model Qwen3-VL attains a leading F1-score of 0.911. Conversely, models pre-trained on general document datasets suffer from "domain interference", causing performance degradation. This establishes a robust technical foundation for automated IE in AEC.

AI.tldr: AEC-specific layout detection dataset and benchmarks show RF-DETR achieves 0.949 mAP50; Qwen3-VL achieves 0.911 F1; domain-general models suffer from domain interference; supports automated IE in AEC.
AI.motivation: IE in AEC drawings is manually intensive; existing general layout models underperform on engineering drawings due to domain gaps; a dedicated AEC-layout dataset and benchmarks are needed to validate and guide model choice.
AI.method: Constructed a custom AEC-specific layouts dataset; evaluated five deep-learning architectures on layout detection tasks; compared transformer-based detectors (e.g., RF-DETR) with a Vision-Language model (Qwen3-VL) and with models pre-trained on general document datasets.
AI.result: RF-DETR achieved state-of-the-art mAP50 of 0.949; Qwen3-VL achieved the leading F1-score of 0.911; models pre-trained on general document datasets suffer from domain interference, degrading performance.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a robust technical foundation for automated IE in AEC and highlights the importance of domain-specific data and architecture choices for AEC layout detection.

title: What General Intelligence Requires: Non-Reducible Constraints Across Levels of Description
summary: General intelligence, of the kind that underwrites the full range of human cognitive achievement, is not a property of computational architecture alone. This paper advances a single thesis: the structural constraints on general intelligence occupy distinct levels of description and are mutually non-reducible, in the sense that the special-sciences tradition gives to that term. It follows that no single architectural advance, and no continuation of the scaling programme by itself, can produce artificial general intelligence (AGI), and that research programmes must be evaluated against the full constraint profile rather than against performance on any one benchmark. The thesis is developed through a method that reads general intelligence through four evidential lenses, AI systems research, anthropology, law, and economics, each anchored to a distinct level of description, supplemented by speculative fiction used as a disciplined heuristic in the context of discovery rather than the context of justification. Applying the method yields a taxonomy of twenty-three structural constraints organised into eight clusters; six are examined in depth and ordered as an ascending ladder of levels, with explicit bridges showing why progress at one level cannot carry to the next. The argument issues in five falsifiable predictions, each stated with a named benchmark family and a disconfirmation condition, converting a descriptive framework into a research programme with a longer horizon than the scaling hypothesis implies.

AI.tldr: AGI cannot be achieved by architecture advances or scaling alone; a multi-level, non-reducible constraint framework is required.
AI.motivation: Challenge the claim that scaling/architectural progress alone suffices for AGI by articulating a non-reductionist, multi-level theory of general intelligence aligned with the special sciences.
AI.method: Cross-disciplinary analysis reading general intelligence through four evidential lenses anchored to distinct levels of description (AI systems, anthropology, law, economics), complemented by speculative fiction as a discovery heuristic; derive a taxonomy of structural constraints and map inter-level bridges; formulate falsifiable predictions.
AI.result: Taxonomy of 23 structural constraints organized into eight clusters; six constraints explored in depth and arranged along an ascending ladder of levels with explicit inter-level bridges; five falsifiable predictions with named benchmark families and disconfirmation conditions.
AI.conclusion: Progress toward AGI requires addressing the full constraint profile rather than relying on a single architectural advance or scaling trajectory; the framework converts the descriptive account into a long-horizon research program.

title: Operational Proto-Introspection in Looped Language Models: Process-Quality Taps, Executable Branching, and the Readout-Control Boundary
comment: 49 pages, 8 figures. Paper 1 of a two-paper series; companion methodology paper submitted separately
summary:
Can a language model read the quality of ongoing computation, and can an external intervention turn that readout into better outcomes? We test both questions in a frozen 2.6B looped transformer, Ouro-RLTT. On GSM8K, a strict pre-answer probe excludes the answer region and gold value yet predicts eventual success: hidden states plus length and log-probability shortcuts reach AUROC 0.797, versus 0.731 for the shortcuts alone (incremental +0.066; task-clustered 95% CI [+0.021, +0.112]; 170 tasks, 680 candidates). Low-capacity taps also read role-specialized properties: task-disjoint branch survival reaches 0.9697 oracle retention, content ranking reaches 0.6310 macro top-1, and generated-branch correctness reaches AUROC 0.7755. A non-looped control replicates a candidate-quality readout, so recurrence is not required for every signal.
  We build branch/carry/prune machinery over Ouro's 192-slot recurrent cache, including branch-specific cache lineage and a bit-exact residual-capture splice that recomputes only the affected suffix and saves up to 88% of per-branch layer passes. No frozen intervention produces a validated capability gain. Directional steering is an established negative; a four-task matched-sampling comparison removes evidence for a frozen-fork gain but cannot estimate a general deficit; terminal selection remains unresolved and underpowered; and bounded LoRA changes surface behavior without improving net reachability. A two-null audit does not support the simplest span-misalignment explanation.
  We call this readable-but-not-yet-usable property operational proto-introspection.
