AI.result: Tokenization cost reduced by more than 10x; end-to-end training throughput improved by ~2.5x. At 1024^2 resolution on an NVIDIA A100, Mage-Flow-Turbo generates an image in 0.59s and Mage-Flow-Edit-Turbo edits in 1.02s with a small memory footprint. The 4B model family achieves competitive performance on standard generation and editing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: This work shows that careful cross-layer co-design of tokenizer, backbone, and system enables strong high-resolution generation and editing within a compact 4B model, with Turbo variants making interactive high-res use practical.

title: Supra Cognitive Modes: A Routed Architecture for Agent Memory
summary: Agent-memory workloads mix direct factual lookup, relation-chain and current-state reasoning, and broad synthesis over long histories. We describe Supra Cognitive Modes (SCM), an architecture that maps explicit or automatically selected per-query modes to retrieval and synthesis payloads over one shared ingest substrate. A frozen semantic classifier and runtime gates dispatch queries among fused lexical and dense lookup, graph or iterative multi-hop handling, and stratified long-form synthesis. The substrate combines multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and optional asynchronous enrichments. We characterize the deployed configuration on three benchmarks: Long-term Conversational Memory (LoCoMo; n = 1,986), MemoryAgentBench (MAB; n = 3,671), and LongMemEval (n = 500). The reference run records 84.87% on LoCoMo factoid categories and 68.61% on adversarial abstention, 61.49% on MAB across two repetitions, and 86.00% on LongMemEval. A repository-backed reproduction produces similar aggregate scores and supports task- and mode-conditioned failure analysis. Raw baseline outputs, aligned end-to-end timing for LoCoMo and LongMemEval, and complete token ledgers are unavailable; stored rows also omit some final runtime decisions. The results characterize one implemented routed configuration and its diagnostic failure patterns, while source inspection verifies the per-query control interface and shared-substrate design. Causal routing effects, efficiency gains, and statistical significance remain outside the available evidence.

AI.tldr: SCM architecture routes per-query cognitive modes to retrieval and synthesis on a shared substrate for agent-memory tasks; evaluated on LoCoMo, MAB, LongMemEval with reproduced results; evidence limited for causal routing and statistics.
AI.motivation: Address the integration of direct factual lookup, relation reasoning, and long-form synthesis in memory-rich agent workloads by providing a unified, mode-dispatching substrate.
AI.method: Frozen semantic classifier and runtime gates direct queries to fused lexical/dense lookup, graph/multi-hop handling, and stratified synthesis; substrate accumulates multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and async enrichments; evaluation on three benchmarks with reproduction workflow.
AI.result: Reported metrics: LoCoMo factoid 84.87%; adversarial abstention 68.61%; MAB 61.49%; LongMemEval 86.00%; two repetitions; reproduction yields similar aggregates; raw outputs and token ledgers not available; some runtime decisions missing.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a configured routed workflow and its diagnostic failure patterns; validates per-query control interface and shared-substrate design; however causal routing effects, efficiency gains, and statistical significance remain unverified.

title: Mark, Don't Erase: Token Inoculation for Dual-Use Knowledge in LLMs
summary: Safety interventions on dual-use knowledge typically choose between destroying hazardous content (e.g., unlearning, filtering) and suppressing it at the output layer (e.g., refusal training); both pay a tax in adjacent-domain competence or over-refusal. We argue that the right operation is conditioning, not reduction: we show that hazardous knowledge can be retained in the model and behaviorally gated by a privileged control token. Our method, Token Inoculation, introduces a binding-and-branching approach. First, during continued pre-training, we mark hazardous content by inserting a special token alongside dual-use documents, so the model binds the marker to the underlying semantics of the hazardous domain. Second, during supervised fine-tuning, we teach the model to answer hazardous queries correctly when the special token is present and to refuse them when it is absent, thereby enabling selective refusal without removing dual-use knowledge. On hazardous domain (e.g., WMDP-Bio), Token Inoculation reduces accuracy from 79% to 18% while retaining 93% of the base-model's benign-domain performance (e.g., MMLU), achieving the best safety-utility trade-off against unlearning and refusal-tuning baselines across 1B-14B model scales. We further show that refusal selectivity is controllable through the quality of the conditioning signal and that domain-specific semantic binding during pre-training is critical for the conditional behavior to generalize beyond memorized triggers. Our results suggest that safety alignment is better cast as a conditioning problem than a forgetting one: behavioral control is more precise when sensitive knowledge is retained under controlled access than when it is destroyed.

AI.tldr: A conditioning-based safety method (Token Inoculation) retains dual-use knowledge but gates behavior via a binding token, achieving a strong safety-utility trade-off without unlearning.
AI.motivation: Conventional safety strategies trade off utility or degrade performance; a mechanism to selectively constrain hazardous behavior without destroying knowledge is desirable.
AI.method: Binding-and-branching: insert a hazardous-content token during continued pre-training to bind the marker to domain semantics; during supervised fine-tuning, train the model to answer hazardous queries when the token is present and to refuse when the token is absent, enabling selective refusal without removing dual-use knowledge; critical role of domain-specific binding for generalization.
AI.result: On hazardous-domain task (e.g., WMDP-Bio), hazardous accuracy drops from 79% to 18%; benign-domain performance (e.g., MMLU) retained at 93%; achieves best safety-utility trade-off vs unlearning and refusal baselines across 1B–14B models; selectivity controllable via token quality; domain-binding during pre-training is key for generalization beyond memorized triggers.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment is more effective as a conditioning problem than a forgetting one; controlled access to sensitive knowledge yields precise behavior without fully erasing capabilities.

title: Delineate Anything v2: A Global Foundation Model for Field Delineation
summary: Accurate agricultural field boundary delineation at large scale is a foundational task for food security, supply chain transparency, and carbon accounting. While vision foundation models like SAM show remarkable zero-shot capabilities, they frequently fail in geospatial domains due to topological complexity, cropland texturing patterns, and a lack of physical scale awareness. In this work, we introduce Delineate Anything v2, a globally scalable foundation model designed specifically for wide-area field boundary mapping. We construct FBIS-73M, a 73-million-instance multi-resolution dataset spanning 61 countries. To address the pervasive issue of multi-field administrative parcel merging, we introduce a resolution-specific data curation pipeline that leverages topological image-space adaptation to homogenize merged parcels and strengthen weak physical boundaries. Furthermore, we establish a novel, manually curated evaluation benchmark covering 100 countries to assess independent zero-shot generalization. Our results show that Delineate Anything v2 surpasses the current state-of-the-art, including the Delineate Anything framework, by 0.284 mAP@0.5 (+103.3% relative gain), while maintaining execution speeds suitable for rapid national- and global-scale deployment, as demonstrated by nationwide mapping of Ukraine (603,000 km^2) in 5.4 hours on a consumer-grade workstation. Code, pre-trained weights, the FBIS-73M dataset, and ready-to-use national-scale vector boundary products are publicly available at https://github.com/Lavreniuk/Delineate-Anything.

AI.tldr: Delineate Anything v2 introduces a globally scalable foundation model for wide-area field boundary mapping, backed by the FBIS-73M dataset and a resolution-specific curation pipeline, plus a 100-country benchmark; it achieves a 0.284 mAP@0.5 improvement over prior SOTA and enables rapid nationwide mapping.
AI.motivation: Vision foundation models struggle in geospatial domains due to topological complexity, cropland texture, and lack of physical scale awareness, hindering accurate wide-area field boundary delineation crucial for food security, supply chains, and carbon accounting.
AI.method: Propose Delineate Anything v2 with the FBIS-73M dataset (73 million instances across 61 countries), a resolution-specific data curation pipeline leveraging topological image-space adaptation to homogenize merged parcels and strengthen weak physical boundaries, and a manually curated 100-country evaluation benchmark for zero-shot generalization.
AI.result: Outperforms current SOTA (including Delineate Anything) by 0.284 mAP@0.5 ( +103.3% relative gain ); demonstrates scalable deployment with Ukraine (603,000 km^2) mapped in 5.4 hours on a consumer-grade workstation.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers scalable, generalizable field boundary delineation for large-scale geospatial mapping, providing open-source code, weights, and public datasets to enable national- and global-scale boundary products.

title: OpenRTAG: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Data Quality Degradation
summary: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs) are an important graph data form that combine relational structure with rich node text. However, real-world TAGs are often imperfect, with quality issues arising from text, structure, and labels, and typically manifesting as sparsity, noise, and imbalance. These dimensions define nine representative degradation scenarios that can substantially affect TAG learning. Although prior studies have explored specific mitigation strategies, existing evidence remains fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and model families, leaving TAG robustness insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we present OpenRTAG, a robustness benchmark for text-attributed graph learning. OpenRTAG organizes TAG quality issues into a unified 3 * 3 taxonomy and supports standardized evaluation across nine TAG datasets and three downstream tasks. It systematically evaluates scenario validity and model sensitivity, compares traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative GFM, investigates the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of scenario-matched baselines, and further examines model behavior under composite degradation scenarios. OpenRTAG provides a standardized testbed for understanding robustness in TAG learning under realistic low-quality settings.

AI.tldr: OpenRTAG is a robustness benchmark for text-attributed graph learning (TAG) that unifies degradation into a 3×3 taxonomy, standardizes evaluation across nine TAG datasets and three tasks, and benchmarks GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative GFM under realistic low-quality settings.
AI.motivation: TAGs combine structure and text but face quality issues across text, structure, and label dimensions, causing sparsity, noise, and imbalance. Existing studies are fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and models, hindering understanding of TAG robustness.
AI.method: Introduce OpenRTAG with a 3×3 degradation taxonomy (nine scenarios). Provide standardized evaluation across nine TAG datasets and three downstream tasks. Compare traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative Graph Fault Model (GFM). Assess scenario validity, model sensitivity, and robustness under composite degradations; evaluate scenario-matched baselines for effectiveness and efficiency.
AI.result: A standardized testbed enabling systematic evaluation of TAG robustness, revealing model sensitivity to different degradation types, the performance of scenario-matched baselines, and insights into composite degradation scenarios; serves as a unified framework for comparing robustness across TAG models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: OpenRTAG offers a standardized, comprehensive platform to study TAG learning robustness under realistic low-quality settings, facilitating clearer understanding and benchmarking, and guiding the development of more robust TAG models.

title: Spaghetti Architect: A Contamination-Resistant, By-Construction-Labelled, Multi-Language Code Dataset Generator
comment: 32 pages. Under review at the Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR). Code: https://github.com/KurathSec/Spaghetti-Architect (artifact archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21033174)
summary: Mined code corpora are abundant but uncontrolled: a snippet's semantics, surface "messiness," and difficulty are whatever the wild contained; there is no known-optimal reference to grade against; and any public sample may already sit in a model's training set. We present Spaghetti Architect, a tool that mints code datasets with the control such corpora lack. An anti-optimization transpiler maps a clean, language-agnostic JSON intermediate representation to deliberately redundant, fully-flattened programs in five languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C++); every program is compiled, run, and checked against a reference oracle, so each instance is correct by construction. The clean IR is a known-optimal reference, messiness is dialed by strictly-nested anti-pattern profiles, each instance is labelled along two orthogonal difficulty axes, intrinsic (problem size) and incidental (presentation at fixed semantics), and contamination is resisted by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed. We give construct-validity evidence that the quality order moves established complexity and readability metrics, and report baselines on a four-model open ladder: exact match rises with scale, and the intrinsic knob collapses arithmetic-aggregation accuracy of even the strongest model to zero. Further, development-set scores equal freshly re-minted held-out counterparts within $|Δ|\le 0.012$ (comprehension) and $\le 0.011$ (refactoring); on identical programs, refactoring equivalence ($0.73 \rightarrow 0.99$) is scale-invariant while output prediction collapses; and ablating the generator's self-annotations shows they inflate the weakest model an order of magnitude more than the strongest ($-0.173$ vs $-0.017$): the annotated ladder resolves one of three adjacent pairs where the unannotated resolves all three. Open source (MIT), dependency-free, archived under a persistent DOI.

AI.tldr: Presents Spaghetti Architect, a system that generates and labels synthetic, language-agnostic code datasets with known-optimal references, anti-optimization transformations, and contamination resistance; provides evaluation baselines across multiple languages and models.
AI.motivation: mined code corpora are noisy, lack canonical references, and risk data leakage; there is a need for controlled, reproducible datasets with explicit difficulty axes to rigorously evaluate code-understanding and generation models.
AI.method: An anti-optimization transpiler converts a clean JSON intermediate representation (IR) into redundant, fully-flattened programs in Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, and C++. Each program is compiled, executed, and checked against a reference oracle, making it correct by construction. The IR serves as the known-optimal reference; instances are annotated along two orthogonal difficulty axes—intrinsic (problem size) and incidental (presentation at fixed semantics). Contamination is mitigated by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed. The approach includes self-annotations and a private/open ladder setup to evaluate model performance across scales and configurations.
AI.result: Construct-validity evidence shows the quality order aligns with established complexity/readability metrics. In a four-model ladder, exact-match scores improve with scale, while the intrinsic knob reduces arithmetic-aggregation accuracy of even the strongest models to zero. Development-set scores match freshly minted held-out counterparts within small deltas for comprehension and refactoring. On identical programs, refactoring equivalence rises from 0.73 to 0.99 and remains scale-invariant, whereas output prediction collapses with scale. Ablating the generator’s self-annotations reveals they inflate the weakest model far more than the strongest. The annotated ladder resolves one of three adjacent model-pairs that the unannotated ladder cannot resolve. The dataset is open-source (MIT), dependency-free, archived under a persistent DOI.
AI.conclusion: The Spaghetti Architect framework provides a controllable, reproducible benchmark for code understanding and transformation tasks, enabling precise evaluation of model capabilities while mitigating contamination and messiness through synthetic generation, explicit difficulty labeling, and cross-language evaluation.

title: Context-structured Video Anomaly Detection with Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Training video anomaly detectors is challenging due to the difficulty and cost of annotating diverse and rare abnormal events. Although recent large vision-language models enable training-free inference, existing approaches mostly rely on holistic inference over sampled video and may miss context-specific anomaly cues. In this paper, we present CSI-VAD, a training-free video anomaly detector that identifies abnormal events across diverse contexts. The key idea is to decompose each video into three distinct contexts (environment, objects, time) and perform context-specific inference in separate branches. Because we ground anomaly judgments solely in context-specific visual cues, we do not require predefined text prompts describing abnormal events or dataset-specific tuning. Experiments on UCF-Crime and UBnormal show that CSI-VAD consistently improves over the direct holistic baseline and achieves competitive performance against existing methods, showing the advantage of structured context decomposition for training-free video anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: CSI-VAD is a training-free video anomaly detector that uses context decomposition (environment, objects, time) to perform context-specific inference, improving over holistic baselines without prompts or tuning.
AI.motivation: Annotating diverse and rare abnormal events is costly, and holistic, prompt-based inference may miss context-specific cues. A training-free method leveraging contextual cues can improve anomaly detection across varied scenarios.
AI.method: Decompose each video into three contexts (environment, objects, time) and apply separate, context-specific inference branches. Ground anomaly judgments on visual cues within each context, without predefined text prompts or dataset-specific tuning.
AI.result: On UCF-Crime and UBnormal, CSI-VAD consistently beats the holistic baseline and is competitive with existing methods, demonstrating the benefit of context decomposition for training-free VAD.
AI.conclusion: Contextual decomposition into environment, objects, and time provides a robust, training-free pathway to detect anomalies across diverse contexts.

title: Comparative Study of Multi-Agent Actor-Critic Algorithms in Parameterized Action Reinforcement Learning
summary: Parameterized action reinforcement learning has shown strong performance in environments requiring both discrete action selection and continuous parameterization. Prior work established the effectiveness of single-agent actor-critic algorithms - Greedy Actor-Critic (GAC), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC) - on benchmark parameterized action tasks, but their extension to multi-agent settings remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a comparative study of shared-experience multi-agent extensions of these algorithms: Multi-Agent Greedy Actor-Critic (MAGAC), Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC), and Multi-Agent Truncated Quantile Critics (MATQC). Rather than following the centralized training, decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, the proposed framework uses multiple independent actor-critic agents that share a replay buffer while maintaining separate policy and value networks. We evaluate the algorithms on the Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 benchmarks against their single-agent counterparts, using three-, five-, and ten-agent configurations to assess scalability. Performance is measured by average evaluation return and training time across ten independent runs, with one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc tests used to assess statistical significance. Results show that the multi-agent framework consistently improves Greedy Actor-Critic performance, while MASAC and MATQC show comparatively modest gains over their single-agent versions. Increasing the number of agents beyond five yields limited additional performance while substantially raising computational cost, particularly for MAGAC. These results highlight a trade-off between learning performance and computational efficiency, offering insight into the scalability of shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic methods for parameterized action reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: Shared-experience multi-agent extensions of parameterized-action actor-critic methods (MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC) show mixed gains: MAGAC improves more consistently; MASAC/MATQC offer modest improvements; scalability limited by computation, with diminishing returns beyond ~5 agents.
AI.motivation: Assess scalability and performance of independent, shared-replay multi-agent implementations of parameterized-action actor-critic algorithms, in contrast to centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE).
AI.method: Independent actor-critic agents share a replay buffer but maintain separate policies and value networks. Evaluated MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC against single-agent baselines on Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 with 3-, 5-, 10-agent configurations. Performance metrics include average evaluation return and training time across ten runs; significance tested via one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD.
AI.result: MAGAC consistently improves over its single-agent GAC baseline; MASAC and MATQC show smaller gains. Increasing agent count beyond five yields limited performance gains but substantially higher computation, especially for MAGAC. Overall, a trade-off exists between learning performance and computational efficiency in shared-experience multi-agent parameterized-action RL.
AI.conclusion: Shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic can enhance parameterized-action learning, notably for MAGAC, but scalability is constrained by computational costs. The results underscore the need to balance performance gains with efficiency and motivate further work on scalable multi-agent coordination for parameterized-action tasks.

title: Exposure-Based Reinforcement Learning to Rank
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods for learning-to-rank (LTR) can optimize (almost) any ranking goal, e.g., from precision or discounted cumulative gain to fairness-of-exposure or ranking distillation. However, standard RL is ineffective and computationally costly due to the enormous action space in LTR settings. Existing methods reach computational efficiency through custom gradient computation algorithms, but they are very complex to implement and often clash with auto-differentiation. Consequently, existing RL for LTR is not attractive to many practitioners. We reconsider RL for LTR while actively avoiding reliance on custom gradients. Contrary to the existing approaches, we focus on variance reduction and GPU computation. In doing so, we discover that high sample-efficiency can be reached through baseline corrections and partial marginalization. Furthermore, we propose an abstraction that places gradient estimation behind a document-exposure distribution, this enables seamless plug-and-play integration with auto-differentiation. Thereby, one only has to implement a loss as a differentiable function of exposure and RL for LTR can optimize it using auto-differentiation. Our experimental results reveal that our new exposure-based RL for LTR approach converges considerably faster and at significantly higher ranking performance than existing custom gradients, with no additional costs in computation time when using GPUs. In contrast, existing custom gradients result in severe stability issues when converging over many epochs, which never occur for our methods. Thus, we considerably improve RL for LTR methodology by increasing its effectiveness, efficiency, and ease of application.

AI.tldr: An exposure-based RL for learning-to-rank (LTR) method that eliminates custom gradient engineering, improves sample efficiency via baseline corrections and partial marginalization, and leverages an exposure distribution to enable auto-differentiation. It achieves faster convergence and higher ranking performance with GPU efficiency and better stability than gradient-based RL for LTR methods.
AI.motivation: Standard RL for LTR struggles due to enormous action spaces and reliance on complex, non-differentiable gradient techniques. Custom-gradient approaches are hard to implement and can clash with auto-diff, causing stability and practicality issues. There is a need for a simple, GPU-friendly, stable RL framework for LTR.
AI.method: Introduce an abstraction that routes gradient estimation through a document-exposure distribution. Apply variance reduction via baseline corrections and partial marginalization. Frame gradient estimation as a differentiable loss with respect to exposure, enabling seamless integration with auto-differentiation without custom gradient implementation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows the proposed exposure-based RL for LTR converges faster and achieves higher ranking performance than existing custom-gradient methods, with no additional computation time on GPUs. In contrast, methods using custom gradients exhibit severe stability issues over long training, which do not occur with the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: By re-framing RL for LTR around an exposure distribution and leveraging variance reduction, the method enhances effectiveness, efficiency, and ease of application, enabling plug-and-play optimization via standard auto-differentiation.

title: Advancing Multimodal Fusion on Heterogeneous Medical Data with Hybrid Geometry Attention
comment: ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2026)
summary: Multimodal fusion learning (MFL) has shown great potential in the medical domain, where we are faced with disparate data modalities such as imaging, clinical records, and omics. However, existing MFL strategies face several major challenges. First, they struggle to capture complex cross-modal interactions effectively, which in turn limits performance improvements. Second, they incur high computational costs, restricting their applicability in resource-constrained healthcare AI applications. Finally, they are often designed and evaluated for narrow, fixed modality configurations (e.g., imaging-only, or specific pairs such as image and omics), which limits evidence of their adaptability and generalizability to broader collections of heterogeneous medical modalities. To address these challenges, we propose a novel MFL framework - Cascaded Unified Representation Learning for Efficient Fusion Network (CURE) - a lightweight and scalable framework that progressively integrates various modalities through a novel efficient Hybrid Geometry Aware Fusion layer (HyFuse), where each HyFuse layer is sequentially learned for each modality, making the framework adaptable and generalizable. Within HyFuse, an efficient residual convolution module captures rich multi-scale features to ensure cost-effective learning, while a hybrid-space aware attention mixer learns coarse-to-fine structural cues to better preserve cross-modal relationships. Complementary learnable late-fusion and shared information refinement modules are then employed to learn robust modality-order-invariant shared representations, which in turn yields consistent performance improvements. Extensive evaluations on 16 public datasets show that CURE outperforms leading multimodal fusion methods, boosting performance by up to 3.97% and lowering computational costs by up to 87.8%, ensuring more effective and reliable predictions.

AI.tldr: CURE: Cascaded Unified Representation Learning for Efficient Fusion Network; a lightweight, scalable multimodal fusion framework using HyFuse for progressive, modality-agnostic integration in medical data, achieving higher accuracy with substantial compute savings across 16 datasets.
AI.motivation: Address core challenges in multimodal fusion learning: (i) inadequate modeling of complex cross-modal interactions, (ii) high computational costs limiting clinical applicability, (iii) limited generalizability to broad, heterogeneous modality collections.
AI.method: Propose Cascaded Unified Representation Learning (CURE) with HyFuse layers that sequentially fuse modalities. HyFuse includes a residual convolution module for rich multi-scale features and a hybrid-space aware attention mixer for coarse-to-fine cross-modal cues. Includes complementary late-fusion and shared information refinement modules to learn robust, modality-order-invariant shared representations.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 public datasets, CURE outperforms leading MFL methods, with improvements up to 3.97% and computational cost reductions up to 87.8%.
AI.conclusion: CURE offers a lightweight, adaptable, and generalizable MFL framework for heterogeneous medical modalities, delivering robust cross-modal integration with significantly lower computation.

title: Sequential Learner Modeling Using Multi-Relational Graph Convolutional Networks
summary: User modeling is a critical task in a variety of personalized systems. Recognizing their effectiveness in learning from graph-structured data, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), are increasingly employed for user modeling. However, existing approaches typically treat different relation types in a graph as homogeneous, limiting their ability to capture richer semantics and construct more informative user models. While multi-relational GNNs (MR-GNNs) have been adopted for representation learning and recommendation, their application for user modeling remains unexplored. Moreover, existing GNN-based user modeling approaches ignore the user interaction sequence. To address these research gaps, in this work we propose MR-ConceptGCN, a novel fully unsupervised approach focused on concept-based sequential learner modeling using multi-relational GCNs (MR-GCNs). MR-ConceptGCN effecively combines Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs), MR-GCNs, and the pre-trained language model SBERT to obtain enhanced relation- and semantic-aware representations of the PKG items. The enriched embeddings of the knowledge concepts that a learner did not understand when interacting with learning materials in CourseMapper are then used to construct a sequential learner model that combines long-term and short-term learner interactions. We report the results of an online user study (n = 31), demonstrating the benefits of MR-ConceptGCN in terms of several important user-centric aspects including accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction with an educational recommender system.

AI.tldr: MR-ConceptGCN uses multi-relational GCNs with Personal Knowledge Graphs and SBERT to build unsupervised, concept-based sequential user models for educational recommendations, showing benefits in accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction in a small online study.
AI.motivation: Limitations of homogeneous relation treatment in graph-based user modeling and the under-exploration of combining multi-relational GNNs with interaction sequences and semantic concept representations for learners.
AI.method: Construct Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs) and apply multi-relational GCNs (MR-GCNs) to obtain relation- and semantic-aware item embeddings, enhanced by SBERT. Use enriched concept embeddings (especially for concepts the learner did not understand) to build a sequential learner model that fuses long-term and short-term interactions in an unsupervised framework.
AI.result: Online study with 31 participants showing improvements in accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction for an educational recommender system.
AI.conclusion: MR-ConceptGCN advances concept-based sequential user modeling by integrating PKGs, MR-GCNs, and semantic embeddings, demonstrating enhanced user-centric performance and suggesting broader applicability of MR-GNNs in user modeling.

title: Stale but Stable: Staleness-Adaptive Trust Regions for Stabilizing Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Asynchronous reinforcement learning improves throughput by decoupling rollout generation from optimization, but staleness is an inevitable byproduct compounded by policy lag, engine delays, and mixture-of-experts routing. From a trust-region perspective, this mismatch is critical: training-inference divergence governs approximation error in finite-horizon bounds, whereas PPO clipping only gates sampled outward updates, acting as a sampled surrogate rather than a full-policy constraint. As a result, high-staleness updates remain weakly controlled in the asynchronous regime where stale rollouts matter most.
  We introduce the Staleness-Adaptive Trust Region (SAT), which uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a practical staleness proxy, identifies high-mismatch tails within each batch via staleness-based kernel scaling, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval. This preserves baseline behavior on ordinary tokens while enforcing more conservative updates on newly intercepted outward bands. We prove local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO, showing how the adaptive rule reshapes update geometry under heterogeneous staleness.
  We evaluate SAT in a decoupled asynchronous RL setup built on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, using SGLang as the inference engine and Megatron for training. In this setting, SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieves the best observed AIME24 avg@8, reaching 35.83 at lag 1 and 34.79 at lag 8, while SAT-GSPO reaches 34.17 at lag 1. Adaptive clipping and routing replay act as complementary stabilizers targeting mismatch tails and routing inconsistency, respectively. Overall, aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity effectively stabilizes asynchronous RL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Staleness-Adaptive Trust Region (SAT) for asynchronous RL to bound training-inference divergence caused by stale rollouts; uses staleness proxy and adaptive clipping to constrain updates, with empirical gains on a Qwen3-30B-based setup showing improved AIME24 scores.
AI.motivation: In asynchronous RL, rollout generation decouples from optimization, causing staleness that enlarges approximation error. PPO clipping acts only as a sampled surrogate rather than a full-policy constraint, leaving high-staleness updates under-controlled. A principled, staleness-aware trust-region mechanism is needed to stabilize learning.
AI.method: SAT uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a staleness proxy, applies staleness-based kernel scaling to identify high-mismatch tails within each batch, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval. This preserves baseline behavior on ordinary tokens while enforcing more conservative updates on newly intercepted outward bands. The authors prove local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO. Evaluation is conducted in a decoupled asynchronous RL setup using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, SGLang as the inference engine, and Megatron for training. Variants include SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieving best AIME24 results; SAT-GSPO and adaptive clipping with routing replay acting as stabilizers.
AI.result: SAT variants achieve strong performance on AIME24. SAT-GSPO w/ R3: 35.83 at lag 1, 34.79 at lag 8. SAT-GSPO: 34.17 at lag 1. Adaptive clipping and routing replay stabilize mismatch tails and routing inconsistency, respectively. Overall, aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity improves stability in asynchronous RL.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive, staleness-aware trust-region mechanism reshapes update geometry under heterogeneous staleness and provides a principled means to reduce training-inference divergence in asynchronous PPO-like optimization. The approach yields measurable stability and performance gains in large-scale decoupled RL settings.

title: FlexiAvatar: Unified 3D Gaussian Human Avatars Under Arbitrary Body Visibility
summary: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from monocular video is a fundamental problem in computer vision with broad applications in AR/VR and digital content creation. Existing approaches typically couple parametric body models with neural rendering or 3D Gaussian splatting and optimize all body regions jointly from short videos, which often degrades fidelity in the visible areas. To overcome this limitation, we introduce FlexiAvatar, a unified framework that explicitly optimizes only the visible body regions, effectively eliminating artifacts arising from unobserved limbs. Our method integrates occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking with part-specific residual refinement to capture high-frequency geometric and appearance details. To complete entirely unseen regions (e.g., back views), we leverage a diffusion-based approach to generate texture consistent with the observed appearance. Experiments on full-body (NeuMan, ZJU-MoCap, WildAvatar), upper/half-body (talk-show clips), and head-only (INSTA) inputs show that FlexiAvatar delivers consistently higher reconstruction quality, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by an average PSNR improvement of approximately 3% across datasets. Finally, by restricting optimization to observed regions, our method reduces the effective number of Gaussians that must be optimized and rendered, leading to reduced runtime and memory overhead in partial-visibility scenarios.

AI.tldr: A monocular 3D avatar reconstruction method (FlexiAvatar) that optimizes only visible regions to reduce artifacts, combining occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking, part-aware residual refinement, and diffusion-based texture completion for unseen areas, yielding higher quality reconstructions and lower compute.
AI.motivation: Existing monocular-avatar methods optimize all body regions jointly and across short videos, which causes fidelity degradation in visible regions due to unobserved limbs and global optimization bottlenecks. There is a need to focus optimization on observed regions to improve detail and efficiency.
AI.method: (1) Occlusion-robust SMPL-X tracking to establish accurate correspondences for visible regions; (2) part-specific residual refinement to capture high-frequency geometry and appearance; (3) diffusion-based texture generation to fill entirely unseen regions coherently with observed appearance; (4) optimize only the observed body regions, reducing the number of Gaussians and computational burden; (5) integrate with parametric/body model and neural rendering/gaussian splatting as needed.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across full-body, upper/half-body, and head-only inputs shows consistent higher reconstruction quality; average PSNR improvement of about 3% over state-of-the-art on multiple datasets (NeuMan, ZJU-MoCap, WildAvatar, etc.); reduced runtime and memory usage in partial-visibility scenarios due to fewer optimizable/renderable Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: Focusing optimization on observed regions yields improved reconstruction fidelity, reduces artifacts in unobserved limbs, and enhances efficiency, with diffusion-based completion enabling plausible textures for unseen areas.

title: BioSecBench-Surveillance: A Verifiable Benchmark for AI Agents in Pathogen Genomic Surveillance
summary: As pathogen genomic surveillance scales, the bottleneck is shifting from data generation to analysis. We present BioSecBench-Surveillance, a verifiable benchmark of 100 evaluations testing whether AI agents can infer the right analysis pipeline from raw sequencing data and surveillance context. Each evaluation gives an agent only the data and context a human analyst would have, then grades its structured answer deterministically. The tasks span seven categories, from taxonomic classification to genetic-engineering detection, across diverse sample types and sequencing technologies. Across 3,962 gradable attempts from sixteen model-harness pairs, the strongest configuration cleared only about half. Opus 4.8 with PI led at 50.2 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.1 to 60.3 percent across 83 evaluations, tied with GPT-5.5 with Codex at 50.2 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.8 to 59.6 percent, followed by Opus 4.7 with PI at 49.6 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.0 to 59.2 percent, and Sonnet 4.6 with PI at 48.6 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 38.9 to 58.3 percent. Even when agents invoked the correct workflows, their mistakes came from the choices around them, such as which references, thresholds, filters, and normalization to apply. BioSecBench-Surveillance provides a standard for measuring whether agents can be trusted to perform genomic surveillance when the next outbreak arrives.

AI.tldr: BioSecBench-Surveillance is a large, verifiable benchmark to test whether AI agents can infer the correct genomic-surveillance analysis pipeline from raw data and context. The strongest setups achieve ~50% accuracy across 3,962 gradable attempts, highlighting significant reliability gaps in current AI systems for outbreak-ready surveillance tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the shift in genomic surveillance from data generation to analysis, by creating a standardized, deterministic benchmark to assess whether AI agents can select and apply appropriate analysis workflows under realistic constraints.
AI.method: 100 evaluations across seven task categories (from taxonomic classification to genetic-engineering detection) spanning diverse sample types and sequencing technologies. Each evaluation provides agents with data and context a human analyst would have, and scores a structured answer deterministically. Evaluations involve 16 model-harness pairs and 3,962 gradable attempts. Performance is broken down by configuration (e.g., Opus 4.8 with PI, GPT-5.5 with Codex, etc.) and CI reported per 83 evaluations.
AI.result: Top configurations reach about 50.2% accuracy (e.g., Opus 4.8 with PI; GPT-5.5 with Codex) with 95% CIs around 40–60%. Other leading entries include Opus 4.7 with 49.6% and Sonnet 4.6 with 48.6%. The leading performance suggests only marginal gains above chance, and errors arise even when workflows are invoked correctly—driven by choices of references, thresholds, filters, and normalization.
AI.conclusion: BioSecBench-Surveillance establishes a standard for evaluating whether AI agents can be trusted to perform genomic surveillance during outbreaks. Current systems show limited reliability in inferring and applying correct analysis pipelines, highlighting the need for improved robustness, transparency, and benchmarking approaches in this domain.

title: Contraction-Gauge Preconditioning for Quantized Matrix Multiplication
summary: We study low-precision computation of C=AB with both factors quantized. We derive an exact finite-dimensional identity for the expected squared product error under independent, zero-mean entrywise errors with known variance fields; it holds exactly for non-overloading subtractive dither and for independent stochastic rounding, and we empirically assess deterministic round-to-nearest (RTN). Using the product-preserving equivalence AB=(AT)(T^{-1}B), we formulate contraction-gauge preconditioning: jointly choosing a factor representation and its sharing pattern before quantization. Preconditioning can reduce product error but may require extra transformed, quantized copies of the opposite operand: a shared transform needs one copy, a block-specific transform up to one per block. Within the bounded family of positive diagonal gauges (folds), a geometric program computes a globally optimal shared fold and a linear program decides whether the identity fold is already optimal. For other families we derive computable selection statistics -- tail index for scaling, profile spread for partitioning, coherence and weighted-Gram energy for rotations, slice-energy covariance for hierarchy depth -- with upper bounds for ranking heuristic candidates. Across twelve linear products from a trained three-block image classifier, median within-product rank correlations between dither-model predictions and deterministic-RTN errors are 0.937 at 8 bits and 0.918 at 4 bits. The GP fold cuts held-out product error over the identity fold by 18.0% (8-bit) and 20.5% (4-bit) in geometric mean, beats a SmoothQuant-style grid baseline at both precisions and on ten of twelve products, and lowers composed logit MSE by 15.4% and 26.4%. We thus provide exact stochastic product-error accounting, certified selection within the diagonal family, and a common objective for evaluating reusable transform candidates under RTN.

AI.tldr: Derives an exact stochastic error model for low-precision AB with quantized factors, and designs contraction-gauge preconditioning to minimize product error via diagonal transforms (folds) optimized by a geometric program (and LP to check identity fold). Empirically shows substantial error reductions and competitive performance against baselines on image-classifier products.
AI.motivation: Enable reliable, efficient low-precision matrix products by accounting for and reducing stochastic product error through principled preconditioning and transform selection.
AI.method: Derive an exact finite-dimensional identity for the expected squared product error under independent, zero-mean entrywise errors with known variance fields; prove exact results for non-overloading subtractive dither and independent stochastic rounding; formulate AB=(AT)(T^{-1}B) to enable preconditioning; introduce contraction-gauge preconditioning with shared vs block-specific transforms; optimize within the positive diagonal gauges (folds) via a geometric program for a globally optimal shared fold and a linear program to check identity fold optimality; for other transform families, provide computable selection statistics (tail index, profile spread, coherence/weighted-Gram energy, slice-energy covariance) with upper-bound ranking guidance.
AI.result: Across twelve linear products from a three-block image classifier, median within-product rank correlation between dither-model predictions and deterministic-RTN errors is 0.937 at 8 bits and 0.918 at 4 bits; the GP fold reduces held-out product error relative to identity by 18.0% (8-bit) and 20.5% (4-bit) in geometric mean; outperforms a SmoothQuant-style grid baseline at both precisions and on ten of twelve products; also lowers composed logit MSE by 15.4% and 26.4%.
AI.conclusion: The work provides exact stochastic product-error accounting, certified selection within the diagonal-family folds, and a common objective for evaluating reusable transforms under RTN, enabling principled, computation-efficient low-precision matrix products.

title: GATE-3D: Geometry-Aware Test-time Adaptive Reranking for Open-Set 3D Shape Retrieval
summary: Large pretrained vision models have substantially improved appearance-based 3D shape retrieval, but they still confuse shapes that look similar while differing in geometry. Although geometry-aware features can reduce these errors, naive fusion of geometry and appearance may hurt retrieval when the two modalities are already well aligned. We propose GATE-3D, a lightweight query-adaptive reranking method that incorporates geometry without retraining the retrieval backbone. For each query, GATE-3D predicts how much a geometry-aware score should adjust the appearance-based ranking using features that capture disagreement between the two modalities. This selective design lets geometry contribute where it helps and stay silent where it would hurt. Experiments on three open-set 3D retrieval benchmarks show that GATE-3D improves over appearance-only retrieval and is more robust than always-on fusion. On the primary benchmark, it improves mAP@10 by 2.00 points over appearance-only retrieval (p=0.041); it also improves leave-one-category-out generalization and reduces geometric false positives by 10.8%. GATE-3D achieves competitive zero-shot results against DAC-based baselines. We further find that simple linear routing is more effective than a small MLP in the low-data regime, suggesting that cross-modal disagreement features matter more than model capacity for adaptive routing.

AI.tldr: GATE-3D is a query-adaptive reranking method that selectively injects geometry into appearance-based 3D retrieval without retraining the backbone, improving accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Appearance-based 3D models often confuse geometrically similar shapes; naive fusion with geometry can hurt when modalities are well aligned. A selective, query-specific integration of geometry is needed to improve retrieval without retraining.
AI.method: For each query, GATE-3D predicts how much a geometry-aware score should adjust the appearance-based ranking using features that capture disagreement between appearance and geometry. The routing is simple (linear) and calibrated to a per-query gate that decides when geometry helps. Evaluations show geometry features matter more than model capacity in low-data regimes.
AI.result: On three open-set benchmarks, GATE-3D outperforms appearance-only retrieval and is more robust than always-on fusion; primary benchmark mAP@10 improves by 2.00 points (p=0.041). It enhances leave-one-category-out generalization and reduces geometric false positives by 10.8%. It attains competitive zero-shot results against DAC-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Selective, query-adaptive geometry integration boosts 3D shape retrieval without backbone retraining; cross-modal disagreement features drive effective routing, and simple linear routing suffices in low-data settings.

title: Graph-Based Agentic AI with LangGraph: Workflow Pathways for Long-Running Stateful Business Processes
summary: This paper is a practitioner guide to graph-based workflow pathways for long-running, stateful, multi-step generative AI systems in business processes. Rather than treating LangGraph, a low-level orchestration framework for stateful agents, as a model-quality benchmark target, we present three executable recipes -- SQL analytics with repair loops, agentic retrieval-augmented generation with evidence gating, and human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupt and checkpoint recovery -- to show how typed state, conditional routing, deterministic tools, retries, interrupts, checkpoints, and traces fit together. LangGraph is positioned by workflow-complexity fit, not as a universal default: simpler ReAct-style or plain SDK loops may be better for basic tool use, schema-first tools for structured extraction and validation, and DSPy when prompt or program optimization is the main goal. Each recipe explains when LangGraph is worth the extra structure and which implementation patterns make routes, pauses, and audit trails explicit product behavior rather than hidden prompt logic.

AI.tldr: A practitioner-focused guide that introduces LangGraph as a structured orchestration for long-running, stateful AI workflows, offering three concrete recipes and a decision framework for when extra structure pays off.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between model-centric benchmarks and real-world business-process workflows by enabling typed state, conditional routing, deterministic tools, retries, interrupts, checkpoints, and audit trails in AI-driven operations.
AI.method: Present three executable recipes: (1) SQL analytics with repair loops; (2) agentic retrieval-augmented generation with evidence gating; (3) human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupt and checkpoint recovery. Discuss LangGraph’s fit via workflow-complexity, compare to simpler ReAct-like loops, plain SDK/tooling, schema-first tools, and DSPy; delineate implementation patterns that make routes, pauses, and audit trails explicit rather than hidden prompts.
AI.result: Provides concrete recipes and an explicit framework showing when LangGraph adds value, along with patterns to implement auditable, trackable behavior in long-running AI workflows.
AI.conclusion: LangGraph should be evaluated by workflow complexity fit rather than treated as a universal default; it excels in structured, auditable, multi-step processes, while simpler approaches may be preferable for basic tool usage or optimization-focused goals.

title: ConceptCF: Concept-based Counterfactuals for the Explainability of Time Series
summary: This paper proposes ConceptCF, a method for counterfactual generation that operates on human-interpretable concepts. In high-stakes domains such as healthcare and predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence models can increase efficiency and safety. Explainability is key to ensure these models rely on causal relationships rather than spurious correlations. Counterfactual explanations identify minimal modifications that would change a model's predictions. Existing methods for time series operate on individual points or subsequences without ensuring interpretability of the mutations. ConceptCF instead modifies meaningful concepts. As a result we can provide explanations in terms of these concepts, for example ``the model's prediction would be `Sit' instead of `Walk' if you increase the scale of the movement''. In this paper, the concepts are constructed through time series decomposition, resulting in concepts such as scale, and frequency bands. Counterfactuals are generated using a genetic algorithm that optimizes the concept mutations. Evaluation against five state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates that ConceptCF consistently achieves top-tier performance across validity, confidence, proximity, sparsity and plausibility metrics.

AI.tldr: ConceptCF introduces counterfactual explanations for time series by mutating human-interpretable concepts derived from time-series decomposition (e.g., scale, frequency bands) using a genetic algorithm; achieves strong performance on validity, confidence, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: High-stakes domains require explanations that rely on causal, interpretable factors rather than spurious correlations. Existing time-series counterfactual methods mutate raw points or subsequences and often lack interpretability. ConceptCF aims to align explanations with meaningful concepts to improve trust and usefulness.
AI.method: Concepts are constructed via time-series decomposition to form interpretable factors (e.g., scale, frequency bands). Counterfactuals are generated by a genetic algorithm that mutates these concepts to minimally alter model predictions while preserving interpretability.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation against five state-of-the-art approaches shows ConceptCF consistently achieves top-tier performance across validity, confidence, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility metrics.
AI.conclusion: By grounding counterfactuals in human-interpretable time-series concepts, ConceptCF provides meaningful, actionable explanations that connect model decisions to understandable signal properties; this approach enhances interpretability without sacrificing predictive relevance.

title: CR-Refiner: An Object-Centric Optimal Transport Reranker for Edit-Conditioned 3D Scene Retrieval
summary: Edit-conditioned 3D scene retrieval pairs a reference 3D room with a natural-language modification and retrieves rooms from a corpus that satisfy the edit. Three lines of prior work each fall short on this task. 2D composed image retrieval reasons over pixel-level edits and has no primitive for 3D object sets. 3D foundation encoders embed individual objects but cannot compose at the scene level. 3D scene-grounding methods localize references inside a static scene rather than rank modified rooms across a corpus. We present CR-Refiner, a training-free reranker that wraps any base retriever's top-K candidates with three components. A frozen LLM parses the edit into a structured query entity, and each candidate is scored by an unbalanced optimal-transport problem over a 1xG cost matrix coupling category, style, material, and geometry. The unbalanced solver lets the single-entity query drop mass on irrelevant objects, modelling the asymmetry directly. An axis-conditional structural prior adds size-keyword cues for geometric edits and subject-anchor direction cues for spatial edits. An LLM verifier refines the top three candidates with continuous confidence. Because no benchmark evaluates compositional matching over 3D object sets, we additionally release 3D-CER, 4,963 edit-conditioned queries over a 23,381-room indoor corpus across five edit axes, with multi-positive ground truth, CIRR-style hard subsets, and zero-target adversarials. Across three qualitatively distinct base retrievers, CR-Refiner consistently improves hard-subset R@1 and mAP@10 on every edit axis.

AI.tldr: CR-Refiner is a training-free reranker for edit-conditioned 3D scene retrieval that augments base retrievers with a structured query from LLM, unbalanced optimal-transport scoring across category/style/material/geometry, axis-aware priors, and LLM-based verification, plus a new 3D-CER benchmark; yields consistent gains on hard subsets across base retrievers.
AI.motivation: To close the compositional matching gap in 3D scene retrieval when edits are specified textually; existing 2D or 3D baselines fail to compose object-level edits at the scene level or rank modified rooms across a corpus.
AI.method: Wraps a base retriever's top-K with a frozen LLM that parses edits into a structured query; uses an unbalanced OT with a 1xG cost matrix over category, style, material, geometry; employs an axis-conditional prior for geometric/spatial cues; uses an LLM verifier to refine the top-3; introduces 3D-CER dataset of 4,963 edit-conditioned queries over 23,381 room corpus across five edit axes; evaluation on CIRR-style hard subsets and zero-target adversarials.
AI.result: CR-Refiner yields consistent improvements in hard-subset R@1 and mAP@10 across three base retrievers for all edit axes.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, compositional reranking approach for 3D scene retrieval is effective and complemented by a new benchmark to enable robust evaluation of edit-conditioned 3D object-set matching.

title: LLM Detection as an Intervention: Downstream Impact under Strategic User Behavior
summary: As LLM adoption becomes more widespread, there is a growing interest in detecting LLM-generated content, for example through LLM detection tools and through heuristics based on language patterns. Detectors operate as an intervention that steers not only the detected attribute itself, but also downstream metrics such as LLM usage and output quality. In this work, we demonstrate how imperfect LLM detectors lead to counterintuitive impacts on these downstream metrics, by distorting how users are incentivized to use LLMs in their workflow. We develop a stylized model which captures how users strategically choose how much to use the LLM and how to post-process content to reduce the detected attribute. Using this model, we show that LLM detection can counterintuitively lead humans to increase their LLM usage. Moreover, even when reducing the detected attribute improves output quality, we find that introducing an LLM detector can lead users to produce lower quality outputs. In contrast, we show that detectors result in a clean "rise-then-fall" pattern for the detected attribute, which we empirically reproduce for word frequencies on arXiv abstracts. Altogether, our work illustrates how LLM detection can distort LLM usage and output quality, uncovering failure modes when LLM detectors operate as an intervention on these downstream metrics.

AI.tldr: LLM detectors, as imperfect interventions, can backfire: they may increase usage and even degrade output quality; detectors also show a rise-then-fall pattern in detected attributes; highlight nontrivial downstream effects of detection tools.
AI.motivation: As LLM adoption grows, detecting LLM-generated content is of interest; detectors act as interventions that can shape user incentives and downstream metrics, potentially causing unintended consequences.
AI.method: Develop a stylized theoretical model of users choosing LLM usage and post-processing to reduce detectable attributes; derive counterintuitive effects; provide empirical support by showing a rise-then-fall pattern in word frequencies of arXiv abstracts.
AI.result: Imperfect detectors can incentivize more LLM use; reducing detected attributes may still worsen output quality; detected attribute exhibits rise-then-fall pattern in practice.
AI.conclusion: Detectors can distort downstream metrics; need to account for strategic user behavior and possible adverse effects when deploying detection tools; further empirical validation and modeling required.

title: Is EEG-to-Text Feasible in Real-World Scenarios? An In-Depth Analysis Using a Neuropsychology-Inspired Benchmark
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Published in Proceedings of ACL 2026 Main Conference
summary: Translating brain signals into text could restore communication for people with severe paralysis, yet practically usable systems to date rely on invasive electrocorticography (ECoG). Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive alternative, and EEG-to-text (EEG2Text) has been widely explored. Interestingly, however, EEG2Text models generally rely on teacher-forcing evaluation; without it, they fail to generate meaningful decoding. This reliance prevents EEG2Text from being applied in real-world, non-academic settings. This has fueled numerous debates about whether EEG2Text is a meaningful direction, by extension, and whether EEG truly contains decodable linguistic information. Here, using a neuropsychology-informed paradigm, we find that existing EEG2Text benchmarks have neglected EEG instability, a flaw that has confounded inference and sparked debate. Our experiments furnish key evidence for the feasibility of teacher-forcing-free EEG2Text decoding. Accordingly, we assemble the Corpus OF Eeg-To-Text (COFETT) using a 128-channel high-density EEG cap, providing a benchmark dedicated to evaluating EEG2Text models. In comparisons with multiple existing benchmarks, COFETT achieves SOTA ability to distinguish among model performances and enables robust, teacher-forcing-free evaluation, thereby opening a path toward practical EEG2Text applications. COFETT is open sourced in https://github.com/baoyudu/COFETT.

AI.tldr: Introduces COFETT, a high-density EEG benchmark for EEG-to-text without teacher-forcing, showing feasibility and state-of-the-art discrimination of models.
AI.motivation: To resolve debates about whether non-invasive EEG contains decodable linguistic information and to move EEG2Text from teacher-forced evaluation toward practical, real-world use by addressing EEG instability and benchmarking gaps.
AI.method: Employed a neuropsychology-informed paradigm to analyze EEG instability; collected 128-channel HD-EEG data; built COFETT benchmark; compared EEG2Text models across benchmarks under teacher-forcing-free conditions.
AI.result: COFETT achieves state-of-the-art in distinguishing model performances and enables robust, teacher-forcing-free evaluation; supports feasibility of non-invasive EEG2Text decoding.
AI.conclusion: COFETT provides a dedicated benchmark enabling practical EEG2Text evaluations and contributes to the debate on decodability of linguistic information from EEG, potentially accelerating real-world EEG-to-text solutions.

title: Latent Riemannian Flow Matching for Geometry-Grounded 3D Foundation Models
summary: Geometric foundation models, such as the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT), provide strong 3D priors from unposed images. However, such models operate purely in a feed-forward, deterministic regime, \ie~they cannot generate plausible geometry beyond what the input views directly support. Generative models for 3D scenes, on the other hand, must rely on strong geometric priors to produce coherent outputs from sparse inputs. We bridge these two paradigms by performing flow matching directly in VGGT's latent space, leveraging its learned 3D priors without committing to any explicit downstream representation such as Gaussians, meshes, or video-VAE latents. This requires respecting the latent geometry: VGGT tokens occupy a product of high-dimensional hyperspheres on which standard Euclidean flow matching fails. We address this with a Riemannian Flow Matching framework defined on a product manifold of four hyperspheres, aligned with VGGT's multi-scale encoder, which keeps generated tokens on the valid data manifold required by the frozen decoding heads. On RealEstate10K, ScanNet++ and ETH3D, our method achieves strong performance against recent scene generation baselines in both per-view appearance and aggregated 3D geometry, establishing latent-space flow matching on geometric foundation models as a viable paradigm for 3D generation. The project page can be found $\href{https://lisaweijler.github.io/geometry-grounded-rfm/}{\text{here}}$.

AI.tldr: Latent-space Riemannian flow matching on VGGT's hyperspherical latent space enables 3D scene generation leveraging geometric priors without explicit representations; shows competitive results on RealEstate10K, ScanNet++, ETH3D.
AI.motivation: To fuse predictive capabilities of geometric foundation models with generative 3D scene synthesis by performing flow-based generation directly in the model's latent space while respecting its manifold geometry.
AI.method: Define a Riemannian Flow Matching framework on a product manifold of four hyperspheres, aligned with VGGT's multi-scale encoder, ensuring latent tokens stay on the valid data manifold; perform flow in VGGT latent space without committing to Gaussians, meshes, or video-VAE latents; use frozen decoding heads.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance against recent scene generation baselines in per-view appearance and aggregated 3D geometry across RealEstate10K, ScanNet++, ETH3D.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space flow matching on geometric foundation models is a viable paradigm for 3D generation that preserves strong geometric priors while remaining representation-agnostic; provides coherent outputs from sparse inputs and broad potential for future integration.

title: ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D
summary: As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, we need ways to assess whether their outputs are safe to deploy, even when the agents themselves may be untrusted. AI control offers one such approach: rather than trusting the agent, it treats it as a potential adversary and uses a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deployment. We evaluate AI control for automated AI R&D with ResearchArena, a framework spanning four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Because the deliverable in AI R&D is an artifact that will be deployed and run, we pair each main task with two kinds of hidden side task: an embedded side task that sabotages the submitted model, adapter, kernel, or server itself, and an independent side task that takes a covert out-of-scope action in the sandbox while leaving the artifact honest. We evaluate frontier agents at both sabotage and monitoring, across four monitor types that vary along two axes: whether the monitor may execute and probe the produced artifact, and whether it sees the agent's chain-of-thought. We find that sabotage hidden in the training data is the hardest to catch, flagged fewer than half the time. Letting the monitor run experiments on the artifact, rather than only read the trajectory, helps, but it is not enough: monitors still miss embedded sabotage by inspecting only the surface, by noticing the anomaly but explaining it away, or by probing the artifact with the wrong test. We release ResearchArena as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.

AI.tldr: A framework (ResearchArena) to evaluate sabotage and control in automated AI R&D across four long-horizon tasks, showing that sabotage embedded in training data is hardest to detect; monitoring helps but is not foolproof; release of a modular evaluation platform.
AI.motivation: As AI agents automate AI R&D, there is a need to assess safety of their artifacts before deployment, even when agents may be untrusted; AI control treats the agent as adversarial and uses monitors to detect covert sabotage.
AI.method: Four long-horizon tasks (safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, inference-server optimization) with two side tasks per task (embedded sabotage and independent covert action); four monitor types varying in executable probing and access to chain-of-thought; evaluation of frontier agents (sabotage vs monitoring) within the ResearchArena framework.
AI.result: Training-data–embedded sabotage is the hardest to detect, flagged fewer than half the time. Allowing monitors to run experiments on the artifact improves detection but remains insufficient: they miss embedded sabotage at the surface, misinterpret anomalies, or fail to test the right aspects. ResearchArena is released as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.
AI.conclusion: ResearchArena provides a modular, extensible platform to evaluate sabotage and monitoring strategies in automated AI R&D and highlights the challenges of detecting covert sabotage, especially when embedded in training data.

title: Decafs: Disentangled Conditional adversarial Flows
summary: Flow-based models have established state-of-the-art performance in generative modeling across domains, but are hard to interpret due to their complex latent embeddings. In particular, the entanglement of generative factors in the latent space hinders controlled generation. We circumvent this issue by appealing to a novel conditional generator based on Lie groups that disentangles an alternative latent space, which is aligned closely with the latent flow space using an adversarial loss. Our approach facilitates interpretable conditional generation while obviating the need to expand the dimensionality of the flow space (owing to its invertibility requirements). The proposed model demonstrates strong performance across conditional image (including, outperforming StyleGAN on MNIST, dSprites) and molecule (using standard QM9, ZINC and MOSES) generation tasks

AI.tldr: A Lie-group–based conditional generator disentangles an interpretable latent space in flow-based models, enabling conditional generation without expanding flow dimensionality; achieves strong results on both image and molecule benchmarks, surpassing StyleGAN on MNIST and dSprites.
AI.motivation: Flow-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art performance but suffer from entangled latent factors, hindering controllable generation; there is a need for interpretable conditional generation without increasing latent dimensionality.
AI.method: Introduce a conditional generator built on Lie groups that creates a disentangled alternative latent space aligned with the latent flow via an adversarial loss, preserving invertibility and avoiding flow-space dimensionality expansion.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong conditional generation performance across image datasets (MNIST, dSprites) and molecule datasets (QM9, ZINC, MOSES), including outperforming StyleGAN on MNIST and dSprites.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides interpretable conditional generation without inflating flow-space dimensionality and transfers across domains (images and molecules) via a Lie-group–based latent disentanglement strategy.

title: Text Template Tokens Are Implicit Semantic Registers in Diffusion Transformers
summary: Text-to-image diffusion transformers (DiTs) jointly process text and image tokens, yet their internal computation during denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a causal interpretability framework for modern large-scale DiTs that combines attention decomposition with targeted interventions across token spans, heads, and layers. Using it to separate prompt-content tokens from structural template tokens, we find that the structural tokens carry little prompt-specific information at the encoder output. Yet surprisingly, they emerge as dominant image-to-text attention sinks and causally maintain object identity inside the DiT, acting as implicit semantic registers. We show that they acquire this identity indirectly, with prompt semantics first injected into the image latents and then read back into the template tokens rather than transferred directly from the prompt tokens. Inspired by the above findings, we design a training-free pruning rule for DiTs. Heads that attend most strongly to prompt tokens are dispensable, and pruning them removes $20\%$ of attention FLOPs with only a $1.4$-point drop on GenEval. We further reveal how generative computation in DiTs is organized across heads and depth, separating semantic routing from visual synthesis and progressing from identity formation to propagation and refinement. Our work not only reveals that the tokens encoding semantics at input need not be those that maintain it during generation, but also provides a causal view of internal mechanisms in DiTs.

AI.tldr: A causal interpretability framework for diffusion-based text-to-image transformers reveals that structural template tokens are semantic sinks that preserve object identity, with prompt semantics entering via image latents; a training-free head-pruning rule reduces attention FLOPs with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: To understand how modern DiTs compute during denoising and how semantic information flows across tokens, heads, and layers, and to explore efficiency gains.
AI.method: Combine attention decomposition with targeted interventions across token spans, heads, and layers; separate prompt-content tokens from structural template tokens; analyze encoder outputs and the flow of semantics; propose a pruning rule based on attention to prompt tokens.
AI.result: Structural tokens carry little prompt-specific information at the encoder output but act as dominant image-to-text attention sinks and causally maintain object identity; identity semantics are injected into image latents and read back into template tokens rather than transferred directly from prompt tokens; pruning heads that attend most to prompt tokens removes about 20% of attention FLOPs with ~1.4-point GenEval drop; reveals organization of semantic routing from identity formation to propagation and refinement across heads and depth.
AI.conclusion: Semantics encoded at input tokens need not be the same tokens that maintain it during generation; provides a causal view of DiT internal mechanisms and suggests effective, training-free pruning for efficiency.

title: Associative Emotional Learning in Convolutional Neural Networks
comment: The article has been accepted for publication in Neural Computation
summary: Associative emotional learning enables organisms to adaptively link pleasant or unpleasant outcomes to the presence of predictive stimuli. Whereas computational models such as the Rescorla-Wagner model have shed light on this important function, the limitations of these models are also known, especially when they are applied to neural data. The advent of deep neural networks has opened another avenue for modeling associative emotional learning. In this work we proposed a deep neural network model of visual valence processing, consisting of a visual module that encodes complex natural scenes and a module that recognizes their emotional significance in terms of valence, a key dimension of emotion, and tested a novel Pavlovian learning paradigm on the model. The results showed that with learning, the model reproduced several observations from human associative learning studies, including association formation and generalization, and that the neural representations of the conditioned and the unconditioned stimuli became increasingly aligned both at the single unit and at the neural population level. Comparison between the model and human experimental data provided further validation of our approach. This study thus suggests that deep neural network models, when combined with appropriate learning algorithms, can be used to model behavioral and neural signatures of associative emotion/valence learning.

AI.tldr: A deep neural network model of visual valence learning captures associative emotion formation and generalization, aligning CS/US representations and corroborated by human data.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of classical associative-learning models when applied to neural data by leveraging deep networks to model visual valence processing and Pavlovian learning, thereby linking behavioral and neural signatures of emotion.
AI.method: A two-module DNN with a visual module encoding complex natural scenes and a valence module assessing emotional significance. The model is trained under a novel Pavlovian learning paradigm; analyses include association formation and generalization, examination of CS–US representation alignment at single-unit and population levels, and comparison with human experimental data.
AI.result: The model reproduces key associative-learning phenomena, with CS–US representations aligning more with learning and generalization emerging; these neural signatures show parallel trends to human data, providing validation of the approach.
AI.conclusion: Deep neural networks with appropriate learning rules can model behavioral and neural signatures of associative emotion/valence learning, offering a bridge between computational modeling and neural data and extending insights beyond traditional models.

title: Relative Positions Generalize, Absolute Positions Memorize: An Implicit-Bias Account of Length Generalization in Attention
summary: Transformers with relative positional encodings often extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen during training, whereas transformers with learned absolute encodings typically do not. This is a robust empirical regularity, and the explanations offered for it so far are chiefly about expressivity, that is, about whether a length-generalizing solution exists. We give an optimization explanation. On a minimal fixed-offset retrieval task that isolates positional selection, the gap is governed by the implicit bias of the trained attention head: among the many solutions that fit short sequences, which one gradient descent actually selects.
