Under finite-horizon compactness and Lipschitz assumptions, we prove that UAT strictly enlarges the observation-only Transformer class and can uniformly approximate feedback-dependent decision maps. Across four non-stationary benchmarks: synthetic navigation with hidden goal shifts, non-stationary sepsis treatment, cross-market portfolio allocation, and delayed-feedback recommendation, UAT consistently improves performance over observation-only, test-time adaptation, and input-level feedback baselines, with particularly large gains in noisier regimes that require stronger adaptation.

AI.tldr: A feedback-conditioned retrieval mechanism (UAT) for Transformers that uses a compact utility state to modulate attention, enabling action-reward histories to influence retrieval; proven theoretically and validated empirically on four non-stationary tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard attention is feedback-blind; observation-based histories with differing rewards cannot be distinguished, hindering adaptation to latent regime changes.
AI.method: Introduce Utility-Augmented Transformer with utility state modulating Q/K/V; exact zero-gate property recovering Vanilla Transformer when feedback is uninformative; theoretical results: enlarges function class, universal approximation under finite-horizon compactness and Lipschitz; training uses feedback signals; experiments across four benchmarks.
AI.result: Theoretically, UAT strictly enlarges observation-only Transformer class and can uniformly approximate feedback-dependent decision maps; empirically, UAT improves performance over baselines, especially in noisier regimes.
AI.conclusion: UAT provides robust, feedback-aware retrieval enabling faster adaptation in non-stationary, partially observable environments; potential broad applicability.

title: Circuit Claims Depend on What Is Extracted and How It Is Compared
summary: Circuit extraction identifies a small set of model components whose presence preserves a target behavior under ablation, and the resulting circuit is often read as the mechanism behind that behavior. We argue that this reading is under-determined: preserving behavior does not single out one circuit, because the claim it supports depends on which circuit is reported and how two circuits are compared. We make this concrete in a synthetic Lean tactic-prediction benchmark -- predicting the next step of a proof -- where fixed proof rules with randomized surface form let differences between extracted circuits be attributed to these choices rather than to the task. Across dense and weight-sparse checkpoints (most weights constrained to zero) of the same transformer, evaluated on atomic (single-rule) and compositional (multi-rule) proofs, we vary which extracted object is reported (a compact prediction-preserving circuit, a broader graph that also keeps surrounding read, write, and routing structure, or the smallest subgraph meeting a post-ablation loss threshold), and whether each attention head's query and key are represented jointly or separately. Exact component-to-component edge overlap is low and sensitive to these choices, at times dropping to a random baseline, while two coarser summaries stay stable: the set of selected attention heads, and the circuit-size ranking of conditions that differ in which supervised checkpoint initializes reinforcement learning (RL). The largest accuracy gains from RL on compositional proofs come with the most structure beyond the atomic circuits. A circuit-level claim is therefore well defined only once one states which circuit is reported, the pruning threshold used to extract it, and the level at which circuits are compared. We distill these requirements into a reporting practice for circuit-extraction studies.

AI.tldr: Circuit-extraction results are under-determined: which circuit is reported and how it is compared changes conclusions. Coarser summaries (which heads are selected and circuit-size ranking) are more robust than exact edge-level matching. The paper argues for explicit reporting standards (which circuit, pruning threshold, and comparison level) and demonstrates this on a synthetic Lean tactic-prediction benchmark with RL-initialized checkpoints.
AI.motivation: To improve reproducibility and interpretability of circuit-extraction claims by showing that exact circuit reconstructions depend on reporting choices, not just the task, and to propose a standard reporting practice.
AI.method: Evaluate dense and weight-sparse transformers on atomic vs compositional proofs in a synthetic Lean tactic-prediction benchmark with fixed proof rules and randomized surface form. Systematically vary: (i) which extracted object is reported (compact circuit preserving predictions, broader graph with surrounding IO structure, or smallest subgraph meeting a post-ablation loss), and (ii) whether attention head queries/keys are represented jointly or separately. Measure exact component-to-component edge overlap and coarse summaries (selected heads, circuit-size ranking). Also analyze RL-initialized checkpoints and the impact of extra structural priors.
AI.result: Exact component-to-component edge overlap is low and sensitive to reporting choices, sometimes at random baseline levels. Two coarse summaries are stable: (i) the set of selected attention heads, and (ii) the circuit-size ranking of conditions differing in RL initialization. RL yields largest accuracy gains for compositional proofs when there is more structure beyond atomic circuits.
AI.conclusion: Circuit-level claims require explicit specification of the circuit type, pruning threshold, and comparison level. The authors propose a reporting practice for circuit-extraction studies to ensure well-defined claims and reproducibility.

title: Visual Semantic Decoding of Electrocorticography from Video Stimuli using End-to-End Deep Learning
comment: This is a preprint and has not yet undergone peer review
summary: ECoG-based visual semantic decoding enables inference of semantic interpretation of visual perception from complex, noisy brain activity. This study examines the feasibility of visual semantic decoding using an end-to-end deep learning framework using electrocorticography (ECoG). Specifically, the decoding task is to predict visual categories from video stimuli using time-series neural inputs. A previously collected ECoG dataset from participants ($n=17$) with drug-resistant epilepsy is used for analysis. With fewer than 50 training samples per visual category, this study evaluates multiple deep learning approaches, artificial neural network architectures, and frequency-band filtered inputs. The best-performing approach is analyzed to shed light on the discriminative information it relies on across spectral, temporal, and cortical dimensions. The selected decoding system uses mixup augmentation, a Transformer-based encoder, and high-gamma (80-150 Hz) inputs with a 900 ms post-stimulus window. Further analysis shows that early visual cortex (V2-V4), ventral stream visual cortex, MT+ complex with neighbouring visual areas, and lateral temporal cortex contributed substantially to decoding performance. This study demonstrates that an end-to-end deep learning framework can yield promising decoding performance from dynamic visual stimuli without handcrafted features, while the model behavior remains interpretable through spectral, temporal, and cortical dimensions, which are broadly consistent with established neuroscience knowledge.

AI.tldr: End-to-end deep learning on ECoG can decode visual categories from dynamic stimuli with limited data; mixup augmentation, a Transformer encoder, and high-gamma (80–150 Hz) inputs within a 900 ms post-stimulus window yield promising results, with substantial contributions from early visual, ventral stream, MT+ and lateral temporal cortex.
AI.motivation: Assess feasibility of end-to-end deep learning for visual semantic decoding from ECoG with small training samples and without handcrafted features, and to identify the spectral, temporal, and cortical drivers of decoding.
AI.method: Using a previously collected ECoG dataset from 17 epilepsy patients. With fewer than 50 training samples per visual category, comparing multiple deep learning architectures and frequency-filtered inputs. The best model uses mixup augmentation, a Transformer-based encoder, and high-gamma (80–150 Hz) inputs with a 900 ms post-stimulus window. Cortical/spectral contributions to decoding are analyzed.
AI.result: An end-to-end DL framework yields promising decoding performance for dynamic visual stimuli. The discriminative information relied upon by the best model spans spectral, temporal, and cortical dimensions; decoding performance is substantially influenced by activity in early visual cortex (V2–V4), ventral stream, MT+ complex with neighboring areas, and lateral temporal cortex.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end DL can decode visual semantic information from ECoG with limited data, offering interpretable insights that align with established neuroscience. The approach avoids handcrafted features and demonstrates feasibility for dynamic visual decoding, while highlighting key cortical regions and spectral bands involved.

title: Functional Equivalence and Geometric Diversity in Neural Network Approximations: An Empirical Characterization
summary: The Universal Approximation Theorem states that a neural network with a single hidden layer is sufficient to approximate any continuous univariate function on a compact domain to arbitrary error. However, the uniqueness of such neural network representations is not guaranteed, raising questions about practical identifiability. In this work, we address this concern by analyzing functional equivalence and geometric diversity of neural network approximations to a few elementary mathematical functions. The analysis includes an extensive study of single-layer neural networks and multilayer perceptrons under noisy and noise-free conditions. Beyond just network capacity, we study the geometric properties through the lens of sloppiness, characterized by the eigen spectrum of the Hessian of the cost function and the effective rank to quantify the dimensionality of parameter space. The study reveals large equivalence classes of functionally indistinguishable yet geometrically diverse networks that consistently exhibit low effective rank and structural redundancy. Finally, a model select criterion is proposed for identifying optimal models based on parsimony, ease of estimation, and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Examines practical identifiability of neural nets by exploring functional equivalence and geometric diversity; reveals large equivalence classes with low effective rank, and proposes a parity-based model selection criterion focused on parsimony and inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: To address non-uniqueness in neural network representations implied by universal approximation, and to quantify the geometry of solution spaces via sloppiness and Hessian spectra.
AI.method: The study analyzes single-layer networks and multilayer perceptrons under both noisy and noise-free conditions, assessing functional equivalence for elementary functions. It evaluates geometric properties through the Hessian eigen-spectrum and the effective rank to quantify parameter-space dimensionality and redundancy, comparing diverse networks that realize the same function.
AI.result: Identifies large classes of functionally indistinguishable networks that are geometrically diverse yet exhibit consistently low effective rank and structural redundancy, across settings.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a model selection criterion prioritizing parsimony, ease of estimation, and inference efficiency to identify optimal, interpretable networks; highlights the role of redundancy and sloppiness in neural network representations.

title: H$^2$SD: Hybrid Hindsight Self-Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models on tasks such as mathematical reasoning and code generation. However, most RLVR methods assign a scalar outcome reward to an entire trajectory, resulting in sparse supervision and limited token-level credit assignment. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides denser supervision by distilling token-level distributions from a stronger teacher model, but requires an additional teacher and typically assumes a shared vocabulary. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes this dependency by conditioning the same model on privileged information to construct a teacher policy. However, directly matching the teacher distribution may cause information leakage and unstable optimization. RLSD avoids direct matching by using the teacher signal only to modulate update magnitudes, but it cannot provide an explicit correction direction when the sampled reasoning fails. To address this tradeoff, we introduce $\mathrm{H}^{2}\mathrm{SD}$, a hybrid hindsight self distillation framework that uses the teacher differently according to trajectory correctness. For successful trajectories, the teacher receives the student response confirmed as correct together with a rephrasing instruction, and its probabilities on the original response tokens are used to modulate update magnitudes without changing the direction determined by the reward. For failed trajectories, we condition the teacher on a reference hint containing key reasoning steps and a verified answer, and minimize the reverse KL divergence from the student to the teacher. Experiments on multiple challenging reasoning benchmarks show that H$^2$SD consistently outperforms representative RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD baselines while maintaining stable optimization and favorable generation efficiency.

AI.tldr: Introduce H^2SD, a hybrid hindsight self-distillation framework that uses teacher signals differently for successful vs failed trajectories to enhance RLVR-based reasoning in large language models; achieves improved performance and stable optimization over RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD.
AI.motivation: Address sparse, scalar trajectory rewards in RLVR and weaknesses of existing distillation methods (OPD/OPSD/RLSD): need dense, reliable token-level credit and explicit correction directions for reasoning tasks.
AI.method: Hybrid hindsight self-distillation (H^2SD): for successful trajectories, use teacher with the confirmed correct response and a rephrasing instruction; modulate update magnitudes using the teacher's token probabilities without changing the reward-driven direction. For failed trajectories, condition the teacher on a reference hint containing key reasoning steps and a verified answer; minimize the reverse KL from student to teacher. This combines magnitude-based modulation with explicit corrective guidance across trajectory outcomes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on multiple challenging reasoning benchmarks shows H^2SD consistently outperforms representative RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD baselines, with stable optimization and favorable generation efficiency.
AI.conclusion: H^2SD effectively balances credit assignment and correction directions by tailoring teacher signals to trajectory success, yielding improved reasoning performance and stable training in RLVR settings.

title: SFGA: A Statistics-First Gating Architecture with Adjudicative Escalation for Trustworthy SFT Data Procurement
summary: Procuring supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data forces a buyer to decide, before any downstream training, whether a candidate corpus is worth acquiring. We present \sys{}, a statistics-first gating architecture that treats procurement as a cost-aware routing problem over three intrinsic quality axes -- diversity, utility, and redundancy. Cheap blind measurements are summarised into per-axis estimates with confidence intervals; a gate accepts a decision only when intervals are tight, sample sizes are adequate, and the axes agree, otherwise it escalates the case to an adjudicative debate between a buy-advocate and a reject-advocate judge, resolved by a presiding verdict. On a controlled benchmark of 12 datasets ($2{\times}3{\times}2$ grid over the three axes) with 5 seeds, the gate reaches 0.90 accuracy and 0.83 $F_1$ at \$0.017 per unit, sitting between an always-verify baseline (0.75) and an oracle upper bound (0.98) while spending less than always-escalate (\$0.020). We further report honest negative diagnostics of the debate path: a con-side win rate of 0.80 ($p\approx3{\times}10^{-6}$) and a 52\% position-flip rate under advocate swapping expose negativity and positional biases that a naive LLM-judge would hide. We frame the injected-knob evaluation explicitly as a controlled synthetic benchmark for measurement fidelity and routing calibration, and delimit external validity as future work.

AI.tldr: A cost-aware, statistics-first gate for procuring SFT data that routes decisions across three intrinsic axes (diversity, utility, redundancy) using confidence-based per-axis estimates and an adjudicated debate, achieving strong accuracy at low cost on a synthetic benchmark.
AI.motivation: Reduce procurement risk and expense in data acquisition for supervised fine-tuning by reframing procurement as a decision problem with uncertainty quantification and debatable adjudication.
AI.method: Three quality axes (diversity, utility, redundancy); cheap measurements produce per-axis estimates with confidence intervals; gate accepts a decision only if intervals are tight, sample size is adequate, and axes agree; otherwise escalates to a debate between a buy-advocate and a reject-advocate judge, resolved by a presiding verdict; evaluation on a controlled benchmark of 12 datasets (2×3×2 grid) with 5 seeds; comparison against an always-verify baseline and an oracle upper bound; includes honest negative diagnostics of the debate path (e.g., con-side win rate, position-flip rate) and frames the setup as a controlled synthetic benchmark for measurement fidelity and routing calibration; external validity acknowledged as future work.
AI.result: Gate achieves 0.90 accuracy and 0.83 F1 at $0.017 per unit, sitting between always-verify (0.75) and oracle upper bound (0.98) while cheaper than always-escalate ($0.020); debate-path diagnostics show a con-side win rate of 0.80 (p≈3×10⁻⁶) and a 52% position-flip rate under advocate swapping, indicating biases exposed by the adjudicative setup; results supported by synthetic benchmarking for measurement fidelity and routing calibration.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields cost-effective procurement with near-optimal decision performance via calibrated gating and adjudication, highlights biases in naïve adjudication setups, and establishes a controlled synthetic benchmark for routing calibration; external validity remains to be demonstrated in real-world data collections.

title: Variational meta-learning inference for low dimensional neural system identification
summary: Deep learning has proven highly effective for nonlinear system identification, but heavily parameterized neural networks are prone to overfitting in low-data regimes and lack reliable uncertainty quantification. The recently developed manifold meta-learning framework addresses the data efficiency problem by restricting the model parameters to a meta-learned low-dimensional manifold. However, that method is purely deterministic. We propose a fully probabilistic extension of the manifold meta-learning framework, based on amortized Variational Inference, where a generative prior over the low-dimensional parameter manifold is learned. During task-specific adaptation, we combine Maximum A Posteriori estimation with the Laplace approximation to yield a mathematically grounded posterior approximation. Evaluated on a static regression task and the Bouc--Wen dynamical system benchmark, the proposed approach achieves predictive accuracy comparable to its deterministic counterpart while successfully providing calibrated uncertainty bounds in severely low-data regimes.

AI.tldr: Probabilistic extension of manifold meta-learning for data-efficient nonlinear system identification. Uses amortized variational inference with a generative prior on a low-dimensional parameter manifold; adapts with MAP and Laplace approximation. Matches deterministic performance and provides calibrated uncertainty in very low-data regimes on static regression and Bouc–Wen benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reduce overfitting and enable reliable uncertainty quantification for deep models in low-data nonlinear system identification by combining meta-learned low-dimensional manifolds with a probabilistic framework.
AI.method: Introduce a fully probabilistic extension of manifold meta-learning using amortized variational inference with a generative prior over the low-dimensional manifold; during task adaptation, perform Maximum A Posteriori estimation augmented by the Laplace approximation for posterior uncertainty. Evaluate on static regression and Bouc–Wen dynamical system benchmark.
AI.result: Achieves predictive accuracy comparable to the deterministic manifold meta-learning model while providing calibrated uncertainty bounds in severely low-data regimes.
AI.conclusion: A probabilistic manifold meta-learning framework can deliver data-efficient learning with reliable uncertainty quantification, retaining competitive accuracy relative to deterministic baselines and enabling robust predictions in low-data scenarios.

title: Subject-Conditioned Glucose Forecasting in Type-1 Diabetes
comment: Accepted at the IEEE EMBC 2026 Conference
summary: Accurate forecasting of blood glucose concentration is key in the management of Type 1 Diabetes, facilitating early detection of adverse glycemic events and supporting timely therapeutic interventions. Despite recent advances in glucose prediction, most existing approaches rely on population-level representations or implicit personalization strategies that fail to deliver effective subject-specific forecasts. In this work, we propose Subject-Conditioned Glucose Prediction (SCGP), a novel multimodal deep learning architecture conceived for personalized blood glucose prediction. SCGP conditions glucose predictions based on observed glucose data and a compact subject-specific representation learned from contextual information. By explicitly separating subject characterization from glucose dynamics modeling and avoiding early fusion of heterogeneous inputs, the proposed framework effectively captures inter-subject variability while preserving robust and reliable temporal modeling. Experiments on two state-of-the-art benchmark datasets demonstrate that SCGP consistently improves forecasting performance, enabling reliable detection of adverse glycemic events across multiple prediction horizons, highlighting the benefits of explicit subject conditioning for personalized diabetes management.

AI.tldr: SCGP: A multimodal, subject-conditioned deep learning model for personalized blood glucose prediction that separates subject representation from glucose dynamics to improve forecasting and adverse event detection.
AI.motivation: Current glucose prediction methods largely rely on population-level representations or implicit personalization, which underperform for individual patients due to inter-subject variability and limited temporal modeling. A subject-conditioned approach aims to capture individual differences while maintaining robust temporal dynamics.
AI.method: SCGP is a multimodal architecture that learns a compact, subject-specific representation from contextual information and uses it to condition glucose forecasts. It explicitly separates subject characterization from glucose dynamics modeling, avoiding early fusion of heterogeneous inputs and enabling explicit subject conditioning on observed glucose data and context.
AI.result: On two state-of-the-art benchmark datasets, SCGP consistently improves forecasting performance and enables reliable detection of adverse glycemic events across multiple prediction horizons.
AI.conclusion: Explicit subject conditioning improves personalized diabetes management by capturing inter-subject variability and enhancing the reliability of glucose forecasts and event detection.

title: ROMS-IMLE: A Minimalist Approach to Competitive Single-Step Generative Modelling
summary: Generative models have undergone many generations of evolution, from VAEs/GANs to diffusion/flow matching. Along the way, the underlying techniques have become more complicated and various beliefs about what drives strong empirical performance have taken hold. Due to the success of diffusion models and flow matching, one of the more common beliefs is the importance of transforming the noise distribution to the data distribution gradually through many small transformations. We ask whether this is truly necessary, and take a minimalist approach to designing a competitive generative model. We start with the bare-bones essentials, namely just a training objective and a model. We purposefully make both simple. For the training objective, we choose Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE), and eschew more complicated alternatives such as variational inference, adversarial training and numerical integration. For the model, we eschew transformers and instead choose a moderately sized convolutional network. Then we judiciously added elements that are truly essential, which surprisingly do not include iterative denoising. The result is a single-step parameter-efficient generative model that produces high quality samples at fast speed: it achieves an FID of 2.56 on ImageNet 256 and simultaneously attains good precision and recall.

AI.tldr: A minimalist, single-step generative model using IMLE with a CNN backbone achieves high-quality samples quickly without iterative denoising, challenging diffusion-like approaches; reported FID 2.56 on ImageNet-256.
AI.motivation: Question whether the common belief that gradual noise-to-data transformations (as in diffusion/flow matching) are essential is correct; pursue a lean design to test if strong generation is possible with simpler objectives and architectures.
AI.method: Train with Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE); use a moderately sized convolutional network instead of transformers; avoid iterative denoising and other complex training paradigms (no VI, no adversarial training, no heavy numerical integration); produce single-step samples with a compact model.
AI.result: Single-step generation achieves FID 2.56 on ImageNet 256 and exhibits good precision and recall; the approach is parameter-efficient and fast.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that minimalist design can rival diffusion-based methods; iterative denoising and complex architectures are not strictly necessary for strong generative performance; IMLE can be a viable training objective for efficient, high-quality generation.

title: Biological Amnesia in ICU Time-Series Prediction: A Drift-Adaptive Two-Stream Architecture with Temporal Retrieval
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code and aggregate audit logs available at: [https://github.com/empresst/ClinicalRag]. Under Review
summary: Background: Clinical decision support systems degrade silently as treatment protocols evolve, yet standard adaptation methods treat models as monolithic blocks, unable to distinguish stable patient physiology from shifting institutional practice. Methods: We propose an adaptive clinical intelligence architecture for ICU intervention prediction that structurally decouples physiological from treatment representations, confining parameter updates to the treatment stream upon a dual distributional and accuracy trigger. Automated audit logs record which treatment features drove each adaptation event and how their importance shifted. At inference, an attribution-driven Temporal RAG module grounds each prediction in patient-specific, era-matched PubMed evidence anchored to the patient's dominant physiological features. Experiments used 84,792 MIMIC-IV stays (2008-2022) under strict chronological split. Results: Drift localised entirely to the treatment stream, validating the structural prior. Selective adaptation improved vasopressor and septic shock discrimination and calibration over the static source model. A fully retrained baseline yielded marginally higher aggregate discrimination but missed 26 septic shock cases the framework correctly identified, with none in the reverse direction; retrieval consistency with the pre-adaptation source model was preserved by the framework but degraded substantially in the retrained baseline. Conclusions: Structurally constraining adaptation to drifting components while preserving stable physiological representations enables clinical AI to evolve with practice without distorting learned patient biology. This architecture offers a template for governable, interpretable deployment of adaptive models in high-stakes clinical environments.

AI.tldr: Adaptive ICU prediction with decoupled physiology and treatment streams, triggering updates only in the treatment path; audit logs and PubMed-grounded retrieval; validated on MIMIC-IV, improves septic shock/vasopressor predictions and calibration, maintains retrieval consistency.
AI.motivation: Clinical decision support systems degrade as treatment protocols evolve; monolithic models cannot distinguish stable patient physiology from shifting institutional practice, risking distortion of learned biology.
AI.method: Architectural decoupling of physiological vs. treatment representations; updates confined to the treatment stream via dual distributional and accuracy triggers; automated audit logs record driving treatment features and shifting importance; inference uses an attribution-driven Temporal RAG grounded in era-matched PubMed evidence linked to dominant physiological features; validated on 84,792 MIMIC-IV stays (2008–2022) with strict chronological split.
AI.result: Drift localized to the treatment stream, validating the structural prior; selective adaptation improved vasopressor and septic shock discrimination and calibration versus static source; a fully retrained baseline achieved marginally higher aggregate discrimination but missed 26 septic shock cases correctly identified by the framework; retrieval consistency with the pre-adaptation model was preserved by the framework but degraded in the retrained baseline; no reverse-direction drift observed.
AI.conclusion: Constraining adaptation to drifting components while preserving stable physiological representations enables evolvable, governable, and interpretable clinical AI in high-stakes settings; offers a template for adaptive deployment that maintains patient biology integrity.

title: Unsupervised Multi-kernel Learning for Automated Algorithm Selection
summary: Automated algorithm selection in black-box optimization typically relies on supervised models that map landscape features to algorithm performance labels. Such models are costly to train, benchmark-dependent, and often fail to generalize to unseen problem classes. We study an unsupervised alternative: multi-kernel clustering over heterogeneous landscape representations, in which problem instances are grouped without using performance labels in the clustering stage, and the resulting clusters are mapped post hoc to solver recommendations through a strictly separated three-stage evaluation protocol. Drawing on two decades of advances in multiple kernel learning, we adopt a multi-kernel k-means formulation that jointly learns cluster assignments and kernel weights over four heterogeneous landscape views: ELA, DeepELA, DoE2Vec, and TransOptAS. On affine BBOB-derived selector tasks for Differential Evolution (DE) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) at a fixed evaluation budget, we report mean plus or minus standard deviation selector profiles over 50 independent random seeds for stochastic configurations. Multi-kernel clustering obtains the strongest mean profile on the DE portfolio and remains competitive with, and nominally ahead of, the leading baselines on the more compressed PSO portfolio, where differences among the best methods are small relative to stochastic variation. In representative median-seed runs used for visualization, the learned kernel weights retain ELA and TransOptAS while assigning zero weight to DeepELA and DoE2Vec, providing a task-specific interpretation of which representations are retained by the multi-kernel model for selector-oriented grouping.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised, multi-kernel clustering for algorithm selection in black-box optimization using four heterogeneous landscape views; achieves competitive performance and interpretable kernel weighting.
AI.motivation: To address limitations of supervised algorithm selection (costly labeling, benchmark dependence, limited generalization) by clustering problem instances without performance labels and mapping clusters to solvers post hoc.
AI.method: Multi-kernel k-means over four landscape views (ELA, DeepELA, DoE2Vec, TransOptAS); jointly learn cluster assignments and kernel weights; evaluate on affine BBOB-derived selector tasks for DE and PSO at a fixed budget; 50 seeds; report mean ± std; three-stage evaluation with post hoc mapping to solvers; analyze learned kernel weights.
AI.result: For DE, achieved the strongest mean selector profile; for PSO, competitive with leading baselines with small differences relative to stochastic variation. Median-seed runs indicate kernel weights preserve ELA and TransOptAS while assigning zero weight to DeepELA and DoE2Vec, enabling task-specific interpretation of representations used for clustering.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of unsupervised, multi-view clustering for algorithm selection in BBO, with interpretable representation weighting and competitive performance. Suggests potential generalization benefits and a direction toward representation-robust selector design; future work could explore broader problem classes, alternative post hoc mappings, and stability of kernel weights.

title: Spectral Higher-Order Neural Networks Have Sharp Expressivity Bounds
summary: Neural hypergraphs are a natural generalization of neural networks, the reference models in modern machine learning. Yet, their deployment has proven demanding: the number of weighted hyperedges required leads to an intractable parameter explosion. However, a novel parametrization that leverages spectral attributes for neural hypergraphs has been recently proposed, that enables to recycle parameters via a weight sharing scheme and consequently yields a significant reduction of the associated computational cost. Preliminary tests carried out on spectral higher-order architectures pointed to meaningful improvements in both performance and interpretability. Building on these results, we advance the benchmarking efforts by evaluating the spectral higher order framework on N-bit parity tasks, a well-established testbed known to be particularly challenging. As we will convincingly argue, Spectral Higher-Order Neural Networks (SHONNs) possess a versatile and highly tunable hypothesis space.

AI.tldr: Spectral Higher-Order Neural Networks (SHONNs) propose a spectral parametrization for neural hypergraphs enabling parameter sharing and reduced computational cost, yielding preliminary improvements in performance and interpretability; validated on N-bit parity tasks.
AI.motivation: Neural hypergraphs incur parameter explosion due to numerous weighted hyperedges; spectral attribute-based weight sharing offers compactness, efficiency, and potential interpretability gains.
AI.method: Introduce a spectral-aware parametrization for hypergraph neural networks; implement SHONN framework with weight-sharing across hyperedges via spectral attributes; benchmark on challenging N-bit parity tasks.
AI.result: Preliminary tests show meaningful improvements in performance and interpretability; on N-bit parity tasks, SHONNs demonstrate a versatile and highly tunable hypothesis space.
AI.conclusion: Spectral parametrization yields compact, interpretable, and adaptable higher-order networks; results encourage broader evaluation and theoretical analysis.

title: Adopting Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Molecular Generation
summary: Leveraging large language models (LLMs) for molecular generation has shown remarkable potential in chemical and drug design. Current methods primarily rely on supervised training or fine-tuning with limited datasets, which are insufficient to capture complex molecular design objectives. While some approaches attempt to guide generation toward specific goals, they often lack direct optimization mechanisms, making it difficult to align generated molecules with desired properties. To tackle these challenges, we propose \textbf{LLMol}, a principled reinforcement learning framework that directly incorporates verifiable rewards for targeted molecule generation. The key insight is to formulate molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task, where verifiable rewards serve as explicit supervision to drive generation toward desired objectives. LLMol follows a two-stage training paradigm combining supervised learning and reinforcement learning. In the first stage, large language models are supervised fine-tuned to capture chemical syntax and molecular distributions. In the second stage, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which directly integrates property-based reward signals to guide molecular generation toward task-specific objectives. To address the high variance and instability common in discrete sequence optimization, we adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a stable on-policy algorithm that smooths reward signals and improves training robustness. This framework enables LLMol to effectively handle a range of molecular design tasks, including single-property targeting (e.g., penalized logP, QED) and structure-constrained optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMol consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving higher success rates and improved efficiency across diverse molecular benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A two-stage LLM-based molecular design method (LLMol) that uses supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and GRPO for stable optimization of discrete sequences, achieving superior single-property targeting and structure-constrained goals across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current molecular generation methods rely on limited supervised data and lack direct, verifiable objective-based optimization for molecular properties; discrete sequence generation poses high variance and instability in RL. A principled RL framework with verifiable rewards can better align generation with design goals.
AI.method: Stage 1: Supervised fine-tuning of a large language model to capture chemical syntax and molecular distributions. Stage 2: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) using property-based reward signals to guide generation toward objectives. To stabilize discrete sequence optimization, employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an on-policy algorithm that smooths reward signals and improves training robustness. The design is framed as goal-conditioned sequence prediction with verifiable rewards to enable various tasks (single-property targeting and structure-constrained optimization).
AI.result: Experimental results show that LLMol consistently outperforms existing methods in multiple molecular design benchmarks, achieving higher success rates and greater efficiency across tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLMol provides a principled, verifiably-rewarded RL framework for targeted molecule generation, with GRPO addressing training instability and enabling effective handling of both single-property targeting and structure-constrained objectives.

title: Probabilistic Physics-Aware Machine Learning Predictions of Electric Truck Energy Consumption with Field Data
summary: In this work, we incorporate first principle physics into the construction of data-driven methods by considering a model that accounts for the different sources of energy losses during vehicle operations. Our results show that Bayesian linear regression based on this physics-aware model can improve the reliability of the expected energy consumption, as compared with standard linear regression. Further, it is shown that more complex machine learning models such as neural networks and gradient boosted regression trees, based on the same physical model, can further improve the accuracy in energy forecasting and significantly outperform standard versions of the same machine learning models. In addition to point predictions of the energy consumption, we develop a framework for estimating the corresponding uncertainty in the form of predicted standard deviation. Our results show that all of the models learn to estimate the uncertainty reasonably well.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed Bayesian and ML models improve energy forecasting for vehicle operation; they provide uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Integrate first-principles energy loss physics into data-driven models to improve prediction reliability and forecast uncertainty for vehicle energy consumption.
AI.method: Develop a physics-aware model of energy losses; apply Bayesian linear regression; extend to neural networks and gradient-boosted regression trees using the same physics-informed features; implement a framework to estimate predictive uncertainty (standard deviation).
AI.result: Bayesian linear regression with the physics-aware model improves reliability compared with standard linear regression; physics-informed neural networks and gradient-boosted trees further improve accuracy and outperform standard versions of these models; all models learn to estimate uncertainty reasonably well.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed data-driven approaches enhance energy consumption forecasting and provide reliable uncertainty quantification, with more complex models offering additional gains.

title: Where Should Optimizer State Live? Tiered State Allocation for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Code and training logs available at: https://github.com/nuemaan/skewadam
summary: Optimizer state is the largest single line item in the memory budget of mixture-of-experts (MoE) training: on a 6.78B-parameter MoE language model, AdamW keeps 50.6 GB of first and second moments to update 12.6 GB of bfloat16 weights. We study SkewAdam, an optimizer built on the observation that the three parameter populations of an MoE - the dense backbone, the experts, and the router - differ enough in size and gradient statistics that they should not receive the same state. SkewAdam keeps float32 momentum plus a factored second moment for the backbone (5% of parameters), a factored second moment alone for the experts (95%), and an exact second moment for the router (<0.01%). The resulting state occupies 1.29 GB, 2.6% of AdamW's, and peak training memory falls from 81.4 GB to 31.3 GB, within the budget of a 40 GB accelerator. In a controlled comparison from identical initializations over 82M tokens, SkewAdam reaches validation perplexity 108.4, ahead of AdamW (126.8), Muon (120.2), and Lion (393.7), and settles router load balance to within 1% of its uniform floor. The allocation is not what earns that perplexity: a tier ablation matches it with twenty times the state, and Adafactor, which shares the factored estimator but drops momentum, plateaus 40 points behind. The tiers buy memory at no cost to accuracy; the accuracy comes from keeping momentum, which a uniform optimizer shares too. Sweeping the baselines' learning rates narrows but does not close the gap: the best tuned AdamW reaches 118.5, tuned Adafactor 139.7. Where optimizer state lives, these results suggest, matters at least as much as how much of it there is.

AI.tldr: SkewAdam reduces MoE optimizer memory by tailoring state to three MoE populations, achieving 31.3 GB peak memory and better perplexity compared to AdamW and other optimizers.
AI.motivation: MoE training imposes large, heterogeneous optimizer state. The standard uniform AdamW state allocation is memory-inefficient and can limit performance. The paper argues that the three MoE populations (dense backbone, experts, router) differ enough to warrant distinct optimization statistics to improve memory and accuracy.
AI.method: Partition optimizer state by MoE components: backbone (~5% of parameters) uses float32 momentum plus a factored second moment; experts (~95%) use factored second moment only; router (<0.01%) uses exact second moment; total state size targeted at 1.29 GB; comparisons against AdamW, Muon, Lion, Adafactor; controlled 82M-token training; ablations to separate effects of state size vs. distribution; evaluation of perplexity and load balancing.
AI.result: The approach reduces peak memory from 81.4 GB (AdamW) to 31.3 GB, well within a 40 GB accelerator. State for backbone is 1.29 GB (2.6% of AdamW's), for experts 2.6%, and for router <0.01% of parameters. In 82M-token validation, SkewAdam achieves perplexity 108.4, versus AdamW 126.8, Muon 120.2, and Lion 393.7; router load balancing is within 1% of a uniform floor. A tier ablation with twenty times more state matches performance, and Adafactor without momentum lags by ~40 points; tuned AdamW reaches 118.5 and tuned Adafactor 139.7.
AI.conclusion: Where optimizer state lives matters at least as much as how much of it exists. Tailoring optimizer statistics to the MoE subpopulations enables memory savings without sacrificing accuracy, and momentum contributes to the accuracy gains beyond what larger, uniform state affords.

title: Deep learning-based prediction of time-resolved adhesive forces in viscoelastic Hertzian contacts
summary: Fast prediction of the response of adhesive soft viscoelastic contacts represents a current challenge in soft robotics and for gripping and manipulation tasks. Determining the complete time-resolved force trajectory requires full numerical simulations, whose computational cost is strongly parameter-dependent, making them impractical for real-time application or design-optimization loops. In this work, we overcome this limitation by training a scalar-conditioned, stateful, sequence-to-sequence deep learning model to predict the full force evolution from a prescribed displacement history for both short- and long-range adhesion regimes. The data set spans four orders of magnitude in loading and unloading rates and includes varied dwell times, with the Tabor parameter ranging from $0.2$ to $3.2$. To enable learning across these heterogeneous time scales, we introduce a fixed-measurement-step (FMS) representation that converts variable-length trajectories into fixed-length sequences while preserving their physical-time information. Different architectures were trained, including long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, temporal convolutional neural (TCN) networks, and time-distributed dense layers with three different Tabor-conditioning mechanisms. The models were compared using global waveform and error metrics. We found that the best-performing model has an LSTM architecture with concatenated conditioning, which achieves a held-out mean-squared error of $5.0\times10^{-4}$, a median pull-off-force error of $\approx2.2\%$, and a median hysteresis error of $\approx1.1\%$. For the held-out protocols, the model predicts a complete force trajectory with a median inference time of $0.16$ s. The model is tested across unseen parameter combinations and against analytical limiting cases, providing a rapid surrogate for repeated numerical evaluations with potential use in control-oriented applications.

AI.tldr: A neural surrogate model predicts full force trajectories for adhesive soft viscoelastic contacts from prescribed displacement histories, using a fixed-measurement-step representation and a scalar-conditioned LSTM with stateful seq2seq architecture; achieves real-time inference and generalizes across wide loading rates and Tabor parameters.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational cost of full numerical simulations for time-resolved force response in adhesive soft contacts, enabling real-time control, design optimization, and rapid prototyping in soft robotics and gripping applications.
AI.method: Train a scalar-conditioned, stateful sequence-to-sequence model on displacement histories to predict the full force evolution for short- and long-range adhesion. Use a dataset spanning four orders of magnitude in loading/unloading rates and varying dwell times with Tabor parameter 0.2–3.2. Introduce fixed-measurement-step (FMS) representation to convert variable-length trajectories into fixed-length sequences while preserving physical time. Compare architectures (LSTM, temporal convolutional networks, time-distributed dense with three Tabor-conditioning mechanisms). Evaluate with global waveform/error metrics; identify best model as LSTM with concatenated conditioning.
AI.result: Best model (LSTM with concatenated conditioning) achieves held-out MSE 5.0×10^-4, median pull-off-force error ~2.2%, median hysteresis error ~1.1%; inference time for held-out protocols ~0.16 s, generalizes to unseen parameter combinations and analytical limits, providing a rapid surrogate for repeated numerical evaluations.
AI.conclusion: A scalar-conditioned, stateful LSTM with FMS encoding robustly predicts complete force trajectories across wide adhesion and rate regimes, enabling real-time prediction and control-oriented applications in adhesive soft contact problems.

title: GEqTrain: A Configuration-Driven Framework for Retargeting Equivariant Graph Neural Networks Across 3D Scientific Tasks
summary: Equivariant graph neural networks provide a powerful modeling language for three-dimensional scientific data, but their reuse is often limited by implementations tied to specific tasks, outputs, and training regimes. We present GEqTrain, a configuration-driven framework that separates dataset semantics, model composition, and training objectives. Raw data are mapped to typed node-, edge-, and graph-level fields, while model stacks, losses, and training workflows are assembled declaratively through Hydra configurations. A shared equivariant backbone and training infrastructure can therefore be retargeted to a new task primarily through configuration. We demonstrate this flexibility on three different problems handled within one software stack: coarse-grained-to-atomistic backmapping of biomolecular systems, prediction of NMR chemical shifts in molecular solids, and equivariant generative modeling. Our aim is not to surpass individually optimized task-specific systems, but to show that a shared representation and training infrastructure can achieve competitive accuracy across qualitatively different tasks at the cost of a configuration change. We further introduce GEqDiff, a generative extension based on equivariant flow matching. GEqDiff treats user-defined equivariant fields as first-class generation targets, jointly transporting Cartesian positions and non-scalar node fields spanning representations up to l=3 within a single equivariant flow. We validate this capability on a controlled synthetic benchmark inspired by protein secondary-structure motifs, showing that fields with heterogeneous transformation properties can be reconstructed jointly and with high fidelity. By reducing the software overhead of moving between predictive and generative, scalar and tensorial settings, GEqTrain aims to make equivariant modeling more reproducible, extensible, and reusable.

AI.tldr: GEqTrain is a configuration-driven framework for equivariant GNNs that decouples dataset semantics, model composition, and training objectives, enabling rapid retargeting across tasks; GEqDiff extends this with equivariant flow-based generative modeling.
AI.motivation: To improve reuse, reproducibility, and extensibility of equivariant graph neural networks by separating concerns (data, model, training) and enabling task-agnostic backbones that can be retargeted via configuration.
AI.method: GEqTrain maps raw data to typed node/edge/graph-level fields and assembles model stacks, losses, and training workflows declaratively via Hydra configurations. It shares an equivariant backbone and training infra, retargetable to new tasks. Demonstrations cover three problems: coarse-grained-to-atomistic backmapping of biomolecules, NMR chemical shift prediction in molecular solids, and equivariant generative modeling. GEqDiff extends this with an equivariant flow matching-based generative extension that handles fields up to l=3 as first-class generation targets, jointly transporting Cartesian positions and non-scalar fields. Validation includes a synthetic benchmark inspired by protein secondary-structure motifs showing high-fidelity reconstruction of heterogeneous fields.
AI.result: The framework achieves competitive accuracy across qualitatively different tasks by configuration changes rather than bespoke task-specific systems. GEqDiff demonstrates joint generation of scalar and tensorial fields with high fidelity in a controlled synthetic benchmark, suggesting practical interoperability between predictive and generative, scalar and tensorial regimes.
AI.conclusion: GEqTrain and GEqDiff aim to reduce software overhead in switching between predictive and generative, scalar and tensorial, promoting reproducibility, extensibility, and reuse of equivariant modeling across diverse domains.

title: An unsupervised clustering analysis of breast cancer data derived from electronic health records enhanced through UMAP dimensionality reduction
comment: Accepted at the CIBB 2026 conference ( https://cibb2026.teralab.ai/ )
summary: Breast cancer is one of the most widespread types of cancer, affecting approximately 8 million women worldwide. Electronic health records of patients diagnosed with this disease can serve as valuable datasets for computational analyses, enabling the discovery of new insights about the pathology. Unsupervised clustering, in particular, can identify groups of patients with medically significant features, revealing data trends that might otherwise go unnoticed by medical doctors. In this study, we first applied the DBSCAN density-based clustering method to three independent datasets derived from electronic medical records of patients with mammary carcinoma. Subsequently, to enhance our results, we preceded the DBSCAN application with a dimensionality reduction phase using UMAP. We evaluated our clustering outcomes using three statistical indices (DBCV, DCSI, and DISCO). Our results confirm the effectiveness of combining UMAP with DBSCAN for clustering data derived from electronic health records, paving the way for the medical interpretation of the patient groups identified by our approach.

AI.tldr: UMAP dimension reduction followed by DBSCAN on three EHR-derived breast cancer datasets yields meaningful patient clusters, improving over DBSCAN alone, as validated by DBCV, DCSI, and DISCO metrics.
AI.motivation: Unsupervised clustering of heterogeneous electronic health record data can reveal clinically relevant patient subgroups in breast cancer, potentially informing pathology and treatment insights. Dimensionality reduction can improve clustering performance on high-dimensional EHR features.
AI.method: Two experiments on three independent mammary carcinoma EHR datasets. (1) Apply DBSCAN directly to the original features. (2) Apply UMAP for dimensionality reduction, then DBSCAN on the reduced space. Clustering quality evaluated using DBCV, DCSI, and DISCO indices to assess compactness, separation, and density-based cluster validity.
AI.result: Using UMAP prior to DBSCAN improved clustering performance, with results indicating that the UMAP-DBSCAN pipeline yields more interpretable and clinically meaningful patient groups than DBSCAN alone.
AI.conclusion: Combining UMAP with DBSCAN is effective for clustering EHR-derived breast cancer data, enabling better medical interpretation of identified patient subgroups and illustrating the value of dimensionality reduction in downstream clustering analyses.

title: Predicting Activities in Aqueous Electrolyte Solutions with Hybrid Machine Learning
summary: Activities in aqueous electrolyte solutions, usually described by ionic activity and osmotic coefficients, are important properties for modeling many processes in industry and nature. Established activity models, such as those of Pitzer or Bromley, require fitting to experimental data for each electrolyte of interest and thus cannot predict properties for unstudied systems. While some predictive approaches exist, they are typically limited in scope and rely on additional ion-specific descriptors. In this work, we introduce a new hybrid model that combines the physics-based Bromley model with a matrix completion method (MCM) from machine learning. The MCM is employed to predict the electrolyte-specific parameters of the Bromley model, exploiting the fact that these parameters can be arranged in a matrix with cations and anions as rows and columns, respectively. Due to the lack of experimental data for many electrolytes, the initial parameter matrix is sparsely populated, making the prediction of the Bromley parameters for unstudied electrolytes a matrix completion problem. The hybrid model, Bromley-MCM, was trained end-to-end on experimental data for mean ionic activity coefficients and osmotic coefficients of aqueous solutions of 478 electrolytes at 298 K from the Dortmund Data Bank. As output, we obtain a completed matrix of Bromley parameters for 83 cations and 112 anions, enabling consistent prediction of concentration-dependent activities in aqueous solutions of 9,296 electrolytes at 298~K. This substantially extends the applicability of the Bromley model while maintaining high predictive accuracy, as demonstrated through evaluations on electrolytes excluded from model training.

AI.tldr: Hybrid physics-driven and ML matrix completion approach (Bromley-MCM) predicts Bromley model parameters across 83 cations and 112 anions, enabling predictions for ~9k electrolytes at 298 K with high accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing activity models require electrolyte-specific parameter fitting and fail to predict properties for unstudied electrolytes; a data-efficient, generalizable approach is needed.
AI.method: Integrate the Bromley activity model with a matrix completion method (MCM). Represent Bromley parameters as a cation-by-anion matrix; sparsely populated due to limited data. Train end-to-end on experimental mean ionic activity coefficients and osmotic coefficients for 478 electrolytes at 298 K from Dortmund Data Bank to complete the parameter matrix.
AI.result: Obtained a completed Bromley parameter matrix for 83 cations and 112 anions, enabling concentration-dependent activity predictions for 9,296 electrolytes at 298 K. High predictive accuracy demonstrated on electrolytes excluded from training.
AI.conclusion: Bromley-MCM significantly extends the applicability of the Bromley model while maintaining predictive accuracy, providing a scalable framework for predicting electrolyte thermodynamics across a large chemical space.

title: Parallel Noising in Neural Markov Logic Networks
summary: Neural Markov Logic Networks (NMLNs) are a flexible neurosymbolic relational model. Previous work has shown that, although NMLNs achieve strong performance as generative models for small relational structures, they underperform diffusion-based generative graph models on larger structures. In this paper, we strengthen NMLNs along two main dimensions: (i) we increase the expressive capacity of their potential functions using graph neural networks, and (ii) we develop a new training and inference algorithm inspired by parallel-tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, which we name parallel noising. Together, these enhancements enable NMLNs to attain strong performance in graph generation relative to general diffusion-based generative graph models. Furthermore, they allow NMLNs to match the performance of specialized text-based recurrent models when generating small molecular structures.

AI.tldr: Enhance Neural Markov Logic Networks with GNN-based potentials and a parallel-noising training/inference algorithm to boost graph generation, achieving competitive performance with diffusion models on large graphs and with RNNs for small molecules.
AI.motivation: Address underperformance of NMLNs on larger graphs and in molecular generation by increasing expressivity and offering an efficient sampling/training method.
AI.method: 1) Replace/augment potential functions with graph neural networks to raise expressivity. 2) Introduce parallel noising, a training/inference scheme inspired by parallel-tempering MCMC, for better exploration and convergence.
AI.result: NMLNs achieve strong performance in graph generation relative to diffusion-based models and match text-based recurrent models for small molecular structure generation.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that neurosymbolic models can be competitive with specialized deep generative models across graph and molecule domains by combining expressive potentials with advanced sampling.

title: One Model, Many Graphs: Learning over Attributed Graphs across Heterogeneous Modalities with Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a unified representation space for textual and visual information, yet their potential as general-purpose backbones for graph-structured data remains largely unexplored. In practice, attributed graphs exhibit substantial modality heterogeneity: some graphs contain only textual node attributes, others only visual attributes, while still others provide both. Existing graph learning approaches are typically designed for fixed modality schemas, requiring separate models for different settings and limiting scalability and cross-graph generalization. To bridge this gap, we present OMG-VLM (One Model, Many Graphs with Vision-Language Models), a unified framework for learning over attributed graphs across heterogeneous modality schemas. OMG-VLM leverages a pretrained VLM as a shared backbone and introduces structure-aware graph adapters that integrate neighborhood information while remaining compatible with the VLM's native embedding space. This design enables effective learning over text-attributed, image-attributed, and multi-attributed graphs within a single model. Extensive experiments across diverse domains show that OMG-VLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art GNN- and LLM-based baselines on attributed graph learning tasks such as node classification and link prediction, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen graphs and varying modality schemas. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jo-eyang/OMG-VLM.

AI.tldr: OMG-VLM uses a pretrained vision-language model as a unified backbone and adds structure-aware graph adapters to handle graphs with heterogeneous modalities (text, image, or both). It achieves state-of-the-art performance on node classification and link prediction and generalizes to unseen graphs and modality schemas.
AI.motivation: Attributed graphs often have heterogeneous attribute modalities (text, images, or both). Existing GNNs/LMMs typically require modality-specific models, limiting scalability and cross-graph generalization. A single model that can handle varying schemas is highly desirable.
AI.method: Leverage a pretrained VLM as a shared backbone and introduce structure-aware graph adapters that integrate neighborhood information while remaining within the VLM's embedding space. The adapters enable learning across text-only, image-only, and multi-attributed graphs within one model, without modifying the backbone embeddings.
AI.result: Empirical results show consistent outperformance of state-of-the-art GNN- and LLM-based baselines on attributed graph tasks (e.g., node classification, link prediction) and strong generalization to unseen graphs and varying modality schemas. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: OMG-VLM provides a scalable, generalizable framework for attributed graph learning across heterogeneous modalities by unifying graph data processing under a single VLM backbone with structure-aware adapters.

title: Incomplete Observations Boost Evolutionary Performance in Ocean Modeling
summary: Data-driven methods have revolutionized ocean modeling, yet current approaches rely heavily on complete reanalysis datasets, imposing computational constraints and limiting model performance to that of the training data. Here, we present a generative state-space model and an optimization framework that enable learning directly from sparse and noisy observations. The model is essentially a hidden Markov model with a continuous state space, where oceanic physical quantities are treated as hidden states and measurements as observations, enabling a unified representation of ocean fields and observational data. Both the initial-state and state-transition modules are implemented as neural networks to capture the complexity and temporal evolution of ocean states, while the emission module is formulated as a masked Gaussian distribution. To train the model from sparse observations, we derive an optimization framework based on the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. The framework alternately reconstructs high-fidelity ocean fields via Langevin dynamics and optimizes deep neural networks to capture temporal evolution. Theoretical analysis shows that the framework maximizes the likelihood of observations under the generative model. For efficiency, we assume that ocean-state evolution follows a stationary, ergodic, and Markovian stochastic process and adopt only length-two state sequences during optimization. Experiments on CMIP6 simulation data and FY-3D satellite data demonstrate high-fidelity reconstruction and accurate prediction, showing that sparse observations can directly improve the model's representation of ocean-state dynamics. This work offers a scalable pathway for next-generation Earth system models to learn directly from sparse, incomplete real-world observations.

AI.tldr: Generative state-space model learns ocean dynamics from sparse, noisy data via a neural HMM (continuous latent state) with EM training and Langevin-based reconstruction, yielding high-fidelity reconstructions and predictions on CMIP6 and FY-3D data.
AI.motivation: Overcome reliance on complete reanalysis datasets, reduce computational load, and improve ocean-state representations by learning directly from sparse observations.
AI.method: A continuous-state hidden Markov model where initial-state and state-transition distributions are parameterized by neural networks; emission modeled as a masked Gaussian; EM-based training with Langevin dynamics to reconstruct fields; stationary ergodic Markov process with length-two sequences for efficiency.
AI.result: Experiments on CMIP6 and FY-3D datasets demonstrate accurate reconstructions and predictions from sparse observations, indicating improved ocean-state representation and potential for scalable Earth system modeling.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a scalable pathway for learning ocean dynamics from sparse data, integrating observational information with dynamical evolution to enhance future Earth system models.

title: Breaking the Homogeneity Assumption: Specialized Multi-Generator Adversarial Learning for Rare Failure Detection in Predictive Maintenance
summary: Supervised learning models in the predictive maintenance field are regularly trained on highly imbalanced industrial datasets: machine failures occur rarely but have a disproportionate effect on operations. In addition to the clear class disparity, failure data are typically non-homogeneous, with different failure modes arising from distinct physical processes and exhibiting a multimodal distribution across minorities and classes. Traditional imbalance-management methods, e.g., undersampling, SMOTE-based interpolation, or cost-sensitive learning, typically assume that the minority population is homogeneous. This means their effectiveness is severely limited in the multifaceted conditions encountered in industrial practice. This paper determines the possibility of a failure-type-conscious generative augmentation program to improve the identification of infrequent failures in predictive maintenance systems. An experimental design that is leakage-safe is used to compare five imbalance-handling methods: cost-sensitive learning, random undersampling, SMOTE oversampling, single-generator GAN augmentation, and a specialized multi-generator GAN architecture that has independent generators that are asked to learn individual failure subtypes. Precision/Recall-oriented measures are used to quantify model performance; the main evaluation measure is the PR-AUC. Experiments conducted on the AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance dataset indicate that the proposed multi-generator GAN framework produces more realistic minority samples, yielding higher PR-AUC and recall scores compared to traditional resampling methods and individual-generator GAN augmentation.

AI.tldr: Multi-generator GAN augmentation tailored to failure subtypes improves minority sample realism and predictive maintenance performance (PR-AUC, recall) over traditional methods and single-generator GANs on AI4I 2020.
AI.motivation: Predictive maintenance data are highly imbalanced and multimodal; minority Failure types are heterogeneous; standard resampling assumes homogeneous minority, limiting effectiveness.
AI.method: Leakage-safe experimental design; compare five imbalance-handling methods: cost-sensitive learning, random undersampling, SMOTE oversampling, single-generator GAN augmentation, and multi-generator GAN with independent generators per failure subtype.
AI.result: Multi-generator GAN yields more realistic minority samples and higher PR-AUC and recall than others on AI4I 2020 dataset.
AI.conclusion: Failure-type-conscious generative augmentation is a promising approach for imbalanced, multimodal predictive maintenance data, with improved detection of rare failures; further work needed on generalization and computational cost.

title: Neural Kolmogorov Equations: Parallelizable Learning of Stochastic Dynamics under General Noise
summary: Neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning noisy or stochastic dynamics directly from data; however, existing approaches largely assume uncoupled and continuous noise, limiting their applicability to realistic stochastic drivers, and often scale poorly in time, requiring expensive autoregressive training. To address these limitations, we propose Neural Kolmogorov Equations (NKEs), a deterministic, infinite-dimensional reformulation of Neural SDEs based on the Kolmogorov Forward equation, transforming the learning problem from modelling individual stochastic trajectories to modelling the evolution of probability densities. NKEs learn general Lévy-type stochastic forcing directly through the operator structure of the KFE, and enable parallel-in-time training via a Lagrangian Galerkin projection and operator splitting. We evaluate NKEs on several stochastic benchmarks, including systems with coupled noise and jump processes, and verify that NKEs provide flexible models that accurately recover deterministic and stochastic dynamics with competitive predictive accuracy and improved training efficiency. Code and pretrained models will be released.

AI.tldr: Reformulates neural SDE learning as a deterministic Kolmogorov Forward equation problem (NKEs), enabling Lévy-type noise modeling and parallel-in-time training with improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of current neural SDEs: reliance on uncoupled/continuous noise, poor temporal scaling, and costly autoregressive training; extend to general stochastic drivers including jumps.
AI.method: Deterministic, infinite-dimensional reformulation via the Kolmogorov Forward equation; learn stochastic forcing through operator structure; apply Lagrangian Galerkin projection and operator splitting for parallel-in-time training.
AI.result: Demonstrated on benchmarks with coupled noise and jumps; achieves competitive predictive accuracy with improved training efficiency; flexible in recovering deterministic and stochastic dynamics.
AI.conclusion: NKEs offer a scalable, flexible framework for learning stochastic dynamics, enabling parallel training and direct inference of density evolution; code and pretrained models forthcoming.

title: Conservative Query and Adaptive Regularization for Offline RL Under Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn an effective policy from a static dataset, but its performance is fundamentally limited by dataset coverage. Action preference queries leverage expert feedback without additional environment interaction, enabling policy improvement during offline training. However, existing methods still face two key challenges: selecting informative preference queries and effectively exploiting the collected feedback. Current approaches typically rely only on the distance between policy actions and dataset actions for query selection, while enforcing fixed constraints that keep the policy close to queried preferences. Such strategies often lead to unstable policy updates and integrate poorly with value regularization. To address these limitations, we propose Conservative Query and Adaptive Regularization under Uncertainty Estimation, a lightweight framework that jointly improves preference querying and preference exploitation. Specifically, we employ a Morse network to estimate the uncertainty of policy actions with respect to the offline dataset. Based on this uncertainty, we introduce a conservative query strategy that selectively queries actions near the dataset to preserve Bellman-update stability, together with an uncertainty-aware adaptive regularization scheme that dynamically adjusts data-level constraints during policy optimization. We integrate our framework with CQL and evaluate it extensively on the D4RL benchmark. Experimental results demonstrate superior or competitive performance across a wide range of tasks.

AI.tldr: We propose Conservative Query and Adaptive Regularization under Uncertainty Estimation to improve offline RL with action-preference feedback. By estimating policy action uncertainty via a Morse network, we perform conservative, dataset-near querying and adapt regularization during training, integrated with CQL. Evaluations on D4RL show competitive or superior results.
AI.motivation: Offline RL is limited by dataset coverage; current preference-query methods rely on action-dataset distance and fixed constraints, causing unstable updates and poor synergy with value regularization.
AI.method: Estimate action uncertainty with a Morse network relative to the offline dataset; apply a conservative query strategy that selects queries near the dataset to stabilize Bellman updates; use an uncertainty-aware adaptive regularization that dynamically adjusts data-level constraints during policy optimization; integrate within CQL.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the D4RL benchmark show superior or competitive performance across a range of tasks.
AI.conclusion: Jointly improves preference querying and exploitation in offline RL, balancing stability and performance via adaptive regularization and uncertainty-guided querying, with strong compatibility with CQL.

title: AdaFlash: Adaptive Speculative Decoding via On-Policy Distilled Diffusion Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding, in which a lightweight draft model first generates a draft sequence that is then verified in parallel by the target model, has become a prevalent paradigm for accelerating large language model inference. Recent work such as DFlash further boosts drafting efficiency by leveraging diffusion drafters, whose parallel denoising mechanism enables draft generation in a single forward pass. In this work, we uncover a central pitfall of diffusion drafters: bidirectional attention is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it endows the model with parallel generation and global contextual modeling capabilities; on the other hand, this inherent global dependency introduces high variance at both the domain-level and the token-level: acceptance rates fluctuate substantially across different domains, and draft token quality also varies heterogeneously at different token positions. To tackle this issue, we propose AdaFlash framework, comprising two components: (i) an on-policy distillation (OPD) algorithm with reverse-KL divergence tailored for diffusion drafters, bringing stable convergence and effectively reducing domain-level variance; and (ii) an adaptive length head that dynamically adjusts the candidate sequence length on the fly, substantially lowering the verification cost of the target model and handling token-level variance. Experiments demonstrate that AdaFlash consistently improves speedup rate during deployment, with especially significant gains in high-concurrency scenarios, achieving up to approximately 66% higher throughput than previous state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: AdaFlash improves diffusion-based draft generation by tackling variance from bidirectional attention with two components: on-policy distillation (OPD) using reverse-KL for stable domain-level convergence, and an adaptive length head for dynamic candidate sequence lengths, yielding up to ~66% throughput gains, especially in high-concurrency deployment.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by drafting with a lightweight model and verifying with the target model. Diffusion drafters enable single-pass draft generation but introduce high domain- and token-level variance due to bidirectional attention, harming efficiency and reliability.
AI.method: AdaFlash comprises two innovations: (i) on-policy distillation (OPD) with reverse-KL divergence tailored for diffusion drafters to stabilize convergence and reduce domain-level variance; (ii) an adaptive length head that dynamically adjusts the candidate sequence length during generation to lower target-model verification costs and address token-level variance.
AI.result: Empirical results show AdaFlash yields consistent speedups and significantly higher throughput, achieving up to approximately 66% improvement over prior state-of-the-art methods, with the gains being more pronounced in high-concurrency scenarios.
AI.conclusion: AdaFlash mitigates the variance issues inherent in diffusion drafters and delivers substantial deployment-time efficiency gains, making diffusion-based drafting more reliable and cost-effective.

title: S3: Stable Subgoal Selection by Constraining Uncertainty of Coarse Dynamics in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
comment: Manuscript accepted to the Eighteenth Workshop on Adaptive and Learning Agents (ALA), at the 25th International Conference of Autonomous Agents and Multi Agent Systems 2026
summary: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) intends to separate strategic planning from primitive execution. It has been widely successful in solving long-horizon and complex tasks, where flat-RL algorithms have difficulty in learning.
