However, while the low-level agent in HRL benefits from dense feedback and abundant trial opportunities, the high-level agent receives sparse, delayed feedback from the environment and its performance depends on the low-level execution capability. In this paper, we study whether subgoal selection by the high-level agent can be performed more strategically, by providing it with dynamics-aware intrinsic motivation. Since motivation based on primitive transition dynamics would require broad coverage of the state-action space, we propose to use coarse dynamics, i.e., environment transitions aggregated over multiple steps at the temporal scale at which the high-level agent operates. This approach stabilizes the high-level policy by learning to minimize the predictive uncertainty associated with the coarse dynamics, and provides a guided structure for navigation. We model the predictive uncertainty by evaluating different dispersion metrics as approximated by a Mixture Density Network (MDN). Empirically, we observe that a dense, dynamics-aware intrinsic reward leads to risk-averse subgoal selection, enabling it to outperform state-of-the-art HRL methods in non-stationary long-horizon environments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a dynamics-aware intrinsic reward for hierarchical RL by using coarse, multi-step dynamics and MDN-based predictive uncertainty to guide high-level subgoal selection, improving stability and performance in non-stationary long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: High-level subgoal selection in HRL suffers from sparse, delayed feedback and dependence on low-level policy quality. Introducing an informative intrinsic signal aligned with the high-level timescale can stabilize learning and improve decision-making.
AI.method: Define coarse dynamics by aggregating environment transitions over multiple steps at the high-level temporal scale. Use a Mixture Density Network (MDN) to model predictive uncertainty of these coarse dynamics, and derive an intrinsic reward based on dispersion metrics to guide the high-level policy toward uncertain-but-informative subgoals (risk-averse behavior).
AI.result: Empirically, the method yields a dense, dynamics-aware intrinsic reward that leads to risk-averse subgoal selection and improved performance, outperforming state-of-the-art HRL methods in non-stationary long-horizon environments.
AI.conclusion: Coarse-timescale dynamics with MDN-based uncertainty as intrinsic motivation stabilizes high-level learning, guiding subgoal selection and enhancing robustness of HRL in challenging, long-horizon tasks.

title: In-Context Time Series Classification with Random Convolutional Features
summary:
Time series classification is central to domains like medical signal analysis, industrial monitoring, and sensor-based activity recognition, where class information manifests as localized shapes, specific frequencies, temporal shifts, or complex cross-channel interactions. Random convolutional transforms efficiently map these sequences to fixed-dimensional tabular features but are traditionally paired with simple linear classifiers. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model can more effectively harness these rich representations.
  We propose MASHT, a pipeline that marries MultiRocket and Hydra features with the power of in-context tabular foundation models. By leveraging a pretrained tabular foundation model, our approach completely bypasses task-specific model training, requiring only feature extraction and direct inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MASHT matches state-of-the-art time series classification baselines on univariate tasks, achieving a lower average rank than HIVE-COTE 2.0. On multivariate datasets, MASHT remains highly competitive with the strongest reference methods.

AI.tldr: MASHT uses pretrained tabular foundation models with MultiRocket and Hydra features to classify time series without task-specific training, achieving competitive performance with state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: To better leverage rich representations from random convolutional transforms by using a pretrained tabular foundation model, enabling effective zero-training inference on extracted features.
AI.method: A pipeline that extracts features via MultiRocket and Hydra from time series and then applies a pretrained tabular foundation model for direct inference, bypassing task-specific model training.
AI.result: Univariate tasks: MASHT matches state-of-the-art baselines and has a lower average rank than HIVE-COTE 2.0; multivariate datasets: MASHT remains highly competitive with the strongest reference methods.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained tabular foundation models can effectively harness rich time-series representations from random-convolution transforms, enabling strong performance without task-specific training.

title: DBMol: Design of High-Affinity, Target-Specific Small Molecules through Structure Prediction Models
summary: Designing small molecule ligands that bind with high affinity to specific protein pockets is a fundamental goal in drug discovery, as small molecules constitute a major fraction of approved therapeutics. Recent breakthroughs in structure prediction, such as AlphaFold-3 and Boltz-2, enable accurate biomolecular interaction prediction and show promise as foundation models for downstream tasks, including binding affinity prediction. We propose to leverage these models and introduce DBMol, a new structure predictor-guided framework for de novo small molecule design. DBMol formulates an alternating optimization and projection process. In the optimization stage, DBMol starts from an initial molecule and uses gradient-based optimization to improve pocket-specific interactions and predicted binding affinity using a structure prediction model. In the projection stage, a flow-matching model maps the optimized molecular graph to discrete and chemically valid molecules. Experiments show that DBMol effectively optimizes the Boltz-2 affinity proxy and generates molecules with strong predicted affinity and specificity under Boltz-2 evaluation. To reduce self-confirmation bias, we further evaluate generated molecules using held-out metrics, including AF3-based evaluation. DBMol substantially improves pocket coverage while maintaining molecular diversity over unconditional generation, and is competitive under held-out metrics despite the absence of reference-ligand supervision. These results support the promise of structure prediction models as effective optimization signals for de novo molecular design.

AI.tldr: DBMol integrates structure-prediction-guided optimization with a flow-based projection to design de novo ligands. It alternates gradient-based optimization against a structural affinity proxy and a molecular graph-to-molecule projection, achieving strong predicted affinity and broad pocket coverage with diversity.
AI.motivation: Leverage advances in biomolecular structure prediction (e.g., AlphaFold-3, Boltz-2) to provide reliable optimization signals for de novo ligand design and address limitations of unconditional generative approaches.
AI.method: An alternating optimization/projection framework: (1) optimization stage uses gradient-based updates to improve pocket-specific interactions and predicted Boltz-2 affinity; (2) projection stage uses a flow-matching model to map the optimized graph to discrete, chemically valid molecules. Held-out AF3-based evaluation is used to reduce self-confirmation bias.
AI.result: DBMol substantially improves the Boltz-2 affinity proxy and generates molecules with high predicted affinity and specificity. It achieves greater pocket coverage and maintains molecular diversity compared with unconditional generation, and performs competitively under held-out metrics despite lacking reference-ligand supervision.
AI.conclusion: Structure-prediction models can serve as effective optimization signals for de novo molecular design, enabling targeted binding while preserving diversity; the DBMol framework demonstrates the viability of using structure predictors to guide de novo design without reference ligands.

title: Thermodynamics-Informed Input Reparameterization for Neural Prediction of Real-Fluid Thermodynamic Properties in Supercritical Combustion
summary: Real-fluid thermodynamic property evaluation is a major computational cost in supercritical combustion simulations. In the enthalpy-based pressure-correction formulation, the closure evaluates temperature T, density $ρ$, and compressibility coefficient $ψ$ from the solver state (h,p,Y) through enthalpy-temperature inversion and repeated real-fluid equation-of-state evaluations. Neural-network surrogates offer fixed-cost inference, but direct mapping from (h,p,Y) to $(T,ρ,ψ)$ must capture the enthalpy-temperature relation and non-ideal equation-of-state response, resulting in a complex regression problem. This work introduces a thermodynamics-informed input reparameterization strategy, termed target-aligned input reparameterization (TAIR). TAIR replaces the raw enthalpy coordinate of each property network with a target-matched thermodynamic coordinate: the temperature network uses a temperature estimate obtained by inverting a constant-$c_p$ ideal-gas mixture enthalpy approximation, whereas the density and compressibility networks use an ideal-gas density estimate. These algebraic transformations use only solver-available variables and species constants, guiding the networks to learn real-fluid departures from ideal-gas baselines rather than reconstructing the full closure from raw enthalpy. The method is assessed using supercritical methane-oxygen counterflow flame data against a raw-input baseline and target-inconsistent cross-reparameterization controls. TAIR reduces held-out RMSE by factors of about 1.5, 2.0, and 7.5 for T, $ρ$, and $ψ$, respectively. For an unseen strain-rate flame within the augmented thermodynamic envelope, the corresponding factors are 3.6, 14.5, and 6.0. The target-inconsistent controls perform worse, indicating that the gains arise from thermodynamically matched input design rather than generic preprocessing.

AI.tldr: Thermodynamics-informed input reparameterization (TAIR) improves neural surrogates for real-fluid properties by aligning inputs to thermodynamic coordinates, reducing error compared with raw-enthalpy baselines and showing good extrapolation within augmented thermodynamic envelopes.
AI.motivation: Real-fluid property evaluation is costly in supercritical combustion; neural surrogates offer fixed-cost inference but must map from (h,p,Y) to (T,ρ,ψ) involving enthalpy-temperature inversion and EOS evaluations. TAIR seeks to simplify learning by reparameterizing inputs to thermodynamically meaningful coordinates.
AI.method: Introduce TAIR: replace raw enthalpy inputs with target-aligned coordinates. Temperature network uses a temperature estimate from a constant-cp ideal-gas enthalpy approximation; density and compressibility networks use ideal-gas density estimates. These algebraic transforms rely only on solver variables and constants to highlight departures from ideal-gas behavior. Train/evaluate on supercritical methane-oxygen counterflow flame data, compare against raw-input baseline and target-inconsistent controls.
AI.result: TAIR reduces held-out RMSE by ~1.5x (T), 2.0x (ρ), 7.5x (ψ); for an unseen strain-rate flame, reductions are ~3.6x, 14.5x, 6.0x. Target-inconsistent controls perform worse, indicating gains come from thermodynamically matched inputs rather than generic preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamics-informed input design enables neural surrogates to learn real-fluid departures more efficiently, delivering substantial error reductions and improved generalization within augmented thermodynamic envelopes; the approach hinges on thermodynamically grounded coordinate transformations rather than raw enthalpy inputs.

title: Benchmarking Generalization in Financial Statement Fraud Detection: robust evaluation and novel tasks
summary: Financial statement fraud detection (FSFD) is crucial for market integrity but faces challenges from increasingly sophisticated schemes and under-utilized textual data in financial reports. Existing methods often rely on random data splits, leading to overoptimistic performance estimates that do not reflect real-world generalization to new companies or future periods. To address this recurring problem with the state of the art, we propose a robust FSFD framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to integrate both structured financial data and unstructured textual information from financial reports. We provide a more realistic evaluation through a novel and challenging benchmark task called Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD). We construct and make publicly available a comprehensive U.S. company dataset combining financial statements, summarized MD&A text, and fraud labels. Our approach achieves the best performance on the challenging CI-FSFD task, demonstrating the critical value of textual data and robust evaluation for reliable financial fraud detection.

AI.tldr: A robust LL/M-based FSFD framework that fuses structured financial data with unstructured MD&A text, evaluated on a novel Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD) benchmark using a publicly released U.S. company dataset; achieves state-of-the-art performance on CI-FSFD.
AI.motivation: To address inflated performance from random data splits and under-utilization of textual data in financial reports by providing a realistic evaluation and generalization to unseen companies and future periods.
AI.method: Leverages Large Language Models to integrate structured financial statements with unstructured MD&A summaries; constructs and publicly releases the CI-FSFD benchmark and dataset (financial statements, MD&A text, fraud labels); evaluates FSFD in a company-isolated setting.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves the best performance on the CI-FSFD task, highlighting the added value of textual information and robust, realistic evaluation for financial fraud detection.
AI.conclusion: Textual data and rigorous, realistic evaluation are crucial for reliable FSFD; CI-FSFD offers a more challenging and practical benchmark; the LLM-based fusion framework demonstrates strong detection performance.

title: Toward Auditable Fraud Detection: Combining Graph Features, Model Explanations, and Agentic Case Investigation
summary: Fraud detection systems must scale with rising transaction volume while remaining explainable and reviewable. We study a layered pipeline on the PaySim dataset that combines a gradient-boosted classifier, graph-derived structural features, an autoencoder-based anomaly signal, TreeSHAP explanations, and a bounded LLM investigation agent applied to cases the classifier scores uncertainly. Before any model comparison, we identify and remove a simulator-specific balance shortcut that would otherwise inflate baseline performance. After this correction, neither the graph features nor the anomaly signal improves Average Precision on the full test set. Both, however, rank fraud better within the subset of cases receiving intermediate baseline scores. In a controlled experiment with injected multi-account fraud rings, engineered structural features recover all injected test transactions, while the tabular baseline misses roughly a quarter of them. The investigation agent underperforms direct thresholding of the classifier it relies on, reaching 65.0% accuracy against 71.7% on a balanced 60-case sample, despite having access to model explanations, graph context, and retrieved reference cases. Of the eight decisions the agent changed, six replaced correct classifier outputs with errors, and it produced a coherent written rationale in each case. An exploratory disagreement-based escalation rule flagged two of these agent errors for human review without flagging any correct decision. We conclude that each component of a layered fraud system contributes only under specific conditions, and that a plausible rationale from an investigation agent is not evidence of a better decision.

AI.tldr: Layered fraud-detection pipeline shows limited general gains: graph and anomaly signals help mainly in mid-score cases and in synthetic fraud rings; an investigation agent with explanations underperforms simple thresholding; explanations do not guarantee better decisions; overall, components matter only under specific conditions.
AI.motivation: Evaluate the contribution and explainability of a layered fraud-detection pipeline (gradient-boosted model, graph features, autoencoder anomaly signal, SHAP explanations, and an LLM investigation agent) on PaySim, addressing scalability and reviewability while controlling for simulator biases.
AI.method: Train and evaluate a pipeline combining a gradient-boosted classifier, graph-derived structural features, an autoencoder anomaly signal, TreeSHAP explanations, and a bounded LLM investigation agent. Remove simulator-specific balance shortcut, test on full PaySim test set and on injected multi-account fraud rings; compare against a baseline classifier and thresholding; measure Average Precision and accuracy; assess escalation rule.
AI.result: After bias correction, graph features and anomaly signal do not improve Average Precision on the full test, though they rank fraud better within intermediate baseline-score cases. In injected fraud rings, engineered structural features recover all injected test transactions; baseline misses ~25%. The LLM investigation agent achieves 65.0% accuracy vs 71.7% for balanced thresholding; explanations exist but do not yield better decisions; six of eight agent changes were incorrect despite coherent rationales; an escalation rule flags two agent errors for human review with no false positives.
AI.conclusion: Components contribute under specific conditions; having plausible agent rationales is not evidence of better decision quality; overall, a carefully tuned, multi-component system yields benefits only in particular scenarios and must be validated against robust baselines.

title: GUIDED Network-Agnostic Feature Initialization for Spatial Transferability in GNN-based Models
summary: The Traffic Assignment Problem is a fundamental but computationally expensive component of transportation planning. While Graph Neural Networks have emerged as fast, data-driven surrogates, their practical deployment is severely constrained by a spatial generalization gap. Standard models rely on transductive feature initializations that tie travel demand to fixed network topologies, preventing seamless transfer to new urban environments. To overcome this structural limitation, this research proposes a network-agnostic initialization layer, termed Geometrically Unconstrained Inductive Demand EmbeDding (GUIDED). By injecting travel demand as a scalar attribute on auxiliary virtual links rather than as specific node features, this modular framework standardizes the input space regardless of network scale. Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple urban topologies demonstrates that a Heterogeneous Graph Attention Network (HetGAT) model integrated with the proposed GUIDED layer maintains state-of-the-art predictive accuracy on single-network tasks, while demonstrating superior robustness to out-of-distribution demand patterns and maintaining a distinct performance advantage over the baseline even under severe data scarcity. Notably, the proposed feature initialization enables highly parameter-efficient domain adaptation for inter-network transfer learning without artificial input homogenization, establishing a robust foundation for truly inductive models. At the same time, the optimized scatter operations of the initialization layer yield an approximate 50% reduction in training time per epoch compared to the baseline approach. Furthermore, while demonstrated on vehicular traffic, this fundamental abstraction of spatial topology provides a versatile blueprint for generalized origin-destination spatial problems, such as freight logistics and multimodal network optimization.

AI.tldr: Introduce GUIDED, a network-agnostic initialization layer for GNN-based traffic assignment, enabling inductive inter-network transfer with higher robustness and faster training; pair with HetGAT to preserve accuracy while reducing dependence on fixed topology.
AI.motivation: GNN surrogates for traffic assignment suffer from a spatial generalization gap due to transductive, topology-fixed initializations that tie demand to a specific network; this limits transfer to new urban environments and reduces data efficiency.
AI.method: Propose GUIDED: a network-agnostic initialization layer that injects travel demand as a scalar attribute on auxiliary virtual links rather than as node features; integrate GUIDED with a HetGAT model; optimize scatter operations to accelerate training; evaluate across multiple urban topologies and data scarcity conditions to assess transferability and efficiency.
AI.result: Guided-HetGAT achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-network tasks, exhibits superior robustness to out-of-distribution demand, maintains performance under data scarcity, and enables parameter-efficient inter-network transfer without input homogenization; training time per epoch is reduced by about 50% due to optimized initialization scatter.
AI.conclusion: GUIDED provides a robust, topology-agnostic initialization that supports inductive, cross-network traffic-demand modeling and generalizes to other origin-destination spatial problems like freight and multimodal networks, while offering practical speedups and data-efficiency benefits.

title: A Reinforcement-Learning-Augmented Liquid-Fueled Reactor Network Model for Predicting Lean Blowout in Gas Turbine Combustors
summary: This study introduces a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for generating optimal liquid-fueled reactors to improve lean blowout (LBO) predictions in gas turbine combustors. Existing approaches for determining cluster boundaries rely on manual heuristics or distance-based metrics in the input space. In contrast, the proposed method is goal-oriented, explicitly accounting for the target metric (e.g., LBO prediction accuracy) during cluster formation. The framework employs a multi-stage clustering--classification strategy: an initial clustering step (e.g., $k$-means clustering) generates a large set of homogeneous micro-clusters, followed by an actor-critic RL agent that merges them into optimal reactor zones. The validation study, performed using a Jet-A mechanism (119 species, 841 reactions), shows the RL framework offers improved predictive fidelity compared to $k$-means and captures the correct LBO trends, while achieving substantial speedups relative to the high-fidelity computational model. Overall, the RL-driven approach demonstrates strong potential as a computationally efficient reduced-order modeling technique that can complement high-fidelity simulations for rapid design-space exploration.

AI.tldr: An RL-driven, multi-stage clustering-classification framework to form optimal reactor zones for predicting lean blowout in gas turbine combustors, improving accuracy and speed vs traditional clustering.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of manual heuristics and distance-based clustering in cluster boundary formation for LBO prediction, by introducing a goal-oriented, data-driven approach oriented to the target metric.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) initial k-means clustering to generate numerous homogeneous micro-clusters; (2) an actor-critic reinforcement learning agent that merges micro-clusters into reactor zones optimized for LBO prediction performance. Evaluation on a Jet-A mechanism (119 species, 841 reactions).
AI.result: The RL framework achieves improved predictive fidelity compared with k-means, captures correct LBO trends, and provides substantial speedups over high-fidelity computational models.
AI.conclusion: The RL-driven approach shows promise as a computationally efficient reduced-order modeling technique that can complement high-fidelity simulations for rapid design-space exploration in gas-turbine combustor LBO prediction.

title: Real-time optimal control with shallow recurrent decoder networks
summary: Controlling dynamical systems in real-time across multiple scenarios is critical to enabling adaptive control strategies, ensuring stability and efficiency. However, to tailor control actions in response to varying scenarios, traditional optimal control problems typically require several system simulations, which are often computationally demanding due to the high-dimensionality of the underlying spatio-temporal dynamics. In this work, we exploit SHallow REcurrent Decoder networks-based Reduced Order Modeling (SHRED-ROM) to synthesize a real-time closed-loop controller for high-dimensional and parametric dynamics, relying solely on limited state sensor readings. After training the model on a few optimal examples given by an expert demonstrator, SHRED-ROM mimics the expert behavior with effective distributed control actions in new scenarios, alleviating the curse of dimensionality. Moreover, a sensor forecaster is synthesized and used to close the loop at the latent level, thus efficiently mitigating possible sensor failures or delays. The performance of the proposed optimal control strategy is finally assessed on three challenging high-dimensional cases dealing with either parametric density control or fluid flow control.

AI.tldr: SHRED-ROM enables real-time closed-loop control for high-dimensional, parametric dynamics by learning a reduced-order model with shallow recurrent decoders, trained on expert demonstrations; it includes a latent-space sensor forecaster to handle failures/delays and is validated on three challenging high-dimensional cases (parametric density and fluid flow control).
AI.motivation: Real-time control across varied scenarios is hampered by the computational burden of simulating high-dimensional spatio-temporal dynamics and by sensor unreliability. A data-driven, reduced-order approach that can mimic expert control actions and operate with limited sensor information is highly desirable for scalable, robust adaptive control.
AI.method: Train SHRED-ROM: shallow recurrent decoder networks to build a reduced-order latent representation from available sensor data; learn a policy by imitating an expert demonstrator (few optimal trajectories); incorporate a latent-space sensor forecaster to close the loop under sensor failures or delays; evaluate on three high-dimensional problems involving parametric density control and fluid flow control.
AI.result: The framework achieves effective distributed control actions in unseen scenarios, reduces the computational burden associated with full-order simulations, and demonstrates robustness to sensor delays/failures via the latent forecaster; successful real-time closed-loop performance across three high-dimensional test cases.
AI.conclusion: SHRED-ROM provides a practical, scalable data-driven paradigm for real-time control of high-dimensional parametric systems, mitigating the curse of dimensionality, enabling sensor-robust closed-loop operation, and showing promise for broader applications pending further data-efficiency and theoretical guarantees.

title: Riemannian Deep Learning:Modules, Networks, and Geometries
comment: PhD thesis, University of Trento. The presentation has revised some typos in the previous published papers
summary: Deep neural networks on manifold-valued representations have attracted growing interest, but many basic components remain tied to specific manifolds, rely on Euclidean approximations, or require costly and numerically fragile geometric operations. This thesis develops a unified framework for Riemannian deep learning from three complementary perspectives: reusable neural modules, manifold-specific network architectures, and the design of underlying geometries. It generalizes batch normalization from Euclidean spaces and individual manifolds to broad classes of Lie groups and gyrogroups, and extends multinomial logistic regression from Euclidean space to SPD manifolds and then to general Riemannian manifolds. It further develops neural networks for several important geometric representations, including an unconstrained model of hyperbolic space, Busemann-based hyperbolic learning, and full-rank correlation matrices. Finally, it introduces adaptive and computationally efficient Riemannian metrics on SPD manifolds, including learnable Log-Euclidean geometries and fast, stable Cholesky-based geometries. The proposed methods are supported by theoretical analysis and validated through numerical experiments and applications in vision, signal processing, graph learning, and genomics.

AI.tldr: Introduces a unified Riemannian deep learning framework that generalizes core components to broad manifolds, develops geometry-aware models (hyperbolic, SPD) and learnable metrics, with theoretical and empirical validation.
AI.motivation: To overcome reliance on Euclidean approximations and manifold-specific tinkering, providing reusable modules and scalable geometry-aware networks across Lie groups, gyrogroups, SPD manifolds, and general Riemannian manifolds.
AI.method: Three complementary perspectives: reusable neural modules, manifold-specific architectures, and geometry design. Generalizes batch normalization to Lie groups and gyrogroups; extends multinomial logistic regression from Euclidean space to SPD manifolds and then to general Riemannian manifolds. Develops neural networks for geometric representations including an unconstrained hyperbolic model, Busemann-based hyperbolic learning, and full-rank correlation matrices. Introduces adaptive and computationally efficient Riemannian metrics on SPD manifolds, including learnable Log-Euclidean geometries and fast, stable Cholesky-based geometries. The methods are supported by theoretical analysis and validated through numerical experiments and applications in vision, signal processing, graph learning, and genomics.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis complemented by numerical experiments; validated across vision, signal processing, graph learning, and genomics applications.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables broad Riemannian deep learning across diverse geometric representations, offering reusable modules, geometry-aware architectures, and efficient metrics and enabling practical, scalable learning on manifolds.

title: Off-Context GRPO: Learning to Reason on Hard Problems using Privileged Information
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in large language models. Yet, typical RLVR approaches fail on difficult problems: when a model cannot generate any correct solutions, it receives \textit{zero} learning signal. Providing privileged guidance during training, such as solution prefixes, can help overcome this learning cliff by steering the model towards {correct solutions with non-zero reward}. {We call these rollouts \textit{off-context}: they are generated from a training prompt that contains privileged guidance, while the target objective is defined by the original prompt without that guidance.} {We introduce} Off-Context GRPO (OC-GRPO), a minimally modified variant of GRPO that uses guided rollouts but applies an importance-corrected objective to steer the update back toward the original unguided objective, avoiding the mismatch that destabilizes uncorrected guided training. Empirically, our algorithm achieves a 3.9\% absolute improvement (13.8\% relative gain) over vanilla GRPO on average across standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks with negligible additional cost.

AI.tldr: OC-GRPO leverages off-context guided rollouts with an importance-corrected objective to align training with the unguided objective, delivering 3.9pp absolute (13.8% relative) gains over GRPO on math reasoning benchmarks with negligible extra cost.
AI.motivation: RLVR methods can provide strong learning signals but fail when no correct solution exists, causing a learning cliff. Privileged guidance (e.g., solution prefixes) can help but risks misalignment between guided training and the original objective. A training scheme that reuses guided rollouts without corrupting the objective is needed.
AI.method: Introduce Off-Context GRPO (OC-GRPO), a minimally modified GRPO variant that uses guided rollouts generated from a privileged training prompt but employs an importance-weighted objective to steer updates back to the original unguided objective, mitigating the mismatch that destabilizes unguided training.
AI.result: Empirically achieves 3.9 percentage points absolute improvement (13.8% relative) over vanilla GRPO on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with negligible additional computational cost.
AI.conclusion: OC-GRPO demonstrates that guided rollouts can boost reasoning performance when paired with an importance-corrected objective to preserve alignment with the unguided goal, offering a practical enhancement over GRPO in RLVR contexts. Further evaluation could explore other task families and longer-horizon reasoning.

title: CircuitKIT : Circuit Discovery, Evaluation, and Application Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Circuit analysis can support not only model explanation but also downstream interventions such as pruning, editing, steering, and selective fine-tuning. However, conducting such analyses currently requires stitching together separate implementations for discovery, evaluation, and intervention, as well as hand-authoring the contrastive prompts required by many discovery methods. This fragmentation makes methods difficult to compare and limits their application beyond canonical tasks. We introduce CircuitKIT, a source-available library that connects the circuit-analysis workflow through a typed, serializable representation. CircuitKIT provides a suite of discovery algorithms, declarative interfaces for mapping structured data into discovery tasks, complementary circuit diagnostics, and downstream application modules. Together, these components provide common infrastructure for conducting and comparing circuit analyses. The library, examples, notebooks, and documentation are released at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/CircuitKIT .

AI.tldr: CircuitKIT unifies circuit-analysis workflows into a typed, serializable library, enabling discovery, diagnostics, and downstream interventions with a common interface to facilitate comparison and application.
AI.motivation: Current circuit-analysis practice is fragmented: discovery methods rely on disparate tools, require hand-authored prompts, and lack a unified interface, making method comparison difficult and limiting downstream applications.
AI.method: Developed CircuitKIT, a source-available library with a typed, serializable representation that connects discovery, diagnostics, and downstream modules. It includes a suite of discovery algorithms, declarative interfaces for mapping data into discovery tasks, complementary circuit diagnostics, and downstream application modules.
AI.result: Provides a common infrastructure to conduct and compare circuit analyses; supports explanations and interventions (pruning, editing, steering, selective fine-tuning); released as open-source with examples, notebooks, and documentation at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: CircuitKIT lowers barriers to conducting and comparing circuit analyses and enables broader adoption of circuit-based interventions across models and tasks.

title: ISO: An RLVR-Native Optimization Stack
summary:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is rapidly advancing the reasoning capabilities of language models, yet the optimization layer that converts reward feedback into weight-space updates remains poorly understood. Building on our prior analysis (Zhu et al., 2025), we study this missing layer through the singular structure of model weights and identify spectral inheritance: RLVR can reuse the base model's weight spectra while acquiring new behavior through changes in the associated input and output singular frames.
  We operationalize spectral inheritance as Isospectral Optimization (ISO), an RLVR-native, fixed-spectrum optimization framework with complementary offline and online instantiations. Offline, ISO-Merger combines the frame changes of shared-base specialists into a single fixed-spectrum model, requiring no post-merge data, rollouts, gradient updates, or on-policy distillation (OPD). It recovers complementary specialist capabilities and achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the compared data-free merging methods. Online, ISO-Optimizer applies a chosen base optimizer, including AdamW and Muon, to the frame variables while keeping the base spectra fixed. Across reasoning and coding tasks ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters, ISO-Optimizer improves accuracy in the reported runs and reaches matched scores with substantially fewer training steps. On Qwen3-8B-Base, AdamW reaches an aggregate accuracy of 0.495 after 270 training steps. ISO-AdamW reaches the same accuracy after only 100 training steps and improves further to 0.509 after 210 training steps. Together, ISO offers a concrete answer to RLVR's missing optimization layer: rather than inheriting pre-training optimization wholesale, design post-training around the structure of reward-driven adaptation: inherit the spectrum, optimize the frames.

AI.tldr: Introduces Isospectral Optimization (ISO) for RLVR, preserving base model spectra while updating input/output frames to induce new behavior; features offline (ISO-Merger) and online (ISO-Optimizer) variants with strong data-free merging and faster optimization across 1.5B–8B models.
AI.motivation: Address the opaque optimization layer translating reward signals into weight updates in RLVR; exploit spectral inheritance to reuse base-weight spectra while enabling new task behavior.
AI.method: Define ISO as a fixed-spectrum optimization framework. Offline ISO-Merger merges frame changes of shared-base specialists into a single fixed-spectrum model, data-free. Online ISO-Optimizer applies a chosen base optimizer (e.g., AdamW, Muon) to the frame variables while keeping base spectra fixed, evaluated across Qwen3-8B-Base and similar scales.
AI.result: Offline ISO-Merger achieves the strongest aggregate performance among data-free merging methods and recovers complementary specialist capabilities. Online ISO-Optimizer yields faster convergence than the baseline; on Qwen3-8B-Base, AdamW reaches 0.495 after 270 steps, while ISO-AdamW reaches 0.495 after 100 steps and 0.509 after 210 steps.
AI.conclusion: RLVR’s missing optimization layer can be addressed by inheriting the spectrum and optimizing the frames—design post-training around reward-driven adaptation rather than wholesale pre-training optimization.

title: Provable diffusion-based posterior sampling for linear inverse problems via DDIM
summary: Diffusion-based methods have achieved remarkable empirical success in solving inverse problems. However, many existing posterior samplers either lack rigorous theoretical guarantees or incur substantial computational overhead. We propose a simple and efficient algorithm, called \pddim, for solving linear inverse problems with diffusion priors via a DDIM-type sampler. Our method requires only lightweight, coordinate-wise modifications to the standard DDIM update, while explicitly incorporating the measurement model. The key idea is to perform posterior sampling separately along each singular direction of the measurement operator: for each direction, the sampler follows the learned diffusion prior when the observation signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is below the corresponding diffusion SNR, and switches to a calibrated measurement-based predictor otherwise. We prove that the proposed sampler converges to the Bayesian posterior conditioned on the measurements. Empirical results show that the proposed sampler performs favorably against existing diffusion-based posterior samplers across a range of image restoration tasks, achieving the best performance on the majority of evaluation metrics considered. Overall, our results convert posterior sampling for noisy linear inverse problems to simple coordinate-wise DDIM updates, yielding an efficient, easy-to-implement algorithm with provable posterior consistency.

AI.tldr: A lightweight DDIM-based posterior sampler (PDDIM) for linear inverse problems with diffusion priors; coordinate-wise along singular directions with SNR-based switching; provable convergence to Bayesian posterior and strong empirical performance.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous theoretical guarantees and computational efficiency for diffusion-based posterior samplers in noisy linear inverse problems.
AI.method: Decompose the sampling along measurement operator singular directions. For each direction, update using the diffusion prior when observation SNR is below the diffusion SNR; switch to a calibrated measurement-based predictor when SNR is high. Implemented as a DDIM-type update with lightweight, coordinate-wise modifications and explicit incorporation of the measurement model.
AI.result: Proves convergence to the Bayesian posterior conditioned on measurements; empirical results show competitive to state-of-the-art diffusion-based posterior samplers across image restoration tasks, often achieving top metrics.
AI.conclusion: Reduces posterior sampling for noisy linear inverse problems to simple, efficient coordinate-wise DDIM updates with provable posterior consistency; easy-to-implement and scalable.
